Being purified, O Indu, invoked by many, enter the ocean—the wooden vat—as one who is dear to these people. || 27 || Being purified, O Indu, invoked by many, enter the ocean—the wooden vat—as one who is dear to these people. || 27 || O Soma, invoked by many, being purified and cleansed, entering this sacrifice as one beloved by these people who offer hymns of praise, enter the ocean—the *droṇakalaśa* vessel. With a luster spread by the ladle, with a form that resounds all around, the bright Somas are mixed with the milk of cows. || 28 || The bright, radiant Somas, joined with a luster shining by means of the ladle, with a form that resounds all around, and with a flowing stream, become mixed with the milk of cows; that is to say, they are blended with cow’s milk. Urged on by the inciters, the vigorous one has stepped forth toward the prize, like warriors settling into battle. || 29 || The vigorous, powerful Soma, urged on by the inciters—the singers who impel him with hymns—having been restrained, has stepped forth toward the prize, which is the battle known as the sacrifice. The illustration is: just as warriors, the slayers, stepping forward and entering the fray, advance; so it is here. O Soma, wise seer of heaven, coming together for our well-being, flow forth clearly to be seen like the sun. || 30 || O Soma, wise seer (*kavi*), you who are the Sun of great heroism, flow forth clearly (*ṛdhak*) for our well-being. Thus says Yāska: "The word *ṛdhak* is an expression of separation, and it is also used in the sense of rising up" (*Nirukta* 4.25). Coming together, uniting for our well-being, flow forth for the sake of sight, like the sun from heaven. || 41 || May the Great Lord of Vidyātīrtha, dispelling the darkness of the heart by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the four aims of human life. Thus ends the first chapter of the seventh book in the *Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa*, a commentary on the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā* composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the minister of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka, the supreme sovereign of kings and promoter of the Vedic path.
1. Possessing the seed of existence;
2. they overcome that;
3. by the minister named Gatabhasāyaṇa.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.

The fifth hymn, consisting of thirty verses beginning with “hinvanti,” is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, or alternatively of Jamadagni of the Bhṛgu lineage; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity. Accordingly, it is enumerated thus: “hinvanti [is by] Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, or Jamadagni. The ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.

The sisters, his female companions, loving him greatly, urge on the mighty Indu, the lord, as they seek him. 1. They urge on the vigorous one; the sisters, the female companions, urge on the great Indu, their husband, as they desire him with great love. 1.
In all these [verses], Soma Pavamāna is praised.
Therein, at the beginning, the seer says to Soma:
"My fingers impel you forward to flow."
That is explained: "Svasāraḥ" (sisters);
this is a name for the fingers.
They are the sisters who, with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), urge [the sacrifice] well toward the ritual acts;
they are the kinswomen (*jāmayaḥ*), for they are mutually related as kin because they have sprung from one and the same hand.
*Usyaḥ*:
dwelling for the sake of work;
the meaning is that they go everywhere.

Such fingers, the young maidens of the earth, desiring your victory, being true, impel the flowing *indu*—the Soma—which is a cause of excellent heroism (*suvīrya*), for it is said that "heroic power arises when the Soma is drunk," or which is the impeller of all actions; such a lord, the master of all things moving and stationary, for whose sake he is thus worshipped, they therefore urge forth and send out the great *indu*, who is great because he is given to the gods, or who is worthy of honor.
[The root] *hi* means "to increase" and "to go";
it belongs to the *svādi* class.
O Pavamāna, with light after light, as a god from among the gods, enter into all treasures. 2. O Pavamāna, with light after light, as a god from among the gods, enter into all treasures. 2.

O Pavamāna, being purified by the ten-stranded filter, or indeed while being cleansed, O pure Soma, with every luster—[the root] *ruca* meaning "to shine"—you, as a god blazing with all splendor, from the gods (*pari devebhyaḥ*), bring to us all pervasive, manifold riches (*vasūni*). Enter into us! Bring them to us!
Or rather:
for the sake of the gods, enter—that is, pervade from all sides—all the riches, the dwelling places, the vessels (grahas), and so forth.

O Pavamāna, flow toward us with fair praise, rain for the gods, and strength; flow for our nourishment in abundance. 3. O Pavamāna, [flow] toward us with fair praise, rain for the gods, and strength; flow for our nourishment in abundance. 3.
O Pavamāna Soma, being purified, flow toward us for the sake of worship—meaning, bring to the gods a rain accompanied by beautiful hymns;
"duvas" is the dative case (the *luk* elision of the fourth case ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*), used here for the purpose of service (*paricaraṇa*). Flow hither! Bring it!
The meaning is: "Act in such a way that rain shall come through my hymn of praise.
Furthermore, for our sake—*iṣe* meaning for food—bring about rain that comes together properly (*saṃyatam*) toward us.
Or else:
Bring this "duvaḥ"— the excellent praise consisting of beautiful hymns, performed with a view toward service—
to the gods; that is to say, convey this profuse eulogy to them.

For you are a bull by your radiance; we, with pious thoughts, invoke you, O Pavamāna, the resplendent one. 4. Bull indeed you are; by your light, we, with devout minds, call upon you, the radiant Pavamāna. 4.
O Soma, you are indeed a bull (*vṛṣā*), for you are truly the showerer (*varṣitā*) of desired fruits.
Therefore, O Pavamāna: 1. *bha1*(2)—because of repetition in one hand;
2. *ta3-bha1.2.7*—that [is] from here.

O Soma, being pressed or being purified, we— possessing good deeds (*svādhyaḥ*) or being well-concentrated (*suṣṭhu dhyānavantaḥ*)— bring you, who are radiant with splendor (*bhānunā tejasā dyumantam*),
that is, exceedingly brilliant or possessed of praise,
into the sacrifices; we invoke you.
O you who rejoice in your own weapons, bestow heroic strength upon us at the joints of the year;
find for us a dwelling here.
Flow forth, O Indu, bestowing heroic vigor; rejoicing, O you of excellent weapons, come here and enter our dwelling.

He who possesses beautiful weapons (*svāyudha*). The sacrificial implements, such as the potsherds (*kapāla*) and so forth, are called his ten weapons; he whose these are beautiful is thus described. Or alternatively, he is one whose weapons are the bow and so on. O Soma, being such, *mandamānaḥ*—rejoicing—or rather, with the causative sense implied, *mādayan*—gladdening the gods yourself—*ā pavasva*: flow toward us. *Suvīryam*: endowed with excellent heroic power, [grant] sons and so forth to us. *Ā prāpaya* (the root *gar* has the sense of reaching). Furthermore, O *Indo*, O Soma, you who are characterized by flowing through the cups (*graha*) and the *dhamas* vessels, come well indeed to this very sacrifice of ours, *iha u*—"here indeed," the particle *u* being used for emphasis. || 1 ||
When you are sprinkled with water and cleansed by the hands, you take your place upon the wooden vessel to flow.
When you are poured out from here, being cleansed by the two hands, you flow toward your wooden dwelling for the sake of the one who hears.
He [is] Soma, the one with rays in his hands; he has extended his two arms.
He shines and illuminates with his two hands; his two arms are the rays that measure out [the world].
Being cleansed—being purified by those two—you are the Angir.
For the purpose of pouring the *soma*, there are four kinds of waters;
when you are sprinkled all around by those *vaṃsatīvarī* and *ekadhanā* waters, being then taken up with a wooden vessel made of tree-wood, [you reach] the common dwelling-place (*sadhastha*).
That wherein they stand together is the *sadhastha*, the place—the cups, ladles, and so forth;
you reach it, O seeker of food (*aśuṣe*).
Sing forth to Soma as he flows,
to the great one who possesses a thousand eyes.
Sing forth to Soma as he flows, who possesses swift horses, for the sake of the great one who has a thousand eyes.

O singers, sing forth—perform the Sāman chant with excellence—to the purifying Pavamāna, to the Soma being purified by the tenfold filter, or indeed to him as he is being cleansed. Or rather, praise him. How so?
Like Vyaśva;
just as formerly the ṛṣi named Vyaśva sang praises to Soma, so may you also [sing].
To what kind of one?
To the Great One, to the Most Exalted;

to Him who possesses greatness through qualities and other attributes because He is being accepted by the gods; to the Thousand-eyed One—this statement is made with reference to the abundance of His manifestations.
To him who is joined with hymns numbering a thousand;
or rather,
to Soma, who is to be beheld in manifold ways by various kinds of gods.
Whose honey-dripping golden hue they urge forth with the pressing-stones—
the drop for Indra’s drinking.
Whose color is honey-like, who is heard as sweet, the golden one—him they urge forth with the stones, the drop for Indra to drink. ||8||
O Adhvaryu and others, [he is] the destroyer of the enemies' color;
by that which he drinks, when it is drunk, the enemies are utterly crushed—thus he is capable of warding off enemies.
He is the honey-dripping, the bringer of sweet flavor, the golden-hued, the green-colored Indu.
It is maintained that it is obtained even in a mere form;
it is blazing on all sides.
[The root] *undī* is stated [to mean] "moistening."
Immediately after the pressing, it flows into the vessels;
they urge forth—that is, they impel—the stalk which is the cause of you, O Soma.
In other words, they press you.
"For Indra's drinking," "for Indra's consumption";
the meaning is: for that purpose.

1. Singing the *gā-sāman*, singing the song; being made to sing the *ta-bha-sāman*; being measured by the *tara-sāmagāyana*; being caused to sing the *ta-sāma*. 2. One who causes [the enemy] to flee (*vyāvayitṛ*), one who causes [the enemy] to waste away (*kṣārayitṛ*).
3. [One who possesses] the essence (*rasa*).
Of you, the vigorous one, who have conquered all riches, we choose the friendship. 9. Of you, the vigorous one, who have conquered all riches, we choose the friendship. 9.

O Soma, we—possessors of strength (*vājinaḥ*) who have prepared the oblation (*saṃbhṛtahaviṣkāḥ*)—having conquered all, that is, all pervasive riches of the enemy, choose for ourselves your friendship, characterized by praise and the act of praising you, you who are thus described or renowned. The meaning is: "We cultivate this friendship so that you may grant us wealth. [The word] *jigyuṣaḥ* [is the genitive plural of the perfect participle of *ji*].
In *jije*,
because of the rule *vasvekājāt*, there is an absence of *iṭ* [augment] in the *liṭ* [perfect tense];
and by the rule *saniṭojeḥ*, there is a substitution of a guttural (*ka-varga*) for the letter following the reduplication.
When *ḍas* follows, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel of *vasu*;
the accent is that of the *kamuc* suffix.

Flow as a bull with your stream, O exhilarating one, for the sake of him who is accompanied by the Maruts, bestowing all things through your might. 10. Bull! Flow! With your stream! For him who is accompanied by the Maruts! And! Exhilarating! Bestowing! All! Through your might!
O Indu, you who are by nature flowing or by nature illuminating; O Soma, you who are "visible to all" (*viśvadarśataḥ*), meaning visible to all or worthy of being seen by everyone;
or else, that by which the entire multitude of things is seen—that is, made known.
He is the illuminator of all—this is the meaning. As such, "flow forth" (pavasva) for us—that is, bring to us—"great food" (mahīmiṣam), meaning abundant nourishment. The sense is: bestow it upon us.
Furthermore, O Soma, being purified as you flow, become for us a "finder of the path"—that is, one who procures and makes known the way to heaven.

The jars have sung in response; O Indu, with your streams and with might, enter for the drinking of Indra. 14. The jars have sung in response; O Indu, with your streams and with might, enter for the drinking of Indra. 14.
O Soma, whose nature is to flow, O Indu, the jars—meaning the *droṇakalaśas*—are joined by your continuous streams, you who are endowed with vigor and power;
this plural number is used in view of the multiplicity of applications.
They have resounded, being praised by the chanters through the process of pressing.
For at the time of the Soma-pressing, the officiating priests indeed offer hymns of praise;
therefore, do you enter for the drinking—that is, for the consumption—of Indra; enter into the cups and the portions.

He from whom they milk the intoxicating, sharp juice with the stones—may he, the slayer of adversaries, flow forth. 15. From whom, for you, they milk the intoxicating, sharp juice with the stones—he, the slayer of adversaries, flow forth. 15.

O Soma, you whose exhilarating, intense, swift, and intoxicating juice the Adhvaryu priests milk with the pressing-stones (*adri*)—that is, they extract and purify—you, being such, are the slayer of the arrogant. Those whose minds are directed toward hostility are enemies;
as the destroyer of such evil-natured foes, flow forth and move everywhere.
The meaning is that those who fulfill [this] become devoid of evil and are doers of good deeds.

The King, being purified, moves by means of the prayers of wisdom, over the mind, through the intermediate space, in order to travel. 16. King; by means of the prayers of wisdom; he moves; being purified; over the mind; above; through the intermediate space; in order to travel. 16.

When a human being (*manu*) is performing a sacrifice—or alternatively, according to the rule regarding *manu*: *manu* is that which is to be meditated upon, namely the sacrifice—in that [sacrifice], the King who is "purifying" (*pavamāna*) or "being purified" (*punāna*), by the word "King" (*rājā*) Soma is designated, as seen in such passages as "They purchased King Soma" (*ai. brā. 1.27*). That King goes forth (*īyate*) together with "wisdoms" (*medhābhiḥ*), that is, with hymns of praise. For what purpose? To go (*yātave*) toward the *droṇakalaśa* vessel by way of the atmosphere (*antarikṣeṇa*), via the path of space; for indeed, at the time of approaching the *droṇa*, he is praised by the chanters.

O Indu, bring to us a hundredfold increase of cattle and excellent horses; bring Bhagasti for our protection. 17. O Indu, bring to us a hundredfold increase of cattle and excellent horses; bring Bhagasti for our aid. 17.

O Indu, you who have the nature of flowing or illuminating within the vessels, O Soma, bring to us for our protection—that which possesses hundreds of thousands [of cattle], the nourishment of cows and other livestock that increases their prosperity, a multitude of excellent horses, and the attainment of fortune—the gift of desirable wealth. Bring these to us;
the meaning is: grant us cows and the like, as well as their increase.

O Soma, bring us conquering power, like a form for splendor; as a good protector, bring it for the feast of the gods. 18. O Soma, bring us conquering power, like a form for splendor; as a good protector, bring it for the feast of the gods. 18.

1. Of the one who illuminates *ta*; of the light that sustains. 2. Of that heaven (*svarga*). 3. They have sung after him (*anuṣata*). 4. By the priests (*ṛtvigbhiḥ*). 5. O you who are such as this (*etādṛśas tvam*). 6. Praised (*stutaḥ*). Ṛgveda 4.7.

O Soma, being well-pressed—being purified and having been poured out—for the feast of the gods, for the drinking of the gods, or for the desire of the gods, do thou become [the essence]. Bring hither, bestow upon us, strength that is ever-conquering and capable of overcoming; "juvaḥ" means swift, for the root *ju* signifies motion—it is the power that moves rapidly against enemies, or rather, the power whose nature is to move everywhere. And for the sake of splendor—for the purpose of radiance, as the root *varcas* means to shine—and for the sake of form, bring it to us, bestow it upon us.
Flow, O Soma, most resplendent, roaring toward the wooden vats; settle there like a hawk upon its nest.

Flow forth, O Soma, most radiant one, roaring toward the wooden vats, settling like a falcon upon his nest. O Soma, being purified, O Pavamāna, you who are most radiant—exceedingly luminous—you come toward the wooden vats (droṇāni). This plural number is used out of regard for the great frequency of the vessels. Having them as your goal, you come while "roaring"—uttering sound repeatedly and intensely. Indeed, the Soma, having emerged from the midst of the woollen filter, makes a sound as it falls into the wooden vat (droṇakalaśa) in an unbroken stream. Therein lies the illustration: "like a falcon," just as a falcon—a bird of praiseworthy flight—comes toward its "nest" (yoni), its own place, uttering a loud cry as it approaches from all sides; even so do you.
The Soma, flowing as water, moves toward Indra, Vāyu, Varuṇa, the Maruts, and Viṣṇu.

The water-winner: for Indra; for Vāyu; for Varuṇa; for the Maruts; Soma flows; for Viṣṇu. (20) The "water-winner" (*apsā*) is the distributor of the waters known as *vasatīvarī*. [The root] *paṇ* is used in the sense of "distribution. [The suffix] *viṭ* is applied by the rule "janasana-," and the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule "vidvanoḥ. Such a Soma "flows" (*arpati*), that is, it comes to the wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*). For what purpose? For Indra. Among all the gods, Indra drinks the Soma first; therefore, he is mentioned first. For him, [and] for Vāyu, to assist him. Indeed, immediately after Indra’s station, Vāyu drinks the Soma in the cup dedicated to Indra-Vāyu; therefore, Vāyu is mentioned next. And for him, [and] for Varuṇa, [and] for the Maruts—those gods who produce measured sound—and for Viṣṇu, who pervades the entire universe. The meaning is that the Soma flows so that these may drink it. (4)
Bestowing nourishment upon our offspring, O Soma, flow for us from every side with thousandfold wealth.

Bestowing nourishment upon our offspring, O Soma, flow for us from every direction, bringing thousandfold wealth. (21) O Soma, bestowing—that is, providing and granting—nourishment (*iṣam*) for our offspring (*tokāya*), that is, for our son, flow toward us from all sides (*viśvataḥ*), in every direction, bringing thousandfold (*sahasriṇam*) wealth. The meaning is: "Flow so as to bestow food and other provisions both upon us and upon our son."
Those Soma juices which are in the distance, those which are nearby, those which are pressed by the sages, or those which are at Śaryaṇāvat;

"Those Soma juices which are in the distance, those which are nearby, those which are being pressed in Munvare, or those which are here at Śaryaṇāvat... (22). With these words and others, he declares that the pressing of Soma for Indra exists everywhere. "Those Soma juices (*somāsaḥ*) which are in the distance (*parāvati*), in a very remote region; or those which are nearby (*arvāvati*), in a proximate region, are being pressed (*munvare*) for the sake of Indra—both those that were pressed in the past and those being pressed now; or those which are at Śaryaṇāvat. There is a place near Kurukṣetra called Śaryaṇāvat, which is rich in sweet juice and abounds in Soma. "In this season (*adaḥ*), those Somas which are being pressed for Indra, may they grant us our desired fruit"—this is the connection with what follows.

1. In the *ga-ma3-bha1.5* manuscript, the phrase "in the droṇakalaśa" is absent. 2. In the *na* manuscript, it reads "he goes to Gaṅgā. 3. In the *ga-ta3-bha1.4* manuscript, it reads "firstly. 4. In the *ta-mu-vā* manuscripts, it reads [as follows].

Come! *Pavati* means "to go. Or rather: come to the jar together with this my bright flow (*rucā snutyā*), for they indeed pour out the Soma at the time of its arrival at the jar. 28. We choose today your power, which brings bliss, your vehicle, the protector, the one desired by many. O Soma, we choose today—at this day of sacrifice—your own inherent power (*dakṣaṃ*) which brings bliss (*mayobhuvaṃ*), your vehicle (*vahim*) that brings wealth and other goods, the protector (*pāntaṃ*) who guards against enemies, and the one desired by many (*puruspṛhaṃ*), that is, the strength longed for by all. 29. We choose the delightful one, the most excellent, the wise one, the intelligent one, the protector, the one desired by many. O Soma, we choose you, the delightful (*mandraṃ*) one who causes exhilaration or is worthy of praise; the most excellent (*vareṇyaṃ*) one who is to be chosen and honored by all; furthermore, the wise (*vipraṃ*) one, full of intelligence; likewise, the intelligent (*manīṣiṇaṃ*) one—one whose mind is intent on prayer or who possesses hymns of praise—we choose you. The prefix *ā* is used here in relation to each qualifying attribute. Furthermore, we honor you, the protector (*pāntaṃ*) of all, and the one desired by many (*puruspṛhaṃ*). 30. O you of good wisdom, bestow upon us wealth with good insight; flow forth, O wise one, the protector, the one desired by many. O Soma of good wisdom (*sukrato*), we choose your wealth (*rayim*). Furthermore, [bestow] good insight (*sucetunam*)—"cit" meaning to perceive, with the suffix *-un* in the sense of an abstract noun—meaning excellent knowledge. Bestow wealth and good knowledge upon our bodies (*tanūṣu*) and our sons. Or rather, we choose these for the sake of our sons. Likewise, we honor you, the protector of all and the one desired by many. The sixth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with "Pavasva," is thus enumerated: "Pavasva...; the hundred [verses] are by Vainanamāyya; eighteen are Anuṣṭubhs, the last three are addressed to Agni. The seers are the hundred Marīcis, the descendants of Vainanamāyya. The verse "Tvaṃ soma sūraḥ" is an Anuṣṭubh; the remaining ones are Gāyatrīs. The three beginning with "Agnā āyūṃṣi" have Pavamāna-Soma as their deity, while the others have Pavamāna-Soma as the deity. The application of the hymn has been explained. 1. Flow forth, O you who are seen by all, toward all poetic insights, a friend to your friends, worthy of praise. O Soma, *viśvacarṣaṇe*, you who are the observer of all through your omnipresence, you who are a friend to your friends by virtue of the relationship between the singer and the one praised, being worthy of praise (*īḍyaḥ*), flow forth (*pavasva*) toward all poetic insights (*kāvyā*)—the works of a sage (*kaveḥ karma*)—which are hymns of praise, directed toward us, your friends, because you assist us by providing the oblation. (Notes: 1. 'saṃbhajāmahe' does not appear in manuscript Ta. 2. Manuscript Bha reads 'kiṃca tanūṣu'.)
O Soma Pavamāna, you rule over the universe through those two abodes which stand facing one another.
By those two,
you rule over the universe.
"Ye" refers to Pavamāna; "dhāmanī" refers to the two abodes.
"Westward," O Soma,
they have both stood.

O Pavamāna, being purified by the *daśāpavitra* filter, O Soma, as you are being cleansed—those two stations (*dhāmanī*) belonging to you, the Soma of such form, which are the prior and posterior fortnights (the waxing and waning phases), exist as your own inherent nature through the increase of each leaf and the *sāman* chants;

or rather, those two stations, the names (*nāmanī*), the stalks and the essence of the Soma, moving toward you or having approached you as your two wings or two names, stand there—and through them, you reign as the sovereign lord of the entire world.
Because you lead all the world through the phases beginning with the first quarter, you are its master.

On earth, by granting the desires of all men under the name of the Moon (Anuśa), and in the heavenly world, by giving to the gods their own portion consisting of nectar from your digits, you become their delighter;
for the gods indeed drink the digits of Soma through its successive increase and decrease.

O Soma, you are present on all sides around those stations which are yours; O Pavamāna, O Sage, [you exist] through the seasons. O Soma, since your stations—those specific divisions of time consisting of days and nights—are encompassed by you and remain pervading everywhere; or rather, since your stations, your splendors, revolve around [the world], therefore, O Pavamāna, being purified, O Sage whose actions are far-reaching, O Soma, you exist on all sides together with the seasons, such as spring and the rest. Wherever day and night are pervaded, there Soma exists, conditioned by the seasons such as spring; for both of these are dependent upon him—this is the meaning.

Flow on, generating nourishments, toward all desirable things, as a friend for the sake of helping your friends. O Soma, you who are a friend, having become our companion, flow on—directing yourself toward all desirable things (*vāryā*) that are worthy of being chosen by us, namely our hymns of praise—and for the sake of protection and sustenance for us, your friends, generate and bestow nourishments (*iṣaḥ*). Flow on; come hither. The root *pav* signifies the act of moving.

Thy bright rays, O Soma, extend the filter across the back of heaven by means of thy powers. O Soma, thy bright rays—those luminous beams worthy of praise, belonging to thee who art accompanied by thy powers (dhāmabhiḥ), that is, thy splendors—extend the filter, the means of purification, which is water, across the back of heaven; that is, upon the lower part of the sky, meaning upon the earth. They spread it out extensively; the sense is that they perform this everywhere.

These seven rivers wait upon your command, O Soma; for you the milch-cows run. (6) In connection with his role as the cause of rain, [the poet] says: O Soma, these—these very ones—created by you, the seven, numbering seven, flowing rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others; or rather, the seven rivers characterized by their habit of flowing—wait upon (*siṃsate*), that is, they follow, your *praśīrṣam*, your supreme command through your ordinances. 1. *ta*-bhavati | anusaranti | (The variant reading *ta* means "they become"; it follows.)

The meaning is that they go to the ocean following your command. Furthermore, the cows—meaning the milch-cows who have recently calved and who shall delight the gods by providing oblations—are running and coming toward you, saying, "We shall offer the milk-mixture (āśira) for your sake alone."

Flow forth, O Soma, with your stream, pressed for Indra, exhilarating, bestowing imperishable renown. 7. Flow forth, O Soma, with your stream, pressed for Indra, exhilarating, bestowing imperishable renown. 7.

O Soma, being pressed out, you are the exhilarating god who causes intoxication for Indra; as you are pressed by us, proceed forth toward the wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*) with your own continuous stream passing through the *daśāpavitra* filter for the sake of Indra.
Or rather:
O Soma, being pressed, you who are most intoxicating for Indra, approach your own Indra together with your stream that falls from the vessel accompanied by the cry of *svāhā*.
Of what kind?
"Possessing imperishable fame"—*akṣita* means undiminished; *śravaḥ* is a name for food—bestowing it, that is, granting it to us, "go forth. Thus [it is said].

"Seven [priests] have stirred you with their prayers, desiring to sacrifice. Your streams have been released; they flow forth—this is the meaning. Therein lies a simile: "like coursers. Just as horses emerge from a stable, so do they flow through the filter; this is the sense. And here, the state of being carried in streams is intended in view of the ritual application. 8.

Toward the vessel that distills honey, they have poured forth; in the woolly filter, the wise ones have lowed. 11. Toward the vessel; honey-distilling; they have poured forth; in the woolly filter; the wise ones have lowed. 11.
This is stated in connection with the flow of the stream:

"The Soma juices have been released (*asṛgram*)—by the priests they are poured forth—toward the *kośa*, the wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*), which is the shedder (*acyutam*), the one that causes the sweet flavor to flow out. Toward this, characterized by the *avyaya* [wool-filtration], in the highest [filter] or in that which has become the *avi* [sheep's wool], into the *vāra*, the *vāla*, the ten-fold purifier. Regarding the verb *sṛj*, in the sense of the object, the substitution of *tiṅ* for *tiṅ* (according to the rule *tiṅāṃ tiṅo bhavanti*) results in the form *asṛgram*.
Furthermore: "The *dhītayaḥ* (senses).
[They are so called] because they do not bend the fingers;
or because by them one drinks (*dhayanti*) and consumes."
Our fingers "have lowed," meaning they desire those Soma juices for the sake of purifying them again and again.
Toward the ocean, the drops have gone, like milch-cows to their stall, unto the womb of Ṛta. 12. Toward the ocean, the drops, like milch-cows, have gone home, unto the womb of Ṛta. 12.
The *indavas*, the flowing Soma drops, go toward the *samudram*, the vat (*droṇakalaśa*) which is the meeting place where all Somas converge.
Therein lies the illustration:
just as *gāvaḥ* (cows)—the yielders of milk who delight people and have recently calved—go to their home, the *astam*, even so do they proceed.

Furthermore, those Soma juices have come toward—the womb, that is, the place—of the *ṛta*, the sacrifice which has become reality (*satya*). [This is derived from] the root *gam* in the luṅ tense, with the elision of the suffix *sic* and the elision of the penultimate vowel.

O Indu, for our great joy the waters flow forth like rivers, when you shall clothe yourself in milk. 13. O Indu, for our great joy the waters flow forth like rivers, when you shall clothe yourself in milk. 13.
"O Indra, let the Soma flow for us toward our own *araṇa*, that is, toward the *raṇa*.
*Raṇa* is the sacrifice (*yajña*), so called because the gods rejoice (*raṇanti*) and praise [therein]; the suffix *ap* is used here in the sense of a locus."
The substitution [of *ḍe* for *ṅe*] does not occur by virtue of Pāṇini’s rule 7.1.13 (*ḍeryaḥ*), because in the Vedic language all grammatical rules are optional.

For the sake of "great joy" (*mahe raṇāya*)—that is, for the great sacrifice (*yajñāya*)—the "streams" (*sindhavaḥ*), meaning the waters known as *vasatīvarī*, flow toward it at that time for the purpose of sprinkling the Soma.

"When" (*yat*)—that is, when you are "to be mixed" (*vāmayiṣyase*), meaning when you are covered or prepared with "your own" (*svam*) products of the cow, such as curds and milk, then the waters go toward you.

In this friendship of yours, we, desiring to sacrifice, with you as our protectors—O Indu, we long for your companionship. 14. In this friendship of yours, we, desiring to sacrifice, with you as our protectors—O Indu, we long for your companionship. 14.

O Indu Pavamāna, we who desire to sacrifice (*iyakṣantaḥ*)—or rather, who desire to move forward (*ejayitum icchantaḥ*)—standing in your friendship (*sakhye*), that is, in the act of befriending you, we, being your protectors (*hvotayaḥ*), yearn for and desire (*uśmasi*) nothing other than friendship itself (*sakhitvam*).
1. *ga*-ta³-bhara⁴.⁷-vimṛjaṃti; bha¹.⁷-visṛjaṃti | 2. *ga*-nagarataḥ; ta¹.⁵.⁷-maṃgugato; tara-maṃgugato; ta³-naṃdurato; ta⁴-maṃdurgatayo; bha⁴-naṃdurāto | 3. *ga*-avisvabhūte; ta-bha⁴-aviśvabhūte |

4. *ga-bha1-mu* undergoes the substitution of *ira*; *ta1-na-ra* undergoes the substitution of *ora*; *tara4.5.6.7-na* undergoes the substitution of *ima*. 5. *ta1.5* [becomes] *indavaḥ samudraḥ*; *ta4* [becomes] *indavaḥ samudrāḥ*.

Flow forth for the sake of the seeker of cattle, O Soma, for the great one who beholds men; enter into the belly of Indra. (15) *ā* | *pavasva* | *gaviṣṭhaye* | *mahe* | *soma* | *nṛcakṣase* | *ā* | *indrasya* | *jaṭhare* | *viśa* || 15 ||

O Soma Pavamāna, for the sake of the search for cattle, you seek out the cows of the Aṅgirases. Flow for Indra, who is great, who is the beholder of men, and who perceives the fruit of the deeds of men—the leaders of actions—within the vessels, purified by the ten-fold filter. Then enter into the belly of Indra, or into the *droṇakalaśa* which serves as his stomach.

Great art thou, O Soma; the eldest of the fierce ones, O Indu, the most powerful. As a warrior, thou hast evermore been victorious. 16. Great art thou, O Soma; the eldest of the fierce ones, O Indu, the most powerful. As a warrior, thou hast evermore been victorious. 16.
O Soma, you are great because you are the one who gratifies the gods.
Indeed, you are the eldest and most highly praised.
Furthermore, O Indu, O Pavamāna, you are the most powerful even among those whose strength has been uplifted.
Being a warrior, even while engaged in battle with your enemies, you have always—indeed, at all times—been victorious; you have conquered them and their wealth.
[The root] *ji* means "to conquer.
In the form *jigetha*, the substitution of a guttural (*ka-varga*) for the letter following the reduplication occurs by the rule *san-liṭor jeḥ*.

He who is more powerful even than the fierce, more heroic even than the heroes, and greater even than the bountiful giver. 17. He who—more powerful even than the fierce; more heroic even than the heroes; greater even than the one from whom much is received. 17.
That Soma who is more powerful than even the fierce, more mighty than even the strong;
furthermore, he who is more heroic than even the brave, being exceedingly capable;
likewise, that Soma who bestows abundant gifts.
The root *bhṛ* is used in the sense of "giving.
By the rule *āto manin*, the suffix *vic* is applied.
Thus, he becomes the greatest giver (*dātṛtama*), even greater than those who give much wealth.
The connection is with the following phrase: "We choose you."

O Soma, you are the sun; come hither for the winning of offspring and for the acquisition of our bodies. We choose you for friendship; we choose you for alliance. 18. O Soma, you are the sun; come hither for the winning of offspring and for the acquisition of our bodies. We choose you for friendship; we choose you for alliance. 18.

O Soma, you are the sun, the possessor of great heroism; or rather, you are the impeller of all rites such as sacrifice. Bestow strength upon us. (The verb "place" [dhehi] is supplied here because of the presence of the prefix [upa]). Furthermore, be the giver (*sātā*) of offspring—of sons (*tokasya*) and of "bodies" (*tanūnām*); for "bodies" (*tanvaḥ*) refers to grandsons, so called because they extend (*tanvanti*) the lineage. [The root *ṣaṇu* means "to give. The suffix *vid* is applied by the rule *janasana-*; the vowel change to *ā* occurs by the same rule. We choose you—that is, we honor you—for friendship (*sakhyāya*), for the sake of companionship or ritual action; likewise, for association (*yujyāya*). "Associate" (*yuj*) means a companion; the suffix *vyañ* is added to denote its state or action. Since the rule is conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), the vowel change and augment are not mandatory. Thus, we also choose you for assistance characterized by the slaying of enemies and the like.

When the first libation has been offered in the Agnihotra, the sacrificer, having approached, should worship [Agni] every day and every year with the three verses beginning with *dhāman*. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the verses addressed to Agni, namely *ā yāhy arvāṅ* and *āyūṃṣi pavase*, he should worship every year. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.22.24).
2. Joined with *ga*; 3. joined with *bha* (1.7);
3. *tara*.6.7—*mu*: "by one who has fasted" (*upoṣitena*); *tapa*: "by one who has undertaken [the vow]" (*upasthitena*) (Śrauta Sūtra 2.3–4).
In the ceremonies beginning with the *caula*, four oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) are to be offered; in that very context, three [of these] are prescribed.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “Before those [oblations], one should then offer oblations of clarified butter with the three verses beginning ‘O Agni, you purify our lives’” (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 1.4.3–4).
In the *pavamāna* sacrifice at the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), this verse ‘O Agni, you purify our lives’ serves as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the god Agni Pavamāna.
"O Agni, purify yourself"—this is the *yājyā*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "In the first [offering], 'Agni is the purifier,' 'O Agni, you purify the lifespans,' and 'O Agni, purify yourself, O skillful one'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 2.1).
In the *punarādheya* (re-consecration), this verse "O Agni, [you purify] the lifespans" is an optional *anuvākyā* for the second *ājyabhāga* offering.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The first [verse] always belongs to the Anubrāhmaṇins; 'agne āyūṃṣi pavase' is the second" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.8).
O Agni, you purify our lives; bring us strength and nourishment, and drive misfortune far away.
O Agni, you purify our lifespans; send forth strength and nourishment.
O Soma Pavamāna, you go beyond those who are hostile and harmful enemies;
likewise, you approach—that is, you move toward—the beautiful hymns of the chanters.
The root *ṛṣ* means "to go. It belongs to the Taudādi class; the suffix *śap* is applied according to the rule "it is frequent in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Furthermore, like the sun (*sūra*), he is the "all-seeing" (*viśvadarśana*); that is, he is the observer of everything, or he is one who is worthy of being seen by all.
He knows the vital points, he is surrounded by long lives, he is beneficial for the surrounding world; he is the drop, the steed, the far-seeing one.
He who knows the vital points, who possesses long life, who is all-encompassing, who is beneficial for the protection of the world, the drop (Indu), the steed, the far-seeing one. 23.

Being repeatedly cleansed and purified by the men who lead the ritual through their lives and who know the vital points (*marmajña*), that *indu*, that *soma*, becomes a steed that goes continuously toward the gods.
Of what nature is he?
He is full of milk (*payasvān*) and possesses the quality of pleasing (*prīṇanaśīla*).
Or rather:
he is joined with the wealth to be given to the praisers;
for that very reason, he becomes one who approaches the oblation, beneficial for nourishment, far-seeing—either the maker of all things visible or the knower of all—and Soma goes toward the gods.

The root *cakṣiṅ* is used in the sense of "distinct speech. The suffix *yuc* is applied [to form *cākṣuṣa*] according to the rule: "And after a root that is anudātta and ends in *hlād*, [the suffix *yuc* is added]."
Pavamāna has generated the great *ṛta*, the bright light;
he has struck down the black darknesses.
Pavamāna has generated the great *ṛta*, the bright light; he has struck down the black darknesses. 24.

Pavamāna has generated—that is, brought forth in the heavenly world—the *ṛta*, which is truth, real, vast, abundant, pervasive in all regions, pure, radiant, white-colored light and splendor. What was he doing? Destroying—that is, utterly annihilating—the dark, black-colored darknesses.
The form [is derived] from the root *han* with the suffix *yaṅ* elided and the present participle suffix *śatṛ*;
the initial vowel receives the udātta accent by the rule "the first syllable of reduplicated stems (*abhyasta*) is acute."
As the tawny one is being purified and strikes down [obstacles], the bright drops have been released— swift, with rapid brilliance.
As the tawny one, being purified, strikes down [the foe], his bright drops have been released—quick, with rapid purifying power. 25.

Of Hari, the green-colored one, who destroys the increasing darkness—that is, the slayer of the ever-increasing gloom—and who possesses a purifying brilliance that moves everywhere, the moons are the drops of Pavamāna Soma.
[The root] *cad* means "to delight"; thus, they are the delighters of the gods. The swift streams, characterized by their rapid flow, have been, and continue to be, released.
The meaning is that the purifying fire goes forth.
Pavamāna is the best of charioteers, most resplendent with his brilliant rays, golden-hued,
and rich in manifold wealth.
Pavamāna, the best of charioteers, most radiant with splendors, golden-hued and bright, accompanied by the host of Maruts. 26.
Pavamāna is the god who is the best charioteer, possessing a chariot in the highest degree;
the vowel *ī* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 8.2.16.1 (*īdvin*);
likewise, he is the most brilliant among those endowed with splendor, being exceedingly radiant even through his glorious lusters.

Alternatively, Hariścandra is possessed of a fame that is even more stainless than the stainless [moon]; the *suṭ* augment is applied according to the rule of Pāṇini’s grammar: "When a short vowel precedes and 'candra' follows as the second member of a compound."
The host of Maruts is either radiant with a green color or possesses a green stream;
he whose host of Maruts serves as his companions is thus described.
Such a one has, by means of his own rays—that is, his own splendors—overwhelmed all the worlds, having deluded them; this is to be connected with what follows.
Being purified, winning the prize through his rays,
he bestows heroic strength upon the singer.
Pavamāna has spread out with his rays, bestowing upon the singer most excellent strength, winning the prize of victory. 27.
1. *ga-ta-bha-soma*: [He] attains all; *ta-sarvān*.
*Pavamāna Soma*, with his rays—that is, with his own splendors—reaches the entire world like a horse.
Of what nature is he?
*vājasātama*: one who is preeminent as a giver of food (*anna*) or a distributor of strength (*bala*).
Likewise, bestowing (*dadhat*) or granting (*vidadhat*) a son endowed with great heroism (*suvīrya*) or wealth to the *manu* who performs the *pavamāna-stotra*, he pervades (*vyāpnoti*).
[The form] *akṣota* contains the augment *aṭ*.

Being pressed, Indu has flowed forth; he has passed through the woolen filter. Purifying himself, Indu flows toward Indra. 28. pra | suvānaḥ | induḥ | akṣāḥ | pavitram | ati | avyayam | punānaḥ | induḥ | indram | ā || 28 ||

The flowing *indu*, the Soma being pressed, having passed through the *daśāpavitra*—the woolen filter made from the fleece of a sheep—flows forth (*pra akṣāḥ*) toward the jar. In the *luṅ* tense, after the suffix *tip* and the *sic* augment, there is an absence of the *iṭ* augment by Vedic rule; furthermore, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.2.2: *ato lāntasya*.

In the word *rāsasya*, there is the elision of the suffix *sic*. The vowel *i* is used to clarify that the word ends in the letter *r*. The absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.3.97).
By the rule *halṅyādi*, there is elision of the suffix *ni*.
Then, being purified by the strainer (*pavitra*), the pure *indu*—that is, Soma—enters *indra*. Because of the hearing of the prefix (*upa*), the action of conjunction (*yoga*) is to be supplied.

This Soma plays upon the skin of the cows with the pressing-stones; he loudly calls Indra for exhilaration. 29. This—Soma—upon—the skin—of the cows—plays—with the stones—Indra—for intoxication—loudly calls. 29.
This Soma, in the form of a shoot, plays upon the hide of a bull—that is, on the ox-hide;
the word *adhi* indicates the sense of "upon.
Upon the hide, he plays together with the pressing-stones—the *grāvan*—for the purpose of being pressed; he sports for the sake of extraction.
Doing what?
He was "invoking Indra intensely" (*johuvat*), calling him repeatedly in order to "intoxicate" (*madāya*) him with the drinking of Soma.
By this, it is understood that they were at that time offering praise directed toward Indra.

O Pavamāna, with that glorious milk of yours which has been brought down from heaven, be gracious to us so that we may live. 30. O Pavamāna, with that milk of yours which is full of splendor and has been brought down from heaven—with that, be gracious to us for the sake of life. 30.

O Pavamāna, O Soma being purified, you who have been brought from heaven by the Gāyatrī in the form of a falcon—since that food characterized as Soma, which is full of vigor and endowed with glory, belongs to you, therefore, with that food, be gracious to us for the sake of long life; be merciful, grant us happiness.
‘Tvaṃ somāṃsa’: this is the thirty-second hymn, the seventh [in the section].
Bharadvāja, son of Bṛhaspati, is the seer of the first triplet;
Marīci Kaśyapa is the seer of the second.
For the third [book], Rāhūgaṇa Gautama;
for the fourth, Bhauma Atri;
for the fifth, Viśvāmitra Gāthin.
The seer of the sixth [verse] is Jamadagni Bhārgava;
of the seventh, Vasiṣṭha Maitrāvaruṇi;
and of the remainder of the hymn, Pavitra Āṅgirasa or Vasiṣṭha, or both together as the seers.
The three verses beginning with "pavasva soma mandayan" are two-pāda Gāyatrīs.
The thirtieth verse, "alāyyasya," is a Purauṣṇih consisting of twelve, eight, twenty-seven, thirty-one, thirty-two, and thirty syllables respectively. The following three verses are Anuṣṭubhs.
The remaining *gāyatrī* verses—
beginning with "avitā no ajāśvaḥ"— are three in number; they have Pavamāna-Pūṣan as their deity,
or alternatively, they have Pavamāna-Soma as their deity.
The five verses beginning with “*yat te pavitram arcisi*” have Pavamāna as their deity.
Among these five, the third, “*ubhābhyāṃ deva savitar*,” has both Pavamāna and Savitṛ as its deities;
the fourth is “*tribhis tvā deva savitar*.”
1. *ga-ta-bha-punāna*: a deity named thus.
2. *ga-prayacchatu*; *tara-prayatna*; *bha1.7-prayacchate*. 3. *ga-droṇa*.

4. *ga*: ending in *ta* and *lāṃ*; *ta4*: ending in *ta* and *rlāṃ*; *ta5*: ending in *la* and *ti*; *ta6*: ending in *tra*; *bha4*: ending in *rlaṃ*; *bha1(2)*: *supā*. Sūtra: ending in *rlāṃ*. 5. *ga*, *ta*, *bhara.4*: the word ‘*mṛḷa*’ is absent. 6. *ta*, *bhara.5*: having Pavamāna-Soma as the deity; *bha1*: having Pavamāna-Savitṛ as the deity; *bha4*: having Pavamāna-Savitṛ-Soma as the deity.
Thus, this [verse] "Punantu mā" is, by way of alternative, dedicated to the deity Savitṛ Pavamāna;
"Punantu mā" is, by way of alternative, dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
Furthermore, the two verses beginning with "Yaḥ pāvamānīradhyeti" serve to set forth the praise of those who study the Pavamāna collection.
Therefore, that alone is the deity;
all the remaining [verses] have the purifying Soma as their deity.

And it is recited accordingly: "O Soma, you are the thirty-two straight ones; Kaśyapa, Gotama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha—thus indeed are the seven seers of the three-verse hymns (ṛcas). The remainder is the Pavitra; or both [Kaśyapa and Gotama] are Vasiṣṭhas. 'Pavastra soma' consists of three Gāyatrīs, always two-footed. 'Avitā naḥ' belongs to Pūṣan. 'Yatte pavitram' consists of five verses addressed to Agni. 'Sāvibhyam' is addressed to Savitṛ, or to the Viśvedevas. The others are Triṣṭubhs. The last twenty-seven are Anuṣṭubhs, and they are praises of the Pavamāna hymns by those who study them. Thus ends the application of the hymns (sūktaviniyoga).

You, O Soma, are the sustainer, the delightful, the most powerful at the sacrifice; flow on, bestowing abundant wealth. (1) O Soma, being purified, you are the exhilarating, the most vigorous one at our unimpeded sacrifice. You are the sustainer, desiring the stream of the pressing; therefore, as the giver of wealth to the singers, flow on—be purified by the woollen filter in the wooden vats and other vessels. Or rather: *dhāryuḥ* is formed with the suffix *-yu* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), meaning "possessing a stream"; thus the connection is: "O Soma, you who possess such a stream, flow on."

You, when pressed, are the exhilarator of men, flowing forth, most intoxicating—for Indra, as a wise patron, with the soma-juice. (2) O Soma, you who exhilarate men—that is, who delight the officiating priests who lead the ritual—therefore you are "flowing" (*dadhanvān*), bestowing wealth upon them, or rather, the sustainer of the sacrifice. As a wise patron (*sūriḥ*), being pressed by us, you, together with the *andhas* (the food in the form of the oblation), become most intoxicating (*matsarintamaḥ*) for Indra, providing him with supreme exhilaration. [The *nakāra* is used according to the rule "nādrasya"].

Pressed by the stones, flow toward us, making a loud sound; [attain] the most excellent, resplendent strength. O Pavamāna Soma, being pressed by the stones—the pressing-stones—being extracted and purified, you, making a loud sound (*karnikadat*), flow toward the jar or the vessels. Likewise, attain the most excellent, resplendent (*ghumantam*) strength (*śuṣmam*) that withers the enemies. Alternatively, it may be construed as a single sentence: "Being pressed, you go toward strength. The root *kad* (in the form *kadi-kradi*) means "to take" or "to seize. In the formation of *karnikadat*, the suffix *haL* is elided, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) of the reduplicated syllable, and everything is irregularly formed according to the rule *dhāditidardharti*. From that, the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is added; the accent is determined by the rule *avyastānāmādiḥ*.

The drop, being urged forward, flows across the woollen filters; the tawny one has bellowed for the prize of strength. (4) *Induḥ*: the drop. *Hinvānaḥ*: being urged forward, being impelled by the pressing-stones, being purified. *Arṣati*: flows. *Tiraḥ*: across. *Vāryāṇi*: the desirable things. *Avyayā*: made of sheep’s wool, belonging to the sheep. That is to say, the filters. *Tāni tiraḥ*: having passed through them, having set them aside as an obstruction. *Arṣati*: he goes; that is to say, he flows forth abundantly. *Saḥ ayam hariḥ*: this very tawny-colored Soma. *Vājam*: food. *Acikradat*: he bellows; that is to say, he calls out, "With you, I summon Indra."
1. In Ga, Ta, Bha, and Mu, "ha" does not exist.
2. In Ga, Ta, and Bha, "soma" does not exist.
3. In Ga, Ta, Bha, and Mu, read "cābhigaccha."
4. "O Indra, I gladden you" means "I cause you to win the prize"; "O Indra, I gladden you" means "I cause you to win the prize."

O Indu, you flow forth to another; O Soma, you flow forth to fame, to prosperity, and to strengths consisting of cattle. (5) O Indu, O Soma, you flow apart toward the other [filter]; you flow forth in various streams. Furthermore, you flow forth to glories—sacrificial offerings and foods—and to prosperity (*saubhaga*). Prosperity is the state of being fortunate; the word *subhaga* is listed among the *utratra* group, and its vowel strengthening in the final syllable is not desired here. You attain various riches. Likewise, O Soma, may you attain various strengths (*vājān*) consisting of cattle—that is, possessing livestock. The intention is: "May you cause all of these to reach us. (13)

O Indu, bring us wealth consisting of hundreds, abounding in cattle and horses; O Soma, bestow upon us riches in the thousands. O Indu, flowing into the vessels, O Soma, bring to us—that is, accomplish and grant to us—wealth consisting of hundreds (*śatagvinam*). One who possesses a hundred cows is called *śatagu*; [bring] that which is rich in cattle (*gomantam*), possessing excellent livestock, accompanied by horses (*aśvinam*), and amounting to thousands (*sahasriṇam*)—bring such wealth, or sons.

Flowing through the filter, the swift drops of Soma have reached Indra by these paths. (7) *Pavamānāsaḥ*, *indavaḥ*, *tiraḥ*, *pavitram*, *āśavaḥ*, *indram*, *yāmaibhiḥ*, *āśata*. The *pavitram* is the *daśāpavitra* made of woolen threads; having passed through it—that is, making it an intervening barrier—the *pavamānāsaḥ* (flowing ones), pouring forth in many streams toward the jar, the *āśavaḥ* (swift ones), which quickly produce intoxication or pervade the *camasa* cups and other vessels, the *indavaḥ* (drops), the Somas, by their own *yāmaibhiḥ* (paths/movements), have *āśata* (reached/pervaded) *indram* (Indra). They reach him.

The preeminent, Soma-like juice, the Indu, the ancient one, flows for Indra—the life-force for the living one. *Kakuhaḥ*, *somyaḥ*, *rasaḥ*, *induḥ*, *indrāya*, *pūrvyaḥ*, *āyuḥ*, *pavate*, *āyave*. The preeminent (*kakuha*)—Soma is "preeminent" because he stands most highly exalted above all by virtue of being the impeller of all actions. This very one, the "ancient" (*pūrvya*)—meaning either prepared or pressed in the early morning—is the "life-force" (*āyu*), the Indu that goes toward Indra, flowing into the vessels. The suffix *ya* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.4.138 (*mayaṭ ca*), thus it is "Soma-like" (*somya*), a juice consisting of Soma. For the "living one" (*āyave*)—for Indra, who moves everywhere—it "flows" (*pavate*), meaning it becomes purified through the filter in the jars. Alternatively, it goes forward toward Indra for his sake; the root *pavi* signifies the act of going.

The three fingers impel the hero, the flowing one who distills sweetness; with song they have sounded together toward him. (9) The three fingers—moving here and there for the sake of performing the ritual—impel the *sūra*, the one of great heroism, the impeller of all rites such as sacrifice, the *pavamāna* Soma who distills (*madhuśruta*) the intoxicating juice; they proceed toward him for the purpose of pressing. Then the singers, with their song (*girā*), have sounded together toward him; they praise him perfectly.
1. Those who possess good fortune through the support of the *ga* [sound]. 2. That Soma which belongs to you (*ta*).
3. O Indra, he who comes with those [Somas] (*tebhiḥ*).

May Pūṣan, whose steeds are goats, be our protector on every journey; may he grant us a share among desirable maidens. (10) *Ajāśvaḥ*: "The goats belong to Pūṣan"—as it is said—thus he is called *ajāśva*, meaning one whose vehicles are indeed goats. That *Pūṣan*, the deity of this name, may be our *avitā* (protector) on *yāmani-yāmani*, that is, on every movement characterized as either terrestrial or celestial. Furthermore, may he *ā-bhakṣat* (grant a share to) us *kanyāsu*, among beautiful and desirable women; the meaning is: "May he bestow daughters upon us. This is a form derived from the root *bhaj* in the sense of service (*sevā*), in the *leṭ* mood, second person singular, with the augment *ḍā*. Alternatively: *Ajāśvaḥ* means the goat-vehicled Pūṣan, the nourisher of all, or Soma, on *yāmani-yāmani*. A *yāma* is a sacrifice, so it is that which is reached or attained by the gods. Therein, in the sacrifice, may he be our *avitā*, our protector. Likewise, among *kanyāsu* (women), those who are desired, may he *ā-bhakṣat*, cause us to attain them. (14)

This Soma flows for the one with matted locks (Kapardin), like clarified butter and honey; may he partake [of it] among our maidens. 11. This Soma flows for the one with matted locks, like clarified butter and honey; may he partake among our maidens. For the sake of the one with matted locks—be it for the auspiciously crowned Soma or for Pūṣan—this exhilarating, purified Soma belonging to us flows and proceeds. He reaches him. Therein is the illustration: just as clarified butter, or honey—that is, the intoxicating oblation in the form of *ghṛta*—goes toward Soma or Pūṣan, so it is here. Then he brought [the fruit] among our maidens.

This [Soma] pressed for you, O radiant one, flows pure like clarified butter. May it partake among our maidens. (12) O *āghṛṇe*—[the root] *ghṛ* meaning "to flow" and "to shine"—O Pavamāna or Pūṣan who shines everywhere, this Soma pressed for you has been extracted; it flows toward you. Or rather, for your sake, it becomes purified through the filter in the vessels or flows forth. Therein lies the illustration: like pure clarified butter (*ghṛtaṃ na śuci*). Just as pure clarified butter reaches you, so may it reach us. Therefore, grant us our desired objects.

O Soma, as the progenitor of the speech of the sages, flow with your stream; you are the bestower of jewels among the gods. (13) O Soma, you are the progenitor (*jantu*) of the speech of the sages (*kavīnām*), that is, the generator of praise for those of beautiful wisdom who offer hymns. Alternatively, among the wise, you alone generate speech. Flow (*pavasva*) with your stream (*dhārayā*) into the wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*) and reach the sacrificial cups (*graha*). Thereafter, you are the bestower of jewels (*ratnadhāḥ*)—the depositor of the delightful Soma—among the gods such as Indra. Or else, you are the giver of jewels, such as gold, to us who are performing the work of praising the gods.

In the Grāvastotṛ’s chant, according to the opinion of Gāṇagāri, when the Soma is being poured into the jars for the sake of a suitable vessel, the second and third verses of the triplet to be recited—one beginning with "ā kalaśeṣu"—are to be used.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning with 'ā kalaśeṣu dhāvati' and 'iyeno varma vi gāhate'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.12).

The falcon rushes toward the jars; he plunges into the armor, crying out toward the wooden vats. 14. He rushes toward the jars; the falcon plunges into the armor, crying out toward the wooden vats. 14.

1. In manuscripts ga, ta-bha1.2.4, the word "abhakṣat" is absent. 2. In manuscript ga, it reads "kanyā asmān āgamanayat"; in ta1, "kanyās tasmān āgamanayat"; in ta2, "kanyāsvamānāgamanayat"; in bha1, "kanyāsmānāgamanayat"; in bha4, "kanyāmayat"; and in bha7, "kanyāsu no'smānāgamanayat". 3. In manuscript ta, the phrase "tvam eva" is absent.
Being consecrated by the officiating priests, a certain Soma flows— that is, moves everywhere— into the jars, the vessels for holding Soma, namely the *droṇa* jars;
"like a hawk" (*śyenaḥ*) is an elliptical simile.
Just as a hawk (*śyena*) dives into its chosen nest (*varma* = *varaṇīyaṃ kulāyam*), so too does [the Soma],
crying out loudly (*kanikradat*), go toward the wooden vats (*droṇa* = *droṇakalaśān*).
Or alternatively:
This refers to the intention of those who designate the *droṇakalaśa*, the *adhvaryu’s cup*, and the *pūtabhṛt* as the three [vessels].
One portion of the Soma being poured out goes first toward the *droṇa* while making a sound;
thereafter, it goes to the two vessels.
On the far side, O Soma, thy juice, pressed out, has been released into the jars;
like a hawk darting forth, it flows onward.

O Soma, your juice, pressed in the jars, has been poured forth all around; like a hawk darting swiftly, it flows onward. O Soma, your juice, pressed in the jars—the large wooden vats—has been poured forth all around; it is distributed into the *pra-ha* vessels and the *camasa* cups. How so? Like a hawk darting swiftly: the root *tak* signifies motion; just as a hawk, a bird of swift movement, flies everywhere, so does this juice flow. Or rather, just as a hawk is one who goes everywhere, so the Soma, having gone into the vessels, flows toward the gods such as Indra. [The form *arpati* is derived from the root *ṛp* "to go" with the suffix *sip* (present indicative), or alternatively, it is formed from the root *ṛp* "to go" with the suffix *śap* (present indicative). 15 || 0 || 15 ||
O Soma, being most sweet, exhilarate Indra at the ritual joints.

Flow, O Soma, exhilarating for Indra, most rich in sweetness! 16. O Soma, you who are most rich in sweetness (*madhumattamaḥ*), being the one who exhilarates (*mandayan*)—that is, the one who causes intoxication—or rather, for Indra (the dative case being used because "the mention of the action" [in the rule] must be applied), flow while gladdening Indra; that is, come forth for the sake of Indra.
They have been let loose for the feast of the gods, like chariots seeking booty.

They have been poured out for the feast of the gods, seeking booty like chariots. (17) These Soma juices, being pressed, seeking booty, have been poured out—that is, they are released and offered by the officiating priests—for the feast of the gods, that is, for the drinking of the gods. Therein is the illustration: "like chariots. Just as chariots, seeking booty—meaning desiring the wealth of enemies or strength for their masters—and seeking to go to the gods, are sent forth for the feast of the gods, so too are these Somas.
These pressed juices, most exhilarating and bright, have flowed toward Vāyu.

Those pressed juices, most exhilarating and bright, have flowed toward Vāyu. Most exhilarating—that is, exceedingly intoxicating—and bright—that is, shining—those pressed Soma juices have flowed toward Vāyu; they have emitted sound, or rather, they have caused him to flow. Or else, they have sent forth Vāyu himself for the purpose of drinking the Soma. Indeed, when the Somas are pressed, Vāyu surely comes for the sake of drinking them.
Praised by the pressing-stone, O Soma, you go toward the filter,
bestowing heroic vigor upon the singer.
Pressed by the pressing-stone, O Soma, you go toward the filter, bestowing great heroic vigor upon the singer. 19.

1. Ga-bha4: *sṛjyate*; Ta-bha1.2.7: *prasṛjyate*; Su-pāmārji: *pariprasṛjyate*. 2. Ta3-bha1.4.7: *vibhakto bhavati*. 3. Ga-bha5: *yajamānānām añjhicchantaḥ*; Ta3-bhara.4: *yajamānānām añjhicchantaḥ santaḥ*.
4. bha1 (2) lacks "sutāsaḥ. 5. ta lacks "suteṣu.
6. ga, ta3, bha1, and bha7 lack "satsu."
O Soma, pressed by the pressing-stones for you and poured out, being shaken by the praisers, you go to and reach the filter.
What are you doing?
Bestowing—that is, granting—to the praiser, the person who performs the hymn of praise, wealth and other riches endowed with excellent heroic power (*suvīrya*).
This has been offered for you; O pure-minded one, go through the woolly filter, slaying the demons.
This one, praised by you, the slayer of demons, plunges through the filter, across the woolen strainer. 20.
For you:
[the root] *tud* means "to afflict.

This Soma of ours, pressed by the *prāva*s (the pressing-stones) and thus afflicted on all sides, has become the slayer of *rakṣases*—that is, the destroyer of the wicked ones or demons who create obstacles to our ritual actions.
O Agni, [be] the imperishable, the unshakeable, that which has become the imperishable constituent part; O Agni, [be] the purifier, the cleanser, the radiant one—
[the suffix] *matup* becomes *-vat* according to the rule "chandasīraḥ."
With that very light of your own which exists as your splendor, endowed with the radiance of the sun and other luminaries, purify us—make us pure.
Furthermore, [purify us] with the *brahmasavas*, the Soma-pressings performed by Brahmins;
or alternatively:
Brahman is Soma;
with its pressings, purify us.

O Savitṛ, O God, purify me on all sides with both [your] means: with the filter and with the impulse. (25) O Savitṛ, O God, O radiant Soma, purify me from every direction with both of these: with your own brilliance that cleanses away sin, and with the impulse [of the pressing] through the extraction of the Soma. Make me pure. (17)

O God Savitṛ, O Soma, O Agni, purify us with your three most excellent, most powerful, and skillful abodes. (26) O God, worthy of praise or resplendent; O Savitṛ, impeller of all toward their respective duties; O Soma, distinguished by the quality of purification; O Agni—you, with your three most excellent (*varṣiṣṭhaiḥ*), and therefore most powerful (*dakṣaiḥ*) abodes (*dhāmabhiḥ*), consisting of the bodies of Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, purify us (*punīhi naḥ*), making us completely pure.

May the divine beings purify me; may the Vasus purify me with their wisdom. O All-Gods, purify me; O Jātavedas, purify me. (27) May the *devajanāḥ*—those for whom the manifestation (*jana*) of the gods occurs during sacrifices, namely the sacrificers—or alternatively, the hosts of gods such as Indra and others—purify (*punantu*) me, making me completely pure. Likewise, may the *vasavaḥ*—the gods who provide dwelling—purify me through their own *dhiyā*, that is, through their ritual action. Now, addressing them directly: O *viśve devāḥ*, all you gods, purify (*punīta*) me, make me pure. O *jātavedaḥ*—so called because you know (*veti*) the born classes of beings, or because your wisdom is born—O Agni, purify (*punīhi*) me.

Swell forth, flow forth, O Soma, with all your rays; [be] the most excellent oblation for the gods. 28 O Soma, swell forth—cause us to increase exceedingly; or rather, cause the gods to increase by means of the Soma. Furthermore, with all your rays, for the sake of the gods, flow forth—that is, stream toward the jars and other vessels—the most excellent, most praiseworthy oblation in the form of Soma. [In other words,] bestow it. Regarding the leading forward of Agni and Soma, this verse "upa priyam" is used. It is stated in the Sūtra: "He should begin with the half-verse 'upa priyaṃ panipnatam'. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.10).

Bearing homage, we have approached Agni—the beloved, the one praised by all, the youthful, who increases through oblations. *Priyam*: the one who gladdens all; *panimatam*: sounding exceedingly; *yuvānam*: the youthful; *āhutivṛdham*: to be nourished by oblations; *agnim*: Agni; *bibhrataḥ*: bearing; *namaḥ*: homage (or the sacrificial offering). We, while maintaining *namaḥ*—whether as the sacrificial oblation or as an act of salutation—have approached the purifying Agni, who is dear to all, who is celebrated with hymns, who is ever-youthful, and who thrives upon the offerings.
1. [Note: The commentary glosses "ga-api" as "also."]
2. Increase the existing [wealth]!
3. The Brahmins of the Ga family.
Rigveda 4.8.
We would approach.

In the aorist (luṅ) of the root *gam*, when there is elision (*luk*) of *cal* by the rule "in a mantra, *ghas*" [is substituted for *gam*], the letter *n* occurs by the rule "also after *myo*. This is merely an illustration (*panimātram*).
This is the form of the root *pan*, meaning "to praise," in the absence of the *yaṅ* affix (*yaṅluk*).

According to the rule *dādharti dardharti*, because the particle *iti* serves to indicate that this is an illustration, the augment *nig* is applied to the reduplication and the penultimate vowel is elided as irregular forms (*nipātana*).
The joint of Alārya has perished; O divine Soma, flow over it! Even as for a mole, O divine Soma. Of Alārya, the joint has perished; that, O divine Soma, flow over! Even as for a mole, O divine Soma.
The word *valāya* is derived from the root *val*, with the suffix *āya* added according to the *uṇādi* rules; the substitution of *la* for *ra* occurs because it belongs to the *kapilaka*-class.
O Pavamāna, you who cut away the vital parts of the enemy who is intent on attacking, destroy that very enemy and those whose sins are unequal [to yours].
Then, O radiant Soma, flow toward us;
furthermore, O shining and praiseworthy Soma, [protect] our speech.
The root *khanu* means "to tear open.
Therefore, strike down even that enemy who strikes everyone, but do not strike those whose sins are not equal [to his].

He who studies the Pāvamānī verses—the essence gathered by the seers—eats everything purified and made savory by Mātariśvan. 31. He who... the Pāvamānīs... studies... the essence... gathered by the seers... he... eats everything... purified... made savory by Mātariśvan. 31.

That person who studies the *Pavamānī* verses—all the ṛks dedicated to the deity Pavamāna—which have been compiled and prepared by the seers (*ṛṣis*), the perceivers of the hymns, through the meters and other means—that person eats all kinds of food as something already purified and perfectly cleansed.
He consumes food that is thoroughly refined and free from sin.
To explain how this [food] attains such purity, he says:
Even before his own food is consumed, he has already been purified by Mātariśvan.
Mātariśvan is the wind (vāyu), so called because it breathes (*śvasiti*) within the mother, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
And that wind is indeed the purifier (*pavitra*).
Afterwards, that person eats food that has been made savory and thoroughly purified by the purifying wind, which has rendered it delicious.

To him who studies the Pāvamānī verses—the essence gathered by the seers—Sarasvatī milks forth milk, clarified butter, honey, and water. 32. pāvamānīḥ | yaḥ | adhyeti | ṛṣibhiḥ | sambhṛtam | rasam | tasmai | sarasvatī | duhe | kṣīram | sarpiḥ | madhu | udakam || 32 ||

The Sarasvatī—the goddess of speech who flows everywhere—milks for herself milk, clarified butter, honey, and water; that is, she yields the Soma, which is the essence of the Veda, consisting of the *pavamānī* verses (hymns dedicated to the deity Pavamāna) collected by seers such as Madhucchandas and others. She milks this for the person who studies those *pavamāna* hymns;
the meaning is that she makes this man devoted to sacrifices and the like, and a knower of the Vedic scriptures.
The root *duh* is used in the sense of "filling.
In the reflexive construction (karmakartṛ), the suffix *yak* is prohibited by the rule "na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau.
The elision of the *ta* is effected by the rule "lopas ta ātmanepadeṣu."
In the fourth Anuvāka, there are eighteen Sūktas.
Among them, the first Sūkta, "pra devam," consisting of ten verses, has Vatsaprī, the son of Bhalandana, as its seer (ṛṣi); it is addressed to Pavamāna-Soma as its deity.
The tenth verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter, while the remaining verses are in the Jagatī meter.
And thus it is enumerated: "The seer Vatsapri Bhālandana [recited] 'pra devam' ending in a triṣṭubh; [the deity is] Indra.
The application [of the hymn] has been explained.
1. The sacrificer has brought his burden.

Toward the god, the honeyed drops have flowed forth like milch-cows toward us. Seated upon the sacred grass (*barhis*), eloquent and with uplifted voices, they have clothed the encompassing cow in her mantle.

Toward the god, the honey-sweet drops have flowed forth like milch-cows toward us; seated upon the sacred grass, eloquent and with uplifted horns, the cows have cast off their covering and released their bright color.
1. *Madhumantaḥ*: rich in honey, i.e., mixed with intoxicating juice.
2. *Indavaḥ*: drops of Soma. 3. *Devam*: the shining one, worthy of Soma. 4. *Accha*: towards. 5. *Prati*: against. 6. *Prāsiṣyadanta*: they have flowed forth; they stream out.
They flow forth from the great [vessels] and so on. This is the form of the causative of the root *syand* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the augment *caṅ*.
In that regard, there is an illustration:

Like cows that are milch-cows— cows full of milk that nourish and cause their milk to flow toward their calves— so [is this]. Furthermore, they are seated upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and they possess speech, making sounds such as the lowing of cows.
13. Regarding the camels:
just as they will be unexhausted and full of vigor, so did that Soma swell—that is, he poured out—with milk, meaning with his own essence in the form of milk;
that is to say, he nourished them.
Furthermore, he has caused the two great worlds— the vast and therefore boundless, limitless regions (rajasī)—
namely heaven and earth,
to tremble.
The root *vid* means "to know. This is the form in the present participle (*śatṛ*) with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix. The accent is that of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Distinguishing this earth from the sky by means of his brilliance for all beings, making them manifest, and moving forward—going everywhere on all sides—that Soma has taken unto himself *pājaḥ*, indestructible and imperishable strength;
that is to say, he has become exceedingly powerful.
Seeking his two mothers, the wise king, impelling them, swells his station by his own inherent power;
when the stalk is fashioned with skill, he comes together with the men, his kinsmen, and protects the head.

He, moving about, seeking strength, the wise one, swells his station with his own inherent power; the stalk is adorned by his own nature as he joins with the men, his kinsmen, and protects his head. 4.
Medhiraḥ:
By the rule *medhārathābhyāmarinaracau* (Pāṇini 5.2.109), the suffix *in* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).

Thus, *medhāvān* means "the wise one. He who is Soma, moving intensely between the two mothers—the Heaven and Earth who are the fashioners of the world—and likewise impelling the waters situated in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
The form *vajeryanta* is the present participle in the *śatṛ*-suffix.

Such [a one], together with *svadhayā*—that is, with food characterized by its own nature (*sakula*)—causes his own place (*pada*), which is the form of the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), to swell (*pinvate*) intensely.
Then, by the men (*nṛbhiḥ*) who are leaders of the ritual, the stalk (*aṃśu*)—the Soma—is restrained (*yataḥ*) and fashioned with effort (*yatnena*). It is thus joined (*saṃyataḥ*) by the singers.
The root *piś* means "to divide.
It is used here in the sense of being divided;
that is to say, "mixed."
Soma, indeed, is celebrated as the vessel of barley;
he, this very one, unites and comes together with his sisters who have emerged from a single hand and possess uplifted fingers;
and he protects the head, the multitude of beings that has been shattered.
He protects and nourishes with his own essence;
the root *nas* signifies motion,
and there is no suppression of the accent (*nighāta*) because of the rule "when *ca* and others are elided, it is optional."
He is born with a skillful mind as the embryo of the one who has been transformed; he was deposited by Yama in the past.
Being young, they two first brought him forth; he who was placed in the house did not neglect this birth.

With a skillful mind he is born; is he not the embryo of Cosmic Order deposited with Yama? As two youths, they first brought him to birth; he is established in the house, his origin is not hidden. ||5||
He describes the manifestation of the moon and the sun at dawn:
"Together with the mind increased by the right [side], he is born from the earth;
he is born perfectly."
Likewise, he is the embryo of *ṛta*, that is, of water, worthy of being called an embryo; or rather,
he is the embryo within the midst of the sacrifice of truth, worthy of being called an embryo— namely, man.
That very Soma which is beyond, on the far side in the intermediate space, deposited by Yama through self-restraint along with the gods—
that [Soma] becomes rain from the sun.
Therefore, the meaning is that Soma exists as being of the nature of the sun.
Thus, the word *yūnā* is used with the restrictive particle *ha*;
it means that those two, being indeed young, first became manifest at the time of their birth. Then, this one is specifically known as Soma and this one as Sūrya.
Of these two, one half is the birth; it is hidden, placed within the cave.
Of those two, the other half is said to be manifest:
the sun appears by day and the moon by night.
The wise have discerned the form of the mild one, when the falcon brought the plant from afar.
They purified him, the one easy to slay; they have driven away the eager fury that pursues the wild beast.
1. The accent of *ga-na-bha* is abhyasta; the accent of *ta4.5* is abhyasta.
2. [The accent] of *ta4-bhara2.7* belongs to the root *vāj-*.
3. *bha6-ca* does not exist.

The wise have discerned the form of the low-toned one, when the falcon brought the plant from afar. They purified him, the well-increasing one, in the rivers—the yearning stalk who moves about, worthy of praise. (6)
The wise ones, the prudent and vigilant, have discovered—that is, they know—the form of that exhilarating Soma.
That which is the bond, the food characterized by Soma, the falcon, whose form is the Gāyatrī, brought from afar—from the distant world of heaven.
(The substitution of *bh* for *h* occurs according to the rule: *hrasvād bhakṣaś chandasi*).

The officiating priests cleanse or adorn the Soma—referred to as *vaṃśu*, which is "well-increasing" (*suvṛdhaḥ*), meaning either growing excellently or causing excellent growth—within the "rivers" (*nadīṣu*), that is, within the waters known as *vasatīvarī*. Of what kind [is he]? He is being purified.
They cleanse Soma—the one who desires the gods, who moves about, who goes everywhere, and who is worthy of praise through hymns.
The ten young women cleanse you, the pressed Soma, who have been established by the seers with prayers and meditations;
through the woolly filters and the invocations of the gods, you, being guided by the men, bestow strength for our gain.

The ten young women cleanse you, the pressed Soma, with the seers’ prayers, thoughts, and insights; thus, directed by the men who invoke the gods through the sheep’s wool filters, you strike out for the prize to win it.

O Soma, you who are most vigorous, the ten fingers—produced by dividing [the hands] with both hands—are purifying you with prayers (matis), with hymns (dhitibhis), with actions (karmabhis), and with the non-hairy strainers (avivālais pavitrais)—you who have been pressed, poured out, and placed within the vessels by the seers (ṛṣibhis) such as Madhucchandas and others. They cleanse you.

Furthermore, by the *vṛta*—the men who are leaders of the ritual, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) engaged in the invocation of the gods (*devahūti*)—you are restrained and gathered within the vessels (*graha*). For the sake of winning (*sātaye*) or for the granting (*dānāya*), you rain down (*varṣi*) strength (*vāja*) or food;
that is to say, you burst it open, you make it manifest, and you bestow food and other such things upon the singers of praise.
The wise have celebrated with hymns the Soma as he flows forth, the well-seated bird-like one;
he who, with his honeyed wave, sends forth his voice from heaven like a mortal guardian of wealth.

The wise have celebrated with hymns Vāyu as he moves around, the one who sits well together, the Soma; he who, immortal guardian of wealth, sends forth his voice from heaven with a honeyed wave in a stream. 8.

The inspired hymns (*manīṣāḥ*)—the praises (*stavaḥ*)—have celebrated, that is, they extol, Soma as he proceeds with his vessels full, being prepared by the priests, desired by the gods, possessing a beautiful seat, and as the lord of the mind. [Note:
*vayyam* is derived from the root *vi* in the sense of "going" etc., with the suffix *yat*, and is a Vedic form established by Pāṇini 6.1.83.]
In this instance, there is also an irregular formation (*nipātana*) even for a word that is not a prefix.

*Madhumān* means "possessing honey," i.e., possessing the intoxicating juice. That *soma*, with its own *dhārā*—that is, with the wave-like water known as *vasatīvarī*—falls from *divaḥ*, the sky, into the *droṇakalaśa*. *Riṣipāt* means "the overcomer of the wealth of enemies. *Amartyaḥ* means "immortal," being devoid of human limitations. That *soma* *vācam iyarti*, it impels the voice; for at that time, the singers offer praise.
This Soma, being purified, sends forth everything from heaven through the entire mid-air and settles in the jars;
he is cleansed by the stones and with milk. Pressed by the stones and being purified, the drop finds the dear source of wide space.
