This one speeds forth from heaven across the entire mid-air; Soma, being purified, settles in the jars. He is cleansed with stones and with milk; pressed by the stones, the drop, being purified, shall find wide space and what is dear. 9.
We, as Soma, from the sky— the world of light— drive open every stall; that is,
we cause all the water to flow forth and extend everywhere.
Furthermore, being purified by the *daśāpavitra* filter, Soma settles within the jars known as *droṇa*.
Likewise, he is cleansed, refined, and adorned by the pressing-stones (*grāvan*), by the *vasatīvarī* waters, and by the "cows"—that is, the products of the cow such as milk, curds, and so forth.
Then, being purified and becoming a drop, Soma finds for the singers desirable wealth (*varivaḥ*)—wealth that is most dear and brings delight.
That is to say, it bestows [it].
Thus, O Soma, as you are being poured out, bestow upon us manifold and wondrous vitality; while flowing clear, purify yourself.
We invoke the benevolent Heaven and Earth; O gods, grant us wealth accompanied by heroic sons.
Thus, O Soma, being poured out, bestowing most wonderful vitality, flow on. We invoke the benevolent Heaven and Earth. O gods, grant us wealth accompanied by heroic sons. 10.
This is performed through direct perception.

O Soma, bestowing—that is, granting—while being poured out on all sides by the stones (*adri*), do thou *pavasva*, i.e., cause to flow, *vayaḥ*—food—which is most wonderful (*citratama*), that is, variegated or most worthy of being sought after (*cāyanīyatama*), *naḥ*, for us;
that is to say, grant it to us.

Furthermore, O you two who are free from hatred, we invoke Heaven and Earth for the purpose of offering oblations. O gods, bestow upon us wealth consisting of heroic sons— sons who are capable in their duties—
and place such riches within us.
‘Ipurna’: this second hymn consists of ten verses; it is the seer’s work of Hiraṇyastūpa Āṅgirasa, dedicated to the deity Pavamāna Soma.
The ninth and tenth verses are Triṣṭubhs;
the remaining verses are Jagatīs.
And thus it has been introduced: “*Iṣur na hiraṇyastūpaḥ* and *anyaiḥ* are two Triṣṭubh verses.
The application [of the verses] has been explained.
Like an arrow is fixed upon the bow, like a calf is let loose toward its mother, so is the prayer directed toward the head [of the sacrifice].
Like a wide-streaming cow, O Agni, she yields her milk; under his ordinances, Soma is impelled.

The arrow is not fixed upon the bow; the prayer has been released like a calf toward its mothers at the udder. Like one yielding a broad stream, O Agni, Soma is impelled toward his observances as he approaches.
In this Indra, whose form is Pavamāna, our meditative praise—the thought worthy of reflection—is placed or deposited by us;
*dadhāti* is the verbal root used here.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

Just as a well-feathered arrow is fixed upon a bow by the archer, so too is the Soma released by us for exhilaration into Indra, who stands at the head of all as the nourisher and sustainer. How is this done? [As follows:]...
Like a calf at the udder of its mother cow—which holds the milk—as it is released for the sake of drinking milk, even so [Indra];

like a cow yielding various streams of milk, as she moves forward before us, he yields milk; in that same way, this Indra, moving ahead of these worshippers who have become like calves, yields manifold desires. Furthermore, even within the ritual acts (*vrata*) of such a one, Soma is indeed poured out by the sacrificers.
1. Bha: *iyarti*. 2. Ga, Ta, Bha: *evam*; Mu: *eva evam*. 3. In Ga, Ta, 1.2.5.6, and Bha, 1.4.6, the word "citratamam" is absent. 4. In Ta, 1.2.4.5.6: *hiraṇyastūpote*.
The thought is joined; the honey is poured out; the sweet-sounding tongue is urged within the mouth.
Being purified, like a slayer with a continuous line, the honeyed drop flows through the filter.

"Upoṃ!"—the thought is joined; the honey is poured. The sweet-sounding tongue stirs within the mouth. Being purified, like a jointed reed, the honey-rich drop flows through the filter like one who strikes down his enemies. || 2 ||
In this Indra, whose form is Pavamāna, the prayer—the hymn of praise—is joined, is closely united, and is brought into connection by the worshippers;
[the root] *pṛc* means "to join.
Likewise, the honey—Soma, which causes exhilaration—is poured for the sake of Indra; it becomes sprinkled with water and with barley-flour.
And thus, *mandrājanī*: this is the form derived from the root *aja* (meaning "to move" or "to impel") with the suffix *lyuṭ* and the feminine suffix *ḍīp*.
She is the impeller of the exhilarating juice—the stream of Soma—and she is impelled within the mouth (*āsani*, i.e., the face) of that Indra by means of the pressing-sticks (*codate*).
The word *āsya* undergoes a modification of its action (*āsankriyādeśa*) by [the rule] beginning with *padmromās*.

Furthermore, the *saṃtaniḥ*—the Soma who is well-spread among the *prahādi* vessels, who is honeyed (*madhumān*), possessing intoxicating juice, and who is being purified (*pavamānaḥ*)—being a drop (*drapsaḥ*) characterized by swift motion, or rather, characterized by swift destruction, flows around (*arpati*) the *vāra*, the woolen filter that has no gaps.
Therein lies the illustration.
Like a continuous stream of arrows discharged by excellent slayers and warriors, which, once released, travels swiftly toward its target from all sides, so it was.
The unaging one, seeking a bride, has been bound upon the mountain; the daughter of Aditi binds herself for him who goes toward the Truth.
The golden-hued, worshipful, well-restrained exhilaration has ascended; sharpening his manly powers, he shines like a mighty bull.

The unaging one flows; the life of the bridegroom purifies itself. Around you, the granddaughters of Aditi spread the garment as you proceed toward the *ṛta*. The golden-hued, worshipful, well-restrained exhilaration has leaped forth; sharpening his manly powers, he shines like a buffalo. 3.
*Vadhūyuḥ*:
the waters that have become the bride (*vadhū*), accompanied by the *vasatīvarī* and *ekadhana* waters;
Soma, possessing those, flows around—that is, revolves or becomes purified—upon the sheepskin (*avyai tvaci*), his own natural covering.
Furthermore, "nasīr naptrīḥ":
the word *naptr* denotes a fourth-generation descendant;
thus, "the granddaughters of Soma."
For Soma pours forth seed at the forefront of the plants;
according to the Śruti: "The seed of Prajāpati is the gods; the seed of the gods is rain; the seed of rain is the plants" (Ai.
Ā. 2.1.3). Or else:
The word *naptṛ* signifies offspring;
[the phrase] "their offspring" refers to those.
Soma causes the plants to grow with his own nectar-filled rays.
Therefore, they are her offspring.
Of Aditi;
this is a name for the earth.

The herbs produced from the undepressed earth, being the *ṛta*— the sacrifice whose form is truth— separate the fruit-bearing [plants] for the sake of the sacrificer who goes toward the sacrifice and is unremitting at its forefront.

Furthermore, the golden-hued (*hari*) one, worthy of worship (*yajataḥ*) by all and therefore restrained (*saṃyataḥ*) among the gods such as Prahlāda— the exhilarating drink (*madaḥ*), that is, Soma— such as he, has stepped forth (*akrān*).
It remains in the vessels;
or rather,
it overcomes the enemies.

In the case of *śrameluṅi tipi*, because of the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is an absence of the augment *huṭ*. When *dhau* has been substituted and the *s* of *sip* is elided, the *tip* is dropped by the rule *halṅyādi*. Then, when *natva* is applied by the rule *mo no dhātoḥ*, the form is established. For this very reason, [the text says] *somaḥ nṛmṇā svabalāni śiśānaḥ*, meaning sharpening his own powers;
or alternatively, making the forces of the enemies thin.
"Like a buffalo"—this [word] belongs to the *mahan* [class]. He shines with his own splendor as if great, as if pervading everywhere; he blazes everywhere.
Alternatively,
*naḥ* is used in the sense of inclusion (*saṃgraha*):
"Now this great Soma, endowed with such qualities, shines."

The bull, the shedder of seed, the vigorous one, bellows loudly from the front;
"mā" is used in the sense of measuring and sounding.
The milch-cows, the female cattle, follow after that bull.
Thus, they approach—that is, they go toward—the prepared and consecrated place of the shining god;
by this meaning, a praise of Soma is also expressed.
Being Soma, he makes a sound at the time of approaching the *droṇa*-vessel.
Following him, the milch-cows—the hymns of praise—move about, desiring to please; the hymns of praise go toward the station of the god.
Likewise, this Soma has passed through, or is passing through, the *vāra*—the white-colored, unchanging, woolen filter made of sheep’s wool.
Having passed through it, he goes to the vessels; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, Soma, like his own armor (*atka*), has clothed himself all around with the bright *nikka*—the substance used for mixing—which completely envelops him.

With his unsoiled, radiant garment, the golden-hued immortal, adorning himself, has clothed himself all around. With his expansive, shining robe, he has made the back of heaven his couch, as worthy of honor as the Soma-vessel in the sky. With his expansive, shining robe, he has made the back of heaven his couch, as worthy of honor as the Soma-vessel in the sky.

The immortal one, free from human attributes, Hari, who is green-hued Soma, being purified by water (*nirṇijānaḥ*), clothes himself (*pari vyata*) all around with an unsoiled (*amṛktena*)— the root *mṛj* meaning "purification and adornment"—
and even with an unstained (*aniśrktena*), naturally white-colored garment in the form of milk (*payas*). He completely envelops himself.
Some indeed mix it with purified cow's milk;
that is what is said.

Then this Soma, standing upon the back—that is, on the upper part—of *divaḥ* (the heavenly world), performed purification (*nirṇije*) for the sake of cleansing (*nirnejanāya*), which is to say, for the sake of purifying (*paripavanāya*), for the sake of the uprooting (*barhaṇāya*) of evil—that is, for the destroyer of sin (*pāpanāśine*). He performed this in the heavenly world (*dyuloke*).
For he indeed purifies everything by his own radiance.
[Regarding the form] *akṛta*: it is from the root *kṛ* in the *luṅ* tense; there is the elision of *sic* according to the rule "after a short vowel."
That very [is the case] for the two *camū*s; this is the name of Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*).

3. According to Ga, Soma is the one who pours out desire (kāmasektā).
4. Not produced from cow-products. 5. The substance for boiling (ga-bha4: *śravaṇadravya*; ta4: *aryaṇadravya*; ta5: *ayaṇadravya*; bha6: *śrapaṇadravya*). 6.
For the one who is purifying (ta-bha1.2.4.7: *paripavamānāya*).
7. For one who is cleansing oneself (ta3-bha2); for one who is about to cleanse oneself (ta7); for one who is being cleansed (bha1.7).

The rays of the Sun—the impeller, the possessor of great heroism, the Āditya—are like rays that illuminate everywhere; they are flowing forth, having the nature of moving everywhere; they are exhilarating, providing intoxication; they are slumber-inducing, causing enemies to sleep, and are destroyers; they are swift, pervading the cups and the chalices; and these effusions, the Somas being poured out, go around simultaneously, together with the extended thread, as if with a cloth woven from threads.
These Soma juices do not flow toward, nor do they go to, any other *dhāman*—that is, any other divine body (*deva-śarīra*)—except for Indra. The singular number is Vedic;
[in the plural] they do not go.
They go toward the very abode of Kṛśānu;
that the sacrificial post is the abode of Indra is understood from the wording of the mantra: "He has gone to the dear abodes of Indra" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 21.47).
Like swift waters rushing down a slope toward the depths, the Madras, impelled by the Bull, have found their path.
May there be well-being for our bipeds and quadrupeds in our dwelling; O Soma, may strength and prosperity abide with us and our people.

Like swift waters rushing down a slope into a valley, the Madras, impelled by the Bull, have found their path. May there be peace for our two-footed and four-footed creatures in their dwellings; O Soma, may strengths and subjects abide with us. 7.
*Vṛṣacyutāḥ*:
[The Soma drops] have been poured forth by the *vṛṣa*s—[the word *vṛṣa* being used here] also in the senses of "injuring," "afflicting," and "giving.

By the *vṛṣa*s, the givers of Soma, the *vibhiḥ* (the active ones), these *madrāsaḥ*, the intoxicating Soma juices that have flowed forth (*parisrutāḥ*), have reached (*āśata*) and obtained (*prāṃsadhyai*) a path (*gātuṃ*) of movement toward Indra through our hymns of praise.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like the slope of a river.
That which water flows down toward is called a "slope" (*pravaṇa*).
Just as the swift waters of the river Sindhu flow across that low-lying ground, so [should you].
Now, it is directly perceived:
O Soma, in our dwelling—whether upon entering our own home or departing—grant well-being (*śam*) to our bipeds, such as sons and others, and to our quadrupeds, such as cattle and other livestock.
Furthermore, O Soma, may *vājāḥ*—foods—and *kṛṣṭyaḥ*, offspring such as sons and so forth, abide within us (*asme*).
The meaning is: "Grant us food and the like."
Flow for us with wealth, O golden one, increasing our horses and granting us strength and heroic power;
for you, O Soma, are my fathers, the heads of heaven, established as the makers of vitality.

Flow for us with wealth, with gold, with horses, with cattle, with barley, and with great heroic power. For you, O Soma, are my fathers, set forth as the heads of heaven, the makers of vital strength. 8.

O Soma, you—endowed with wealth (*vasu*), accompanied by gold (*hiraṇyavat*), possessed of horses (*aśvavat*), accompanied by cattle (*gomat*), and possessing barley (*yavamat*)—[that is,] barley being a specific kind of grain;
[grant us] wealth distinguished by grain, endowed with excellent vigor (*suvīrya*); O Pavamāna, flow toward us and bring it to us.
"Grant [it]," so much is meant.
Furthermore, O Soma, since you are the father even of my fathers, the Aṅgirases, therefore you yourselves become my fathers in this way.
Here, the plurality of "fathers" refers to Soma.
Of what sort are they? They are the "heads" (mūrdhānaḥ) of heaven (divaḥ), that is, those who stand at the summit of the celestial world.
The meaning is that through their ritual acts (karmabhiḥ), they obtain the heavenly realm and other such rewards.
Those who have set out and remain always engaged in performing their duties, the makers of this oblation-form—such are my fathers; you become that.

1. They go to the six bhūs. 2. They go to the *u*. 3. To the son. 4. And to the cattle for the sake of support. 5. Food and so forth, and cattle and so forth. 6. Yoked with oxen and horses; or yoked with horses. 7. You are the sovereign lord of the Bhṛgus.

These Soma juices, being pressed, have sped forth toward Indra like chariots toward booty; once pressed, they pass through the sheep’s-wool filter, casting off the residue, while the tawny ones rush toward the rain. 9. These | Somas | being pressed | toward Indra | like chariots | have sped forth | toward booty; | pressed | they pass through | the filter | made of sheep's wool; | casting off | the dregs, | the tawny ones | toward the rain. 9.

Being purified by the filter while being cleansed, these Soma juices of ours have gone forth toward Indra—who is to be honored (*sāti*) by all; [the root] *ṣaṇ* means "to share in" or "to honor," and the suffix *ktin* is used here in the sense of the object. They go forth pre-eminently. In this regard, there is a simile: like chariots. Just as Indra’s chariots go toward *sāti*—[the word] *sāti* is derived from the root *sī* meaning "to end" or "to conclude," and is formed as a nipātana according to the rule beginning with *ūti-yūti*; that in which one sits or is engaged is *sāti*, namely, battle—they go forth toward that, even so. Furthermore, the pressed Somas, extracted by the pressing-stones, pass across and go beyond the filter that has become wide-spreading. These are the golden ones (*harita*).
The cows, the *dhenavaḥ*, who are sources of delight, yield the *āśiram*—the means for mixing, such as milk—which is *satyām*, that is, real and corresponding to its purpose.
Or rather:
twelve months, five seasons, these worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first—by all these together, milk is produced within the cows; it is those [cows] which yield that milk.

Furthermore, this Soma has made for himself four other beautiful and auspicious waters—namely, the *vasatīvarī* waters and the three *ekadhana* waters—for the purpose of cleansing, purifying, or nourishing.
When does he do so?
He does so at the very moment when he has strengthened himself through the *ṛta*, the sacrifices.
Seeking the lovely nectar of immortality, he has separated both heaven and earth by his poetic wisdom.
With majesty, he has spread himself across the most brilliant waters when they recognized his seat through the glory of the god.

He, begging for the beautiful nectar, has with his poetic wisdom separated both heaven and earth; he has encompassed the most brilliant waters with his greatness when they recognized the seat of the god through his glory.
That *pavamāna* [is the giver] of the beautiful, auspicious, immortal water.
Since it is stated that "the mention of the action [in the rule for the recipient] must be made," the object (*karman*) receives the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.62: "The genitive is used diversely in the sense of the dative."

When the sage Cārudaka was being entreated by the sacrificers, he caused both Heaven and Earth to be separated by means of his poetic power (*kāvyena*), that is, through his work as a seer (*kavikarmaṇā*);
the meaning is that he filled them with water for the sake of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, with his great roar (*maṃhanā*), he completely enveloped the most brilliant waters for the purpose of containing them.

When the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), being endowed with fame and the oblation (*śravasā haviṣā yuktaḥ*), know— that is, they understand and obtain— the seat (*sadaḥ*) or place of the shining god Soma for the sake of the sacrifice, then [the sun] encompasses it from all sides. In the root *vid* (to know),
the substitution of *jhi* by *jhas* occurs according to the rule *sijabhyasta*.
May those rays of his be immortal and inviolable, following both generations,
by which they purify both human and divine powers, and then the sages seized him as their king.
May his rays be immortal and invincible, following both races of beings—by means of which they purify both human and divine powers; then indeed, the wise ones seized him as their King.

The rays (*ketavaḥ*) of this such Soma— the indicators, all worthy of refuge, immortal (*amṛtyavaḥ*), and therefore invincible (*adābhyāsaḥ*) [the suffix *ṇyat* being applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.124.3]— those rays, which cannot be harmed by others, may they protect both births (*januṣī*), the two states consisting of the stationary and the moving, having taken them as their mark.
This Soma drinks the seed of the plants at the sacrifice, and indeed the streams of men flow forth.
By whatever banners he impels heroic powers, heroic powers, divine gifts, and acts of wisdom, immediately after the pressing, the wise hymns have seized King Soma—they encompass him;
that is to say, they reach him.
The letter *bha* [is substituted] by the rule "hagrahoḥ°."
1. ta2-bhara.6-yathārthabhūtaṃ; bhā1.7-yathārtha bhūtaṃ | 2. ga-ta3-bhā1.7-paripoṣanāya vā does not exist | 3. ta3-bhā1.2.5.7-vipnute |
4. In the *ga* and *ta-bhara.4.6* [recensions], by means of the sacrifice (*yajña*) as the cause; in the *bhā1* [recension], by means of the sacrifice as the cause.
5. In the *ga* [recension], with nectar-water (*amṛtodaka*); in the *ta-bhara.4.6* [recensions], with life-sustaining water (*prāṇodaka*).
6. In the *bha6* [recension], it is radiant (*dīptā*).

7. ta1.4—*ṛrjusādeśaḥ*; tara.6—*ṛrjusādeśaḥ*; ta5—*harjusādeśaḥ*; bha6—*matubādeśaḥ*. 8. ga-ta-bhā1.2.4.6—at the beginning of the names of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhīnām agre*). 9. ta-bha6—those worthy of the Goddess (*devyārhāṇi*).

Being cleansed by the ten skillful workers, he shines forth among the middle mothers; drinking all the laws of the lovely nectar, the observer of men looks upon both races. He, being cleansed by the ten skillful workers, shines forth among the middle mothers; drinking all the laws of the lovely nectar, the observer of men looks upon both races.

Being purified by the ten fingers—those endowed with beautiful actions—that Pavamāna, accompanied by [the verses] beginning with "He has reached the oblation in Agni," stands within the middle regions situated in the atmosphere, in order to measure the worlds.

Prame: From the root *mā* preceded by *pra*, with the suffix *kvip* and the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs due to the rule "ātaḥ" being split off as a separate yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*).

Furthermore, the purifying one (*pavamāna*), who beholds men (*vṛścakṣas*), the beautiful one, while protecting the ordinances (*vrata*)—namely the sacrificial acts such as the *yajña* for the sake of the auspicious immortal water (*amṛta*)—beholds both worlds, the humans and the gods, as he moves through the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
He looks upon humans by granting their desires and upon the gods by the offering of oblations (*havis*).

Being cleansed for the sake of his power and for nourishment, he, being established between both worlds, rejoices. As a bull, with his vigor, he drives away the malevolent ones, pointing them out like arrows at the spoils. He, being cleansed, for the sake of his power and for nourishment, rejoices, established between both heaven and earth. As a bull, with his vigor, he drives away the evil-minded ones, aiming them like arrows at the prizes.

Being cleansed by the filter, being purified— that Pavamāna, for the sake of sustenance (*dhāyase*)— that is, for the support of the world (*jagataḥ*), for the sake of sensory power (*indriyāya*), and for the sake of Indra’s sufficient strength (*balāya*)— he,
situated between both worlds (*ubhe rodasī*) [the accusative case is used here according to Pāṇini 2.3.5],
existing in the midst of both heaven and earth, exults and moves everywhere.
For Indra's strength indeed arises from Soma.

He is a bull (*vṛṣan*), a showerer of desires or of waters; he, by means of his *vśuṣma*—his drying or consuming power—*vi bādhate*, that is, he especially oppresses the *durmatīḥ*, the evil-minded Asuras. What is he doing?
*Vśurudhaḥ*:
they obstruct others with pain (*śucā*);
it belongs to the *pupodarādi* group [of irregular formations].
Addressing the Asuras who have acted wickedly, he calls them again and again and slays them.
Therein is an illustration:
"as one might drive away a dog."
Just as a heroic slayer destroys his adversaries with arrows that are the means of killing, so too [does he act].

He, not seeing his mother, did not bellow like a bull; he went forth with a sound like that of the Maruts. Knowing the primordial *ṛta*, the one of excellent wisdom chose the celestial hero for the sake of praise. He, not seeing his mother, did not bellow like a bull; he went forth with a sound like that of the Maruts. Knowing the primordial *ṛta*, the one of excellent wisdom chose the celestial hero for the sake of praise. 6.

Pavamāna, beholding his two mothers, Heaven and Earth, again and again, roars loudly from there and goes everywhere. Regarding this, there is an illustration: like a calf (*vatso na*), for *ustrī* is a name for a cow; just as a calf, seeing its mother cow, makes a sound, so it is. Furthermore, like the host of Maruts—*marutām iva svanaḥ*; the suffix *-ya* is added after the root *svan*—just as the host of Maruts goes everywhere making a roar, so it is. He [goes] toward the water, the celestial light (*svarṇaram*). *Svarita*.
1. *ga-ta3.4-bha5.6-mṛjyamānaḥ* means being cleansed or purified. 2. *ta-bha6-paśyan* means seeing. 3. *ta-bhara.6-ā harṣati*; *bha1.7-ārṣati* means he rejoices.
This is the complete method.
It brings benefit to all human beings;
for all humans gather at the water because it serves their purpose.

Knowing that such a first, primary *ṛta*—which is water—the wise one, the performer of good deeds (*sukṛta*), or the one of excellent insight, that Pavamāna chose for his own praise—that is, for the purpose of composing a hymn of praise—which man? He favored him;
the meaning is: "none other than us."
The formidable bull bellows with his mighty strength, sharpening his horns as he gazes far and wide.
Soma settles into his well-fashioned seat; his skin becomes a cow-hide, his covering a goat-skin.

He roars; he is the terrible bull, sharpening his two horns with great power. Far-sighted, the golden-hued Soma settles into his well-fashioned womb. His skin becomes cowhide, and his woolly garment is made of sheep’s wool. 7.

Bhīma is the one who causes fear to enemies; Vṛṣabha is the showerer of desires or of waters; Vicakṣaṇa is one whose nature is to discern everything. That Pavamāna [is called] *taviṣyā*, where *tu* has the sense of increase (*vṛddhi*).
From this [root], by the rule *aca haḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.138), the suffix *i* is applied;
from that, the suffix *kyac* is added in the sense of intense desire.

The augment *suk* is added according to the rule *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.51). By his own will and power, sharpening—that is, making sharp—the two antelope-like horns which are green in color, he draws the *āgrayaṇa* from the vessel into the *droṇakalaśa* by means of two streams.
This is what is being described.
He bellows—that is, he makes a sound—while sharpening his horns on the mountain ridges.
[The root] *ru* means "to sound.
The suffix *śa* is applied according to the rule: "In the Vedic language, [suffixes are] frequently [applied]."
Then that Soma settles down—that is, it stands all around—in its well-made, well-prepared womb, its own place, the *droṇakalaśa*.
The *nirṇij* (the cleansing cloth) of that Soma becomes a cowhide—that is, made of cow-dung—as a purifier;
for the pressing of the Soma takes place upon a bull's hide.
In this way, the skin becomes free from impurities and free from hair;
for that has been stated with reference to the *daśāpavitra* (the fringe filter).
Pure and purifying his body, he has clothed himself in a tawny robe upon the back of the sheepskin;
acceptable to Mitra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu, the threefold honey is prepared by skillful workers.

Pure, purifying his stainless body, the golden-hued one has flowed down upon the sheep’s fleece. Acceptable to Mitra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu, the honeyed juice is prepared in three portions by those of skillful deeds.
"Free from blemish" means devoid of evil;
or alternatively,
[it derives] from the root *rip* "to go."
"Without motion" means staying in the vessel.

Purifying—that is, cleansing—his own body which is such, the Soma, who is therefore pure (*śuci*), purified, or radiant, and who is "harit-colored" (*hari*), has been poured down upon the high ridge (*sānavi*), upon the elevated sheep's-wool filter (*avye*) made of *avika* wool; he is deposited there by the officiating priests.
The root *dhruj* means "to shake.

According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.4.62, *syasicsīyutāsiṣu*, there is the augment *iṭ* as if it were *ciṇ* in the *luṅ* tense in the passive voice; furthermore, due to the presence of the *ṇic* suffix, there is vṛddhi.

Then, for Mitra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu—pleasing and sufficient for these—the three-layered Soma, distributed in three ways and mixed twice with milk from the *vasatīvarī* waters, such honey-like, intoxicating Soma is prepared by the priests endowed with beautiful rites and offered for the sake of the gods beginning with Mitra.
O Soma, at the joints [of the sacrifice], enter the heart of Indra, the bull, the receptacle of Soma, for the banquet of the gods.
Before the distress reaches us, carry us across the wide expanse. As one who knows the field, point out the directions to him who asks.

Flow forth, O Soma, for the feast of the gods! As a bull, enter the heart of Indra, the vessel that holds the Soma. Before we are overcome by distress, carry us across to safety. For he who knows the land has declared the directions to the one who asks. 9.

O Soma, you who are the bull—the sprinkler of desires or of waters—flow for the feast of the gods; that is, pour yourself out into the jars and other vessels. Now, O Soma, you are the heart-pleasing, beloved vessel of Indra, the "Soma-holder" (somadhāna)—so called because the Soma is deposited within it.
Therefore, enter into that;
furthermore, before our affliction—that is, before the torment and oppression—carry us across the difficulties, leading us beyond the demons that are hard to traverse.
Moreover, a man who knows the land and is familiar with the way indeed tells the directions—the paths—to the person who asks variously about the road.
Having spoken thus, he who knows the path of sacrifice said, "Protect us by explaining the way of sacrifice to us, so that we may be preserved."

Like a man [pouring] clarified butter, flow toward the prize, O Indu; as the *Ṛbhu*, flow into the belly of Indra. Like one crossing a river with a boat, do thou, the knowing one, carry us across; like a hero fighting, protect us from our enemies. 10. Like a man [pouring] clarified butter, flow toward the prize, O *Ṛbhu*; O Indu, flow into the belly of Indra. Like one crossing a river with a boat, do thou, the knowing one, carry us across; like a hero fighting, protect us from our enemies. 10.
O Soma, being impelled by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), go toward the *droṇakalaśa*, the vessel that is the repository of the Soma, for the sake of the prize (*vāja*).
Therein lies the illustration:
like a well-placed arrow.

Just as a well-trained horse, being urged forward, gallops toward the prize— the battle— so too, O Indu, flow into the belly of Indra, that is, enter the *droṇakalaśa* vessel. Furthermore, knowing all things, carry us across, leading us beyond all misfortunes.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"not by a boat.
Just as boatmen ferry people across the *sindhu*, the river, by means of a boat, so it is here.
Furthermore, O Soma, like a hero (*śūra*)—that is, like a warrior (*vīra*) fighting and striking down enemies—protect us from reproach (*nidaḥ*), that is, from the reviler who is our enemy;
deliver us from harm, destroy our affliction, and preserve us.
Or alternatively: [the verse continues...]
"O Spṛ, destroy our revilers, our enemies; strike them down with their faces turned downward.
The root *spṛ* is used here in the sense of "to injure.
The suffix *kṣā* is elided according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73).
By the rule "halṅyādi," there is the elision (lopa) of the suffix *tip*.
The fourth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "ā dakṣiṇā," belongs to the seer Vaiśvāmitra; its deity is Pavamāna Soma.
The ninth verse is a Triṣṭubh, while the remaining verses are Jagatīs.
Thus it has been enumerated: "ā dakṣiṇā [nine]; these two [hymns] belong to the descendant of Viśvāmitra."
By the word “those two,” the previously mentioned Reṇu and Ṛṣabha are referred to.
For it is heard in scripture: “Then Viśvāmitra addressed his sons: ‘Madhucchandas, listen! Ṛṣabha, Reṇu, Ṣṭaka! (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.17).
Thus ends the application of the hymns.

The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is bestowed; the impetuous one seeks his seat. The watchful one protects against the malevolent demon. The tawny one makes the sky his head-ornament; he spreads the waters as a covering for the golden-hued one, and the sacred prayer (brahman) serves as his mantle. 1. The sacrificial fee is released; the vigorous one goes to his seat. The wakeful one guards against the malicious demon. The tawny one makes the sky his crest-ornament; the waters are spread beneath him for the golden-hued one, and the sacred prayer serves as his mantle.

In the sacrifice which is Soma’s own domain, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is released—that is, it is bestowed by us—upon the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The powerful (*śuṣmī*) Soma goes to, that is, enters, his seat (*āsadam*), the vessel called the *droṇa*.
Furthermore, the watchful (*jāgṛvi*) Soma protects the singers from the harmful (*duhaḥ*) *rākṣasa*.
Moreover, *hariḥ* (the golden) Soma is *haritavarṇaḥ* (golden-colored). He is *opaśaḥ*: one who lies down (*upaśete*) everywhere; thus he is *opaśaḥ*.
He makes *nabhaḥ payaḥ*—the water that is the very nature of *nabhas*, the sun—the sustainer of all; he produces it everywhere.
The meaning is that he acts according to the sequence beginning with "The oblation cast into the fire...
Alternatively,
*nabhaḥ* refers to the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*), and *payaḥ* refers to milk.
"He makes it a holder.
Furthermore, this *soma* is [contained] in the two "bowls" (*camvoḥ*); this is a name for heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*).
Human beings and gods "camanti" (sip) or consume [the offerings] here.

For those two, he makes the "brahma"—the great, shining [sun] which destroys the darkness, or rather, the sovereign [sun]—into a "upastara," that is, for the purpose of spreading out or covering [them].
Likewise, he makes that very sun into a "nirninaja," for the purpose of washing away or purifying all things.
For the sun indeed overspreads heaven and earth with his own splendor;
he indeed purifies everything with his own light.
Like a plowman at the furrow, he goes forth bellowing; he sheds his dark, asuric hue. He leaves behind the covering of his father and, having gone forth, prepares his bright garment for the journey.

Like a ploughman who strikes the earth, he goes forth bellowing; he casts off his asuric color. He leaves that behind and goes to his father’s appointed place; the swift one makes for himself a path of easy passage.
The powerful Soma, the witherer of enemies, roaring—that is, making an intense sound—goes forth like a warrior who slays men;
moreover, he releases—that is, causes to flow out—the *asurya*, the power or green-hued covering belonging to himself which obstructs the Asuras.
Then that Soma [reaches] Vatri.
It is called *jarā* (old age) because it envelops (*vṛṇoti*) the body. It "leaves" (*jahāti*), that is, it abandons [the body].
If one asks how this is so, it is explained as follows:
Soma goes now to his father’s food, to the prepared and refined *droṇakalaśa* vessel, or indeed to heaven.
Furthermore, Soma has poured himself out into the *daśāpavitra* filter, which is extended and renowned as a means of protection.
*Ninija* is a name for form.
He makes his own form *upaprataṃ*, meaning "having the nature of approaching";
the sense is that he therefore abandons old age.
Pressed by the stones, he flows; within the two hands, the bull exerts himself; through the manly power, he trembles with the prayer.
He rejoices, he breathes, he unites with the song; he cleanses himself in the waters and is honored in the surrounding vessel.

Pressed by the stones, he flows from the two hands; as a bull, he displays his vigor through his manly power. He trembles with inspired thought; he rejoices like one who possesses wealth, responding to the song. He is cleansed in the waters and is sacrificed in the circling vessel.
Pressed out by the stones with the hands—that is, from the two arms—and poured forth, that Soma flows toward the vessels.
That Soma acts like a bull (*vṛṣāyate*);
moreover, being stirred by the hymn (*matī*) and shaking through the atmosphere (*nabhasā*), he goes everywhere; that Soma rejoices and becomes glad.
Likewise, he *nasate*, meaning he becomes closely united with the vessels and other implements.
Furthermore, being praised by *girā*—that is, by hymns of praise—he *sādhate*, meaning he procures for the worshippers wealth, food, and the like.
Moreover, he *ninikte*, meaning he becomes purified, within the *apsu*—the desirable waters.
Then, in that divine rite which is being measured out, or in that sacrifice which nourishes through the offering of oblations to the gods, he who sacrifices becomes honored.
They pour out the honeyed [draught] for him who dwells in heaven, who increases the mountains, the conqueror of the stronghold;
in whom the well-offered [oblations] are mixed upon the height, the foremost [Soma], with wide expanses.

They pour out the honeyed draught for him who dwells in heaven, who is strengthened by the mountain, the conqueror of the dwelling; in whom, upon the high back, they mix the foremost milk with wide expanses through the well-offered oblation.

O powerful one, the exhilarating Soma juices of the mighty [Indra]— who dwells in the shining world of heaven, who causes the clouds or mountains to grow, and who is the conqueror and protector of the fortress of the enemy— surround Indra. He is stirred by the prayer,
as it were, from his place of praise, like rain falling through the atmosphere.
3. [The rays] enter that which has gone forth, bearing [the oblation], and shining.

Likewise, the "well-fed" (*suhutādaḥ*)—that is, the consumers of the well-offered oblations (*suhuta*), the cows—[enter] him who stands at the head (*mūrdhan*), in the elevated place of the udder (*ūdhan*) which holds the milk. Into that Indra, who is distinguished by the quality of *pavamāna*, they pour (*ā śroṇanti*) the beloved, principal [portion] of the path with wide and great expanses.
Indeed, the skillful ones mix Soma with milk;
that is what is said.
Like a chariot urged by two drivers, he has been brought forth from the lap of Aditi by his ten sisters;
he has moved forward and wins the desirable station of the cow, which his prayers have generated for him.
Together, like two arms, the ten sisters have impelled the chariot toward the lap of Aditi. He approaches and wins the secret place of the cow, which his inspired thoughts have brought forth. ||5||
The Soma, shining like Varuṇa, is a seer (kavi) of far-reaching wisdom; he is manifest, endowed with clearly distinct streams—or alternatively: [the two bhurij meters].
Being especially sprinkled within by the *ghasatī-varīs*, he comes forth from *div*—that is, from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—turned away (*parāṅmukham*).
The meaning is that he moves away from the filter (*pavitra*) toward the *droṇakalaśa*.
He is the bull (*vṛṣā*), the stallion (*vṛṣabha*), the three-backed one (*tripṛṣṭha*).
He whose *pṛṣṭhas* (chapters) are three *savanās* (pressings) is called *tripṛṣṭha*. This is because Soma is present in all [three].
Therefore he is *tripṛṣṭha*. Soma, directed toward the hymns (*gāḥ*) being performed by the chanters, has uttered sounds;
[the root] *van* is used here in the sense of "sound."
Furthermore, he is "sahasranītiḥ," meaning one who has a thousand ways of leading;
this refers to the fact that, in view of the multiplicity of applications, there are a thousand methods of leading [the Soma] among both the cups (*graha*) and the goblets (*camasa*).
For this very reason, he is *vyati*, one who returns toward the vessels and so forth, and *parāyati*, one who goes away toward the jars (*kalaśa*).
This very [person], through many—meaning numerous—dawns; the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*.
He has not been seen during many dawn-times.
The root *rebh* means "to sound.
Resounding like a chanter, he strides forth— that is, he shines forth preeminently—
because the Soma is being pressed within them.
Indeed, the praiser shines by means of the performance of praise for the gods.
He assumes his brilliant, color-bestowing form; wherever he lies, he drives away those who attack.
Winning the waters, he goes by his own power to the divine folk; he unites with our fair praise, with that which begins with cattle.

He assumes his radiant form, worthy of praise; where he has rested, he stirs my thoughts. The winner of waters, he goes by his own power to the divine folk. He unites with our fair hymns, with the foremost of cattle.
Regarding *vasya*: in the case of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), there is the substitution of *aś*.
The color (*varṇa*) belonging to this Soma—the ray that wards off enemies—makes its form (*rūpa*) *tveṣam*, that is, shining. It brings it about.
The ray has spread across; the form has been manifested. A battle (*saṃgrāma*) is so called because it is encountered together (*samyak prāpyate*) by warriors here.
In this battle, he lies down or stands, bringing [the enemy] under his control;
in the *laṅ* tense of the root √śī, there is no elision of the suffix *śap* due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi.
In that battle, that ray (*raśmi*) is victorious; it withers the enemies or restrains them.
It means "he injures.
Because it constitutes a separate sentence, there is no *anighāta* (lack of accentuation). Furthermore, there is the repetition (*vapsā*).
The form [of the word] is derived from the root *san* with the suffix *viṭ* and the addition of *an*.
He is the giver of waters— that is, of liquids—
or rather, he is the distributor of the waters known as *vasatīvarī*.
This very [sacrifice], together with *svadhā*—that is, with food in the form of oblations (*havīṣ*)—goes forth toward the divine folk (*jana*), those belonging to the gods (*deva*).
Moreover, this very [sacrifice] comes together with *suṣṭuti*, that is, with excellent praise (*su-stuti*).
Because of the hearing of the prefix (*upa-*), the action of joining (*yoga*) is to be supplied.

Furthermore, that Soma, with that speech by which the praisers—beginning with "gavāgrayā" (with the foremost cows) and so forth—ask for cattle, with that same speech he "nasate," meaning he comes together or unites;
the root *nas* has the sense of going.
Because it constitutes a separate sentence, there is no *anighāta* (lack of accentuation).
Like a bull lowing as he circles the herds, he has bellowed; he has pierced through the firmament of the sun.
The divine eagle looks down upon the earth; Soma beholds all creatures with his wisdom.
Like a bull moving toward the herds, he has bellowed; he has clothed himself in the waters. The divine, well-winged one has looked down upon the earth; Soma beholds all creatures with his wisdom. 9.
Like a bull entering the herds of cattle, he comes toward them and makes his will; even so this Soma, moving around the hymns of praise, bellows.
Then, he surpasses the splendors—the lights—of Sūrya, the impeller of all;
that is to say, he establishes himself in the heavenly world in the form of the Sun.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *dadhāti*, by the rule "sthā-dhvorica," there is the substitution of a short vowel and the augment *kit*.

Furthermore, the divine (*divyaḥ*), born in heaven (*divi bhavaḥ*), the well-flying (*suparṇaḥ*)—the Soma who possesses beautiful flight because he was brought down by the Gāyatrī in the form of a hawk—has reached the earth (*kṣām*). It is so called because people dwell (*kṣiyanti*) and reside here.
He gazes upon the earth, he looks down;
1. he shines forth (virājati). 2. The word "janaṃ" is not present in Ta, Bha, and Preraka-Āditya. 3. [This refers to] the impelling Āditya. 4. Śobhana° in Ta₁, Ta₂, Ta₆, and Ma₆; Śona° in Ta₅.
In Ṛgveda 4.1, because of the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is no elision of the *śap* suffix in the verb *caṣṭe*, which means "he adorns."
Then Soma, as the "born" one, beholds—that is, he surveys from all sides—the "born" creatures with "kratu," meaning with wisdom;
the middle voice is used here by way of grammatical substitution (vyatyaya).
The fifth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "hariṃ mṛjanti," is the seerly work of Harimant, a descendant of Aṅgiras; its deity is Pavamāna Soma.
According to the metrical rule, "That which follows [the first part] up to Uśanas is Jāgata" (Anuvāka 9.67), it is composed in the Jāgata meter.
Thus it has been cataloged: "hariṃ mṛjanti; [the seer is] Harimant."
The application is concluded.

They cleanse the tawny one; he is harnessed like a ruddy steed. Soma is mixed with milch-cows in the beaker. He sends forth his voice; they urge him on with hymns. He is the beloved of the one praised by many, even at the place of sacrifice. They cleanse the tawny one; he is harnessed like a ruddy steed. Soma is mixed with milch-cows in the beaker. He sends forth his voice; they urge him on with hymns. He is the beloved of the one praised by many, even at the place of sacrifice.

"The priests cleanse (*mṛjanti*) Hari, who is green-colored like Soma. According to the rule "In the case of *mṛj*, when there is an initial [augment], vṛddhi is optionally prescribed" (Pāṇini 1.1.58; Kāśikā 1.1.5), there is an absence of vṛddhi here.
Thus, he is "the ruddy one" (*aruṣaḥ*).
The suffix *atru* has the sense of habit (*śīla*).
Thus, like a horse whose nature is to move, [the Soma] is "yoked," that is, joined with Indra and the other gods.

Furthermore, the Soma "situated in the *kalaśa* vessel called the *droṇa*" is "anointed" (*ajyate*), meaning it becomes thoroughly mixed, by means of the "cows"—that is, by products of the cow such as curds and the like.
Moreover, when Soma raises up speech— that is, sound—
meaning he produces sound,
then there are those who praise and those who reflect.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the second case ending [of *stutim*] undergoes a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).
They "impel" or "set in motion" the praise.
The root *hi*—meaning "to go" and "to increase"—belongs to the *svādi* class and is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Then, he who is held by hymns—that is, dear to the praiser who is "puruṣṭuta," meaning one joined with many hymns—[is described]. [The root] *śrīṅ* means "to satisfy";
[the suffix] *kip* is applied.
In the word *śasi*, the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs;
it retains the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound.
He bestows some—meaning "how many"—wealth that gladdens on all sides.

Together many wise ones offer praise when they have milked the Soma into the belly of Indra; when the men with beautiful hands cleanse the desirable honey with the ten sisters who share a common dwelling. Together | they praise | many | the wise ones | of Indra | the Soma | in the belly | when | they have milked | if | they cleanse | with beautiful hands | the men | with the ten sisters | the desirable | honey || 2 ||
"The wise ones"—those who are masters of their minds and possessors of insight—"many singers" together, simultaneously, "speak" the mantras;
that is, they praise.
When the officiating priests have "milked the Soma" into Indra's "belly," that is, into the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, then they praise him.
The form [is] *duher luṅ asi*.

Due to the optionality of the dual number in Vedic (*chandas*), there is either the absence of the dual or its presence. Furthermore, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "When (*yadi* = *yadā*), the men (*naraḥ*), meaning those who perform actions, having beautiful arms (*sugabhastayaḥ* = *śobhanabāhukāḥ*), cleanse (*mṛjanti*) with the ten fingers (*daśabhiḥ*)—which are of equal origin (*sanīḷābhiḥ*)—the desirable (*kāmyam*) Soma, which causes exhilaration (*madhu* = *madakaram*), and praise it, then they speak."

Not resting, he passes beyond the cows toward the beloved roar of Sūrya’s daughter; for him, Vinaguṣas brought pleasure; he dwells together with his two kinds of sisters, his female kin. *aramamāṇaḥ* (not resting), *ati* (beyond), *eti* (he goes), *gāḥ* (the cows), *abhi* (toward), *sūryasya* (of Sūrya), *priyam* (beloved), *duhituḥ* (daughter), *tiraḥ* (across), *ravam* (the roar). *anu* (after), *asmai* (for him), *joṣam* (pleasure), *abharat* (he brought), *vinaguṣaḥ* (Vinaguṣas). *sam* (together), *dvayībhiḥ* (with two kinds), *svasṛbhiḥ* (sisters), *kṣeti* (he dwells), *jāmibhiḥ* (female kin). 3.
1. *ga*-born [beings] are those born from this; they are born from *ta1.2.6.7*; they are born from *ta3.4.5-bhara.6.7*.
2. When *ta* [occurs], there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "before a *dhātu* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffix."

Just as a bird (viḥ) sitting on a tree while purifying itself (duṣan), so too [is it here]; “purifying” (duṣat). The substitution of the sibilant ṣ is by the rule “after a preceding word-element” (pūrvapadāt).

The skillful, wise poets milk the radiant, thundering, imperishable Sage; the lowing thoughts, like cows, go toward him who is gathered together in the womb of Order, in his seat, he who is born again.

The wise, skillful, and thoughtful ones milk the radiant, thundering, imperishable Sage. My cows and my thoughts go toward him as he is being gathered, reborn in the seat, the womb of Eternal Order (Ṛta).
The *kavayas*— those of transcendent wisdom, endowed with vigor (*vapasaḥ*), performers of ritual action (*karmavantaḥ*), and possessors of inspired thought (*manīṣiṇaḥ*)—

the officiating priests who are masters of the mind through their *manīṣā* (insightful intellect)— milk and press the *vaṃśu*, the Soma; that which roars and resounds, which is inexhaustible (*akṣīṇam*), the seer (*kaviḥ*) of transcendent vision.

Then, the *punarbhuvaḥ*—the waters that come into being again—have carried across (*apīparan*) the sacrificer who performs good deeds (*sukṛtam*), meaning he performs excellent rites; they either honor him with delight or cause him to cross over. [Grammatical note: In the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix, there is the treatment as a reduplicated form (*sanvadbhāva*), the substitution of *abhyāsetva*, and the lengthening of the vowel.
The two bulls bellowed together; the wild oxen roared. They sent forth their longing cries toward the surging waves of the river.
Generating the hymn with streams of honey, they have strengthened the beloved body of Indra.

Properly, truly; the horses, the buffaloes, have bellowed. Upon the wave of the river, the longing ones have stirred; with streams of honey, generating the hymn of praise, they have indeed strengthened the dear body of Indra. 2.

The "mighty" (mahiṣāḥ), meaning the venerable and great priests, being "well-yoked" (samyak-śvāḥ)—that is, being united with one another—have "well-roared" (samyag ahepata); this means they impel the Soma well, that is to say, they press it. [The root] *hi* [is used] in the senses of "going" and "increasing";
the form is that of the *luṅ* tense with the *sic* suffix.

Then, the *venās*— Yāska [states in Nirukta 10.38] that "the root *ven* means 'to desire'"— that is, the officiating priests desiring the fruit of heaven and so forth, have caused the Soma to vibrate (*avīvipan*) upon the waves (*ūrmi*) of the flowing water (*sindhoḥ*), within the waters of the *vasatīvarī*s and other [ritual waters].
In this context, the meaning is "impelling.
Regarding the root *vap*, which ends in *i*, there is a shortening [of the vowel] by the rule "in the case of the causative (*ṇic*), there is shortening of the penultimate vowel.
Furthermore, generating—that is, performing—the *arka*, the hymn of praise for worship, they have strengthened with streams of honeyed soma the beloved, most dear body and abode of Indra.
This is the form [of the root] *vṛdh* in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix.
Wearing the purifiers, they sit around the sacred speech; their ancient father guards their vow.
Varuṇa has established the great ocean as a crossing; the wise one indeed finds support in the firm foundations.

Wearing the purifiers, they sit around the sacred word; their ancient father protects the holy law. Varuṇa has spread himself across the great ocean; as a wise one, he alone is able to hold fast among the powers of Varuṇa. 3.
The rays of Soma, endowed with the purifying power of the *pavitra*—the means of purification—sit around, that is, they surround, the *vāc*, the intermediate speech situated within Soma;
for it is stated in scripture: "Soma, indeed, was King Gandharva" (AiB 1.27). Thus, Soma indeed abides in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

Then, the ancient one—the father of these rays—and this Soma protect—that is, they favor—the *vrata*, the activity consisting of manifestation. Furthermore, Varuṇa, the self-shrouder of all, this very Soma [protects] the great ocean;
this is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
By those rays, he veiled the great intermediate space; that is to say, he made it hidden, meaning he pervaded everything. The wise ones [perceive] this very Soma.
The word *it* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).

Only those who are skillful—that is, wise—in their ritual duties (*karmaṇi*) are capable of undertaking (*ārabham ārabdhum śakuḥ śaknuvanti ca*), that is, performing, the *varuṇeṣu*—referring to the waters (*udakeṣu*) which sustain all—or the dwellings (*vasatīḥ*).
Regarding the suffix *kamul*, it is applied after the root *rabh-* in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*) by the rule "after the root *śak*, [the suffixes] *namul* and *kamul*" (Pāṇini 3.4.12).
By means of the pitch-accent (svara), it has the acute accent (udātta) on the middle syllable.
Like [birds] at a thousandfold stream, they have sung together in the vault of heaven, honey-tongued and unfailing.
His spies do not close their eyes; watchful, at every step there are bridgers who carry nooses.

In the thousandfold stream, they have resounded together for you in the vault of heaven—those honey-tongued, unfailing ones. His spies, the protectors of the earth, do not close their eyes; at every step there are ensnaring fetters.

1. *ga*-pūrayanti; 2. *ga*-vepate; *ta-bha4.6*-patate; *bhara*-kampate; *bhava*-vatapate; 3. *ga*-aṃśānām; 4. *ga*-have. *Sahasradhāre*: That [intermediate space] from which many streams of water flow is thus described as *sahasradhāra*.
Abiding in that [place], those rays of Soma, standing from below, resounded together;
the meaning is that they joined the earth with rain. Moreover, abiding in the *nāka*, the lofty region of heaven (*div*), they are honey-tongued, having honey at their tips.
For from the tips of the moon's brilliance, honey flows; hence they are called "honey-tongued.

These spies of this Soma—his own inherent rays, which are his very essence—are situated separately in various directions; being swift-moving (*bhūrṇyaḥ*), they do not close their eyes, that is, they do not blink.
However, the meaning is that they are always awake to distinguish between the sinful and the virtuous.
Alternatively,

just as royal servants remain constantly vigilant to investigate the wicked, so too these rays— being bound as "bridges" (setavaḥ) at every step, in every place— are "possessors of nooses" (pāśinaḥ), acting as obstructors for evildoers.

Those who have resonated together with the *ṛc* from the father and the mother, glowing and utterly consuming the untruths—by their power they blow away the skin of the enemies of Indra, the scorched hide from the high heaven. 5. From the father. From the mother. Over. Up. Those who. Have resonated together. With the *ṛc*. Glowing. Utterly consuming. The untruths. Of the enemies of Indra. Away. They blow. By their power. The skin. Scorched. From the high heaven. 5.
Regarding the father and mother, heaven and earth:

because of the lack of knowledge that heaven and earth are the fashioning parents, as seen in such passages as, "Heaven is my father, the progenitor; here is my navel. My kinsman is the great earth, my mother" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.33).

Those rays of Soma which, from Heaven and Earth, have resounded—that is, have become fully manifest—blazing and shining by means of the *ṛc* being performed by the priests, completely consuming—that is, utterly destroying—the unrighteous (*anṛtān*), those sacrificers devoid of ritual action; they [the rays] [are directed] toward the enemies of Indra (*indraviṣām*), meaning those who harbor hatred toward Indra.
[The compound takes its accent on the first member] according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.2.45, *ke ca*, or it may mean "those hated by Indra."
*Asikī*:
this is a name for night;
it refers to the skin, which is black in form like the night.
The meaning is "a Rākṣasa.
By means of *māyā*—whether through action or wisdom—they blow away, that is, they cause to depart, the vast-bodied *bhūmanas* from the sky, that is, from the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
The sense is that they strike them down.

Those who from the ancient measure have raised their voices together, controlled by the *śloka* and dwelling within the impetuous one—let them be blind and deaf; the evildoers do not traverse the path of *ṛta*. From the ancient measure, those who have sounded forth together, constrained by the *śloka*, dwelling within the impetuous one—they shall indeed become sightless and deaf; the evildoers do not cross the path of *ṛta*.
*Ślokayantrāsaḥ*: *Ślokāḥ* means praises;

those who restrain praise through their impetuosity, whose internal selves are being struck by speed—such are the rays of Soma which, from the ancient, primordial measure, from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), resounded together and manifested. Men who are eyeless (*anakṣāsaḥ*), lacking sight and unable to perceive the true nature of things, and men who are deaf, deprived of hearing the hymns to the deities and being evildoers—they have abandoned them; they cast them aside.
Those who possess vision, those who have heard [the truth], and those who are wise do not abandon [them], but rather praise them.
To that very effect: "The evildoers, men of sinful deeds, do not cross over, nor can they cause to cross over, the host of these [sages] who has become the path of *ṛta*, the eternal order."
The intended meaning is that those who have performed good deeds cross over.

In the wide, thousand-streamed filter, the wise seers purify their speech. Among them, the Rudras are here—their spies are unerring, possessing noble steeds, beautiful to behold, and keen of vision. (7) 1. ga—by the foremost splendor of Soma; 2. ga—tava—bha6—devoid of attachment; bha7—devoid of company; 3. bha(2)—the Rākṣasī; 4. bha6—from the ancient; 5. bha(2)—"duṣkṛtaḥ" means "evil-doers."

In the filter spread out with a thousand streams, the sages, the wise ones, purify their speech. Among them are the Rudras, the impetuous, the guileless; they are touchers, possessing noble horses, beautiful to behold, and observers of men.

The poets (*kavayaḥ*)—those who have performed their duties and are therefore wise (*manīṣiṇaḥ*), meaning the learned officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*)—utter the *mādhyamikā vācam* (the intermediate speech) while engaged in the *soma*, which is the purifier (*pavitram*) that produces purity, spread out (*vitata*) in a ritual act (*karmani*) possessed of many streams (*sahasradhāre*).
Indeed, Soma dwells in the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*) with the Gandharvas such as Viśvāvasu, according to the scriptural tradition: "King Soma was among the Gandharvas" (*Ai. Brā. 1.27*).
There, the gods purchased the Soma dwelling therein by means of the cow-like speech (*gorūpayā vācā*).
At that time, it can be said that speech desires the *soma*.
Therefore, they purify—that is, they refine—the central speech situated in the *soma*;
that is to say, they praise it.
Then those who possess the aforementioned qualities, being wise and skilled in ritual action, strive toward that station of Varuṇa’s tongue;
for the root *inakṣati* signifies motion.
Being present together, they reached you with their praises; or rather, through their various hymns, they attained you.
Furthermore, as for *katam*:
the accusative case is used here according to the rule "kālādhvanoḥ... (Pāṇini 2.3.5).

One who is *aprabhuḥ*, meaning not capable or competent regarding *karmaṇi* (action), he—this very person—*ava padāti* (falls down) *atra* (in this very world); that is, he falls into decay due to old age and does not go upward.
[The root] *pada* means "to go. The augment *leṭyāṭ* is applied.
Therefore, the meaning expressed is that the Agniṣṭoma and other rites must be performed by everyone.
The seventh hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “*śiśurna*,” is the *ārṣa* (seer’s work) of Kakṣīvat, the son of Dirghatamas; its deity is Pavamāna Soma.
The eighth verse is a *triṣṭubh*, while the remaining verses are *jagatīs*.
Thus it is enumerated: “*śiśurna*: Kakṣīvat [is the seer]; the eighth is [in] *baṣṭha* [meter].”
The application of the hymns has been concluded.
The unborn child has cried out in the wood; he who is like a swift steed desires to win the light of heaven.
He unites with the seed of heaven, which increases the milk; him we implore for his favor and for wide-reaching protection.

The infant, not yet born, has bellowed in the wood; when the prize-winning steed, the ruddy one, desires to win the light of heaven, he accompanies the seed of heaven, increasing with milk. We implore him for his favor, for his far-reaching protection. 1.
This Soma, being purified, born and produced in the *vananīya*—the desirable water of the *vasatīvarī*—cries out like a child; indeed, he cries downward with his face turned below.
At that time, he makes a sound within the midst of the water. When he becomes a vigorous steed (*vājī*), powerful or radiant (*aruṣa*).
Or rather:
like a swift horse, the Soma—
whose nature is to move toward the waters— desires to win over (sipāsati), that is, to share with himself, the heavenly world (svar).
In the word *sanoteḥ*, there is the absence of the suffix *san* and the substitution of *ā*;
the lengthening [of the vowel] is a Vedic (*sāṃhitika*) archaism according to the rule "sanoteḥ...
This [Soma], together with *retas*—the water that increases the milk of cows and plants—*sacate*, that is, it comes together with from the *divaḥ*, the heavenly world, to the earthly world.

We entreat with a beautiful hymn— that is, with excellent praise (the third case ending *sumatyā* is substituted by its long vowel according to Pāṇini 7.1.39)— that well-known Soma, who is such [as described], who is all-pervading (*saprathas*), most extensive on every side, and endowed with wealth and other blessings, for that protection which is a home. We implore him for it.
The root *īh* has the sense of "begging" (*yācñā*).
It is derived from the root *īṅ* meaning "to go," belonging to the *divādi* class.
In Vedic usage, there is the elision of the suffix *iyaN*.

He who is the pillar of heaven, its support, the self-existent stalk that is full on every side—he, the Seer, has encompassed these two great worlds with his mysterious power; he, the Sage, has held them together and maintains all strengthening foods.

That pillar of heaven, the support, well-extended, the full stalk, moves all around on every side. May he worship these two great worlds, heaven and earth, by his turn; the sage has supported the two joined worlds together and all nourishments. 2.
The pillar of heaven—that is, the supporter who restrains the celestial world;
the sustainer—that is, the upholder of all things.
Or alternatively:
He is the supporter of the earth, according to the Vedic revelation: "The pillar of heaven and the sustainer of the earth" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.89.6).

Such is he, well-spreading and extended everywhere; therefore, he is full, completely filling the vessels—that stalk (*aṃśu*) consisting of Soma which moves all around, encompassing everything from every side.
By the rule "tiṅi codāttavati," the verb of motion (gati) is unaccented.

That Soma shall worship (yakṣat)—that is, he shall cause to sacrifice—these two worlds, heaven and earth (rodasī), by means of that which is to be honored (āvṛtā), namely, through praiseworthy action;
the meaning is that he shall unite them with his own power.
Then he has supported—that is, held fast—the two well-united and mutually joined Heaven and Earth;
here, the lengthening of the vowel in the reduplication follows the rule *tujādīnām*.
Subsequently, may the Seer (*kavi*), whose deeds are far-reaching, bestow food (*iṣaḥ*) upon his worshippers.
Because of the hearing of a prefix (upasarga), there is the ellipsis of a verb expressing connection (yoga).
1. In manuscripts ta1, 2, 5, 6, and 7, as well as manuscript bha6, the word "vardhakena" is absent.
2. In manuscripts ga, ta3, and ma, it is read as "pṛthutamaṃ".
3. In manuscripts bha1, 2, and 7, it is read as "pūrṇaḥ".

Great is the food, well-prepared, sweet as Soma; wide is the pasture for the cow, for Aditi belongs to him who goes toward *ṛta*. He who rules over rain, he who is the impetuous one, the bull, the leader of the waters—he who comes with help, who is accompanied by hymns. Great is the food, well-prepared, sweet as Soma; wide is the pasture for the cow, for Aditi belongs to him who goes toward *ṛta*. He who rules over rain, he who is the impetuous one, the bull, the leader of the waters—he who comes with help, who is accompanied by hymns. 3.

For that Indra who goes toward the sacrifice—which is *psaras*, having become reality—for him there is *psaras*: a well-prepared, excellent draught consisting of Soma, great, vast, abundant, sweet-flavored, and fit for consumption.
[The root] *psā* means "to eat.
Furthermore, for Indra and the other gods who are returning to our sacrifice, the path of Aditi—that is, the earth—and the pasture-land (*gavyuti*) become wide and expansive.
The meaning is that the path became wide enough for Indra to travel together with his hundreds of thousands of bay horses (*haris*).
That Indra is the lord (*īśvara*) of the rain that falls back toward this world from here;
likewise, he is *usiyas*.

*Usya* is a name for cattle. He who is beneficial to the cattle (*go-bhyaḥ hitaḥ*), the showerer of waters (*apām udakānām vṛṣā*), the leader (*netā*) and guide of the sacrifice, whose coming is from here (*ita-ūtiḥ*)— that is, he whose approach toward this our sacrifice is from here—
that Indra, who is to be praised with *ṛc*s, is [the one].
Therefore, this Soma must be drunk by him.
In the *pravargya* ritual, during the *abhiṣṭava*, this verse "ātmanvadbharaḥ" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "tadu pratyakṣam asya karma ātmanvadbharaḥ duhyate ghṛtam payaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).

The self-possessed cloud is milked; ghee, milk, and the navel of Cosmic Order are born as immortality. The well-disposed, bounteous ones gratify him; the two heroes and the flowing waters pour forth the beneficial fluid. ātmanvat | nabhaḥ | duhyate | ghṛtam | paryaḥ | ṛtasya | nābhiḥ | amṛtam | vi | jāyate | samīcīnāḥ | sudānavaḥ | prīṇanti | tam | narau | hitam | arva | mehanti | peravaḥ ||4||

"Ātmanvat": by the rule "ano yud," the augment *nuṭ* is added. Ghee and milk, which possess essence (*ātmanvat* = *sāravat*), and from the sky (*nabhas*)—that is, from the moon which is the form of the sun—the [milk] is milked.
Furthermore, it is the "navel" (*nābhi*) of *ṛta*, that is, of the sacrifice.
[The root] *ṇaha* means "to bind.
The form *sālam* occurs due to the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23); this is because in the Veda, all grammatical rules are subject to optionality.
The navel of the sacrifice, the bond, the immortal, and the water are born from it; from that very source they manifest.
Thence, the *sudānavaḥ*—the sacrificers who possess beautiful praise and offerings—being well-disposed and united with one another, gratify this Soma, satisfying him with their hymns.
Now, the *naraḥ*, the leaders, the *peravaḥ* [from the root *pā*, "to protect"].
In the word *māpastve run*, the suffix *run* is applied.
The rays of Soma, the protectors of all, *mehanti*—that is, they rain down—the terrestrial water that is beneficial (*hitam*), deposited (*nihitam*), and present in the lower regions.
[The root] *miha* means "to sprinkle."
It belongs to the *bhū* class (of roots).
Alternatively,
they sprinkle beneficial water toward the earth.

The stalk has roared, accompanying itself with its wave; it swells the skin that nourishes the gods for the sake of man. It places the germ within the lap of Aditi, by which we may obtain both offspring and descendants. It has roared; the stalk; accompanying; with its wave; that which nourishes the gods; for man; it swells; the skin; it places; the germ; in the lap of Aditi; indeed; by which; offspring; and; descendants; we may obtain. 5.

1. That which is to be consumed (ga-ta³-ma¹.².⁴.⁷-bhakṣaṇīyam). 2. Of those who support (ta-bhara-yāḥ); by the two [worlds] (bha⁶-yā dyāvā); of Aditi, the undecaying (su-aditeḥ adīnāyāḥ). 3. The leader of all (ga-ta³-ma¹.².⁴.⁵-netā sarvasya). 4. Of the moving world (ga-jagataḥ). 5. To be given (ga-dātavyo). 6. The navel (ga-bha¹.⁶.⁷-nābhiḥ; ta⁴-nābhi). 7. He pleases, he causes delight with hymns; he causes delight with hymns (bha¹(²)-stutibhiḥ prīṇati prīṇayati stutibhiḥ prīṇayati).
Accompanied (sacamānaḥ) by the wave (urmiṇā)—that is, by the mass of waters such as the *vasatīvarī*—the stalk (aṃśuḥ), Soma, has roared (arāvīt), making a sound.
Furthermore, that Soma is "god-seeking" (devāvyam).
The root *ava* means "to protect.

According to the rule "the suffix *ī* is applied after *avitṛ*, *stṛ*, and *tamitṛ*," the suffix *ī* is added. [Thus, *avitrī* means] "the protector of the gods. [The word *tvacam* refers to] her own body. [The verb *pinvati* means] she causes it to swell or succeed for the sake of the human, that is, for the sacrificer.
That is to say, it flows into the vessels.
Moreover, she places that embryo in the lap—that is, in the vicinity—of Aditi, the undepressed Earth, among the plants; she establishes it with her nectar-like rays.
By means of that embryo, may we obtain *toka*, a son who destroys suffering, and *tanaya*, a grandson.
A *tanaya* is a grandson (*pautra*), so called because he "extends" (*tanoti*) the lineage. We honor (*dadhāmahe*) him—that is, we uphold him—in the act of worship (*dambhe*).
In the present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *dhā*, the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule "the suffix *śap* is frequently elided in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Like those [rivers] at the thousandfold stream, may they be inexhaustible and rich in offspring in the third realm;
four [of them], established at the navel, bring down from heaven the immortal oblation, dripping with clarified butter.

In the thousand-streamed [filter], let those inexhaustible [waters] flow down; let them be rich in progeny in the third realm. The four naves are established below the sky; they bring the oblation, dripping with ghee—the nectar of immortality.

In the seventh thousand-fold world-system, in the third [realm], in the world of heaven, those who dwell there—unfailing, mutually attached, possessing offspring, having produced progeny, belonging to Soma—may they descend; may they fall down upon the earth. As for which ones these are, he says:

The four naves, which are the four radiant digits of Soma that dispel the afflictions of heat, have been placed from heaven—that is, from the celestial world—downward by Soma. These true ones, dripping with clarified butter (ghṛta), meaning water, bring the oblation characterized by Soma and other offerings to the gods; they present it to them.
Likewise, they bring and deposit the nectar (amṛta) in the form of milk among the cows and in the form of essence among the plants.
He assumes a white form; the striving one approaches. Soma, the bounteous Asura, knows the vastness of the earth.
Through wisdom he accompanies the ritual labor; may he, the impetuous one, burst open the water-holding cloud.

He makes his form white when he desires to win; Soma, the bountiful Asura, knows the vastness of the earth. Through prayer, he attends to the sacred rite; he, the seer of heaven, shall burst open the water-holding vessel along the downward slope.
He then makes his form white and shining; that is, he does so when he desires to win, that is, when he wishes to partake of heaven.
When the Soma vessels have arrived, their form becomes white, colored by his splendor.
Then he is the bountiful one (*mīḍhvān*).
Regarding the root *siha*, meaning "to sprinkle":
from this root, the form *kasāṃ* is established through the grammatical rule of *nipātana* (irregular derivation) as seen in the list beginning with *dākṣāṇasāṃhīmmīḍhvāṃś*.

[The word] *kāmasāṃhaḥ* means "the sprinkler of desires"—an *asura* (a wise one) or a powerful one. *Bhūrmānaḥ* means "possessing much wealth. *Veda* means "he knows," that is, he knows how to give [wealth] to the worshippers.
The meaning is "he gives. Regarding *sīm*: by the rule "so'ci lope cet," there is the elision of the suffix *su*.
This very one, through his *dhī*—that is, through wisdom (*prajñāna*)—attends to, or comes together with, the *pra-vat*, meaning the excellent or preeminent ritual acts (*karmāṇi*).
[Note: The long vowel in the second word is due to the rule of *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*.
He attends to them from all sides; he unites with them completely.
Furthermore: from heaven and from the intermediate space, [he brings] the *kavandha*—that is, the cloud, for the word *kavandha* denotes a cloud;
this is a metaphorical designation (*tācchabdyam*). It is full of water (*udrin*).
"megham ava darṣat" means he splits it open;
he makes the door wide open.
The meaning is that having split the cloud, he causes rain from the atmosphere.
Half-white, with his lineage reddened by cattle, the prize-winning steed has stepped upon the goal;
those seeking the gods have incited him with their minds for Kukṣīvat, who possesses a hundred winters of cattle.

Immediately thereafter, having won [the prize], Soma has stepped upon—the white, now white-colored through contact with the *soma*, and anointed (*akta*) with the waters (*gobhiḥ*)—the wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*). "At the goal" (*kāṣman*):
the word *kāṣman* denotes the limit (*kāṣṭhā*).
Just as a certain vigorous horse (*vājī*), participating in battle, steps upon that goal toward which warriors rushing forward desire to go, so too does he step upon it.
The meaning is that Soma falls into the *droṇakalaśa* at the end of the wooden trough (*kāṣṭhā*).
Then, for that Soma, the priests, desiring the gods (*devayantaḥ*), impel him with their minds; they send forth hymns toward him.
Therein, for Kakṣīvat—the singer of praises of this name who has lived for a hundred winters (*śatahimāya*) and has traveled far—Soma sends forth the cattle (*gonām*).

The augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule *goḥ pādānte* (Pāṇini 7.1.57). The designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is assigned by the principle that "the mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) must be supplied [to the rule defining the recipient].
Thus, the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.

The juice of you, O Soma, as you are pressed by the stone, flows through the sheep’s wool filter, O Pavamāna. Being cleansed by the sages, O most exhilarating one, be sweet for Indra to drink, O Pavamāna. Of you, O Soma, as you are pressed by the stones, the juice, O Pavamāna, flows through the sheep’s wool filter. Being cleansed by the sages, O most exhilarating one, be sweet for Indra to drink, O Pavamāna.

O Pavamāna Soma, being purified by the filter, as your juice—blended with the waters such as the *vasatīvarī*s—is mixed, it flows through and reaches the sheep’s wool, the fringe, and the ten-stranded filter (*daśāpavitra*).

Then, O most exhilarating Pavamāna Soma, being cleansed and purified by the sages (*kavi*s), the far-striding officiating priests, do you become sweet-tasting for Indra’s drink; be a source of delight for Indra.
The eighth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “abhi priyāṇi,” is the seerly work of Kavi Bhārgava; it is composed in the Jāgata meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity.
It is thus enumerated: “abhi priyāṇi pañca kaviḥ. Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.

The mighty one, well-disposed for our pleasure, flows toward his dear names, upon which he grows great. Great and far-seeing, he has mounted the all-pervading chariot of the lofty Sūrya. abhi priyāṇi pavate canohito nāmāni yahvo adhi yeṣu vardhate | ā sūryasya bṛhato bṛhannadhi rathaṃ viśvañcamaruhat vicakṣaṇaḥ || 1 || He flows toward his dear names, the mighty one who increases over them, bringing delight. Great and far-seeing, he has mounted the all-pervading chariot of the lofty Sūrya.
*Canohitaḥ*. *Cana* is a name for food (*anna*).
It is derived from the root *cāyati* with the suffix *asun*, and is established as such by the *Uṇādi-sūtra*.

Soma flows toward—that is, he prepares on all sides—the waters which are beneficial for the one who knows the sacrifice, or rather, those waters which are dear to him, which delight the world, and which are prone to bowing down.
In those waters situated in the intermediate space, this great Soma increases, becoming fully grown;
Soma dwells in the midst of the waters.
Then the great Soma, the all-seeing one, having mounted the far-reaching chariot of the vast, supreme, and all-pervading Sun, ascends above it;
for it is said: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the Sun."

4. A chariot that goes everywhere (ga-bha²-viśvagāminam ratham); 4. A chariot whose course is everywhere (ta⁴-bha¹-viśvagāmanaratham); 7. A chariot that moves everywhere (bha⁷-viśvagāñcanam ratham); 1(2). A chariot that is the means of motion (bha¹-gamanasādhanam ratham).
