The tongue of *Ṛta* flows forth as the beloved honey; the speaker, the lord of this prayer, is inviolable. As a son, he bestows upon his parents their secret third name in the luminous realm of heaven. The tongue of *Ṛta*—of the sacrifice that has become reality—is Soma, who stands in the place of the tongue. He flows forth, pouring out the beloved, exhilarating honey, the juice that brings delight. Of what nature is he? He is the "speaker," the creator of sound; or rather, the one who grants a favorable hearing to the hymns being performed by the singers. He is the "lord" (*pati*) of this ritual action (*dhi*), its protector; he is "inviolable" (*adābhya*), incapable of being harmed by demons. As a "son" (*putra*), the sacrificer bestows upon his "parents"—his mother and father—their "secret" (*apīcya*) "third name. This name was unknown to them at the time of the naming ceremony; therefore, it remains hidden from them. 1. *stutayaḥ*: hymns. 2. *sādhīyasya*: more effective or excellent. 3. *pratiśravaṇasya*: of the act of listening or granting a response. 4. *rakṣobhiḥ*: by demons or obstructive spirits. 5. *antarhitaṃ*: hidden or concealed. 6. *tau*: they (the parents). 7. *nāmakaraṇavelāyām*: at the time of the naming ceremony. 8. *tasmāt*: therefore. 9. *tayor*: of those two (the parents). 10. *aparijñātam*: unknown.
Regarding the word *matibhiḥ*:
[it is derived from] the root *man* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*).
[In the rule] *mantre vṛṣapapacamana°*, why is it [the suffix] udātta?

Praised with hymns, pressed by the priests, and poured out—beneficial for food (or beneficial for the eyes)—he illuminates and makes manifest with his own splendor the two mothers, Rodasī, Heaven and Earth, the fashioners of the world; thus pure and radiant, Soma flows through and across the purifying filters made from the woolly hair of the sheep on both sides.

Furthermore, being poured out like fire being sprinkled, the stream of the exhilarating Soma purifies itself day by day, every day, within the long sacrificial sessions, flowing through the filters from both sides.
Flow forth, O Soma, for our well-being; being purified by the men, clothe yourself in the milk-mixture.
With those exhilarating draughts of yours that are impetuous and far-reaching, urge Indra to grant us wealth.
O Soma, flow forth for our well-being; being purified by the men, clothe yourself in the milk-mixture (*āśira*). Those exhilarations of yours—let them be established.
Soma, the sustainer of all, flows and is purified from heaven, from the intermediate space, and from the filter situated in the intermediate space.
Of what nature is Soma?
*Kṛtsya* means that which is to be done; the sense is "that which is to be purified.
*Rasa* refers to that which consists of essence (*rasātmaka*), the *dakṣa* (skillful/efficient) one who bestows strength upon the gods.
Or rather:
Dakṣa is to be praised for the sake of the gods;

likewise, he is to be rejoiced in or praised by the *nṛ*—the leaders, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The tawny-colored (*hari*) one is being released or impelled by the *satvan*s—living beings or riders—as a steed (*atya*) is. Just as a well-trained horse goes with ease (*vṛthā*), so too does he, with ease and without effort, manifest his own powers (*pājāṃsi*) and speeds.
"In the rivers" means in the *vasatīvarī* waters; "with them" is the intended sense; "sprinkled" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
This is the intention regarding the arrival at the pressing.
Like a hero, he takes up weapons in his hands; desiring to win, the steadfast one exerts himself among the challengers.
Stirred by those seeking the waters, the Indu, rushing toward the glory of Indra, is anointed by the wise.

The hero does not hold weapons in his hands; he desires to win for himself as a charioteer in the contests for cattle. Stirring up the glorious [Soma] of Indra with active [fingers], the drop, being urged forth, is anointed by the wise.

This Soma, like a hero, holds—that is, maintains—his two arms and his various weapons. Desiring to partake in the sacrifice, which is the means for attaining the bliss of heaven (*svaḥ*), he is a charioteer, possessing a chariot;
the suffix *rac* is added here to form the word *rathi*.

In the *gaviṣṭis*—that is, during the quests for cattle on behalf of the sacrificer—the Soma-drop (*indu*), the god, impelling the vigorous strength of Indra, being urged forward by the wise and skillful officiating priests who desire ritual action (*apasyu*), is anointed with milk. It means that he possesses a chariot for the sake of gathering cattle for the sacrificer. Thus the Soma-drop, stimulating Indra’s power, is pressed by the seekers of work and the intelligent ones. It is anointed with the products of the cow.

O Soma, being purified with your wave for Indra, entering his bellies while increasing in strength—swell for us, O wielder of the lightning bolt, like heaven and earth; through our prayer, measure out for us eternal strengths.

O Soma, being pressed for Indra, entering with thy wave into his bellies while increasing in strength, swell us like lightning filling the two worlds with clouds; through our prayer, measure out for us eternal strengths. 3.
O Soma Pavamāna, being purified and increasing in strength, enter into the bellies of Indra with a wave—that is, with an abundant stream.
Because the region of the belly is vast, the plural is used.
For our sake, like lightning from the clouds, cause the two worlds, heaven and earth, to swell and flow forth.
Furthermore, "by means of wisdom and action" (dhiyā karmaṇā) "now indeed" (na idānīm).
The word "not" (na) is used here in the sense of "presently. "Eternally" (śaśvataḥ).
This belongs to many;
I fashion many *vāja*s—foods—in close proximity.
The King of the universe flows clear, beholding the light; he, the guardian of the seers, has willed the thought of the Eternal Law.
He who is polished by the sun’s ray, the father of hymns, the peerless sage of inspired song.

The king of the universe flows clear for those who behold the light; he, the protector of the seers, has caused the prayer of the cosmic order to resound. He who is cleansed by the ray of the sun is the father of hymns, whose poetic wisdom is unassailable.

6. "Do you grant? Soma is the king and lord of the entire world, the beholder of heaven, the all-seeing one, [the lord] of *ṛta*—that which has become reality, the opposite of the word *anṛta* (untruth) used for humans, the word *ṛta* having the sense of "divine."
Even there, Indra is accepted according to propriety.
His *dhīti*—his intellect or his action—is extended (*abhivita*) by the sages (*ṛṣibhiḥ*), those who perceive what is beyond the senses.
The sense is that he himself is also a preeminent sage (*ṛṣiśreṣṭha*) due to his greatness.
And so another mantra says: "Brahmā is the pathfinder of the gods, the leader even of the poets" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.96.6).
Such Soma, by his own will, desired the work of Indra.
That Soma is cleansed by the garment—the casting, the ray—of the god Sūrya.

Soma, whose poetic power is unequaled by other poets, is the protector and master of our hymns (*matīnām*); this is the ellipsis. Or rather, the connection is: he who is the father of hymns and whose poetic power is unequaled, being purified, flows forth.
Like a bull rushing toward the herds, you flow toward the vat, bellowing as a bull in the lap of the waters.
You flow for Indra as the most intoxicating one, so that we may be victorious in battle through your protections.

Like a bull toward the herds, you flow around the vessel; bellowing like a bull in the lap of the waters, O most exhilarating one, flow clear for me, for Indra, so that aided by you, we may be victorious in the encounter. 5.
O Soma, like a bull among herds, you enter those herds; just as a bull enters them, so do you go around—the *vṛka*—the vessel-like jar that holds the essence. Abiding where?
In the lap of the *vapā*, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Being what? A bull (*vṛṣabhaḥ*), a showerer [of benefits], bellowing (*kanikradat*) while making sound— O Soma, as such you flow (*pavase*) for Indra, that is, for the sake of Indra.
O you who are most free from envy, you are the one who drinks most;
may we, protected by you, overcome our distress and be victorious in battle.
The tenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "eṣa pra kośe," has the same seer and other characteristics as the preceding one.
It is introduced by the word "eṣaḥ."
The application is concluded.

This honeyed one has bellowed toward the vat; Indra’s thunderbolt, more wondrous than the wondrous. Toward him flow the lowing, milk-yielding streams of nectar, dripping with ghee, like milch-cows to their pasture.

This one, rich in sweetness, has bellowed forth in the vat; Indra’s thunderbolt, more wondrous than the wondrous. Toward him flow the streams of the Eternal Order, dripping with ghee, lowing like milch-cows with their milk.

This Soma, dressed in this attire, rich in sweetness and possessing a sweet flavor, has cried out loudly—resounding intensely—in the vat, the *droṇakalaśa*. Of what nature is he? He is like the thunderbolt (*vajra*) of Indra, occupying the very position of the thunderbolt.
Because it possesses strength and serves as a means of striking like a thunderbolt (*vajra*), it is metaphorically designated as a "thunderbolt.
Indeed, this very Soma is Indra’s thunderbolt in his accomplishment.
Likewise, compared to other sowers of seeds, he is more beautiful (*vapuṣṭaraḥ*)—that is, a superior sower.
Because Soma is the agent of sowing the seed, according to the Vedic revelation: "Soma, indeed, is the placer of the seed" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1.6).
[The phrase] "of this" refers to this Soma, which has truth as its fruit; the word "streams" (*dhārāḥ*) is to be supplied [as the object].
They low toward them and approach them.
Of what nature are they? They are *sudughāḥ*, those that yield well; *ghṛtaśrutaḥ*, those from which clarified butter or the essence of water flows; and *vāśāḥ*, those that low.
What is it like?
It is like cows that are barren yet joined with milk. Thus [it is said].

1. For the word *ta3.bha7*, the meaning is "the gods"; for the word *bha6*, the meaning is "as it were. 2. *Ta* and *Mu*: it is accepted. 3. *Ga*: because he is himself the most excellent even among the sages (*ṛṣi*).
4. *ga*-kāmayate; 5. *ga*-ta1.5.7-*bha*1.2.7-*yūthā* does not exist;
6. *ga*-haviṣyaḥ saṃdhārakaṃ; *ta-bha6*-rasaṃ dhārakaṃ; *bha*1.7*-ravadhārakaṃ*.
He flows as the ancient one, whom the falcon, dispatched from heaven across the straight path, has carried away;
he, quivering with fear in his heart at the sight of the archer’s arrow, draws up the honeyed juice.

He, the ancient one, flows forth—he whom the hawk, sent from heaven, churned out across the straight path. Trembling with fear in his mind at the sight of the emaciated one, he, the archer, draws near to the honeyed draught.
That Soma, ancient and primordial, flows and is purified— meaning he is being pressed—
that Soma whom the falcon, impelled by his own mother from the sky (the heavenly world), brought down, passing through and piercing the obstructed [space].
What? The third world is *rajas*.
That very *soma*—the *soma* of sweet juice (*madhvaḥ*)—he draws toward himself (*ā yuvate*), that is, he separates it from the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).

"Quivering himself, trembling and going downwards, with a mind terrified of Kṛśānu, the protector of Soma, the archer who hurls arrows—he says, 'Draw forth the honey'"; such is the connection [of the words]. That Kṛśānu is the protector of Soma is clearly stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "Kṛśānu is the protector of Soma, the guardian of the left foot" (AiB 3.26).
May those many, later drops of Soma flow for us toward great booty consisting of cattle—
drops that are worthy of being looked upon, as delightful as food, which have been offered as oblation after oblation by those who have performed every sacred prayer.

May those many, most recent drops of Soma flow for us toward great booty consisting of cattle—drops worthy of being beheld, as desirable as food, which have relished every prayer and every oblation. 3.
Those aforementioned *pūrvāsaḥ* (earlier ones) are the *uparāsaḥ* (later ones);
they are called *uparāḥ* because they have ceased (*uparatāḥ*) here.
Such *indavaḥ* (drops), that is, Soma juices, for our great [sacrifice] rich in cattle, let them flow—*dhavantu*—toward our great strength, toward food, for the sake of obtaining nourishment.
Of what kind are the drops (*indavas*)?
They are *īkṣaṇyāsas*, meaning they are worthy of being looked at, beautiful to behold, like those who are to be eaten (*adyo na*).
They are indeed edible.
Because of the striking of women;
they are like women, well-adorned, beautiful, and charming.
To the question "What [is that]? he says: "That."

Those drops (indavas) which have tasted—have partaken of—all prayers (brahma), that is, every collection of hymns used for praise, and all oblations (havis), that is, every collection of sacrificial offerings.
May this Indu, the knower, win for us what is desired, he who is praised by many with a focused mind;
he who, as the embryo in the seat of the Lord, pours forth the wide-open stall of cattle.

May this Indu, the knower, win for us against those who attack him—he who, praised by many with a focused mind, has taken his place as the embryo in the seat of the Lord; he flows toward the wide-open stall of the cows. ||4||
May this Indu, Soma, knowing—that is, being aware of—the enemies who desire to harm us, slay them;
may he strike them down by what means?
By his all-pervading, ever-attentive mind.
Of what nature is he?
He is "much-praised," lauded by many.
That Soma, who, being present in the seat or place of the powerful Agni—either upon the earth or on the sacrificial altar—places and sustains the embryo within the plants.
And he who flows toward the wide enclosure (*vraja*)—the source of abundant waters—which belongs to our cows that have been seized by enemies;
he, like a forest, [is praised].
The active juice of heaven flows clear; the great Varuṇa has established himself for the wide-striding one.
Mitra, the worshipful one, has been pressed out among the people, like a stallion lowing in his herd, eager for the prize.

1. Ga-bha 1.7: *preritaḥ*. 2. Ta-nabhasā saha; Tā3-bhara 2.7: *manasā saha*; Bha6: *namasā saha*; Mu: *manasā aha saha*. 3. Ga-ta 1.3.4-7; Bha 1.4.7: the word *īkṣaṇīyāḥ* is absent. 4. Ta 1.2.4.5: *yata*. Ṛ. 4–10:

*cakriḥ*, *divaḥ*, *pavane*, *kṛtvyaḥ*, *rasaḥ*, *mahān*, *adabdhaḥ*, *varuṇaḥ*, *huruk*, *yate*, *asātri*, *mitraḥ*, *vṛjaneṣu*, *yajñiyaḥ*, *atyaḥ*, *na*, *yūthe*, *vṛṣayuḥ*, *kanikradat* || 5 || 1. Impelled by the womb (ga-bha 1.7). 2. Together with the sky (ta-nabhasā); together with the mind (tā3-bhara 2.7); together with reverence (bha6-namasā); together with the mind and "aha" (mu-manasā aha). 3. In Ga-ta 1.3.4-7 and Bha 1.4.7, the word "īkṣaṇīyāḥ" does not exist. 4. In Ta 1.2.4.5, it is "yata". Ṛ. 4–10: The maker; from heaven; in the purification; the effective one; the juice; the great; the undeceived; Varuṇa; for the one who goes crookedly; Mitra; in the enclosures; worthy of sacrifice; like a steed in the herd; seeking the bull; neighing loudly. || 5 ||

The *cakriḥ* (the mover), the maker of all, the *kṛtvyaḥ* (one who is capable of action), the *karmaṇyaḥ* (one who is fit for ritual acts), the *ramaḥ* (the one whose essence is *rasa*), the *mahān* (great) as superior in qualities, the *adabdhaḥ* (unassailable), he who moves (*yate*) crookedly (*huruk*)—
that is to say, he wanders here and there; for that purpose, he purifies himself (*pavate*) from the realm of heaven (*divaḥ*).
The meaning is that he is purified by the filter of the atmosphere.
Furthermore, this Soma is pressed;
when?

In order to avoid [harm] while the settlements remain unharmed—what kind of one are we?—he is *mitra*, a friend to all; *yajñiya*, worthy of sacrifice; like an *atya*, a steed, in a herd—that is, in a herd of mares—he, being a *vṛṣayu* (desiring the bull), makes a sound; even so, this *vṛṣabha*, the showerer of essence (*rasa*), having bellowed (*kanikradat*) with a roar, has poured forth.
‘Pra rājā vācam’ is the eleventh hymn in the fifth [maṇḍala]. The seer and other details are as before. It is indexed under ‘Pra rājā’.
The application is concluded.
The King, generating the voice and flowing forth, clothing himself in the waters, desires to win the cows.
He seizes the inspired hymn with his body; pure, he goes to the appointed place of the gods.

The King, generating speech, has rushed forward; clothing himself in the waters, he strives toward the cows. He seizes the impurity with his body as a filter; purified, he goes to the appointed place of the gods. 1.
This king, shining as Soma while being pressed, flows forth, generating sound;
likewise, clothing himself in the *vasatīvarī* waters, he approaches the cows—that is, the hymns of praise.
The root *iyakṣati* is listed among the verbs meaning "to go."

At the time of purification, he takes hold of the *ripra*—the impurity consisting of dregs, husks, and other refuse—which is like sin, of this Soma, using the *avi*, the woolen filter (*daśāpavitra*) made from sheep’s wool, or with his own garment.
Afterwards, being purified, he approaches the *niṣkṛta*, the prepared place of the gods.

O Soma, you are poured out for Indra by the men; as a wave, a sage, you are pressed in the wood. For many are your pressings for your journey; there are a thousand bay horses, swelling with the contents of the vats.

O Soma, you are poured out for Indra by the men; you, the seer who beholds men, are anointed as a wave upon the wood. For many are your pressings to come hither; a thousand bay horses are yours, seated in the vessels. 2.
O Soma, you are purified—that is, pressed—by the men, the leaders, the officiating priests, for the sake of Indra.

Likewise, O Soma, you who are the beholder of men (*nṛcakṣas*), looking with favor upon the sacrificers; you who are the wave (*ūrmi*) being impelled or swelling forth, and the wise one (*kavi*), are anointed—that is, impelled—within the wood, that is, the water.
For many indeed are your pressings (*sutayaḥ*), your paths of rushing toward the goal, for you to travel.
Since it is impossible for a limited amount of Soma to undergo immeasurable praise, he speaks of its abundance:
"Of the *camūdas*—those seated upon the two pressing-boards—there are a thousand, immeasurable, swift, bay-colored shoots.
Or alternatively:
Because it has been stated, "O you who are being sprinkled for Indra," the connection between the path and the means of attainment upon reaching Indra is established by the second half of the verse.
Those ancient, swift-moving ones proceed toward Indra;
likewise, there are a thousand bay-colored horses, as indicated by the term *camūṣad*.

The celestial nymphs (*apsarasaḥ*) belonging to the ocean— so called because the ocean is their means of attainment— the ocean being the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)— those certain nymphs associated with it, sitting within the sacrifice in the vessels as the *vasatīvarī* waters, flow toward the wise Soma; they flow toward the Soma as he is being pressed.

These waters indeed impel, increase, and nourish him who is accustomed to the service of the *harmya*—the sacrificial hall that provides comfort like a palace. Or rather, those very waters are the singers who pray for and seek from the purifying Soma his inexhaustible and undiminished favor (*sumna*). This is the underlying sense.

Certain celestial nymphs, desiring King Soma, the wise one, abandoned even the gods and came from heaven; standing near the king, they took his pleasure, increased his vigor with their own essence, and entreated him for happiness.

The Soma that wins cattle, wins chariots, wins gold, wins the light of heaven, wins the waters, wins the mountains, and wins thousands—the exhilarating draught which the gods have prepared for drinking, the sweetest drop, ruddy and a source of bliss. O Soma, winner of cattle, winner of chariots, winner of gold, winner of the light of heaven, winner of the waters, winner of the mountains, and winner of great wealth—[we praise] that exhilarating draught which the gods have fashioned for drinking, the most delicious drop, ruddy and a source of joy.

Soma, the winner of cattle for us, likewise the winner of chariots, the winner of gold, the winner of heaven (the joy of the celestial realm), the winner of waters, the winner of thousands—that is, the winner of wealth numbering in the thousands—purifies himself;
he whom the gods have fashioned.
For what purpose?

For drinking—that is, for the sake of quaffing—what kind of Soma? Intoxicating (*madaṃ*), which produces exhilaration; most sweet (*svādiṣṭhaṃ*), the very best in flavor; *drapsaṃ*, consisting of essence; *aruṇaṃ*, reddish in color; and *mayobhuvaṃ*, the bringer of happiness.

O Soma, flowing forth, making these true riches manifest for us, you flow on. Strike down the enemy, both the one who is near and the one who is far away; grant us wide pasture and security. 5. O Soma, flowing forth, making these true riches manifest for us, you flow on. Strike down the enemy, both the one who is near and the one who is far away; grant us wide pasture and security. 5.
O Soma, making these true riches—the wealth consisting of cattle and mountains mentioned in the preceding mantra—while being purified as Pavamāna, you flow forth.
Slay the enemy; slay him who is our foe, whether he be near at hand or far away in a distant land.
Likewise, grant us a wide pasture and security.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses, begins with “acodasaḥ.
The seer and other details are as before. It is indexed under the heading “acodasaḥ.”
The application is concluded.
1. [The Soma] whose nature is to resort to the body; [it is] for the protection of the body and the womb.

May the pressed drops, the tawny ones, flow forth for us toward those of lofty heaven, unimpelled. And may our enemies be scattered; may the hostile powers perish. May they reach us, and may our prayers be successful. 1. Unimpelled, may the drops flow forth for us—the pressed tawny ones among those of lofty heaven. And may our enemies be scattered; may the hostile powers perish. May they reach us, and may our prayers be successful.
May the Soma drops—bestowing speech, unimpelled, and not urged by another—flow forth for us; that is, may they go forward.
The root *dhanv* signifies motion.
Where?
In the *bṛhaddiva* sacrifices— meaning those characterized by abundant luster—
or alternatively, among those born of the *bṛhaddiva* lineage;
"na" is the connection of the mantra.
Of what nature are the drops?
They are being pressed (*suvānāsaḥ*), being purified (*sūyamānāḥ*), and they are golden-hued (*harayaḥ*).
Furthermore, those who are non-givers (*varātayaḥ*)—those who do not bestow food (*anna*) upon us (*naḥ*) and others—let them perish (*vinaśan*).
Likewise, let even the noble ones perish;
let them not enjoy our deeds, O gods who have become dear to us.

May the drops, distilling exhilaration, flow forth for us—those by which we urge on our steeds for the sake of wealth. Beyond the obstruction of any mortal whatsoever, may we carry away riches in every way.
Let our Soma drops, which cause exhilaration, flow forth toward us—drops that distill intoxication and pour out joy.
Or rather (*vā*): or else; it has the sense of "something more."

May riches indeed flow forth toward us. With those [riches] by which we reach the presence of the powerful enemy who obstructs Soma, we drive him away; driving him away, we attain them. Transcending the encompassing oppression of any whatsoever mortal man, may we always carry forth riches in the form of cattle and other wealth.

Indeed, he is the enemy of his own ill-will, and he is the wolf of the ill-will of others. As thirst overcomes one in the desert, so may he overcome them; O Soma Pavamāna, strike down those evil-minded ones! uta | svasyāḥ | arātyāḥ | ariḥ | hi | saḥ | uta | anyasyāḥ | arātyāḥ | vṛkaḥ | hi | saḥ | dhanvan | na | tṛṣṇā | sam | arīta | tān | abhi | soma | jahi | pavamāna | duḥādhyaḥ ||3|| He is indeed the foe of his own hostility, and he is indeed the wolf of the hostility of another. As thirst prevails in the desert, so let it prevail over them; O Soma, O Pavamāna, strike down those of evil intent.
Moreover, that Soma is the one who goes forth against the enemy's hostility for the sake of slaying him;
moreover, that Soma is the wolf indeed against our own enemy’s hostility, for the enemy (*arāti*) is surely a harmer.
Note that the word *arāti* exists even in the feminine gender.
Now, that which is produced by direct perception:
"thirst in a desert.
A desert is a region devoid of water.
Just as thirst, once it has taken hold of one, overcomes him, so too do you slay those two kinds of enemies.
1. *ta-nosmātyai*; *bha6-nosmākam* | 2. *ga-ta1.2.5.7-bhara.6-naśyantu*; *ta3.4-naśanta naśyantu* | 3. *bha1.7-pra dhanvantu pragacchantu* is not present.
4. In the manuscripts ga, bha1(2), the word "or" (athavā) is not present.
5. In the manuscripts ta and su, it means "something" (kiñcit).
6. In the manuscripts ta, bha6, and mu, [it refers to] the acquisition of a friend from an enemy.
O Pavamāna Soma, strike down those enemies who have come against us; let ignorance fall upon them, and slay those evil-minded foes!

Your highest navel is in heaven, where you were born; your branches have grown over the ridges of the earth. The pressing-stones chew you upon the hide of the cow; the wise have milked you with their hands from the waters.

In heaven, at your navel, he who is supreme has drawn you up; upon the ridges of the earth, the swift fingers of the pressing-stones have climbed. They devour you upon the ox-hide; the wise ones have milked you with their hands from the waters.
O Soma, that supreme and highest portion of yours exists in heaven, at the navel of the sky—in the region that serves as the center of the celestial world;
or rather, at the "navel" which is the source of rain and other benefits, in the realm of heaven.
It is that which, taking the form of a deity, accepts the oblation.
Those parts of yours situated in the heavenly world, having been cast upon the high ridges of the earth—the regions of mountains and the like—have grown; they grow.
The pressing-stones (*adryaḥ*), which are the soma-pressers, devour you, who have become a portion of the heavenly world; *bapsati* means "to eat."
Where?
On the skin of the bull.
The word *ardhī* restates the meaning of the locative case.
This means on the ox-hide used for pressing.
Although nowadays people press upon a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and not on an ox-hide, nevertheless, the Soma is measured upon that [antelope skin] for the purpose of purchase.

And this being so, there is no contradiction, because according to the Sūtra—"The pressing-skin belongs to that upon which one measures"—it is specifically the ox-hide, as the instrument of measurement, that is designated as the "pressing-skin."
In that manner, they have milked, or are milking, you—the *vasatīvarī* waters; the meaning is that the Aṅgirases, having reached you, milk you.
Or else:
They milked [the cows] from the waters, the liquids, and the signs;
by what means?
By their hands.
‘The hand [is derived] from the root han’ (Nirukta 1.7). By whom?
By the *manīṣiṇaḥ*, the wise ones—the Adhvaryus and others.
Thus, O Indu, they press out for you your well-being and well-formed juice, as the first ones who pour it forth.
O Pavamāna, drive away the stingy one; let your impetuous strength be manifest, a dear and exhilarating intoxication.

Thus, O Indu, they press out your juice—mighty and well-fashioned—as the first ones to be honored. O Pavamāna, you have brought low those who lie in ambush. Let your vigor be manifest; let your exhilaration be beloved. ||5||
In the preceding [verse], it was said, "The mountain devours you"; that very thing is now being stated.
O *indu*, O Soma, in this manner (*eva*)—that is, by the method currently being performed—your *subhvaṃ* (well-being), which is a beautiful state of being, is *supeśasam*.
*Peśas* is a name for form (*rūpa*).
The first ones [the Maruts] [attained] beautiful flavor at the very outset;
or rather,
"first" (prathama) is a name for the principal one.

The *prathamaḥ*, meaning the foremost or principal ones— the pressing-stones or the Adhvaryu priests— being *abhidhriyaḥ*, that is, being pressed, *tuñjanti*, meaning they impel [the juice]. O *pavamāna*, *nirdanidaṃ*, meaning the one who cuts us down, destroy *sarvam api śatrum ni tāriṣaḥ*, every single enemy without exception.
May your *śuṣma*, which causes trembling, and your *madah*, the beloved exhilarating juice that has become dear, be manifest.

The thirteenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “*somasya dhārā*,” is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Ghasu, a descendant of Bharadvāja; it is in the *jagatī* meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity.
Thus it is enumerated: “*Somasya*; Vasu [is the name]; [the seer is] Bhāradvāja.
The application (*viniyoga*) has been explained.
The stream of Soma, who beholds men, flows clear; by the Eternal Law he calls the gods from heaven.
O Bṛhaspati, it flashes forth with unswerving light; like the oceans, they have poured out their libations.

The stream of Soma, who beholds men, flows clear; by the Eternal Law, he calls the gods from heaven. Through the impulse of Bṛhaspati, he flashes forth; like the oceans, his libations have spread abroad. || 1 ||

The stream of the Soma being pressed flows forth for the one who hears. Of what kind of Soma? Of that which is "nṛcakṣas," the beholder of men—the sacrificers. And he, by means of *ṛta*—the sacrifice—invokes the gods, Indra and others who partake of the Soma. Where? From above the sky, from the world of heaven.
By the roar, the sound, the hymn of Bṛhaspati—the protector of the mantras and the praiser—it flashes forth like lightning.
Like oceans, the libations pervade and encompass the earth, which is connected with the sacrifice.

O vigorous one, you whom the priests have celebrated with hymns—you, resplendent, now ascend this place of birth. Prolonging the life of the honeyed [draughts], O Soma, you flow as a bull, a great exhilaration, for Indra’s glory.

O vigorous one, upon whom the noble ones have looked down with longing—you, being resplendent, ascend to the womb of the sweet juices. Extending the life-span and great renown, O Soma, you flow as a bull, a gladdening draught, for Indra. 2.

O Soma, possessor of food, you who are swift; you whom the cows of the two days have lowed toward—you praise you. This means that, standing for the sake of the milk-mixture (*āśir*), they make a sound.
You, [Soma], [the juice] struck from iron—*ayas* being a name for gold.
By that [word], the hand is indicated.
With a golden hand, you ascend to the prepared place of origin (*yoni*), being radiant and shining;
thus the reading "abhi yonim ayohatam" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.1.2) is appropriate.
Furthermore, O Soma, extending the life-span and the great glory—whether as food or fame—of the sacrificers who possess the honeyed oblation, you flow clear for Indra;
you are the showerer, the exhilarating one who brings joy.

In the belly of Indra, upon the mountain, he intoxicates himself; clothing himself in vigor, most auspicious for the sake of renown, he has spread out toward all beings. Playing, the tawny bull flows onward.

Into the belly of Indra flows the most intoxicating one, clothing himself in strength for the sake of glory, most auspicious. He has spread himself out toward all beings; playing, the tawny, vigorous steed rushes forward. 3.
This Soma flows into and is poured into the belly of Indra;
for what purpose?
For glory—that is, for his food—in order to accomplish the attainment of food after having sacrificed.
Soma is qualified as *madintamaḥ*, meaning most intoxicating; and *ūrjaṃ vasānaḥ*, meaning clothing himself in strength, that is, enveloping himself in the sap that produces power.
The phrase "the receptacle of waters" (*apām vamānaḥ*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.78.1) is appropriate.
Being most auspicious— that is, bestowing beautiful blessings—
that Soma extends himself toward all beings, pervading every class of living creatures.
Having arisen in the sky, sporting and playing upon the altar, Hari—the green-colored one, the steed skilled in traversing, the showerer—flows in the form of essence.
The men, the ten fingers, milk you out for the gods—you, the most honey-sweet one with a thousand streams.
Soma, pressed by the stones and poured forth by the men, flow as you purify yourself for all the gods, O winner of thousands!
Thee, the most honey-sweet, the men—the ten fingers—milk for the gods in a thousand streams. O Soma, pressed by the stones and impelled by the men, flow for all the gods, O winner of thousands! 4.

O Soma, they—the leaders, the officiating priests—milk you, such as you are, for the sake of the gods and for Indra’s purpose; they milk you who are most rich in sweetness, exceeding full of honey, and possessed of a thousand streams, that is, many streams.
Who [are they]? The leaders, the officiating priests.
Ten fingers—meaning ten in number—are for them;

O Soma, you who are set in motion by men, pressed out and extracted by the stones, you who are the winner of thousands, the conqueror of wealth numbering in the thousands, flow forth and purify yourself for all the gods.
The ten fingers strike you, the honeyed bull, with stones in the waters;
O Soma, exhilarating Indra and the divine host, you flow like the surging wave of the ocean as you are pressed.

The ten fingers milk you, the honey-sweet bull among the waters, with the stones—O Soma, exhilarating Indra and the divine folk. Flowing forth like a wave of the river, you spread out as you are purified. 5.

The ten fingers—the swift-moving hands—of the skillful-handed man milk you, such as you are: honeyed, sweet-flavored, a bull who showers down desires—with stones that are like pressing-boards, in the waters.
O Soma, gladdening Indra and the other divine host, you, being purified and flowing like a wave of the river, proceed.

The hymn beginning with "pra somasya" consists of five verses. The seer and deity are as previously stated. The remaining three [verses] are in the Jagatī meter. This is indicated by the phrase "pra somasya. The application (viniyoga) has been explained.

The well-adorned waves of the purifying Soma go forth into the belly of Indra. When the pressed juices, led by Dabha and accompanied by glory, have exhilarated the Hero for the giving of cattle. 1. The waves of the purifying Soma go forth into the belly of Indra, beautifully adorned. When the pressed juices, led by Dabha and accompanied by glory, have exhilarated the Hero for the giving of cattle. 1.
The "waves"—the streams of essence—of the "Pavamāna," the one being purified, "go forth" (pra-yanti) into the "belly" (jaṭharam) of Indra.
The connection is that these waves are "well-formed" (supeśasaḥ), meaning beautiful in appearance.

When these pressed (suta) Soma juices, having been extracted, are joined with the "glory" (yaśasā)—which is the strength—of the cows, and with "skill" (dakṣā), and thus being uplifted, they exhilarate (udamandiṣuḥ) the heroic and valiant Indra for the sake of giving—that is, for the granting of what is desired by the sacrificer—then they go into his belly.

For Soma has flowed toward the jars like a swift, vigorous steed on its course; he, the bull, knowing both lineages of the gods, hears the nectar from here and that which is beyond. 2. For Soma has flowed toward the jars like a swift, vigorous steed on its course; he, the bull, knowing both lineages of the gods, hears the nectar from here and that which is beyond.
This Soma flows toward, that is, faces, the jars; like what?
Like the "vohā" of this [chariot], that is, like the horse that draws the chariot.
He goes just as one goes to his own destination;
or rather,
this is an illustration for what follows later.
Like a merchant on a road, like Raghuvartani who moves swiftly, and like a bull that rains down;
then, knowing both kinds of birth—that of Agni and of the gods who enjoy the Soma—he has flowed into the jars with his knowledge.
What are those two births? It is explained as follows:
That which, as soon as it is born, "from there"—from the world beyond, the heavenly world—and "from here"—from this world—“hears,” that is, pervades the sacrifice;
the connection is: “knowing the birth of both of those.”

O Soma, as you flow clear, scatter wealth upon us; O Indu, be a giver of great bounty. Bestow strength upon the liberal patron with your gracious wisdom; do not cast us away from our home into the distance. 3. O Soma, as you flow clear, scatter wealth upon us; O Indu, be a giver of great bounty. Bestow strength upon the liberal patron with your gracious wisdom; do not cast us away from our home into the distance. 3.
1. With the strength of a bull;
2. O Soma, being purified as you flow, scatter and spread us [the wealth] on every side for our sake.
What?
"Vasu" means wealth, such as cattle and the like, which provides dwelling.
Furthermore, "O Indu," O Soma, "you are Maghavan," meaning wealthy; "be the giver"—this is the ellipsis—"of 'mahaḥ rādhasaḥ'," that is, of great wealth.
Thus, O *vathodhaḥ*, bestower of food, O Soma, through your excellent wisdom (*cetunā*), grant (*śikṣa*) me, who serve you for the sake of dwelling (*vasave*), that which is easy and auspicious.
Do not cast away (*parā sicaḥ*) from us—that which is to be given to us—the wealth (*gaya*) which is far (*āre*) from us.

May Pūṣan, Parjanya, and the bounteous Mitra come to us; may Varuṇa, who is most gracious, Bṛhaspati, the Maruts, Vāyu, the Aśvins, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, the well-guiding Sarasvatī [come to us]. 4. May Pūṣan, Parjanya, the bounteous Mitra, and Varuṇa of excellent protection come to us; may Bṛhaspati, the Maruts, Vāyu, the two Aśvins, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, the well-guiding Sarasvatī [come to us]. 4.
May the gods Pūṣan and the others—those who are well-disposed, bountiful givers, and who have come together in harmony—come toward us, to our sacrifice.
Likewise, may they be "well-restrained" (*suyamā*); the analysis of the term *yama* is that which is restrained or controlled.
And may Sarasvatī, of beautiful form, come hither.

May both Heaven and Earth, the all-pervading; the god Aryaman; Aditi; the Ordainer; Bhaga; the one who blesses men; the wide mid-air; and all the gods, take pleasure in the one who is being purified. (5) Both: dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth). Viśvaminve: viśvam'inve (the two who encompass everything). Aryamā. Devaḥ (the god). Aditiḥ. Vidhātā (the Ordainer). Bhagaḥ. Nṛśaṃsaḥ (the one who blesses men). Uru (wide). Antarikṣam (the mid-air). Viśve (all). Devāḥ (the gods). Parvamānam (the one being purified). Juṣanta (may they take pleasure in). (5)
"O all-pervading ones! The root *invati* means 'to pervade.

Both *dyāvāpṛthivī*, heaven and earth, who pervade everything; and Aryaman and the others, as well as Bhaga, who is praised by men (*nṛśaṃsaḥ*); and the wide mid-air (*urv antarikṣam*); and all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*)—they enjoy and serve the purifying Soma."
The hymn beginning with "asāvi" consists of five verses and fifteen [syllables per verse].
The seer and other details are as before.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Asāvi... ending in Triṣṭubh."
By this dual designation, it is established that both of the two *prakṛtis*, namely "pra somasya" and so forth, end in *triṣṭubh* meters. The application (*viniyoga*) has been explained.

The Soma has been pressed—the ruddy, virile, tawny one. Like a king from heaven, he has bellowed toward the cows. Being purified, he goes around the woolly filter; like a falcon, he settles upon his ghee-rich womb. 1. The Soma has been pressed—the ruddy, virile, tawny one. Like a king from heaven, he has bellowed toward the cows. Being purified, he goes around the woolly filter; like a falcon, he settles upon his ghee-rich womb. 1.
"Soma has been pressed; it has become infused.
Of what nature is Soma? It is *aruṣa*, shining; *vṛṣā*, raining down [blessings]; *hari*, green-colored."
And he, like a king, being "dasma" (wondrous) and beautiful to behold, "acikradat"—makes a sound—directed toward the "gāḥ" (waters) at the time of his natural release;

thereafter, "punānaḥ" (being purified), he passes through the "avyam" (woolen) "vāram" (filter), that is, the hair-strainer known as the *daśāpavitra*. Then, like a "śyena" (hawk), he purifies himself [the ellipsis being "for the sake of"] "āsadam" (sitting down) upon his own "yoni" (place/seat), which is "ghṛtavat" (rich in water).

1. O Sage, you go about seeking greatness; like a groomed steed, you rush toward the prize. Warding off misfortunes, O Soma, be gracious! Shedding clarity like ghee, you flow around your mantle. 2. O Sage, with the wisdom of a seer, you go about seeking greatness; like a groomed steed, you rush toward the prize. Warding off misfortunes, O Soma, be gracious! Shedding clarity like ghee, you flow around your mantle.

O Soma, being a seer (*kavi*) of lovely vision, you go around the mighty, enduring purifier with the desire for the performance of sacrifice. Then, cleansed and washed like a steed, you hasten toward the prize of battle.
O Soma, driving away and warding off our misfortunes, be gracious and bring us happiness.
Clothing yourself in ghee and water, you go around, that is, you approach;
what?
Your cleansing garment, the purifying filter.

Parjanya is the father of the great-winged bird; he has established his dwelling upon the mountains at the navel of the earth. The sister waters have flowed toward the cows; he unites with the pressing-stones when the sacrifice is performed. Parjanya is the father of the great-winged bird; he has established his dwelling upon the mountains at the navel of the earth. The sister waters have flowed toward the cows; he unites with the pressing-stones when the sacrifice is performed.

Of that great buffalo-like Soma, who possesses leaves or wings and is prone to falling, Parjanya is the father and progenitor; that Soma maintains his dwelling (*kṣayam*) upon the earth—at its very center, in the place of the navel, namely the *havirdhāna*—and among the mountains, that is, among the pressing-stones associated with the hills, at the time of the pressing.
Moreover, the sisters—the fingers, the waters, the *vasatīvarī* vessels, the cows for the milk-mixture, or the hymns of praise—rush toward him and come together;
he unites and comes into contact with the pressing-stones.
Where?
When the beloved sacrifice was concluded.

Like a wife toward her husband, you bestow auspiciousness upon Pajra; hear the embryo [within you], for I speak it to you. Move among the inner voices so that you may live well; O blameless Soma, be watchful at the turning-point. Like a wife toward her husband, you bestow auspiciousness upon Pajra; hear the embryo [within you], for I speak it to you. Move among the inner voices so that you may live well; O blameless Soma, be watchful at the turning-point.

Like a wife [bestowing] upon her husband, as a wife gives happiness to her lord, so [O Agni], bestow—*śeva śevam* (happiness after happiness). The absence of the *ām* suffix in the second case is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). You grant (*maṃhase*) happiness to the sacrificer.
O Soma, you who are the embryo within the *pajrā*, listen; listen to these praises; I speak them unto you.
*Pajri* is a word for the act of moving;
they say that *pajrā* is the earth.
Alternatively, the speech of the intermediate region (mādhyamikī vāk) is *pajrā*.
It possesses that form because it is born upon the earth in the form of plants;
furthermore, since the speech of the intermediate region is also the means for bringing rain, it is its "son."
As such, enter well—most excellently—into the midst of our songs, our words, and our hymns, so that we may live.
O Soma, you who are beyond reproach and worthy of praise, be watchful and awake against the host of our enemies.
As you have brought a hundredfold and thousandfold booty from of old for those who do not fail, O Indu, so flow now for new prosperity; noble seekers of the truth attend to your ordinance.
1. In the regions connected with Ga-giri; 2. In Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.4.5, the word "abhyasaran" is absent.

As follows: From the ancients, O Indu, thou art a winner of hundreds, a winner of immortality, a winner of thousands, and a winner of wealth from the Aryas; even so, flow on for new prosperity, for thy law the waters follow. 5.

O Indu, O Soma, just as you were for the ancient great seers who praised you—a giver of hundreds, a bestower of wealth numbering in the hundreds, and likewise a giver of thousands—so may you now go forth through the mountain passes. Even so, flow and pour out now for a newer, more recent prosperity.
The waters, the *vasatīvarī* waters, follow after your ritual act (*vrata*);
therefore, flow on.
The hymn beginning with "pavitraṃ te" consists of five verses; it is the sixteenth hymn, composed by the seer Pavitra Āṅgirasa, in the Jāgata meter, and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity.
Thus it is enumerated: "pavitraṃ te pavitram.
In this hymn, the first two verses are to be recited as an *abhiṣṭava*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'pavitraṃ te vitataṃ brahmaṇaspate' and 'vi yatpavitraṃ dhiṣaṇā atanvata'—these two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.6).
Your purifier, O Brahmaṇaspati, is spread out; it has encompassed your limbs from every side.
That which is raw does not enjoy what is unheated; only those who are cooked and have offered oblations have attained that.

The purifier is stretched out for you, O Brahmanaspati; as the Lord, you go around all our limbs from every side. One whose body has not been heated does not partake of that [purification]; only those who are cooked [by fire] and carry it [within] attain it. 1.

O Brahmaṇaspati, O Lord of the mantra, O Soma, this *apavitra*—the purifying limb—is spread everywhere, extended throughout. You, the Lord, the powerful one, encompass on all sides the limbs, the various members.
That purifier of yours is not attained—that is, it does not pervade—the raw, unripened person whose body has not been heated by the milk-vow and other such disciplines.
"Being cooked," that is, indeed thoroughly ripened, "carrying," meaning performing the sacrifice, they have "attained," that is, pervaded, "that purifier."
The purifier is spread out upon the station of heaven during the heatings; its radiant threads have extended far.
The swift ones protect its purifier; with their mind, they stand upon the back of heaven.

The purifier of heat is spread across the station of heaven; its glowing threads have extended far and wide. The swift ones protect its purifier; with conscious intent, they stand upon the back of heaven.

The *pavitra*—the purifying limb or the radiant energy (*tejas*)—of Soma, the scorcher of enemies through his heat, is spread out and extended in the lofty place of heaven, the station of the celestial world.
As the Brāhmaṇa states: "In the third heaven from here, Soma was" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.1.1).
His threads—the stalks of the plant—are shining, blazing, and stand stretched across the distance.
On the earth or in the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*):
"The swift-moving juices of this Soma protect— whom?"

The *pavitāraḥ* (purifiers) are those who purify; they protect—that is, they guard—the sacrificer by means of the oblation (*homa*). Being situated "behind" the sacrifice, they "stand upon" (*adhi tiṣṭhanti*), that is, they take their place upon the "back"—the elevated region—of "heaven" (*divaḥ*), the celestial world, through their "consciousness" (*cetasā*), that is, by the power of their intention to go to the gods.
In the *abhiṣṭava* [laudation], the verse beginning with "arūrucat" is to be omitted.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'īle dyāvāpṛthivī' [is recited] prior to the final verse; 'arūrucad uṣasaḥ pṛśnir agniḥ' is likewise to be omitted" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.6).
1. Just as those who do not fail [attain] booty in battle; 2. Just so, even thus, by these [means], indeed thus, thus;
3. They attend upon, they serve.
4. *bha* is for you (*tava*).
5. By [the rule] beginning with *bhaṣ-sthānau* etc.
6. In *ga₁*, *ta₃*, *bha₁.₂.₇*, "carrying" (*vahaṃtaḥ*) is absent.
7. According to the Śruti: "That which is overcooked belongs to Rudra; that which is undercooked belongs to the gods; that which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti.
8. Of that which is pervasive (ta). 9. Of that which causes desiccation (ga).
10. The streams of Soma have been offered; they have been poured forth through the gate of the sacrifice.
The dappled bull has caused the dawns to shine; the prize-winning steed sustains all worlds.
By his creative power, the masters of illusion have measured it out; the fathers, who behold men, have deposited the germ.

The dappled dawn has shone forth; the beloved bull supports all the worlds, seeking strength. By his creative power, the masters of illusion have measured it out; the fathers, who behold men, have deposited the germ. || 3 ||
The *pṛśni* connected with the dawns is the Āditya;
as the Nirukta states: "The *pṛśni* is the Āditya, for his color reaches out [to all]" (Nirukta 2.14).
This *apriya*, the principal one, this very Soma, has shone forth (*arūrucat*)—that is, he causes [all] to shine.
He, the bull, the sprinkler of water, sustains and nourishes the worlds— the multitudes of beings— with water, desiring their food;
he is possessed of *māyā*,
for *māyā* is wisdom.
The wise gods have measured out [the world] through the creative power (*māyā*)— that is, the wisdom— of this Soma;
O possessors of oblations, you whose strength has been born from drinking a single portion of the Soma!
*Havis* is a name for water.
Like Soma, the water has become the sacrificial offering (*havis*);
this is a name for water.
The meaning is "the essence of water.
Enveloping—that is, clothing yourself in—the great, divine sevenfold sacrificial hall, you go around, that is, you traverse it, in order to complete the sacrifice.
Furthermore, O Soma, as King and possessor of the chariot that is the filter (*pavitra*), you ascend to battle.
Alternatively,
since the practice of using terms denoting battle for sacrificial rites is observed here and there, "vāja" here refers to the sacrifice as a battle;
you have ascended that.
The sense is that it is just as when a certain king, having mounted his chariot, enters his own abode.
Furthermore, he is "thousand-spoked" (*sahasrabhṛṣṭi*),
meaning he possesses many parts.
The meaning is "one who goes immeasurably.
Alternatively, *bhṛṣṭi* means a weapon;
thus, he is one who possesses innumerable weapons.
O you of great fame, you conquer great food for us.

The hymn beginning with “*pavasva devamādanaḥ*,” consisting of five verses, is the seventeenth *sūkta*. It belongs to Prajāpati, the son of Vāc; it is composed in the *Jagatī* meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity.
Thus it is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: “*pavasva vācyaḥ prajāpatiḥ*.
Its ritual application (*viniyoga*) has been explained.

The god who gladdens at the joints [of the sacrifice], the far-seeing one, has appeared for Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu. Prepare for us today wide space and well-being; sing praise to the divine host dwelling in the vast expanse.

Pour out [the soma] at the joints [of the sacrifice]. He who gladdens the gods, who dwells among all people, the winner of waters—for Indra, for Varuṇa, and for Vāyu—prepare for us today a wide space accompanied by well-being. Praise the divine host in their broad dwelling. 1.

O Soma, you who exhilarate the gods, the delighter of the deities, the one who observes all with wisdom, the winner of waters, and the giver of water— do you flow and pour forth for Indra, for Varuṇa, and for Vāyu.
O [Agni], create—that is, bring about—for us, for ourselves, *varivas*, wealth that is accompanied by *svasti*; *svasti* is a name for non-destruction (*avināśa*). Make our wealth such as that.

On the vast earth (*urukṣitau*), which is connected to sacrifice, praise (*gṛṇīhi*) the divine host (*daivyam janam*), the assembly related to the gods; for the word *jana* denotes a multitude. Praise that [assembly].
The root *gṛṇāti* has "sound" as its object; it means "make sound.
The sense is: "Make sound in such a way that, upon hearing the sound of your pressing [of Soma], the gods come."
Alternatively, the seer refers to himself as "the divine folk" (*daivyam janam*);
that is, he says, "Regard me as a person connected to the gods; call me a true devotee."
The immortal Soma, who has taken his place over all the worlds, flows around them;
making the gathering and the parting for our aid, Indu follows after us as the sun follows the dawn.
He who stands over all the worlds, the immortal Soma—let him flow around them all, effecting both union and separation for our aid; Indu follows close after us like the sun. 2.
The immortal, divine Soma, who has taken his stand upon all these worlds, flows around— that is, he moves around and protects—
all those entire worlds.

This very drop (*indu*), making the sacrifice or the sacrificer "bound" (*saṃcṛta*)—that is, connected with fruits by the gods—and making it "unbound" (*vicṛta*)—that is, liberated from the Asuras or from sufferings—cleaves to and serves the sacrifice on all sides for the sake of the rite;
he does not [fail] the sun.

Just as the sun, for the sake of the welfare [of beings], makes the world gathered together by means of its lights and dispersed by being freed from darkness—thus making it accessible for the movement of living beings in every direction—it likewise attends upon [the Lord].

He who releases [the waters] with the rays upon the plants, seeking the favor of the gods and hastening toward wealth, flows with his lightning-flash in a stream; pressed, Indu, the Soma, gladdens the divine host.
1. *ga*-sātā; 2. *ga*-sukhair vā;
3. *ga*-viyukte.

He who is released with the rays of light among the plants, hastening to the dwelling-place of the gods and bringing wealth, flows with a stream by means of lightning when pressed—the Soma that exhilarates Indra and the divine host. ||3||

That Soma which is poured out with rays [or] with the rays of light into the plants—that is, they establish that Soma—why? for the sake of the gods' *sunna*, meaning their happiness. Of what nature is he? *Iṣayan*: desiring to reach the gods; from the root *iṣ* "to go. Or, desiring wealth; likewise, *upavāsuḥ*: one who has obtained wealth from his enemies. That Soma, being pressed, flows forth with a flashing stream. What does he do? Gladdening Indra, the divine lord of the gods.
This Soma flows on, the winner of thousands, impelling the vigorous voice that awakens the wise.
Indu drives toward the ocean with the winds; he settles in the jars within the heart of Indra.

This very Soma flows on, the winner of thousands; being urged forth, the fierce drop sends out a vigorous voice. He raises up his awakening from the ocean with the winds; he settles into the heart of Indra within the jars. 4.
This very Soma flows and is purified. Of what nature is he?
He is the conqueror of thousands, the victor over a thousandfold.
Doing what? Impelling—that is, setting in motion—the speech of the officiating priests, which consists of hymns of praise.
What kind of speech?
The active one, moving toward the object of praise,

awakened at dawn— this very Soma, the moon, causes the ocean, the oceanic essence, to rise up by means of the winds, that is, by the moving ones such as the Adhvaryu priests and others, or indeed by the winds themselves, while being delighted; likewise, he fills the heart of Indra.
The *hārda* is that which is dear. That *hārda* of Indra becomes his favorite expression; thus he settles within the jars, beginning with the *droṇakalaśa*.
The cows mix that Soma with milk—the increaser of milk, the bestower of good offerings—with their prayers.
The active, effective juice flows as a bowstring; he is the inspired sage, the seer through his poetic wisdom, and resplendent with celestial light.

The cows surround him with milk—the Soma who increases the milk—with their prayers; he is the finder of light. The winner of wealth, the effective juice flows clear; the inspired sage, the seer, through his poetic wisdom, shines with the light of heaven. 5.
The cows mix that Soma—which increases milk, the increaser of milk—with their own milk; they perform the act of mixing it.
They mix that Soma who, through prayers and hymns, bestows everything; he is the finder of light.
That Soma, the winner of wealth, the conqueror of the riches of enemies, flows and purifies himself through his poetic work.
Of what nature is he?

He is effective (*kṛtya*), capable of action (*karmanya*), essence (*rasa*), having the form of essence, a sage (*vipra*), wise (*medhāvin*), a seer (*kavi*) of far-reaching insight, radiant with his own splendor (*svarcasas*), and complete in all his limbs.
*Cana* is a particle used for emphasis.
The eighteenth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “indrāya,” is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Vena of the Bhṛgu lineage; its deity is Pavamāna Soma.
The eleventh and twelfth verses are Triṣṭubhs, while the remaining verses are Jagatīs.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “indrāya [dvādaśa], Vena Bhārgava; it ends with two Triṣṭubhs.”
The application is concluded.
O Soma, flow well-praised for Indra; let disease vanish along with the demons.
Let not the two deceitful ones delight in thy juice; here let the wealthy gods be present.
1. Support the divine people. 2. Having gone there, the cows mix that Soma with milk.
Of what kind?

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: they mix with [milk] that Soma who increases milk—that is, who causes milk to increase—through prayers and hymns; who finds the light of heaven; who is the bestower of everything; the winner of wealth; the conqueror; the one worthy of action; the one whose form is essence (*rasa*); the wise one; the intelligent one; the seer (*kavi*) by virtue of his poetic work (*kāvyena kavikarmaṇā*); and the one possessing self-radiance and complete limbs. Those who mix [with him] are thus described.
O Soma, well-pressed for Indra, flow around; let the demon be driven away along with his following. Let not the double-dealers delight in your juice; let the drops here be full of wealth. 1.

O Soma, you who are well-pressed and thoroughly purified, flow around for the sake of Indra; go forth, release your juice! May this disease, together with the Rākṣasa, depart and be separated from us. Having drunk their own portion of your juice, let the double-minded—those joined with duality, namely falsehood (the opposite of truth)—the wicked, not exhilarate me. Furthermore, O drops, may these juices of yours be full of wealth in this sacrifice.

O Pavamāna, urge us forward in the battle; for you are the skillful exhilaration of the gods, beloved by them. Strike down the enemies who raise their voices in derision; let Indra drink the Soma, and drive away our assailants.

O Pavamāna, urge us on in the battle; for you are the skillful and beloved exhilaration of the gods. Slay the enemies who raise their shouts of defiance; O Indra, drink the Soma, drive away our adversaries, and destroy our foes. 2.

O Pavamāna Soma, impel and urge us forward in this battle, in this conflict; for you are indeed capable (*dakṣa*) among the gods—or rather, you are capable for the gratification of the gods—or rather, you are the exhilarating one (*mada*), the delighter who is dear to the gods and brings them joy. Slay our enemies and come toward us, O you who are accompanied by praises (*bhandanāyat*). *Bhandanā* means hymns of praise, derived from the root *bhand*, which signifies the act of praising. [Come] desiring those praises. And drink the Soma, O Indra, and strike down our adversaries from the battle.
Unharmed, O Indu, you flow as the most exhilarating; you become the most excellent nourishment for Indra.
Many wise ones sing toward you; they kiss the king of this world.
Unharmed, O Indu, you flow as the most exhilarating one; you become the very self of Indra, his supreme nourishment. Many wise ones cry out toward you; they kiss the king of this world. 3.
O Soma, dwelling in the waters, unassailable, unhurt, most gladdening, and most exhilarating, you flow clear and are purified.
You are yourself the supreme essence; you become the nourishment, the food of Indra.
Many wise singers, chanting praises, call out toward Soma, the king of this world, and press him out.
They kiss and they go away.

The wondrous Indu, with a thousand songs and a hundred streams, flows for Indra as desirable honey. Conquering the field, flow toward us; conquering the waters, O bounteous Soma, create for us a wide path.

With a thousand songs of praise, with a hundred streams, O wondrous one, the drop flows clear for Indra as desirable honey. Winning the field, flow hither; winning the waters, O Soma, bounteous one, make a wide path for us. 4.
The one with a thousand songs, who leads in many ways, possessing a hundred streams and endowed with countless currents—the wonderful, marvelous, and great Indu flows for Indra as desirable honey.
Moreover, winning for us both the field and the waters, flow toward the filter;
O Soma, O bountiful showerer, make wide and spacious for us our path.

Making a sound as you flow into the jar, you are mixed with the rays of light; you pass through the sheep’s wool, O Soma of wondrous power. Being cleansed like a spirited horse on its course, O Soma, you have flowed together into the belly of Indra. *karnikadat* (making a sound), *kalaśe* (in the jar), *gobhiḥ* (with the rays of light), *ajayase* (you are mixed), *vi* (through), *avyayam* (the sheep’s wool), *sumāyā* (O you of wondrous power), *vāram* (the fleece), *arhasi* (you pass), *mṛjyamānaḥ* (being cleansed), *atyaḥ* (like a spirited horse), *na* (as), *sānusiḥ* (one who seeks the goal), *indrasya* (of Indra), *soma* (O Soma), *jaṭhare* (in the belly), *sam* (together), *akṣaraḥ* (you have flowed). O Soma, making a sound (*karnikadat*) as you dwell in the jar, you are mixed (*ajayase*) with the rays of light (*gobhiḥ*). You pass through (*vi arhasi*) the sheep’s wool (*avyayam*), the fleece (*vāram*), which is the filter (*daśāpavitra*), by means of that (*sumāyā*). Being cleansed (*mṛjyamānaḥ*), like a spirited horse (*atyaḥ na*) on its course (*sānusiḥ*), O Soma, you have flowed together (*sam akṣaraḥ*) into the belly of Indra.

Sweet, flow for the divine generation; sweet, for Indra whose name is "the one to whom the invocation is easily heard. Sweet, for Mitra, for Varuṇa, for Vāyu, and for Bṛhaspati—honey-sweet and inviolable. O Soma, you who are sweet, flow for the divine generation, that is, for the host of gods. Likewise, flow as something sweet for Indra, whose name is "the one to whom the invocation is easily heard" (su-havītu-nāman), meaning he whose summons is auspiciously heard. Flow for Mitra, for Varuṇa, for Vāyu, and for Bṛhaspati. You are honey-sweet (madhumān)—possessing a sweet essence—and inviolable (adābhya), being unassailable by others.

The ten fingers cleanse the steed in the jar; the thoughts of the sages send forth their speech. Flowing on, they rush toward the beautiful hymn; the intoxicating drops enter Indra. (7) They cleanse the steed—the swift one who stands like a horse—in the jar; the ten fingers, belonging to the Adhvaryu priest, purify him. Likewise, among the sages, the thoughts—the singers—send forth their voices, their hymns of praise. Flowing on, the Soma juices rush toward the beautiful hymn. The intoxicating drops, the exhilarating Soma juices, enter into Indra. (7)

To Ga-janman, the one born from *ga*; to Ta-janman, the deity born from *ta*; to Ta-ma-janman, the deity born from *ta* and *ma*; to Bha-janman, the birth; to Bha-ja-janman, the deity born from *bha* and *ja*. As for *paribhūti*: may the hater who incites violence against us, the obstructive *māki*, be powerless. O *Indo*, O Soma, by means of you as our instrument, may we conquer every kind of wealth.
The far-seeing bull, the sage, has illuminated the lights of heaven from his station above the filter;
the king, lowing loudly, passes through the purifier, while those who watch over men milk the nectar of heaven.

The bull, marked with diverse signs, has taken his place upon the high station; the sage has illuminated the luminous realms of heaven. The King, bellowing loudly, passes through the filter; those of keen vision now milk the nectar of heaven.
This Soma, the bull, the showerer, the far-seeing beholder, has ascended to the sky, the world of heaven.
Having done so, he has caused to shine in various ways the luminous bodies—the stars and other radiant things—belonging to the sky.
Being a seer of transcendent wisdom, King Soma passes beyond the filter, the ten-stranded sieve.
Roaring, he makes a sound;
the Soma juices, the observers of men (*nṛcakṣasaḥ*), milk—that is, they flow—the nectar, the essence, the sap of heaven (*divaḥ*).
The meaning is that they milk their own juice or the water of the atmosphere.
In the vault of heaven, the honey-tongued, unwearied seers milk the bull dwelling on the mountain;
they milk the drop that has grown great in the waters, in the ocean, in the wave of the river, rich in sweetness within the filter.

In the vault of heaven, the honey-tongued, unceasing, longing ones milk the bull dwelling on the mountain—the drop that has grown great in the waters, in the ocean; they milk the honey-sweet one into the filter within the wave of the river. 10.

In the *nāka*— the pain-free place called the *havirdhāna* (oblation-holder) belonging to the shining sacrifice— the honey-tongued ones (*madhujihvaḥ*), whose speech is sweet, and the unattached ones (*asaśrataḥ*)—
meaning those who move individually or, alternatively,
those who press [the soma] quickly without delay— the *venas*, great seers of this name, milk [the soma]; that is, they press it.
Alternatively, the gods milk the beloved *venā*—that is, the heavenly world itself.

They pour that *soma*, the bull (*ukṣaṇam*) who is the establisher (*setāram*), dwelling upon the mountain (*giriṣṭhām*) in the region of the mountains, into the waters (*apsu*) while possessing the *vasatīvarī* waters; he who is increasing (*vavṛdhānam*) and growing, the drop (*drapsam*) in the form of essence, into the ocean-like (*samudre*) greatly expanded wooden vat (*droṇakalaśe*). The ellipsis is: "they pour [it] into the wave (*ūrmau*) or flood of the river (*sindhoḥ*) water. For that purpose, the ellipsis is: "they pour the honeyed (*madhumantam*) essence, stirred with sweetness, into the filter (*pavitre*), the *daśāpavitra*."
The many songs of the longing ones have yearned for the golden-winged bird who has alighted upon the firmament;
the prayers lick the infant as he is praised—the golden bird established in the dwelling-place of the earth.

In the firmament, the many voices of the longing ones have yearned for the well-winged one who has arrived. The prayers lick the infant, him who is praised with hymns, the golden bird standing upon the earth. 11.
Our many ancient songs of praise, belonging to us—the *venas*—yearn toward Soma as he dwells in the heavenly vault (*nāka*) and subsequently rises upward;
that is to say, they extol him.
Our thoughts—that is, our praises—lick, that is, they caress, that infant Soma who is to be refined like a child.
The meaning is that they attain [it].
Of what kind is the child?
One who is "panimata," i.e., crying out.

From the root *panat* with the suffix *yaṅ*, followed by *luK* and then *śatṛ*, there is the substitution of *ni* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).
*Hiraṇyayam* means made of gold; *śakunam* means a bird; *kṣāmāṇam* means situated on the earth; *stham* means standing or residing in the *havirdhāna* (the sacrificial shed for oblations).

The Gandharva has stood erect upon the vault of heaven, beholding all the forms of this [universe].
His radiance has shone forth with bright luster; pure, he has illuminated both worlds, his parents.
Upright upon the firmament stands the Gandharva, beholding all forms. His radiance has shone forth with brilliant luster; pure, he has illuminated both worlds, the parents. 12.
The Gandharva, the elevated one who sustains the rays, Soma, has taken his stand, he stands upon the *nāka*, the sun.
What is he doing?
Beholding, looking upon all the forms of this sun.

Bhānu, the Āditya, being presided over by Soma, has shone, shines, and will shine with brilliant, glowing luster and splendor. Not only himself, but he also causes the two Mothers, the fashioners, Rodasī—the Heaven and Earth—to shine forth.
Śuci, the radiant Sun.
Now, in the fifth section (anuvāka), there are eleven hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, "pra te," consists of forty-eight verses.
The seers (ṛṣis) who perceived the first ten verses are two groups of seers known by the dual names Ākṛṣṭās and Māpas.
The seer-group of the second *daśarca* consists of two groups of seers named Sikatā and Nīvāvarī;
the seer-group of the third *daśarca* consists of two groups of seers endowed with the two names Pṛṣva and Ajā.
The reason for their having two names should be understood as being for the sake of [completing] the number eight.
The seers of the fourth [section] consisting of ten verses are the group known by the two names beginning with "ākṛṣṭā māpāḥ";
thus, there are forty verses.
Now, for the five [sections], the seer is Atri Bhauma.
Gṛtsamada is the seer of the *natasimaṇām* verses.
The *jagatī* is the meter.
Pavamāna Soma is the deity.

And thus it has been enumerated: "The forty-eight [hymns] beginning with 'pra te' consist of ten verses each; the groups of seers are Ākṛṣṭas, Māpās, Sikatās, Nīvāvarīs in the first [section]; Pṛṣvas and Ajās in the second; three [groups] in the third; Atri in the fourth; and Gṛtsamada for the other three. The application [of these hymns] has been explained.
O Pavamāna, your swift, exhilarating drops, urged by prayer, flow forth like fleet-footed sons;
the celestial, well-winged, honey-sweet Soma-drops sit around the vat, most joyous in their intoxication.

O Pavamāna, your exhilarating draughts, stirred by prayer and swift as coursers, flow forth of their own accord. Like divine, well-winged birds, the honey-sweet drops, most intoxicating, settle around the vat.
O Pavamāna Soma, as you are being purified, your swift, mind-swift streams— your exhilarating,
intoxicating juices— flow forth by their own inherent power.
The meaning is "without effort. Who is he like?
Like the son of Raghu.
*Raghu* means a swift-moving horse;
those born therein are *raghujāḥ*. Like them, they have emerged; they are divine, meaning existing in heaven (*divi*).
The meaning is that they are being held in the intermediate space within the ten-purified filter.

The *suparṇas*, those of beautiful flight; the *madhumantas*, endowed with sweetness; the *madantamāsas*, most exceedingly intoxicating; the *indavas*, radiant juices—these sit around, that is, they settle upon, the *kośa*, the wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*).
Your exhilarating, intoxicating draughts have been poured forth, like chariot-horses racing apart.
As a cow with her milk surrounds her calf, so do the honeyed waves of Soma-drops encompass Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.

Your exhilarating, intoxicating draughts have been poured forth, like chariot-horses racing apart. As a cow with her milk seeks her calf, so do these honey-sweet drops and waves seek Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt. 2.
1. *ga-prādīpayaddhi*;
2. *ga-bha5.6-pṛśva* and *bha6-yajā* are groups of nouns;
3. *ga-raghavaḥ śīghravegā athāḥ*; *ta6-raghuḥ śīghravāḍavā*.
They flow forth; those exhilarating, intoxicating, and swift juices of yours, the pervasive draughts, are being poured out separately, just like chariot-horses.

Those honeyed waves, free from bitterness, taking the form of leaves—the Soma juices belonging to Indra—approach the wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, with their own natural sap, just as a cow approaches Yama with her milk.
Like a steed not lagging behind as he rushes toward the prize,
the Soma, the bull, winner of the light, flows over the filter upon the sheep’s-wool ridge, the mother rock of heaven, to be held for Indra’s sake while being purified.

Like a steed urged forward toward the prize, he hastens to the light; the bull, the winner of heaven, flows onto the mountain of the filter made of sheep’s wool—the Soma, being purified for the sake of Indra’s power, to be held fast. 3.
Like a steed being urged forward, hasten toward the prize, that is, the battle.
Likewise, as one who knows the light (*svarvit*), knowing all, [hasten] toward the vessel, the *droṇakalaśa*, from heaven—the mother-mountain—from the celestial world;
for the mountain is the cloud.
By that, the water produced by it is indicated; entrust it to its maker. Now, that which is produced through direct perception.
The bull, the showering Soma, [is] upon the wool-free back;
the word "ardhi" restates the sense of the locative case.
When that [back] is combined, he becomes *punānaḥ*, i.e., being purified.
For what purpose?
It is for that purpose that you are sustained by the sustaining sense-faculty.

O Pavamāna, the celestial waters of the Aśvins, urged by prayer, have been released with milk into the vessel; the ancient, swelling streams have flowed forth, which the wise sages who protect you cause to flow.

O Pavamāna, your celestial, swift-inspiring, and horse-like streams have been released toward the support of the milk. Within, the seers have cleansed the ancient [streams], those wise ones who, O seat of the seers, groom you.
O Pavamāna Soma, those *āśvinīḥ* [mares] belonging to you are pervasive;
from the root *vi-āp* (to pervade) comes the suffix *vini* according to the *uṇādi* rules,
and from that, the suffix *aṇ*.
The unaccented [syllable] is replaced by another.

The swift ones, impelled by thought, the celestial ones—existing in heaven, falling from heaven, the streams joined with milk—have been let loose; they go forth into the *dhārīmaṇi*, the supporting wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*).

Those who are the ordainers (*vedhas*), the arrangers, the seers (*ṛṣi*)—O Soma, you who are drunk by the seers (*ṛṣipāṇa*)—they cleanse you, they purify you. Those seers [purify] the ancient, steadfast streams within, in the midst of the vessel, they wipe them clean.
O all-seeing one, your rays, the skillful servants of the Lord, go forth encompassing all abodes.
You flow through with your purifying laws, O Sobha; as the lord of the entire world, you reign.
O all-seeing one, your rays, the skillful ones, go forth around all the stations of the Lord; pressed out, O Soma, you flow through with your laws, and as the lord of the entire world, you reign. 5.
O Soma, you who possess all-seeing eyes, the beholder of everything, from you—the sovereign lord—proceed the great rays (ketavaḥ), for "ṛbhvas" is a name for greatness;
these mighty rays encompass (pari yanti) all abodes (dhāmāni), that is, all places of splendor or the bodies of the gods;
the meaning is that they illuminate them.
O Soma, you who are pervasive and whose nature is to spread, you purify yourself through your sustaining and flavorful juices;
as the lord and master of the entire world, you reign as its sovereign.
The rays of the one being purified on both sides, the banners of the steadfast one, move around him as he is pressed;
when the tawny one is cleansed upon the filter, he sits down in his place within the jars.
1. On the summit with two strainers; on the two strainers, these two strainers. 2.
*Taṇḍya Brāhmaṇa* 1.2.4.7 lacks "from heaven.

From both sides. Of the one being purified. The rays. Of the firm one. The pressed juice. Around. They go. The banners. When. Upon the strainer. He is cleansed. The tawny one. Being seated. He settles down in his place, in the jars. || 6 ||

The rays—the indicators—of Soma, who is being purified (*pavamāna*), who is being cleansed (*pūyamāna*), and who is firm (*dhruva*) and self-immutable while existing, go around on both sides, from here and from there. This occurs at the very time of pressing: when this golden-hued (*hari*) one is cleansed upon the *daśāpavitra* filter, then he, whose nature is to exist (*sattā*), sits down in his own place, the womb (*yoni*), namely in the jars such as the *droṇakalaśa*.
The banner of the sacrifice, the well-performed rite upon the mountain, Soma goes to the appointed place of the gods.
With a thousand streams he flows around the vat; as a bull, he passes through the filter with a loud roar.

The banner of the sacrifice, the well-performing one, Soma flows clear; he goes toward the appointed place of the gods. With a thousand streams he glides around the vessel; as a bull, he passes through the filter with a roar. 7.
The banner of the sacrifice, the indicator, the one of excellent rites—the beautiful sacrifice—Soma flows, purifies, and is consecrated.
Such Soma approaches and reaches the prepared and consecrated station of the gods;
for that purpose, he with a thousand streams flows around the vessel, the *droṇakalaśa*.
Having descended for that purpose, the bull, bellowing loudly as he seeks to discharge his seed, passes beyond the filter and goes toward the lower region.

The king plunges into the ocean; the rivers flow toward him, and he, resting upon the streams, gathers the surge of the waters. Ascending the unaging ridge, he stands at the navel of the earth, the supporter of the great heaven.

The King [Soma] plunges into the ocean; the rivers flow apart. He has taken refuge in the waves of the waters, dwelling within the streams. Pressed out, he has mounted the back of the sheep’s fleece, the height of the great heaven, as the support of the earth. 8.
This King Soma plunges into the ocean, the intermediate space, the rivers, and the waters therein.
Having plunged in, he flows forth as a flood of water, gathering the wave of the waters.
Resting within the rivers, the waters, or the vessels (*graha*).
The meaning is that, while being offered as an oblation, it reaches the sun by way of its rays and abides within the clouds in the atmosphere;
for this [fire] alone is the means for bringing rain.
Or else:
This is like the body [of the Soma].

Just as rivers flow into the ocean, so [the two streams] have resorted to and taken refuge in the *sindhu* waters, the *vasatīvarī* waters—the ocean being the vessel that holds the purified soma juice—before the pressing.
Afterwards, the *pavamāna*, being purified, has ascended and stands upon the elevated woolen filter (*daśāpavitra*), which is like a mountain ridge (*avyayaṃ sānu*).
In which place? At the navel of the earth—that is, at the sacrifice which stands in the place of the navel;
the meaning is: in the *havirdhāna* (sacrificial oblation-hall) connected with that.
According to the Vedic revelation, "They call the sacrifice the navel of the world" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.4.18.2).
Of what nature is it?
It is the *dharuṇa*, the supporter, of the great heaven (*maho divaḥ*), that is, of the *Svarga* world.
Thundering like the ridge of heaven, he has roared—the Soma who, by his ordinances, pervades both heaven and earth.
