Making the sun manifest, he flows clear; being purified, he settles within the jars.

Like the ridge of heaven, thundering, he has bellowed; he for whom both heaven and earth exist according to their laws—for that Indra, Soma purifies himself, making the sun known. Being cleansed, Soma settles within the jars. 9.
1. There is no "departed" (*gata*) or "unrequited" (*aniṣkṛta*).
2. Having transcended *bha* (or *bha1* and *bha2*), he goes. 3. Of that very [state], *ga*.

Now, from the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Maṇḍala 7, Sūkta 3, Mantra 14: "Like the ridge of heaven," that is, sounding as it were while making a noise toward the elevated place of the celestial world, he roars without faltering.
By the laws and supports of that Soma, both heaven and earth are sustained.
It is well known that he sustains both through the bestowing of rain—which generates food—and by serving as the sacrificial oblation for the gods.
Such is that Soma, the one of great majesty; being purified, he flows and is cleansed in the filter, seeking to win the friendship of Indra.
That Soma, being purified, sits—that is, dwells—among the Karūṣas.
The light of the sacrifice flows forth as the beloved honey; the father of the gods, their progenitor, the pervasive lord of wealth.
He bestows the secret treasure within the two self-sustaining worlds—the most gladdening thought, the essence of Indra.
The light of the sacrifice flows as the beloved honey. The father of the gods, their progenitor, the pervasive lord of wealth, bestows a secret treasure upon the two who offer the *svadhā*.

Thus, for the sake of obtaining food, strength, or vigor, he partakes in the great battle for wealth. That Soma, the bull, the showerer of benefits, well-armed, is purified by the pressers, the performers of the extraction.

This wise bird-like Soma, being impelled, has sped forth with his wave through the filter, like one sent by others. By your power, O Sage, the pure Soma flows through the two worlds, O Indra, by means of your wisdom for you. This Soma is "wise" (*matavān*); *manas* is that which is esteemed, beloved, and desirable—he possesses that. Being "purifying" (*pavamāna*), being cleansed and purified, and being "impelled" (*hitaḥ*), he moves swiftly like a "bird" (*śakunaḥ*) when sent. O "Sage" (*kave*)—one whose wisdom has traversed [all things] or who is learned; for the Śruti says, "Those who are learned are sages" (*Ai. Brā. 2.38*). O such sacrificer, or rather, O Indra characterized as described above, by your "power" (*kratvā*)—your action—and by "wisdom" (*dhiyā*)—your intelligence—or rather, in the relationship of qualifier and qualified: by your sustaining "wisdom" and your "power," the "pure" Soma flows between the two worlds, O Indra, pervading the two worlds by your mental power.

Clothed in his mantle, worthy of sacrifice, touching the heavens, filling the mid-air, and established among the worlds; being born as the light of heaven, he has stepped forth toward the clouds; he seeks to win over the ancient Father of this [water]. Clothed in his mantle—his armor, which is of the nature of splendor—he who touches the heavens, wearing it as a covering; the worshipful one, who fills the mid-air with water; such is Soma, established within the worlds (the waters). Being born as the light of heaven (*svar*), generating for himself the host of gods to be nourished, or the celestial realm; or rather, generating the water (*svar*); he has stepped forth toward the clouds (*nabhas*) by means of the water. He seeks to win over, that is, he honors and serves, the ancient Indra, the protector (*pitaram*) of this water.

He bestows great protection upon his people, he who first attained his primordial abode. That which is his station in the highest heaven—from there he goes forth toward all encounters, well-prepared. He, Soma, grants great (*mahi*) protection (*śarma*) for the entry (*viśe*) of this Indra; he, Soma, who first (*prathamam*) reached (*vyānaśe*) his (*asya*) abode (*dhāma*), the body endowed with splendor, before other gods could reach it. That which is his station (*padam*) in the highest (*paramē*) sky (*vyoman*)—from that Soma, Indra (or Soma himself) goes forth toward (*abhi yāti*) all (*viśvāḥ*) encounters (*saṃyataḥ*), that is, all battles. "He grants great protection," is the connection. 15.14.

1. *ga*, *ta*³·⁴, *bha*⁴ read *yacchati prayacchati*; *bha*¹·⁷ read *prayacchati*. 2. *ta*, *soma*. 3. *ga*, *ta*³·⁴, *bha*¹·²·⁴·⁶—‘*prathama*’ is not present. 4. *ta*, *bha*⁶—‘*vā padaṃ*’ is not present. 5. *ga*, *ta*³·⁴, *bha*¹·²·⁴, *mu*, *saṃyāti*.
The drop (Soma) has gone forth to the appointed place of Indra; as a friend, he does not violate the agreement with his friend.
Like a youth with young maidens, Soma hastens toward the jars by a path of a hundred courses.

"Yea! he has gone forth—the drop—to the appointed place of Indra. As a friend, he does not violate the agreement with his friend. Like a youth with young women, Soma flows together with the jars by the path of a hundred courses. 16.
The *indu*, the Soma, has gone forth toward the prepared place, the belly of Indra; indeed, he goes forward.

And having gone there, as a friend who has become a companion, the Soma does not fail—that is, does not harm—the "well-swallowing" (*saṃgiraṃ*), the belly which serves as the vessel for Indra’s complete swallowing. Furthermore, just as a young man (*marya*) comes together with young women (*yuvatibhiḥ*), even so this Soma, at the time of pressing, comes together (*samarṣati*) with the *ṛtīvarī* waters, which are by nature prone to mixing.

Afterwards, Soma goes by way of the hundred-pathed route—a path provided with many vehicles and possessing apertures—to the jar associated with the ten fingers, that is, the *droṇakalaśa*; this is the ellipsis.
Or rather, it is a single sentence:
just as a mortal man comes together with young women, so does he come together with the waters in the jar by way of the hundred-pathed route.
Your prayers, joyous, praising, and worthy of praise, have stepped forth for the communal dwelling.
With inspired thought, the chants have celebrated Soma; the milch-cows have poured forth their milk.

Your inspired thoughts—joyous, seeking praise, and longing for wealth—have stepped forth into the dwelling places. With wise intention, the songs of praise have celebrated Soma; the milch-cows have gathered around him on every side. || 17 ||
O Soma-like ones, you— the thinkers of thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*), desiring the exhilarating sound (*mandrayuvaḥ*), desiring praise (*panyuvaḥ*),
and the singers (*vipanyuvaḥ*)—
the chanters proceed forward (*pra akramaḥ*) into the dwelling-places (*saṃvasaneṣu*), that is, into the sacrificial halls suitable for habitation.
He says that very thing:
the *manīṣāḥ*, those who are masters of the mind, the *stubhaḥ*, the praisers, have *abhyanūṣata*, they praise him;
even the *dhenavaḥ*, the cows, with their own milk, *abhy aśiśrayuḥ*, they mix this Soma.

O Soma, flow for us with abundant, swelling nourishment; O Indu, being purified, flow without fail—that which yields for us thrice daily, inexhaustible, rich in food, full of strength, sweet, and endowed with heroic power.

O Soma, pour out for us abundant, swelling nourishment; O Indu, being purified, flow forth an unfailing stream that shall yield for us thrice a day—unfailing, rich in food, full of strength, sweet, and endowed with heroic power.
O Indu, radiant Soma Pavamāna, do thou flow for us—our well-restrained, gathered, swelling, and increased food, which is unfailing and inexhaustible;
that is to say, grant it to us. Such as it is, which for us day by day, three times a day—at the three pressings—flows forth, streaming without obstruction.
What?
It milks out for him a son who is *kṣumat*—endowed with sound and heard everywhere; *vājavat*—possessing vigor; *madhumat*—endowed with sweetness; and *suvīrya*—of excellent capability.
"Purify yourself as the protector of that [milk]" (*tāmipaṃ pavasva*)—such is the syntactical connection.

1. *ga*-bha4: refined, perfected (*niṣkṛtaṃ saṃskṛtam*). 2. *ga*: the proper support for speech (*samyaggirāmādhāram*); *ta1.5*: the proper support for the act of swallowing (*samyagmiranādhāram*); *tara.4.5.6-bha6*: the proper support for the act of swallowing (*samyagiraṇādhāram*).
3. *ga*: there is an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntaḥ*) in that regard.
4. *maryaḥ*: the connection is that, having been mixed with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he flows into the jar.
5. *vājavat*: possessing strength (*bala*).

The bull of hymns, the far-seeing Soma, flows clear; he has extended the days and the dawns from heaven. By his action, he has caused the rivers to roar toward the jars, entering the heart of Indra through the wise ones. 19. The bull of hymns, the far-seeing Soma, flows clear; he has extended the days and the dawns from heaven. By his action, he has caused the rivers to roar toward the jars, entering the heart of Indra through the wise ones. 19.
This Soma flows; it is being purified.
Of what sort is this Soma?
[The Soma] of prayers (*matīnām*).
The *matayaḥ* are the singers of praise;

for them, he is the *vṛṣā*, the showerer of desires, the *vicakṣaṇaḥ*, the all-seeing one; the *ahnaḥ*, *uṣasaḥ*, and *divaḥ*—that is, of the day, the dawn, and the heavenly world (or of the sun)—he is the *pratartā*, the promoter.

Furthermore, regarding the *sindhūnām*, the flowing waters, he is the *krāṇā*, the maker (*karoti*); the suffix *śānac* is applied, and by the rule "the verbal suffix is frequently elided in the Veda," there is an elision of the conjugational suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
*su*: the form *su* [is used] because of the rule *supāṃ suluk...* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], which substitutes the vowel *ā*.
*kalaśān avīvaśat* means he desires to enter the jars.
Doing what? Entering—that is, penetrating—the heart (hārdi) of Indra; the ellipsis is "praised by the wise."
Alternatively,
even though it is separated by other words, the term "by the wise" (manīṣibhiḥ) is connected with "purifies" (pavate).

The ancient sage, impelled by the wise ones, flows forth; guided by men, he has roared around the vessels. Producing the name of Trita, he pours out sweetness to establish friendship with Indra and Vāyu. By the wise ones, he flows forth—the ancient one, the seer—guided by men, he has cried out around the vessels. Bringing forth the name of Trita, he pours out honey to create friendship for Indra and Vāyu.
This Soma is purified— that is, cleansed— by the wise ones, such as the *adhvaryu* priests and others; or alternatively, it flows— that is,
pours forth— by the wise ones, meaning by the streams (*dhārā*) that possess wisdom.
Of what nature is he?
Ancient, a seer, and wise, he has been restrained by men—the leaders such as the *adhvaryu* priests—and, being so constrained, he cries out loudly all around in order to reach the jars and vats.
Producing the water known by the name belonging to Indra, who is extended across the three stations, he flows forth, pouring out the sweet juice.
For what purpose? To establish friendship—that is, to create a bond of friendship—between Indra and Vāyu.

This one, being purified, has caused the dawns to shine; this one has become the creator of space for the rivers. This Soma, yielding the three times seven [cows] as milk-mixture, flows for the heart—charming and exhilarating. 21. This one, being purified, has caused the dawns to shine; this one has become the creator of space for the rivers. This Soma, yielding the three times seven [cows] as milk-mixture, flows for the heart—charming and exhilarating. 21.
This Soma, being purified—being cleansed—makes the dawns shine forth; he causes them to shine in various ways.
This one has become abundant for the flowing rivers, the *vasatīvarī* waters; he becomes prosperous.
The particle *u* is a filler.
Of what nature is he?
He is the "creator of the worlds" (lokakṛt), the maker of the worlds;
his status as the creator of the worlds is due to his being the showerer [of rain] and the bestower of seed.
This Soma, yielding the milk-mixture (*āśira*) through the mouth of the officiating priest, has milked twenty-one cows—three times seven.
Because he is the prompter of the act of milking, he is figuratively designated as the agent.
Intoxicating (*matsara*), that is, exhilarating, and beautiful (*cāru*), that is, delightful, he flows and purifies himself.
For what purpose?
For the heart; for that which goes to the heart.
1. One who causes them to increase;
2. [The reading] *ga-ta1.7-bha6-mu- 'su:* does not exist;
3. [The reading] *ga-ta4-bha6.7- 'praviśan* does not exist.

4. *ga-ta-bha*-*mu*: "Of this sacrificer, Indra... 5. *ta5-bha6*: "...twenty-one times through your mouth"; *bha4*: "...twenty-one times through the mouth of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*")"; *mu*: "...or twenty-one times through the mouth of the officiating priest.
6. *bha6*: "Because it completes [the number]."
7. *ga*-agentive metaphor; *ta1.2*-agentive metaphor; *ta3*-having-made metaphor; *ta4.5*-agentive metaphor; *bha1.2.7*-metaphor; *bha6*-agentive metaphor.
O Soma, being poured out at the joints [of the sacrifice] among the divine abodes, O Indu, flow through the filter into the jars.
Sitting within the belly of Indra while bellowing, you, impelled by the men, caused the sun to ascend to heaven.

Flow on, O Soma, through the divine abodes; being released, O Indu, flow into the jars and the filter. Seating yourself within the belly of Indra while bellowing, you, guided by the men, caused the sun to ascend to heaven.
O Soma, flow for the sake of the gods and the ancestors in those divine abodes and stations;
flow through those joints.
Being of what nature?
O *indu*, radiant Soma, [being] in the jar, in the filter, and in the *daśāpavitra*—
the word *ā* is used here in the sense of "and."
Being emitted and being poured forth— here,
as in the case of "he offers the Agnihotra, he cooks the gruel," a sequential order based on the purpose (ārthika-krama) is to be understood.
Furthermore, while seated within Indra's belly— that is, entering his stomach— he roars loudly, having been grasped by the men, the leaders, the officiating priests.
[He is] the one offered; such being the case, you caused the sun to ascend in heaven—you made him manifest, O Adhvaryu.

Purifying himself with his wave through the filter, the golden-hued one—toward him the seven milch-cows low. In the lap of the waters, the Āyus have kindled Agni, the seer, in the womb of Cosmic Order (ṛta), the great protectors. 25. He is the oblation; as such, you caused the sun to ascend in heaven—you made him manifest, O Adhvaryu. Purifying himself with his wave through the filter, the golden-hued one—the seven milch-cows low toward him. In the lap of the waters, the Āyus have kindled Agni, the seer, in the womb of Cosmic Order (ṛta), the great protectors.

The seven milch-cows—the seven [metres] beginning with Gāyatrī, or the seven rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā—approach and flow toward the golden-hued Pavamāna, who is being purified all around by the surging juice upon the sheep’s wool, the goat’s hair, and the woollen filter;
for the root *nav* is listed as a verb meaning "to go" (*navate kṣodate*).
Furthermore, he [the Soma] is the Seer (*kavi*) in his own lap, in the expanse of the intermediate space, in the womb of Truth.
Regarding the name "water" (*udaka*), it is because that term is recited among the names [of the waters] in the passage: "The truth is the womb; the womb of truth.
In the water, the *mahipās*—that is, the great winds or men—*vahiṣpata*, meaning they impel or drive it forth even more intensely.
Being purified, Indu plunges through the obstacles, making all paths easy for the sacrificer;
making the cows his garment, the beloved sage flows around the filter like a playful horse.

The Indu, being purified, plunges through the enemies, making all paths easy for the sacrificer; the beloved sage, creating the cows as his own raiment, flows like a playful horse through the woollen filter. || 26 ||
This drop—blazing, lunar, being purified and cleansed—plunges into the waters and passes beyond the enemies.
What does it do?
Making all the paths to be traversed easy to travel, both Vedic and worldly, it proceeds.
For whom? For the performer of the sacrifice, the patron (yajamāna); the meaning is that he enters the jar while warding off enemies and making the paths easy to travel.
Furthermore, making his own form (*rūpa*) bright and pure (*v-nirṇijam*),
that is, making it full of essence (*rasamaya*);
he is lovely (*haryataḥ*), meaning desirable.
‘Haryagatikāntyā’:
the suffix *at* is derived from the *uṇādi* [list].

A *kavi* is one whose wisdom is beautiful (*kāntaprajña*). Such a Soma, like a horse (*vājī*), playing (*krīḷan*), flows around (*pari varpati*) the *vāra*, that is, the *daśāpavitra* (the ten-strand filter). It moves completely through it.
The hundred-streamed, unpressed libations flow toward the golden one like rushing waters;
they cleanse him who is enveloped in milk on the third ridge in the luminous realm of heaven.

Unbound, with a hundred streams, they flow toward him; they celebrate the tawny one, the swift steed. These longing waters cleanse him who is enveloped by the rays of light, upon the third ridge in the luminous realm of heaven.

Those well-known rays of the sun, which flow from the east, joined together in a hundred streams, and full of splendor, resting on all sides around the Soma— those rays go toward Hari (the golden one),
being desirous of water (or, alternatively, seeking the waters).
By the word *dhārā* (streams), the streams of Soma are intended here.

The *asr̥ktaḥ* (unbound/unrestrained), *asaṃbaddhāḥ* (unconnected), *abhishriyaḥ* (flowing toward), and *abhigāḥ* (resting upon the cows)—that is, those well-known [streams] which are *śritāḥ* (mixed) with the cows—[these] *udanyuvaḥ* (thirsty ones), desiring rain from Indra, join together with the *harimandram* (the golden-hued joy).

In the case of the fingers: the *aṅgulayaḥ* (fingers) also, by means of the *gobhiḥ* (rays)—in the context of the Soma-streams, by the *gobhiḥ* (cows)—envelop (*āvṛtam*) the *vyāsam* (extended) Soma; they cleanse it, that is, they purify it.

In the sky, in the shining realm of the Āditya—that which the Āditya causes to shine—in that third [place], when there is a requirement for a receptacle, they release Soma who dwells in the heavenly world, which has become the third.

1. *Ga-ta* and *Bha1.2.4.7* mean "having gone" (*ga-ta*). Alternatively, it means "making the cows produce their transformations, namely, milk. 2. *Ga* reads *hari* as "green" (*haritam*). 3. *Mu* [places this] on the third back-verse (*pṛṣṭhe*). 4. *Bha1(2)* [places this] on the third being (*bhūte*) of the back-verse.
"These progeny of yours are divine; you are the seed. You rule over the entire world.
And all this, O Pavamāna, is under your control. O Indu, you are the first establisher of the abodes."

These progeny are thine; thou rulest over all this world that is of celestial seed. Now, O Pavamāna, this entire universe is under thy control. O Indu, thou art the first establisher of the cosmic order. 28.
From your divine seed, these living beings—these creatures—are being produced and have been born;
for the Śruti says, "Soma is indeed the depositor of the seed" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1.6).
You rule over the entire world; you are its Lord.
Moreover, O Pavamāna, this entire universe exists under your control and depends upon you;
O Indu, as the foremost and preeminent one, you are the sustainer, the supporter of all abodes.
You are the ocean, O all-knowing sage; yours are these five directions within the cosmic order.
You have surpassed both heaven and earth; you, O Pavamāna, are the light and the sun.

You are the ocean, O all-knowing sage; yours are these five directions within your wide expanse. You have stretched yourself beyond both heaven and earth; you, O Pavamāna, are the light and the sun. 29.
O poet of transcendent wisdom, since you are like the ocean that brings about the rain of waters, therefore you are the knower of all;
or rather,
you are the ocean of the two-fold self and thus the knower of all.
Furthermore, O Vidharmaṇi (the one who upholds), the five directions—the excellent quarters—become established; this is the sense remaining.
You uphold both the sky and the earth.
O Pavamāna, the divine Sūrya causes your lights to swell.
O Soma Pavamāna, you are purified for the gods in the filter, the support of the mid-world;
the first seers grasped you, and all these worlds have submitted themselves to you.
O Soma Pavamāna, you are purified in the filter, as the upholder of the realm for the sake of the gods. The first eager ones grasped you; all these worlds have submitted themselves to you. 30.
O Soma Pavamāna, you are purified for the sake of the gods upon the ten-strand filter (daśāpavitra) in the support of the realm, the world, or the essence.
The desiring, foremost, most excellent, and principal officiating priests (ṛtvij) seize you.
To you, to you—indeed to you—all these, all these worlds, all living beings, have submitted; they restrain themselves [before you].
The singer goes forth across the sheep’s wool filter; the tawny bull, the golden-hued one, has roared in the wooden vessels.
The prayers have lowed together, yearning; the hymns lick the infant who is worthy of praise.

The singer goes forth across the sheep’s woolly fleece; the tawny bull, the steed, bellows among the woods. The prayers have lowed together in longing; the hymns lick the infant who is worthy of praise.
1. *bha* 1.2.7—*tvaṃ soma*. 2. *bha* 1—*te va*; *bhara* 1—*te tava*. 3. *ga*—*draviṇasādhanāpām*. 4. *ta* 4—*bha*—"*pratamā*" does not exist.
*Vrebha*: one who causes to sound.
*Vrebhu*: to sound.

Soma flows through the sheep’s fleece; he, the bull, the shedder [of seed], passes through it, purifying himself and flowing forth with great intensity. Soma, the tawny-colored one, has bellowed loudly within the waters;
they praise him together.
The meditative thoughts (*dhi-tayaḥ*), the meditators (*dhyātāraḥ*), longing— desiring either the sacrifice or the Soma—
caress, lick, and touch the Child (*śiśum*), who is to be refined like a child, with their prayers (*matayaḥ*) and hymns of praise (*stutayaḥ*).
The meaning is "they cause their own [nature] to be perverted. Of what kind?
Resounding, that is, making a sound.

He has clothed himself all around with the rays of the sun, weaving the threefold thread as he knows how; leading the most recent shoots of Cosmic Order, the husband of the wives goes toward the appointed place. 32. He—with the rays of the sun; all around; has clothed; the thread; weaving; threefold; as; he knows; leading; of the Truth; the most recent shoots; the husband; of the wives; toward; goes; to the appointed place. 32.
Soma, with the rays of the sun, envelops himself; that is, he surrounds himself. What is he doing?
While extending—the *tanu* being the sacrifice—either the threefold libation (*savana*) or the threefold [thread] performed by the gods, he knows it as it is threefold.
In whatever manner he understands it to be complete, extending it accordingly,
he brings about the newest praises for the sacrificer who is truthful and established in his vow; leading those intended praises toward their goal,
he, as the lord and protector of the people, goes forth to the prepared vessel.

The King of the rivers flows on; the Lord of heaven goes forth with wide strides, bellowing loudly. The golden-hued one, with a thousand streams, is poured out all around; being purified, generating speech, he approaches with wealth. 33. King of the rivers, he flows; the Lord of heaven, he goes by wide paths, bellowing loudly. With a thousand streams, the golden-hued one is poured out all around; being purified, generating speech, he approaches with wealth. 33.

The Lord of the hosts of Sindhus—the rivers—and of the waters; the Master of heaven, the sovereign of the celestial world; bellowing with sound along the paths of *vṛta*—the sacrifice—he pervades. Soma, possessed of a thousand streams and many flows, is poured by the men—the leaders, the officiating priests—around into the vessels.
Being purified, generating speech and sound, approaching the wealth, he is poured around; such is the connection of the words.

O Pavamāna, you flow forth like a great flood; brilliant as the sun, you pass through the sheep’s wool. Purified by the hands and pressed by men with stones, you hasten toward great and prize-winning booty. 34. O Pavamāna, you flow forth like a great flood; brilliant as the sun, you pass through the sheep’s wool. Purified by the hands and pressed by men with stones, you hasten toward great and prize-winning booty. 34.
O Soma, flowing forth, you cause the great flood—
the word *arṇa* being a name for water— or rather, the essence— to flow abundantly; that is, you cause it to go forth.

"‘Dhātu gatiśuddhayoḥ’: furthermore, being like the sun—*sūraḥ* meaning *vicitraḥ*, i.e., variegated—and being worthy of praise (*cāyanīyaḥ*) and venerable (*pūjyaḥ*), he approaches the imperishable ones (*avyayāni*). [Variants: 1. *ta-bhara-mu* read *prayeti*; 2. *ga-ta3-bha4.5* lack the phrase ‘of what kind... making sound’; *ta-bha6* read ‘of what kind, making sound’; 3. *ga* reads ‘from that very one’; *mu* reads ‘to him thus’; 4. *bha6* reads ‘he approaches’; 5. *ga* reads ‘the Lord flows’; 6. *ta* lacks ‘from heaven’; 7. *mu* reads ‘the master Soma flows, i.e., is purified’; 8. *ga-bha1.4.6.7* read ‘approaching’; 9. *ga* reads ‘you purify’]. In this regard, there is an illustration."
I go with my feet to the vessels made of sheep's wool.

Furthermore, purified by rays, cleansed by arms, pressed by men who are priests, and filtered by stones—you, being thus purified, proceed toward great strength, toward battle, and toward wealth that is beneficial for riches;
for the root *dhanv* signifies motion.
O Pavamāna, you flow toward nourishment and vigor; like a hawk, you settle within the wooden vats.
Pressed for Indra as a gladdening, exhilarating draught, you are the supreme pillar of heaven, far-seeing.

O flowing one, you bestow nourishment and vigor; like a falcon, you settle within the wooden vats. Pressed for Indra, you are the exhilarating delight, the intoxication, the pillar of heaven, the supreme, far-seeing one. 35.
O Pavamāna Soma, being purified, you flow toward us with food, nourishment, strength, and power.
Like a hawk, you settle in the desirable hollows—the jars—and once seated, you protect us.
Now follows the section composed in the third person.
For Indra: intoxicating, causing exhilaration, a beverage for intoxication, the cause of intoxication, and intoxication itself.

O Soma, you are indeed the beholder of men from every side; O flowing bull, you run through those [waters]. As such, flow for us with wealth and gold; may we be able to live among all beings. O Soma, you are indeed the beholder of men from every side; O flowing bull, you run through those [waters]. As such, flow for us with wealth and gold; may we be able to live among all beings. O Soma, you are indeed the beholder of men from every side—that is, you exist as the observer of men throughout all worlds. O Pavamāna, O Bull, you who rain down waters, you run through those waters in various directions. As such, flow for us—pour forth for us. What? Wealth consisting of many *vasus* (riches or ritual implements) and likewise wealth consisting of much gold. And may we, endowed with riches and gold, be capable of living among all beings in the worlds.
O Indu, finder of cattle, knower of treasures, finder of gold, bestower of wealth, you are established among the worlds.
O Soma, you are a hero of noble lineage; you are all-encompassing for us.

The one who brings praise raises up offspring-providing, all-life-sustaining, and all-well-bearing [streams] day by day. As a bearer, [grant] wealth consisting of offspring and abounding in dwellings. O Indu, once drunk, entreat Indra on our behalf. 41.

Soma is the protector (*pasaḥ*). Soma is the one whose life-span is all-pervading (*viśvāyuḥ*), the one who goes everywhere. "Possessing offspring" (*prajāvatīḥ*) means bestowing the fruit in the form of progeny; "bearing cattle" (*paśubharāḥ*) means being well-carrying. "All" (*viśvāḥ*) refers to all [the hymns]. "Praiseworthy songs" (*abhandanāḥ*) are hymns of praise. He "urges forth" (*udiyarti*), meaning he impels them excellently. At what time? It is said: "In the day" (*ahardivi*), that is, during both day and night. Now, [the following] is addressed directly: "The sacred power" (*brahma*) is the sovereign ritual act, "possessing offspring," meaning endowed with progeny—that is, having offspring as its fruit. Or rather, in this context, it is "possessing offspring," meaning accompanied by progeny. Likewise, "wealth" (*rayim*)—of what kind? "Having horses as its abode" (*aśvapastyam*), meaning a stable for horses. O *Indo*, O shining Soma, when you have been drunk by Indra, pray for that very Indra from us; beg him for us.
Thus, at the beginning of the days, the tawny one, being urged forward,

passes over the fine, minute hairs of the waters— the streams that are naturally swift, being gathered together as they are purified and cleansed. O Indu, O Soma, when you are mixed with the waters upon the two pressing-boards, then, O Soma, being pressed, you sit within the jars.
O Soma, you who know the seasons, flow through the joints [of the filter] as one worthy of praise; run through the sheep’s wool, pouring out your dear honey.
O Indu, strike down all devourers and the voracious ones. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.

Flow through the joints, O Soma, knower of the seasons, worthy of praise; run through the sheep's wool, pouring forth the beloved honey. Strike down all the Rākṣasas and the Atriṇs, O Indu! May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 48.
O Soma, you are our knower of the seasons— that is, the one who knows our ritual actions and praises—
and you are worthy of hymns, meaning you are to be praised.
Since he is worthy of praise, the intention is that he is a knower of the seasons (*ṛtuvit*).
Such as you are, flow for our sacrifice; let your essence stream forth.
Flow around and pour out the beloved honey through the sheep’s wool filter, the ten-stranded purifier (*daśāpavitra*).
O Soma, shining within, strike down all the *atriṇas*—the devourers—and all the *rakṣases*.
Endowed with brave heroes and good sons, may we, at the sacrificial assembly (*vidatha*), speak forth—that is, utter aloud—the great, lofty word; that is to say, may we pray.
Or rather, let us utter abundant praise.

The second hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "pra tu drava," is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Uśanas Kāśya. By the rule governing unspecified meters, it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity.
Thus it is enumerated: "pra tu nava uśanā.
According to the statement "the *jagatī* [meter] applies from here upwards until Uśanas" (Anuvāka 9.67), the jurisdiction of the *jagatī* meter has ceased.
The application is concluded.
Run forward and settle into the vat; being purified by the men, flow toward the prize. Cleansing you like a spirited horse, they lead you with reins toward the sacred grass.
Flow forth; settle into the vat. Being purified by the men, flow toward the prize. Cleansing you like a spirited horse, they lead you with reins to the sacred grass.
O Soma, flow forth quickly; go forward!
Having gone, settle yourself within the *droṇakalaśa* vessel.
Being purified by the leaders—the men—flow toward and bestow food (*vāja*) for the sake of the sacrificer.

Like a vigorous, powerful horse, they cleanse you—the vigorous one—just as they groom a horse; thus purifying you, the Adhvaryu and the others lead you toward the *barhis* (the sacrificial grass) and the sacrifice with their fingers, which act like reins.
The god with his own weapons, the lord of the mountain, the slayer of Indu-foes, protecting his stronghold;
the father of the gods, their progenitor, the skillful one, the pillar of heaven, and the support of the earth.

Well-armed, the divine Indu flows on, slaying the malevolent and protecting the stronghold. He is the father of the gods, their progenitor, most skillful, the pillar of heaven, and the support of the earth. 2.
The god Soma, the moon, possessing excellent weapons, flows pure.

That god is the slayer of those who curse and the slayer of demons; guarding against harm and calamity, he is the father and protector of the gods, as well as their progenitor. Possessing keen insight and great strength, he is the pillar of heaven and the supporter of the earth.
Thus, one of such magnificent power flows pure.
3. *ga*-marjyati; 4. *ga*-marjyantaḥ.
Now, O Soma brought by the hawk (*syenabhṛta*), you who were carried by the hawk, bring—bring hither—the *prayāṃsi*, the foods.
O charioteer, bestowing wealth and granting desirable vigor, flow toward and reach the axle.
This Soma, being pressed, has run through the filter like a released torrent toward the waters;
sharpening his horns like a wild bull with sharp points, he rushes toward the secret [place] like a hero, a warrior.

This Soma, being pressed, has run forth around the filter like a released torrent; like a courser, he rushes on, whetting his two sharp horns like a buffalo, seeking the cows, like a hero, a warrior in secret.
This Soma, being pressed and being purified, like a courser skilled in the race, has been let loose; like a horse released, he runs and rushes around the filter.
Moreover, sharpening his two sharp horns like a great buffalo, a wild beast of the mountains, he rushes forth—this is another comparison.

Seeking cattle that have entered the cave, like a hero [seeking] booty as if with an arrow, just as two powerful bulls fight and run swiftly toward each other, so too does this being, whose nature is to settle, go— this is the remainder of the sense.
She has gone forth through the innermost depths of the mountains; somewhere in the wide expanse she has found the cattle.
Like the thundering lightning from heaven with its rays, O Indra, this stream of Soma flows clear for you.

She has come from the highest interior of the mountain; being present somewhere within the wide space, she has found the cows of heaven like the thundering lightning with its flashes. O Indra, this stream of Soma flows clear for you. 8.
This stream of Soma flowed forth from the highest exalted place toward its destined vessel or region.
Furthermore, she discovered the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis while they were staying in a certain hidden, wide space within the mountain—the dwelling place of leaves;
for that wide space (*ūrva*) was where the Paṇis, having stolen the cows, had placed them.
"Go upward, manifesting great qualities"—for this is another mantra (Ṛgveda 6.17.1). "Like lightning from heaven": like lightning from the light of heaven, thundering—that is, making sound.
Lightning is further specified.
"Propelled by stones"—this is the ellipsis.
Just as [the stone] makes a sound, so too this stream of Soma makes a sound;
O Indra, this very stream of Soma flows and purifies itself for you, for your drinking.
Or it flows away.

And indeed, O Soma, as you are being purified by Indra with his crushing blows, you gather around yourself a mass of cattle; bestowing many great and long-lasting gifts, O Lord of Power, grant us those things for which we have praised you.

And indeed, O Soma, being purified by Indra with his aids, I go around the heap of cattle; bestowing many great refreshments, O giver of life, O powerful one, grant us those [blessings], for you are praised. 9.
Moreover, O Soma, being purified—being cleansed—you encompass, that is, you reach around, the multitude of cattle, the herd carried away by the Paṇis; how so? It is said:
having mounted a single chariot together with Indra, upon one and the same vehicle.
1. There is no "great" [one] (ga-mahān). 2. Like [a horse], he ran around, he runs around the purifier (pavitra).
O Soma, quick-giver, bestowing gifts, being praised, do thou grant us many great and vast refreshments characterized by abundance.
O possessor of power, [grant them]; those refreshments are, as it were, thy own property.
Now follows the third hymn, consisting of eight verses, beginning with "atha somaḥ. The seer and other details are as before; it is cataloged as "ayaṃ somo 'ṣṭau."
The application is concluded.

This Soma, O Indra, is pressed for you; for you it flows clear. Drink of this! For you indeed have you made it, you have chosen it—the drop, the Soma—for exhilaration that is worthy of alliance. This Soma, O Indra, is pressed for you; for you it flows clear. Drink of this! For you indeed have you made it, you have chosen it—the drop, the Soma—for exhilaration that is worthy of alliance.
O Indra, this Soma is pressed for you; it is extracted for your sake.
In the case of the root *śru* (to hear) with the sense of desire (*kāma*) and the suffix *laṭ*, there is the elision of *ta* according to the rule "lopas ta ātmanepadeṣu."
For you, and for your sake alone, it flows and purifies itself;
and in you, drink this—drink that!
For you indeed have made this drop, this Soma.
And you have chosen this for what purpose?
For exhilaration, for a worthy companion, for an ally.
It is well known that Soma is the helper who bestows strength upon Indra;
the syntactical connection is: "O you who act in this manner, protect him."

Like a chariot with many protectors, he has been yoked; the great one [has been joined] for the winning of many riches. Then all the human-born beings, having Svapā as their protector, bowed down like trees standing upright in the forest. He, like a chariot with many protectors, has been yoked; the great one [has been joined] for the winning of many riches. Then all the human-born beings, having Svapā as their protector, bowed down like trees standing upright in the forest.

This very Soma is *bhuripāṭ*, the bearer of a heavy burden; like a chariot, he is *bhuripāṭ*, the bearer of the weight of what has been offered. He is yoked—that is, he is joined. Of what nature is he?
Great (*mahaḥ*).
For what purpose have these many, numerous riches been brought for our gain— that is, to give to us? Then, immediately after the yoking, all— every single one— of the *nahuṣyā* (human) [treasures].
Nahuṣa is a man;
his kinsmen, born again and again, are distinct from us. They are turned upward, facing upwards, in the forest—that which is desirable—toward their own fall.
This is a name for battle.
In this battle joined for the attainment of heaven, let them go down;
"navati" means going or movement.
Or alternatively:
O Māma, those seeking to fight gather for the purpose of battle.

Like Vāyu with his team of horses at the sacrifice, like the two Nāsatyas when invoked, you are most beneficent; possessing all boons, like the Giver of Wealth (Draviṇodas) in person, you are, O Soma, like Pūṣan, the inspirer of the intellect. vāyurna yaḥ niyutvān iṣṭyāmā nāsatyā iva have ā śambhaviṣṭhaḥ | viśvavāraḥ draviṇodā iva tman pūṣeva dhījavano asi soma || 3 || Like Vāyu who possesses a team of horses at the sacrifice, like the two Nāsatyas when called upon, you are most auspicious; possessing all desirable things, like the Giver of Wealth in person, like Pūṣan, you are the one who quickens the intellect, O Soma.
Soma who possesses *niyuts*—
the *niyuts* being the horses of Vāyu—
is like Vāyu himself; he is one who goes to the sacrifice (*iṣṭyāmā*), that is, one who moves toward the sacrifice.
Like the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, having heard the invocation—the call—you are most beneficent, the greatest bringer of happiness from every side.
Like Draviṇodas, the giver of wealth, you are Viśvavāra, possessing all desirable things within yourself; thus you are Viśvavāra.
Like Pūṣan, you are the nourisher; like Savitṛ, you are Dhījavana, swift as thought.
Or rather, O Soma, you are the impeller of actions.
1. Those connected with humans.

Like Indra, you who perform great deeds, O Soma, you are the slayer of Vṛtras and the breaker of forts. Like a steed, you are indeed the slayer of those called "Ahi," O Soma; you are the slayer of every Dasyu. Like Indra—*yaḥ* (who), *mahā* (great), *karmāṇi* (deeds), *cakriḥ* (performer)—you who habitually perform great acts, O *soma*, you are *vṛtrāṇām* (of the enemies) *hantā* (the slayer), *asi* (you are). Likewise, you are *pūrbhit* (the breaker of forts). Furthermore, like a *paidraḥ* (steed), for you are the slayer of those named *ahi* (*ahi-nāmnām*). Having come, you are the slayer of that [serpent]; the meaning is "of those so named. Not only of them, but you are also the slayer of *viśvasya* (every) *dasyoḥ* (Dasyu), of every enemy who causes destruction.

Like Agni when released into the forest, he effortlessly displays his splendors within the rivers; like a warrior-man amidst the great clamor of battle, Soma, as he flows clear, sends forth his wave. Like Agni who is let loose in the woods, he effortlessly (vṛthā) creates his radiant powers (pājāṃsi) within the rivers. Furthermore, like a man who is a combatant amidst the great shouting (upabdiḥ) [of battle], Soma, while being purified (pavamānaḥ), sends forth (iyarti) his swelling wave (ūrmim). Like Agni, he who is being released into the woods—that is, into the forest—effortlessly creates his powers; even so, Soma effortlessly creates his splendors within the rivers, which are the spaces of the atmosphere. Moreover, like a man who is a fighter, making a loud noise against a great enemy—this word *upabdi* is a name for sound—Soma, while being purified, sends forth his increased essence as a wave.

These Soma juices pass through the sheep’s woolly fleece like celestial water-jars raining from the clouds. Like rivers flowing effortlessly toward the ocean, these pressed drops have been released downward into the jars. These being purified, the *somāḥ* (Soma juices) go beyond the *vārāṇi* (woolly fleece), that is, the woolen filters made of sheep’s hair—this is the sense. Therein lies the illustration: *divyā na kośasaḥ*, like celestial water-jars, that is, like waters existing in heaven. They are further specified as *abhra-varṣāḥ*, raining down like from the clouds. Moreover, *vṛthā* (effortlessly), like *sindhoḥ na* (like rivers), the *sutāsaḥ* (pressed) Somas flow *nīcīḥ* (downward) toward the *kalaśān* (jars). They have been released; they go toward the jars.

Powerful like the host of Maruts, fly forth like the blameless celestial folk; like waters, quickly become well-disposed toward us—you who win a thousandfold, you who spread across the earth, like the sacrifice itself. O Soma, "powerful" (*śuṣmī*); "power" (*śuṣma*) is so called because of its drying or consuming nature—being thus strong, "fly forth" (*patrasva*) like "the host of Maruts" (*mārutaṃ śardhaḥ*). He clarifies this very comparison: "like the celestial folk" (*divyā viṭ*), that is, like the blameless (*anabhiśastā*) progeny. "Blame" (*abhiśāsaḥ*) means censure. Like waters, quickly become well-disposed (*sumatiḥ*) toward us—you who win a thousandfold (*sahasrāpsāḥ*), you who spread across the earth (*pratanāpāṭ*), like the sacrifice (*yajñaḥ*).
1. She blazes with flames;
she purifies herself, being blameless.
For the Brāhmaṇa states: "The Maruts are indeed the clans of the gods" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.5.7).
Furthermore: "O you who are like water (*āpaḥ*), cooking quickly and swiftly, be well-disposed toward us.
Moreover: "Possessing a thousand forms.
*Apsaḥ* is a name for form (*rūpa*).
"You are multiform, the protector of armies, the overcomer of armies like Indra; you become the sacrifice, O Sacrifice. Thus it is said.
O Soma, thy laws are indeed those of King Varuṇa; thou art established in lofty domains. Thou art pure, like Mitra the beloved; O Soma, by thy skill thou art like Aryaman.
Truly, O Soma, thy laws are like those of Varuṇa; lofty and profound is thy domain. Thou art pure, dear as Mitra; thou art to be honored like Aryaman, O Soma. 8.
O Soma, I quickly perform your *vratāni*—the remaining sense is "your ritual acts.
O Soma, your *dhāma*—your abode of splendor—is vast (*bṛhat*) and profound (*gabhīra*).
Like Mitra, you are dear (*priya*), radiant (*śuci*), or pure.
O Aryaman, you are indeed Aryaman; like a god, you are worthy of being honored.
"Pro sya vahniḥ" is the fourth hymn, consisting of seven verses.
The seer and other details are as before.
It is introduced by the words "Pro sya sasah."
The application is concluded.
Like rain from heaven, this Soma has flowed forth, purifying himself with broad streams;
the bearer, with a thousandfold stream, has settled among us in the lap of his mothers and in the wooden vessel.

He, the bearer, has flowed with broad streams from this heaven like rain; being purified, he has flowed forth. With a thousand streams he has settled within the fire-vessel, in the lap of his mother, and Soma has entered the woods. 1.
The combination of the two particles *pra* and *ū* is treated as a single particle.
"He (*saḥ*) is the carrier (*vahnih*), the bearer (*voḍhā*), who extends forward (*pra... asyāt*) and spreads out (*prasandate*) by means of the paths of sacrifice (*padhyābhiḥ*).
Like rain from heaven (*divo na vṛṣṭiḥ*), while being purified (*pavamānaḥ*), he pervades (*akṣāḥ*) as it were from the sky."
This Soma, possessing a thousand streams—that is, many streams—has settled, or sits down, among us.
The King of the rivers has clothed himself in you; he has mounted the swiftest ship of Truth.
In the waters, the drop, impelled by the falcon, has grown strong; he milks the father, and he milks the offspring of the father.

The King has clothed himself in the garments of the Sindhu rivers; he has mounted the straightest ship of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*). As a drop impelled by the falcon, he has grown great within the waters. The Father milks him; the Father milks his own offspring.

This King Soma "covers" (avasiṣṭe)—that is, he clothes himself in—the milk and other ingredients used for mixing, which serve as a garment for the rivers (udakānām), meaning the waters, or for the cows that flow with milk and such. Having done so, he mounts—that is, he ascends—the most straight (rajiṣṭhām) ship of the *ṛta*, the sacrifice. That drop (dṛpsaḥ), the essence of the Soma, impelled by the falcon (śyenajūtaḥ), grows—that is, it increases—within the waters, the *vasatīvarī* waters.
"I beheld this Soma, born from that Father—the protector, the one standing in the place of a father, namely the heavenly world. This Father, the protecting world, "milks" (duhe) its essence;
likewise, the Adhvaryu priest also milks it.
Or alternatively:
The father, the protector, the master, and the sacrificer milk this Soma characterized as described above for the sake of fruit; likewise, the Adhvaryu milks its essence.
Or rather, the repetition of "duhe" (he milks) is for the sake of emphasis.
1. Gayā.

They seek the lion, the tireless one, the golden-hued, the ruddy, the lord of this heaven; the hero, foremost in battles, asks for the cows; by his sight, the bull protects [the world]. They seek the lion—the destroyer of enemies, like a lion—who is the tireless impeller of the sweet waters, the golden-hued, the ruddy, the lord and protector of this heaven; the sacrificers reach out toward Soma. In battles, the hero, the foremost among the gods, Soma, asks for the cows stolen by the Paṇis; having slain the Paṇis, he seeks the path of the cows to recover them. Moreover, by his sight—that is, by his power—the bull, the sprinkler Indra, protects the universe.

They yoke to the wide-wheeled chariot the horse with honeyed back, formidable, tireless, and lofty; the sisters, his kinswomen, cleanse him, and those of common origin strengthen the vigorous one. They yoke to the chariot with its broad wheels the horse whose back is honeyed, who is terrible, tireless, and sublime—the Soma, who stands in place of the horse. Just as one yokes a horse to a chariot, so do the priests yoke him to the chariot of sacrifice, which has many wheels and is the means of swift motion. Furthermore, the sisters—those who move by themselves and are mutually related as sisters—or rather, the "kinswomen," meaning the fingers (being produced from the same hand), they both cleanse and purify this Soma. Thus it is said: those of common origin, being bound together, strengthen the vigorous Soma, making him powerful.

Four milch-cows yielding clarified butter attend upon him; established within the same firm support, they honor him with reverence as they purify themselves. These many cows encompass him from every side. Four milch-cows yielding clarified butter attend upon him (Soma). Of what sort are they? Established within the same firm support—the atmosphere which sustains all—they honor him with reverence (namas) as they are being purified by food (anna). These many, abundant cows encompass him from every direction.

The pillar of heaven, the supporter of the earth, and all the peoples are in his hands. For him who praises him, there has been a well, accompanied by steeds; for the sake of Indra, the mountain is a stalk of honey. Pillar of heaven, supporter of the earth, and all the peoples are in his hands. For him who praises him, there has been a well, accompanied by steeds; for the sake of Indra, the mountain is a stalk of honey.
1. ta1.2.3.4.5.6-bha1.2.6-nāvaḥ; bha7-nāgāvaḥ | 2.
ta1.2.3.4.5.6-bha1.2.6-nāvaḥ; bha7-nāgāvaḥ | This Soma is the support of heaven, the celestial world.
Just as the pillar is for a house,
so too is he the supporter— the sustainer— of the earth.
Moreover, all people, all creatures, abide in the hand of this Soma.
The spring (*utsa*): from which desires flow forth, thus it is the spring; [it is] Soma.
May he, being yoked for you who praise and offer oblations, be possessed of horses; may he become so.
That Soma is the bountiful one, the honey;
the genitive case is used in the sense of "action.
Soma is the stalk of sweet juice.
"An *aṃśu* is that which consists of mere tranquility," says Yāska (Nirukta 2.5).
[The term] *indriyāya* refers to the purifying wind; it is purified (*pūyate*) and thoroughly cleansed (*abhipūyate*).
Flowing again and again toward the feast for the gods, O Soma, as the slayer of Vṛtra, flow for Indra.
Be able to grant us great wealth, most resplendent; may we be masters of heroic power.

Flowing onward, toward the feast for the gods, O Soma, flow as the slayer of Vṛtra for Indra. Bestow great wealth, most resplendent; may we be masters of riches consisting of heroic power. (7) || 25 || The fifth hymn, beginning with "pra hinvānaḥ," is the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha’s composition addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa. It is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity. Thus it is enumerated: "pra hinvānaḥ, five [verses], iṣṭaḥ. The application [of the hymn] has been explained.
Urged forward, the progenitor of the two worlds has come forth like a chariot seeking booty,
going toward Indra while sharpening his weapons and taking all treasures into his hands.

Being urged forward, the progenitor of heaven and earth has set forth like a chariot seeking booty, going toward Indra while sharpening his weapons and taking all treasures into his hands. Being urged forward—that is, being impelled by the Adhvaryus and others—the progenitor of heaven and earth (the two worlds), his status as their progenitor arising from the bestowing of rain and the receiving of oblations; such is Soma, who, desiring to win—that is, to grant—booty, meaning food, has gone forth, that is, he moves forward. Going toward Indra, reaching him, and sharpening his weapons—that is, making them well-pointed so as to possess keen arms for the purpose of assisting Indra—he takes all treasures into his hands for the sake of giving them to us. Performing thus, he has set forth.
The voices have cried out toward the bull who dwells upon the three ridges, the bestower of vital strength, whose hands are marked with rings.
Clothed in the forests like Varuṇa among the rivers, he, the mighty one, bestows desirable boons.
1. *ga* for the sense-object (*indriyārtha*); *ta*, *bha*, *mu*, *ya* for the sense-faculty (*indriya*). 2. *ta³-bha⁶* is purified (*abhipūyate*). Something has been abandoned (*tyakta*).
O Soma, winning [the prize], unassailed by enemies, come to the feast of the gods, the sacrifice.
As a slayer of foes, flowing with sweetness, purify yourself for Indra. Bestow wealth that is desirable to many.
And may we be masters of great valor. O Soma, winning [the prize], flow for Indra—the slayer of Vṛtra—for the sake of the gods' drinking at the divine banquet.
How art thou?
Thou art capable, possessed of power.

By your grace, O Puru, may we become masters of abundant wealth—wealth that brings great joy, wealth consisting of excellent heroes (*suvīrya*, meaning one in whom there are beautiful heroes). [The meaning is as stated in Bha4; according to Mu, being a winner (*vanvan*), O Soma, for the sake of Indra, at the *devavīti* (the feast for the gods), you, the slayer of Vṛtra (*vṛtrahā*) and the unassailable one (*avāta*), flow forth for Indra. In what manner? You are capable (*śagdhi*), you are powerful (*śaktimān*), and you are great (*mahaḥ*).]
By your grace, may we become masters of wealth—of that riches which belongs to Puruścandra, who is greatly gladdening and possesses excellent heroism, and in whom there are beautiful heroes.
3. *ta3-bha-pra* hinvānaḥ.
4. *ga-ta3-bha1.2.4.7*—"tayoḥ" is not present.

Toward the three-backed, bull-like bestower of vigor, the voices of the singers have cried out. Dwelling in the woods like Varuṇa among the rivers, the bestower of treasures distributes desirable gifts.

"Tri-pṛṣṭha": he is so called because he possesses three *pṛṣṭhas*—that is, three hymns (*stotra*s), or the locations such as the *droṇakalaśa*, or the *savana*s (pressings). That *vṛṣaṇam* (the showerer), the bestower of vigor (*vayodhām*), the giver of food, Soma—the *vāṇīḥ* (voices) or words of the *āghoṣavatām* (resounding) *vāṇīḥ* (songs of praise).
They have lowed; they cry out.
Enveloping—clothing himself in—the waters, tree after tree, Varuṇa covers them just as Varuṇa covers the rivers.
Soma is the bestower of treasures (*ratnadhāḥ*), the giver of jewels.
He bestows and grants desirable riches to those who praise him.
O hero of the host, possessing all valor, victorious, and triumphant, flow onward as a winner of riches;
armed with sharp weapons and a swift bow, a skillful protector, you are invincible—you who conquer enemies in battles.

The foremost of heroes, the all-heroic, the powerful, the conqueror—flow on! A winner of riches, with sharpened weapons and a swift bow, invincible among the well-disposed, overcoming the enemies in battles by force. 3.

O Soma, flow clear; you are the one who plays. You are the leader of heroes, a host of heroes—that is, one whose assembly consists of heroes. You are possessed of all heroes—one so described is one for whom all are warriors. You are mighty, enduring, and victorious by nature. You are a gatherer, a distributor of riches, with sharp weapons, a swift bowman whose bow is habituated to rapid endurance, and one who is unvanquished in battles (*sumatsu*). Unconquered, you overcome those who oppose you. Where? In the *pṛtanās*, among the enemy armies. Whom? The enemies.

Creating wide pastures and bringing forth riches, flow toward us with your two united inspirations. Desiring the waters, the dawns, the light of heaven, and the cattle, bring together for us manifold and great strengths.

Creating wide pastures and fearlessness, flow toward us, O Soma, bringing together the two well-united worlds. Desiring to win the waters, the highest light, and the cattle, bestow upon us great and wondrous strengths.
O Soma, you who provide wide pastures and broad paths, bringing fearlessness to your worshippers, you who bestow wisdom—
purify yourself, O Steed, uniting these two names of Heaven and Earth as they flow together.
Desiring to obtain—wishing to enjoy for the sake of nourishment—the waters, the dawns, the sun, the cattle, and the rays, you, O giver of wonders, roar aloud;
[you roar] in order to grant us great, mighty, and abundant foods (*vājān*). This is the ellipsis.
O Indu, as you flow clear, exhilarate Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra, and Viṣṇu;
exhilarate the host of Maruts, exhilarate the gods, and exhilarate the great Indra for our intoxication.
To Agni, O Indu, as thou art being purified; to Soma, to Varuṇa, to Mitra, to Indra, to Viṣṇu, to the host of Maruts, to the gods, and to the great Indra, O Indu, for exhilaration—[gladden them] all.
1. *ga-ta-bha* do not have ‘*droṇa*’... or ‘*vā*’. 2. *ga-ta-bha* read ‘*asoḍhā*’. 3. *ga-ta1.2.3-bha* do not have ‘*te*’. 4. *bha1(2)* reads ‘*kṣara*’.
O Pavamāna, being purified, O Indu Soma, you satisfy Varuṇa and the other gods with [the juice] for their exhilaration.
Because Indra is the primary deity, he is mentioned twice.
Thus, like a king, flow with your power, O Seasoned One, purifying yourself and driving away all enemies.
Bestow vital strength upon the singer for the sake of splendor; and do you, O gods, protect us always with your blessings.

Like a king, O Indu, being measured by the seasons, you drive away all misfortunes with your might. Bestow vital strength upon us for our well-spoken hymns and for splendor. Do you protect us always with your blessings. 6.
Concluding the hymn with this [verse], he prays for the fruit: "O Soma— [the word] 'thus' being understood as 'praised in this manner'—

you, being possessed of the season (ṛtumān), like a king, by means of this strength (amena balena), crushing (ghanighnat) all (viśvā) misfortunes (duritā), that is, destroying them, flow forth (pavasva)."

O Soma, being seen within, bestow beautiful splendor upon our hymn for the sake of glory; having understood that which is meaningful for the purpose of liberation, grant us vital strength—bestow food.
Since food has its cause in praise, there is a primary statement regarding those words of praise.
The remainder is established.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness [of ignorance],
may the Great Lord of the Holy Tīrtha bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the third adhyāya in the eighth aṣṭaka of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā-bhāṣya, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
Salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Having explained the third [hymn] of the seventh Aṣṭaka, Sāyaṇācārya, who knows the meaning of the Śruti, now desires to comment upon the Śruti.

In this context, the sixth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "asarji," is the seer's work of Kaśyapa Mārīca; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, concerns Pavamāna Soma, and has Oṃ as its deity.
It is cataloged under the heading "asarji kaśyapaḥ.
Its ritual application (viniyoga) has already been explained.

He was poured forth from the mouth like a steed to be won in battle; the first wise thinker, through his inspired thought, [prepared] the ten fingers on the woolly back. The bearers direct him toward his seats.

He has been released—the speaker, like a chariot-horse in battle—by means of inspired thought. The first thinker, the mental disposer, [is led] by the ten sisters upon the sheep’s back; they drive the bearer toward his seats.

The speaker is "śabdāyamānaḥ" (making sound), from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking," with the suffix *vanip*. Such is the purifying Soma; he is released into the *ājī*. It is called *ājī* because the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) drive (*ajanti*) toward the ritual purpose; that is the sacrifice. Therein, he is released along with *dhī*—meaning either the ritual action or the hymn—into the vessels. In this regard, there is an illustration: "as on a chariot-path in battle. This is a name for a battle (*saṃgrāma*), so called because they cast (*ajanti*) weapons therein. Just as a horse is released there by means of *dhī*—that is, by the hand—so it is here. Of what nature is he? He in whom the gods have their *manotā* (mental impulse).
1. *ga* and *ta* (3, 4): *tādṛśaḥ*; 2. *ga*: *āyuṃdhyatra iti*; 3. *ta* (1, 2, 4, 5), *bha*, *ra*, *mu*: *mucyate*.
Their minds are woven across and through him;
and so it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "For in him their minds are woven" (AiB 2.10).
He is the first, the chief of all the gods, the wise one.
The mind is the impulse; the prayer is the praise.
Possessing that [praise], the ten sisters—the fingers—having directed the sacrificial halls toward him, [bring] Soma, the bearer, to the high ridge.
The prefix *adhi-* expresses the sense of the locative case.
They drive—that is, they impel—the [Soma] into the filter made of sheep’s wool (*avya*), which is produced by the unborn (*avibhava*) or the unweaned (*avivāla*).
[The root *aj* means "to go" and "to impel."]
Pressed by the divine people with their poetic wisdom and by the descendants of Nahuṣa, Indu flows forth—
he who is cleansed by mortal men, purified by these swift ones with milk and water.

The drop, pressed by the sons of Nahuṣa with the hymns of the divine folk, flows forth; the immortal Indu, being purified by these men—by mortals—with the stones, with the waters, and with the milk of cows. 2.

Being pressed—that is, being purified—by the wise and skillful singers, by the Nahuṣya men, the drop, Soma, goes toward the sacrifice for the sake of partaking of the divine host, that is, the company of gods existing in heaven;
here, the dative case ending is replaced by the long vowel of the preceding sound according to the rule "supāṃ suluk.
He approaches the sacrifice for the purpose of consuming the Soma.

Furthermore, that immortal Soma, which is free from the nature of death, being thoroughly purified by men—the leaders of the ritual—by mortals, by stones, by sheep's-wool filters, by cows—that is, by ox-hides used for the three pressings or by cow-products such as milk—and by waters such as the *vasatīvarī* and so forth, goes toward the sacrifice (*yajñam*). Since the prefix (*upa*) is heard in the text, a verb of motion (*yāti*) is to be supplied.
The bull roars for the bull; this flowing drop, shining white, yields the milk of the cow.
The earth, with its thousand rays, bestows wide space upon him; through us, the sun passes through the fine mesh.

The bull, bellowing loudly for the bull, this Soma-stalk flows for him; being purified, he moves toward the bright milk of the cow. With a thousand rays, the thunderbolt stands firm upon the broad earth; like the sun, he passes through the fine mesh without being defiled.

The *vṛṣan*, the showerer of desires— or acting like a bull— *roruvat*, roaring loudly, the *aṃśu* Soma, while being purified (*pavamāna*), goes toward this *vṛṣṇe*, for the sake of the showering Indra; he goes toward the *ruśat*, shining (this is a form derived from the root *ruc*) white milk of the cow, which is the substance used for mixing.
The root *īr* means "to go";
it belongs to the *ādādi* class.
Furthermore, there is the root *ṛk*.
By the rule *chandasīvanipau*, the suffix *vanip* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).

Thus, *stotravān* means "possessing hymns," and *vanot* means "the knower of praises. The *sūraḥ* (heroic one), the possessor of great heroism (*suvīryaḥ*), the impeller of all [priests] in rites such as the *abhiṣṭoma*—that Soma, by means of *adhvasmābhiḥ* (unwearied paths), that is, paths free from destruction or injury, passes through *sahasram pathibhiḥ* (a thousand paths), that is, many ways, into the *aṇvam* (minute) *pavitram* (filter).
Having passed through it, he goes to the *droṇakalaśa* (wooden vat).
O Indu, as you purify yourself, strike down the strongholds of the fiercely-eyed one with your power;
like a tree struck by a growing bolt from above, shatter those who are near and those who are far off, so that they may be brought low.

Crush the dwellings of the Rākṣasas, however firm they may be; O Indu, as you purify yourself, open wide the paths to strength. With your swift and increasing force, strike down from above those who stand near at hand, even from afar, as their refuge fails them.
O Soma, shatter—even those very firm places, the strongholds and cities of the Rākṣasa, which are otherwise difficult for others to approach.
(The root *ruj* belongs to the Tudādi class, meaning "to break").
Furthermore, O Indu, O Pavamāna, as you are being purified by the filters and other means, uncover—that is, bestow—his *vājās*, whether they be his foods or his powers.
The meaning is "bring hither.

Likewise, those *rākṣasas* who come from above, from the upper region; or those who come from nearby, in the vicinity; and those who come from afar, from a distant land—of those *rākṣasas*, strike down their leader, their bringer, their master.
The root *tujati* has the sense of "injuring.
With a "striking weapon"—that is, with a weapon that is an instrument of killing—you must "tear asunder," that is, cut;
the root *vṛśca* meaning "to cut" belongs to the Tudādi class.
As in the ancient time, O possessor of all boons, prepare forward paths for the singer who offers new hymns.
May we, O you who provide abundant food, attain those great ones who laugh with splendor and drink at the appointed seasons.

As in the ancient times, O possessor of all boons, prepare the forward paths for our newest well-spoken hymn. May we attain those irresistible, great paths of yours, O guardian of the seasons, O provider of abundant food—yes, O you who provide abundant food! 5.

O you who possess all desirable things (*viśvavāra*), O Soma—such as you are, being pressed (*prasuvānaḥ*), impelled by the priests (*ṛtvigbhiḥ hīyānaḥ*), golden-hued (*hariḥ*), the stalk (*aṃśuḥ*) Soma, you are poured out (*pari sarji*) into the filter (*pavitre*) made of undivided [wool], the *daśāpavitra*.
For what purpose? [To flow through it.]
For the sake of winning, that is, for the acquisition of wealth or for the worship of the gods;
in this regard, there is an illustration: "like a chariot."

Just as a chariot is sent forth in battle for the purpose of slaying enemies or for seizing the wealth of enemies, even so this Soma, being purified by the filter, attains *indriya*— the characteristic mark of Indra, or that which is sufficient for Indra— and *śloka*, the hymn of praise. (The root) *ā-plu* means "to pervade."
The *luṅ* tense is used here.
Thus, that Soma, with *prayobhiḥ*—pleasing oblations in the form of food—*ajuṣata*, that is, he served or gratified the gods.
[The root] *juṣ* [is used] in the senses of "pleasing" and "serving."
Truly, he has flowed clearly through the filter, assuming his names in the womb of the sage;
settling like a *hotṛ* priest in his seat, the seven inspired seers have approached the vessels with offerings.

He has flowed clearly; he has run through the filter, assuming his names. The sage, settling in his own womb, sits like a Hotṛ priest in his place within the vessels. To him have come the seven seers, the inspired singers. 2.

Soma, the protector (*nṛkṣakṣas*) of men, the seer (*kavi*), whose wisdom has transcended all, bearing (*dadhānaḥ*) the water known as *vasatīvarī*, flows toward the filter (*pavitra*), the place of origin (*yoni*) of this very self, moving around it on all sides;
then he goes to the seat (*sadanam*), where they sit.
In that [Soma], like a Hotṛ priest among the gods, he sits down at the place of praise; even so, Soma sits down in the vessels (*camū*).
"Cam" refers to the *camasa* cups, the *graha* ladles, and so forth.
He flows toward them.
Immediately thereafter, seven wise brahmins—namely the sages Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, Gautama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha—approached this Soma with hymns of praise.

Wise, the knower of the way, belonging to all the gods, Soma goes to his eternal seat while being purified. He becomes the one who delights in all poetic inspirations; the sage extends himself toward the people and toward cattle.

Wise, the finder of the path, belonging to all the gods, Soma goes to his own seat while being purified. May he be the one who delights in all poetic inspirations; the sage strives after the people for the sake of cattle. 3.
Sumedhas:

by the rule "nityamasic prajāmedhayoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.122), the suffix *asic* is applied, resulting in a form ending in *-as*. Thus, he is one of beautiful wisdom (*śobhanaprajña*). Gātuvit: a knower of the path (*mārgasya vettā*).
Or alternatively:
*gātavaḥ* means the singers;
[the one] who causes them to obtain wealth.
*Viśvadeva* means approached by all the gods; or alternatively,
*deva* refers to playing or radiance.

Endowed with pervasive radiance, such Soma, being purified— that is, being cleansed— proceeds toward the eternal, indestructible seat, the wooden vat (droṇakalaśa). Thereafter, he becomes one who delights— that is, one whose nature is to take pleasure— in all poetic works, that is, in all hymns of praise.
He who is devoted to the practice of joy,
being thus steadfast and wise, strives— that is, makes an effort— to follow after the five classes of people, namely the four castes together with the Niṣādas. That is to say, he follows them.
O Soma Pavamāna, all those gods, the thirty-three, are yours;
ten others, the seven priests, cleanse you upon the ridge with their own powers and with swift steeds.
O Soma Pavamāna, all these gods—the thirty-three—along with the ten who possess self-sovereignty, and the seven impetuous ones, cleanse you upon the ridge by their own powers. 4.
1. In *ta-bhara*, "suvānaḥ" is not present.
2. In *ga-ta-bha6*, it is "for the purpose of bringing wealth" (*dhanāharaṇārtham*); in *bhara*, it is "for the sake of wealth, for the purpose of bringing" (*dhanāya haraṇārtham*).
3. In *ga*, it is "they drink" (*camanti*).

O Pavamāna, O Soma being purified, those who are your own— those well-known thirty-three gods (traya ekādaśāsaḥ)— all of them, in their entirety, abide in the secret place (niṇye). [The suffix *ḍat* is used here in the sense of completion.]
This is that which has its name hidden;
it exists in the hidden place, the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).

You, such as you are, the ten fingers discharge (*sṛjanti*)—that is, they purify—with *svadhā*, meaning with waters, upon the summit, that is, upon the exceedingly elevated, non-woolly, non-fleecy filter (*pavitra*).
Furthermore, "yahvīḥ":
by the rule *vā chandasi*, there is a long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*).
The great (*yahvyaḥ*), seven—that is, numbering seven—rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others, emit you.
The meaning is that they purify you with their own waters, namely the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *ekadhanā* waters.
Let there be true strength for the one being purified, wherein all singers have gathered together;
when he won light for the day and the world for Manu, he struck down the Dasyu as he desired.

Then let there be truth for the one being purified, wherein all the singers shall find release; when he has made light for the serpent and won the world, he protected Manu and struck down the Dasyu in combat.
May that true, reality-constituting, and well-known place of the purifying Soma be ours immediately;
may that place be ours where all the poets, the singers, assemble together to offer praise.
May that place belong to this Soma, whose light he makes for the day, providing space, illumination, and radiance.
The particle *u* is used for emphasis. That light (*jyotis*) protected (*prāvat*), that is, guarded with excellence, the king named Manu.
Likewise, who made Soma’s own splendor (*tejas*) into something prone to approach (*abhīkam*) the Dasyu—the Asura who destroys everything?
In the *luṅ* [aorist] tense of the root *kṛ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *cli* suffix by the rule "in a mantra, *ghas*" is substituted [for *kṛ*].
Like a truthful king proceeding to an assembly, Soma, the purifier, has gone toward all the vessels rich in cattle; like a wild buffalo among the woods, he has settled within them.

Like a fetus within the womb, like a true king among cattle-owners, Soma—being purified and seeking "this is mine"—has entered the jars; settling like a wild buffalo in the forests, he has flowed forth. 6.

The Hotṛ is the invoker of the gods; like a skilled butcher, he approaches the sacrificial houses as if they were already filled with cattle. Furthermore, he is like a truthful king whose actions are true—a "Manu-saminī," so called because in him battles are properly won by his warriors.

Going toward those battles—that is, proceeding—so too does Soma, while being purified, sit within the wooden vessels (*vana*) that are desirable, namely in the place of the *vasatīvarī* waters; like a wild beast, a buffalo—a beast called "buffalo"—standing in the waters, he has gone around, he moves about, the jars known as *droṇa*s.
Or rather:
Soma, the great one, or the one worthy of worship, goes around the jars.
"Sākamakṣaḥ" is the eighth hymn, consisting of five verses; it is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Nodhas Gautama.
The meter and deity are as before.
Thus it is enumerated: "Sākamakṣaḥ: five [verses], by Nodhas."
The application has been explained.
May the ten sisters, the fingers, together with the axle, cleanse him; the ten swift thoughts of the sage purify him.
Like a prize-winning steed, the golden-hued one has run around the streams and reached the wooden vat of Sūrya.
1. "Those [words] are well-known" does not exist [in this context].
2. He goes around the sacrificial hall (yajñagṛha).
3. *gacchate* (ta¹); *tara*. 4.1.57. *bha6-gacchaṃta*; *ta3.6-bha1.2.4.7-gacchati*; *mu-yathā parigacchate*.

4. Being purified, being cleansed—O bull, the sisters have cleansed thee for me. The prayers of the wise man, seeking wealth, have sped toward the golden one. On the far shore of the sun, he has reached the vat like a prize-winning steed. || 1 ||
"vmākamukṣaḥ" means those who sprinkle together simultaneously; "ukṣ" is in the sense of "to sprinkle," and this is the form [of the word] in the *kip* suffix.
Such fingers, moving skillfully here and there for the sake of performing their tasks, cleanse—that is, purify—the sacrificial ground;
[the root] *mṛj* is used in the sense of "purification" and "adornment.
Likewise, there are ten—that is, numbering ten—*dhītayaḥ* (devotions or insights).
It is bent by the fingers.
The fingers of the wise, capable, or intelligent one—of the Soma who is to be consecrated by divine lot or who is desired—are the impellers.
Then the golden-hued Soma, the offspring of the Sun, flows around those quarters that have appeared as his wives.

For since they manifest through the splendor of the sun, that [sun] is the "born" (jāta) of the quarters. His [the sun's] "vājī," which is by nature expansive, stands like a horse; Soma reaches—that is, pervades—the *droṇa* vessel. The root *nakṣ* has the sense of pervading (*vyāpti*).

Like a child with its mothers, the bull, desiring the cows, has flowed forth—the stone, rich in boons. Like a youth going to a maiden at the appointed place, he unites with the milk-streams in the jar.

Bellowing, desiring the gods, the bull— the showerer of desires— and therefore possessed of many boons, Soma, the *vṛdhi*, is joined together with the *vasatīvarī* waters that have become his mothers;
he is united there like a child with its mothers.

Just as a desiring son is sustained by his mothers through the giving of milk; the root *dhāv* has the sense of "to go," and this is the form in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) used in the passive voice.

Just as a man approaches a young woman, so too the wind (*vyāna*), approaching its own well-prepared and consecrated place, unites with the *usraiyā*—that is, with the waters or with the products of the cow such as milk—within the *kalaśa*, the wooden vat. Because the root *gam* is used here with the prefix *sam-*, the Atmanepada ending is applied according to the rule "samo gami."

And indeed, the udders of the milch-cow have swelled; the wise one accompanies [the rite] with streams of drops. The cows mix his head with milk from their teats, as if with ornaments, through their cleansing.
Moreover, regarding the word *vadhanyā*:
*aghnyā* is a name for a cow. The Soma has swelled forth from the udder—the place where the milk is—of the cow that is not to be slain (*aghnyā*).
Having entered into the plants and other substances, Soma causes them to swell through his excellence.
Regarding the root *pyai* (to swell), the substitution of *pī* occurs in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) according to the rule "liṅyaṅośca.
This Soma, the drop of excellent wisdom (*vsumedhāḥ*), meaning one of beautiful insight, *sacate*—that is, he accompanies, comes together with, or unites with—the streams (*dhārābhiḥ*).
Then, in the *camūs*—
the *camūs* being the vessels such as the *grahas*, so called because they "sip" (*cam*) or consume the Soma therein—
they mix with white milk the Soma situated within them, which is like a head (*mūrdhan*) raised high, and thus completely cover it.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as they cover [themselves] with garments that have been washed and purified, so it is here.
O Pavamāna, roaring with desire, bestow upon us, through the gods, wealth consisting of horses;
may the chariot-borne, longing Puraṃdhi come to us to grant cattle and riches.

Acting like a poet (*kavi*), that is, behaving as a seer; or alternatively, desiring those who are poets, namely the singers. Therein is an illustration: just as a cowherd goes around the pen (*vraja*)—the place for cows that is to be meditated upon—for the sake of increasing the cattle, so too does he flow toward the vessels for the gratification of the gods.
Twofold, unfolding the law of the mortal, the worlds expand for him who finds the light of heaven.
Like cows swelling with milk in the stall, the prayers flowing toward the Truth have lowed toward Indu.

Twofold, uncovering the law of immortality, he who finds the light of heaven; the worlds have spread out. Like cows swelling in their stall, our prayers, tending toward the Eternal Law, have lowed toward the Soma-drop.

Soma, the sustainer (*dhāma*) and locus (*dhāraṇa*) of the immortal waters, moving through the intermediate space, unfolds himself in two ways (*dvitā*), covering both sides with his own brilliance as he proceeds through the middle.
Then, for that Soma who knows the light of heaven (*svarvit*), the worlds expand;
that is to say, they expand to provide a path for the movement of his rays.

Then, swelling and desiring to please— the prayers characterized by praise, the words seeking the sacrifice and longing for the Truth— they lowed toward this most excellent *indu*, the Soma, at the place of sacrifice (*svasara*).
Or rather, they long for the Soma.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Just as cows, being milked, let forth milk from their bodies at *svasara*.
*Svasara* is a cow-pen, so called because here the cows are well-thrown (*su-asyante*) or driven together.
In that case, they produce sound by aiming at it; it is just like that.
