When the seer bears his poetic visions around all the worlds like a hero on a chariot, he wins glory among the gods for mortals; may he, the ever-renewing one, bring wealth to the skillful man among many people.
When the sage bears his poetic visions like a hero, a chariot [bearing] all beings; may there be glory among the gods for the mortal man, and new wealth for skillful men among the many. 3.

Soma is the poet (*kavi*) whose wisdom has transcended; he brings forth, that is, carries around or encompasses, the *kāvya*—the poetic works, the deeds, or the hymns of the poet. How, one might ask? [As follows:]
Like a hero who is truly a hero, a chariot that overcomes enemies,
so does he encompass all the beings involved in battle.
At that time, the pervasive glory and wealth residing among the gods shall adorn the mortal, the man who offers praise.
The form [of the verb] is derived from the root *bhū* with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) and the desiderative suffix (*san*).

Desiring to cause [the sacrificer] to prosper (*bhāvayitum icchan*), Soma becomes worthy of praise (*navyaḥ*— to be lauded) among the many (*purubhūṣu*) sacrificial abodes for the sake of skill (*dakṣāya*)— that is, for the increase of the wealth (*rāyaḥ*) given by himself.
The suffix *yat* is applied after vowels [ending in a word] when expressing praise (*stuti*).
Born for glory, he has gone forth from glory; he bestows glory and vital strength upon his singers.
Clothed in glory, they have attained immortality; their encounters become true when the measured course is run.

Born for glory, he has gone forth toward glory; he bestows vigor and glory upon his singers. Clothed in glory, they have attained immortality; their battles become true when the mountain is measured. 4.
That Soma was born for glory; he has manifested for the sake of perfection.
He says that very thing:
he has come forth specifically for the purpose of providing support.
It issues forth directly from the rays.

And having issued forth, that Soma [bestows] glory— meaning that which is to be meditated upon, to be understood, and to be protected— for the *jaritṛ*s, the chanters, and for the *stotṛ*s, the praisers.
He bestows, ordains, or grants food, strength, or life.
Clothed in the glory bestowed by him, the singers attain immortality—divinity or deathlessness.
In that [Soma], which moves with measured step, they have gathered together.

The term *yuddhanāman* means "that wherein battle is properly obtained"; the suffix *thak* is applied to the seventh [case-ending] by the rule *samīnaḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.11). Those battles are *satyāni*, meaning they are true and according to reality, and not false.
The meaning is that by that moon they are defeated.
Bestow food and vigor upon both flanks; O mortal, make wide light for the gods.
For all those offerings are well-pleasing to you; O Soma being purified, you destroy the enemies.

Bring us food, bring us strength; drive away the horseless and the cowless. Create wide light for us, O mortal! Bring the gods hither, for all these great deeds are yours. O Soma, being purified, you shall overcome our enemies. 5.

O Soma, bring to us poison, food, and the strengthening essence of food; furthermore, bring the cow that carries all desirable things— the cow who is the means for accomplishing the sacrifice through the gift of milk—
and likewise, create the great light known as the sun, making it the illuminator of the world.
O Sage, satisfy the gods, Indra and the others, with Soma;
[use] the present tense (laṭ) for the root *mad* according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" [Pāṇini 2.4.73], with the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix *śap*,
and [the form] *aninvānaḥ* due to the non-distinction between the middle and active voices (*ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada*).
Moreover, O Soma, all the *rakṣas* are easily overcome by you through your great power, without effort;
indeed, [the particle] *hi* is used for emphasis.
Therefore, O Pavamāna, being purified, O Soma, drive away and slay them all there.
The tenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "kani kranina," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Praskaṇva, the son of Kaṇva.
Thus it is enumerated: "kani kranina: Praskaṇva.
It is composed in two meters (chandas).
The application [of the mantra] has been explained.

Moving with a leap, being swallowed by the tawny one, settling within the belly of the ocean while being purified, he—being guided by men—makes the cow his garment; therefore, generate inspired thoughts through your own inherent powers.

He leaps forth, the tawny one; being pressed, he settles within the belly of the wooden vessel. Being purified and guided by the men, he makes the milk his garment. Thence, generating hymns through his own powers, he produces inspired thoughts.
Being purified, or being purified on all sides, being overcome—the *hari*, the golden-colored Soma—*kanikranti*, he sounds repeatedly.
Regarding the root *krand*, when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided, the reduplication becomes *ni* according to the rule "in *adardhati*, *dardhati*, etc. [Pāṇini 7.4.65]. It is the reduplicated form.
It stands firm.
Thus being purified and cleansed, sitting within the belly of the *vana*, the desirable wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*), he makes a sound.

Furthermore, held and restrained by the men—the performers of the rite and the chanters—Soma, covering the "cows," that is, the products of the cow such as milk and so forth, assumes his own form, the bright cleansing garment (*nirṇij*), within the cups and other vessels.
Therefore, O singers, generate for this Soma hymns worthy of thought, together with the *svadhā* offerings—that is, the oblations. You have generated them.
The absence of the substitution of the final letter of *jha* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively:
O singers, generate—that is, produce—hymns for this Soma.
"Perform [it]"—that is the meaning.
Hari, creating upon the earth, sends forth the speech of immortality like a rower propelling a boat;
he reveals the secret names of the gods among the gods and proclaims them upon the sacrificial grass.
1. *ga*-devatvamamaraṇam;
2. *ga*-janayantu; 3. *ga*-chāndasatādeśaḥ; *ga1*-chāndādeśaḥ; *bha2.4*-chāndodādeśaḥ.
Being released upon the earth, he stirs the voice of Truth like a rower urging a boat. The god makes manifest the secret names of the gods upon the sacrificial grass for all to hear. 2.
Being poured out and being released, the golden-hued Soma impels the divine speech that exists upon the path of Truth (*ṛta*).
An illustration for this is:
just as a boatman, ferrying people to the shore, propels his boat, so does he.
The root *ṛ* means "to go";
it belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class.
By the rule *artipiparyoḥ*, the vowel of the reduplication is changed to *i*.

Then the shining god Soma reveals the secret, hidden names—that is, the bodies—of the gods, Indra and the others, for the singer who has proclaimed them aloud at the sacrifice upon the sacrificial grass (barhis). He makes them manifest so that they may be praised.

Like the surging waves of the waters, our inspired thoughts speed forth toward Soma. Paying homage, they approach him; longing for him, they enter into him who longs for them. Like the surging waves of the waters, our inspired thoughts speed forth toward Soma. Paying homage, they approach him; longing for him, they enter into him who longs for them.

Just as the waves of the waters hasten, so too, being "tattūrāṇāḥ"—that is, hurrying in their task to praise the gods—they proceed with speed. (The particle) *it* is a filler. Thus, they are those who are rushing toward the ritual action.
The root *tur* means "to hasten.
It belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class.
This is the form in the present participle (*śānac*) derived from its *yaṅ*-lopped (*yaṅluk*) stem.
The absence of the doubling (abhyāsa) and the substitution of *r* for *s* are Vedic (*chāndasa*).

It takes the accent of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyastasvara*). Such priests (*ṛtvij*) send forth (*pra īrate*) their mental powers (*manīṣāḥ*), that is, their hymns of praise, toward Soma (*somam accha*).
Paying homage—worshipping Soma—the truthful ones approach him and go toward him;
for [the rule] "the first word is not unaccented when joined with 'ca' or 'vā'," there is no suppression of the accent.
Then, longing—desiring—the praises enter into Soma, who is likewise longing.

They milk him who is being cleansed, like a buffalo on a mountain ridge—the swift, the bull dwelling upon the mountains. To him, as he bellows, the prayers flow together; Trita bears Varuṇa within the ocean.

The priests milk—that is, they extract—the famous stalk (*aṃśu*), the Soma, which is being purified with efforts, being served like a buffalo (*mahiṣa*)—so called because it is like a buffalo—dwelling on a high ridge (*sānu*), a mountain-like place; [the Soma] is a bull (*ukṣan*), a fulfiller of desires, situated upon the stones for the purpose of pressing.
Regarding this, the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* states: "The pressing-stones are the calves; the priests milk [it]. (TS 6.2.11.4).
The *matayaḥ*— the hymns worthy of being meditated upon— accompany, that is, attend upon and serve, that very Soma who thus yearns and desires.
Then Trita, Indra existing in three places, sustains— that is, holds for the sake of slaying the enemies— this Soma, the warder-off (*varuṇa*) of foes, within the ocean, the intermediate space.
Or alternatively:

*trita* is [so called] because he is present in three places—the *droṇa*, the *āvanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt* jars; from there, the *vitata* Soma sustains and nourishes Indra, the repeller of enemies, in the heavenly world.
1. Of the sacrifice that has become true (bha1-2). 2. Waves (ga). 3.
Our hymn impels [him] (ga); the hymn impels them (ta3-bha5).
4. They enter at *ga*, *ta*, *ra*, *bha*, *ca*.
5. They remain at *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *ti*.
6. At *ta* there are creepers (*latāḥ*); at *ta* and *mu* there is "remained" (*sthitaḥ*).

Impelling the voice like the Upavaktr priest of the Hotṛ, O Indu, as you are being purified, expand our inspired thought (*manīṣā*). Since you and Indra rule for the sake of good fortune, may we be masters of heroic power. Impelling the voice like the Upavaktr priest of the Hotṛ, O Indu, as you are being purified, expand our inspired thought. Since you and Indra rule for the sake of good fortune, may we be masters of heroic power. 5.

O Indu, O Soma, impelling our speech—that is, our hymn of praise—just as the Adhvaryu priest encourages [the Hotṛ] by providing the response like an Upavaktṛ, so do you, while being purified, provide encouragement for the recitation of the chanters; release your wisdom, that is, your intellect, and moreover, direct that intellect toward the bestowing of wealth. Furthermore, when both you and Indra dwell together in the sacrifice, may we, the chanters, be possessed of good fortune.
Furthermore, he dwells upon—that is, he sits within—the wealth of excellent vigor, which is endowed with beautiful potency.
Immediately thereafter, Soma—the wise one who has become a friend to Indra—approaches the singer of beautiful praise (*sumati*) by means of this chariot, the purifying filter. He goes toward him.
The meaning is that at that time, he approaches the praise being performed by him.
O God, flow for us through the service of the gods, O Soma, as the great, sweet, and exhilarating drink for Indra;
making the waters flow and raining down upon heaven and this earth, purifying yourself, grant us wide space from the vast expanse.

O God, flow for us from the assembly of the gods, O Soma, for the great exhilaration, as a drink for Indra; making the waters flow and raining down this heaven, bestow upon us wide space as you are being purified. 3.

O shining god, O Soma, you who are such a drink for Indra— being drunk by Indra— flow and pour yourself out into the vessels and other containers for our own sake, into this great and vast sacrifice extended by the gods, for the consumption and drinking of Indra. Furthermore, making the waters flow, you are the progenitor of Viṣṇu, the all-pervading one.
All this occurs when the Soma is being pressed;
for Soma indeed causes the gods to swell with nourishment.
For the oblations of the *devasuvām*, [the offerings] of Soma and Vanaspati, the *yājyā* is “*brahmā devānām*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “And you, O Soma, at our will, are the Brahman of the gods and the path-finder of the seers” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.11).

Brahmā among the gods, the pathfinder among poets, the seer among the wise, the buffalo among wild beasts, the hawk among vultures, the axe among the forests—Soma goes forth over the filter, chanting. 6. Brahmā; of the gods; the pathfinder; of the poets; the seer; of the wise; the buffalo; of the wild beasts; the hawk; of the vultures; the axe; of the forests; Soma; the filter; across; he goes; chanting. 6.
Soma becomes such a form.
He becomes the *brahman*, the one occupying the position of the *brahman* priest, for the gods—the officiating priests who offer hymns of praise.
Or alternatively:
Brahmā becomes the king of the shining gods, Indra and the others;
likewise, he is the *padavī* of the *kavis*, those of far-reaching wisdom. He who arranges words (*pada*) with correctness is called *padavī*.
The form [of the word] is derived from this root *i*, meaning "to go" and so forth, with the suffix *krip*.
Likewise, he becomes a *ṛṣi* among the *vipras*, the wise;
for he who sees what is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*) is a *ṛṣi*, according to the statement: “A *ṛṣi* is so called because of his vision” (Nirukta 2.11).
He becomes the buffalo among wild animals;
that is, he becomes a powerful king known as a buffalo.
Likewise, among the vultures—that is, among a specific class of birds—he becomes the hawk, the praiseworthy king of birds.
Among the *vanānām*— the root *vana* meaning "to injure"— you are the *svadhiti*, a cutter among those who injure and cut. You are the one named *svadhiti*.
Soma, possessing such power, being resonant—that is, making a sound—passes through and transcends the filter made of woolen threads.

Soma, being purified, has caused our songs and inspired thoughts to swell like a river its wave; beholding these dwellings from within, the bull, knowing them, stands among the cows upon the paths. He has caused the wave of speech to swell, like a river; Soma, being purified, [has stirred] our songs and inspired thoughts. Beholding these dwellings from within, the bull, knowing them, stands among the cows upon the paths.
The purifying Soma, the lord of thoughts (*manīṣāḥ*), causes the heart-pleasing songs of praise to vibrate intensely;
he impels them just as a flowing river impels the wave of sound.

Furthermore, Soma—the bull who rains down desires or waters—beholding the multitude of hidden things within (*antar*), takes his seat (*ātiṣṭhati*) among these *vrajanā*, these forces that are difficult for the weak to restrain (*avaraṇi*).
What does he do?
Knowing (*jānan*) [the way] among the cows, being one who knows the cows, he enters the enemy forces.

Intoxicating, choosing for himself in the battles, the steed with thousandfold seed, flow toward the prize! O Indu, being purified for Indra, as a wise one, stir up the wave of the stalk, seeking out the cattle. 8. He, the intoxicating one, choosing for himself in the battles, the steed with thousandfold seed—flow toward the prize! O Indu, being purified for Indra, as a wise one, stir up the wave of the stalk, seeking out the cattle. 8.
1. Desirable. 2. For the cows (plural); ta3.7-bha2.6: for the people of the cows.

O Soma, exhilarating (*v-matsara*), intoxicating (*madakara*), victorious (*vanvan*) over enemies in battles (*pṛtsu*), and therefore irresistible (*v-vāta*); possessed of a thousand powers (*sahasretāḥ*), endowed with a thousand streams (*sahasrodhadhāropeta*): do thou, O Soma, advance against (*abhivardha*) the strength (*vāja*) of the enemies.
O Soma, *Vinda*, being purified (*pavamāna*), wise (*manīṣī*), and impelling sounds (*gāḥ viṣaṇvan*), do thou proceed.
Or rather:
impelling the cows that serve as the means for the sacrifice of the sacrificers,
O Indra, urge on (*vīraya*) the wave— the mass— of the Soma being pressed for the sake of Indra.
The beloved Soma, desired by the gods, flows around the jar for Indra, delightful for his exhilaration;
with a thousand streams and hundredfold vigor, the drop goes like a swift steed to the assembly.
The beloved one, the jar, the wind-god Devavāta— for Indra, the Soma, delightful for exhilaration, with a thousand streams, possessing a hundredfold vigor, the drop,

like a prize-winning steed in the assembly— O Pavamāna, being purified, O Soma, our ancient fathers, the wise Aṅgirases, skilled in ritual action, [attained their goal] through you alone. (The particle *hi* is used for emphasis.)
With you alone as their companion, they performed the rites, such as the *agnihotra* and others;
furthermore, they honored (*vanvan*) the singers,
or alternatively—
The root *van* has the meaning of "to injure. Injuring the enemies,
you have gone around the protective enclosures (*paridhi*) reached by them.

Because everything is enclosed by these, they are called *paridhi*s; [here they refer to] the Rākṣasas. "Uncover" (*aporṇu*) means "uncover" (*aporṇuhi*), that is, "remove the covering"; it amounts to saying "slay them."
In the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *ūrṇoti*, the suffix *hel* is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
The meaning is: "O such as you, grant us—meaning, to us—wealth endowed with sons and other blessings."

As you did for Manu, O bestower of vigor, slayer of enemies, finder of wide space, and possessor of oblations—so flow on, bestowing wealth; unite with Indra and bring forth our weapons. As you sent [the waters], as you bestowed vigor upon Manu, O slayer of enemies, finder of wide space, and possessor of oblations—so flow on, bestowing wealth; unite with Indra and bring forth our weapons.

O Soma, just as in the past you were the bestower of vitality to King Manu, the provider of food, even so—being a slayer of enemies, a destroyer of foes, a finder of wealth, and a bringer of riches—while being possessed of oblations such as the *puroḍāśa* cake, you have flowed forth; that is, you came to grant him wealth and other blessings.
Thus, bestowing—that is, granting—wealth and riches to us, flow; that is, come toward us.
Furthermore, being offered by us, settle well with Indra;
moreover, bring forth—that is, manifest—your weapons for him.
There is no loss of accent (anighāta) because of the difference in sentence structure (vākyabheda).

Flow forth, O Soma, rich in sweetness, observer of the cosmic order (ṛta), clothing yourself in waters upon the sheep’s-wool back. Here, sit within the wooden vats that overflow with clarity; most gladdening, exhilarating, and worthy of Indra’s drink. 13. Flow forth, O Soma, rich in sweetness, observer of the cosmic order, clothing yourself in waters upon the sheep’s-wool back. Here, sit within the wooden vats that overflow with clarity; most gladdening, exhilarating, and worthy of Indra’s drink. 13.
O Soma, you who are rich in sweetness, endowed with intoxicating juice, and true to the cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*)—
the suffix *-van* being used here in the sense of possession according to the rule *chandasi vanipaḥ*—
such as you are, wearing the waters both the *vasatīvarī*s and the *aikadhana*s, flow forth, purifying yourself upon the lofty sheep’s wool filter.

Then, O most intoxicating, exceedingly exhilarating, Indra-drinker—meaning that which is to be drunk by Indra—gladdening Soma, sit down, that is, take your place, within the water-filled wooden vats (droṇakalaśas).

Flow with a hundred streams from heaven, purifying yourself as the winner of thousands at the feast of the gods; uniting with the rivers and the jars, mingling with the rays of light, prolonging our lifespan. 14. Flow with a hundred streams from heaven, purifying yourself as the winner of thousands at the feast of the gods; uniting with the rivers and the jars, mingling with the rays of light, prolonging our lifespan. 14.
1. You yourself have performed these deeds.
Vanvan—striking—the *rakṣases* while approaching the hollows; with them, envelop the *rākṣasa* enclosures (*paridhis*).
[In the *liṭ* (perfect tense),] *ga-ta3-bha6* means "you indeed strike."
2. O Hero, together with our heroes—those wise in action—and with our sons, may you, Maghavan, become possessed of wealth.

Since my ancestors performed their work together with you, therefore, O Soma, you who possess a hundred streams—that is, you who are endowed with many streams—purify yourself; that is, bring down rain from heaven, from the intermediate space, or from the sun.
Or alternatively:
you, who possess a hundred streams, many streams, and manifold streams, flow from the shining purifier of heaven; pour forth the rain in unbroken streams into the vessels. Of what nature are you?
At the *devavīti*— that sacrifice which is the gods' feast (*vīti*) or enjoyment—

in that [sacrifice], you, the giver of thousands of riches to the thousand sacrificers, desiring their food (*vājayu*), come together with the flowing rivers, the *vasatīvarī* waters, into the wooden vat (*kalaśa*), the vessel called *droṇa*.
In that way, extending our lifespan—that is, our life—do thou unite with us in the jar through the products of the cow, such as milk and the like.

This very Soma, being purified by our prayers, like a prize-winning steed, overcomes the stingy ones; he is like the milk of Aditi drawn by the singers, like a wide path, or like a well-guided draft-horse. 15. This very one—this Soma—being purified by our thoughts, like a prize-winning steed, indeed overcomes the stingy ones; like the milk of Aditi [drawn] by the singers, like a wide path, or like a well-guided draft-horse. 15.
Such is this Soma; being purified—that is, being cleansed—by means of *matibhiḥ*, that is, by hymns which are instruments of thought, he becomes [thus].
That Soma, like a swift steed (*atya*)—that is, like a horse capable of traversing the distance—is a prize-winner (*vājī*) who, as it were, overcomes the *arātīḥ*, that is, the enemies, in battle.
The particle *it* is used for emphasis.
It indeed crosses over and indeed destroys,
just as there is no obstruction due to its connection with that;
furthermore, [it is] of Aditi.
The name of the cow is "gonāmā. Just as the milk, the fluid of a cow that is not emaciated, is sought after with efforts (*iribhiḥ*) until it becomes pure, so too is Soma completely purified.
Moreover, like the wide expanse (*urvīva*).

The form *soluk* is derived from the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Just as a broad (*uru*) and expansive (*vistīrṇaḥ*) path (*gātuḥ*) is to be traversed by all, and just as a draft-horse (*voḍhā*) is easily controlled (*suyamaḥ*), being well capable of being restrained, even so this Soma is to be restrained by means of hymns of praise (*stotrabhiḥ*).

Well-armed, being purified by the pressers, flow toward your secret and beautiful name; flow toward booty like a swift runner seeking glory; flow toward Vāyu, O divine Soma, and toward the cows. 16. Well-armed, by the pressers, being purified, flow toward, [attain] the secret, beautiful name; toward booty, like a runner, through desire for renown; toward Vāyu, toward the cows, O divine Soma. 16.
"Equipped with weapons" means endowed with beautiful weapons; or alternatively,
in the sacrifice there are ten weapons, such as the wooden sword (*sphya*) and the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*).

Possessing that [name], being purified by the pressers who extract [the juice], you—[your] beautiful, secret name, which is your essence of sap hidden within the cave—flow forth together with the hymns of praise; cause it to reach the jars and other vessels. Furthermore, like a powerful horse moving forward, you [proceed] for the sake of glory.

By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the substitution of *āj* for the seventh case ending. O God, bring us food (*vāja*) toward our desire for food; furthermore, O praiseworthy Soma, bring Vāyu—the vital breath and life—toward us.
Bring cattle and livestock to us.
1. *ga-ta-bha4.6*: endowed with many streams of water; *bha1*: endowed with many streams of water; *bha2*: endowed with many streams of water. 2. *ga-bha1.4.7*: of many kinds, belonging to oneself.
3. *bha6*: syllable.
4. *ga-ta³-bha¹.².⁵.⁶.⁷-kāmayamānaḥ*: "Desiring what indeed, and lowing, you [are] desiring.
5. *ga-ta³-bha².⁴.⁵.⁶-pravardhayan*; *tā¹.².⁵.⁷-’vardhayan* is absent.
6. *bha⁶-kṣīrādibhiḥ svakalaśe*: "With milk and other [substances], in your own vessel."
7. tā1.2.7—*eṣa sya etādṛśaḥ*; ta4.5—*eṣa sya etādṛśasya*. 8. tā1.2.4.5.6-bha6—*stotṛbhiḥ*.
9. ga-bha4—*yājādeśaḥ*; ta7—*ajādeśaḥ*.

10. *ta-bha2-’vājaṃ* is not present. They cleanse the newborn infant, the beloved; they beautify the bearer with their quality, O Maruts. Being a seer through his songs and poetic power, Soma, being a seer himself, goes forth beyond the filter while singing. 17. *śiśum* (infant), *jajñānam* (newborn), *haryatam* (beloved), *mṛjanti* (they cleanse), *śubhranti* (they beautify), *vahnim* (the bearer), *marutaḥ* (O Maruts), *guṇena* (with their quality), *kaviḥ* (a seer), *gīrbhiḥ* (with songs), *kāvyena* (by poetic power), *kaviḥ* (a seer), *san* (being), *somaḥ* (Soma), *pavitram* (the filter), *ati* (beyond), *eti* (goes), *rebhan* (singing). 17.
Now, [he is] a child who has just acquired speech, standing like a child;
or rather, one who makes evils thin, that is, destroys them.
Being born, he has manifested; for this very reason, he is *haryata* (desirable).
[The root] *harya* means "to move" and "to desire. By the rule beginning with *bhṛ-mṛ-dṛśi* etc., the suffix *tac* is applied.
The Maruts cleanse Soma, who is desired by all;
moreover, they beautify him—the bearer—as their own troop, a group of seven.
Then Soma, the seer of far-reaching wisdom, [acts] through his very work as a seer (*kāvyena*).
It is known from the mantras beginning with "May he, the lord, protect me" and ending with "May the moon, the lord of the constellations, protect me" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.5.1).

Like a handsome youth grooming his body, like a courser that has been groomed for the winning of riches, like a bull going toward the herds, flowing around the vat while bellowing, he has entered the two bowls. *maryo na śubhraḥ tanvaṃ mṛjānaḥ atyo na sūtvā sanaye dhanānām vṛṣeva yūthā pari kośamarṇan kanikradacamyorā viveśa* || 20 || "Handsome" (*śubhraḥ*) means shining and adorned; "like a youth" (*maryo na*) means like a human being; "grooming his body" (*tanvaṃ mṛjānaḥ*) means purifying his own body with the *vasatīvarī* waters. Furthermore, "for the winning of riches" (*sanaye dhanānām*) means for the enjoyment or acquisition of wealth; "like a courser" (*atyo na*) means like a horse accustomed to running; "having been groomed" (*sūtvā*) means having become swift. Moreover, "like a bull" (*vṛṣeva*) means just as a bull makes a sound when approaching herds, so too Soma, "flowing around the vat" (*pari kośamarṇan*)—the vessel made of the pressing-skin—"bellowing" (*kanikradat*) meaning making a sound again and again, "has entered" (*ā viveśa*) the two "bowls" (*camvoḥ*), that is, the two pressing-boards. Regarding the word *kanikradat*: in the case of the root *kadi* with the intensive suffix elided, by the rule beginning with "dādharti dardharti," there is the augment *ni* inserted into the reduplicated syllable. When this takes the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), the initial vowel becomes acute according to the rule "abhyastānāmādiḥ. 9. Translation complete.

Flow on, O Indu, being purified with great splendors; bellowing loudly, flow around the woolen filters. Playing, enter the two bowls; as you are being purified, let your exhilarating juice intoxicate Indra. Flow on, O Indu, being purified with great splendors; bellowing loudly, flow around the woolen filters. Playing, enter the two bowls; as you are being purified, let your exhilarating juice intoxicate Indra. O Indu, Soma, being purified with great splendors—that is, by the officiating priests—you, being purified, flow on. Then, bellowing loudly—making a great sound—flow around the woolen filters, the downward-flowing purifiers. Furthermore, playing—that is, sporting—as you are being purified, enter the two bowls, namely the two pressing-boards. Immediately thereafter, let your exhilarating juice, which causes intoxication, delight Indra. (In the verb *mamate*, the *ślu* reduplication occurs according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.)

His great streams have been let loose; anointed with milk, he has entered the jars. Creating the *sāman*, the skillful singer of *sāmans* goes toward the wise one, crying out like a lover toward his kin. The great, lofty streams of this Soma have been released; they flow forth. Anointed with milk—the products of the cow such as milk and the like—he has entered the jars, that is, the wooden vats. Creating the *sāmans*, the skillful singer of *sāmans*—meaning one who is well-acquainted with chanting melodies—and being all-knowing (*vipaścit*), the Soma goes toward them, crying out and calling upon the gods. He approaches the vessels for drawing the juice and other implements with speed. Therein lies the comparison: just as another lustful man rushes with haste toward his own kin, that is, his wife, so does he.
1. Let [it] cause the earth (bhūmi) to rejoice (mādayatu).
2. It is sprinkled (siktaḥ) after being anointed (aktaḥ) with the juice of the *gata* plant.

Striking down the enemies, O Pavamāna, you go forth; like a lover approaching his beloveds, O Indu, you are celebrated. Like a bird alighting in the woods, Soma, being purified, settles within the jars. O Pavamāna, O Soma being purified, you who are celebrated—that is, pressed by the singers—and who flow into the vessels of Indu, you go forth, striking down and destroying the enemies. How so? Just as a lover approaches his beloveds, that is, a handsome man approaching those he desires while driving away [rivals], so do you approach. Like a bird, a flier, alighting in the woods—that is, settling upon the trees—so are you a flier. Being purified, O Soma, you settle—that is, you take your seat—within the jars. The suffix *tan* is added to the root *sad* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*); the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* applies because the root is monosyllabic.

O Soma, your radiant beams, as you are being purified, flow like women—well-milking, with excellent streams. The golden-hued one, brought hither, rich in boons, has bellowed repeatedly within the waters, in the jar of the god-seeking sacrificers. O Soma, your own radiant beams, belonging to you who are being purified, come forth like women; just as a woman milks milk for her sons, so these rays—well-milking, possessing beautiful streams—are excellent yielders of wealth and other gifts for the sacrificers. Furthermore, the golden-hued one, brought by the officiating priests, the much-desired Soma, has bellowed again and again, crying out within the waters (the *vasatīvarī* waters) and in the jar (the *droṇa*) of the god-seeking sacrificers.
In this section (anuvāka), there are seven hymns (*sūkta*).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifty-eight verses beginning with "asya preṣā," is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity.
Regarding that, Vasiṣṭha Maitrāvaruṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the first triplet (*tṛca*).
The second was named Indrapramati;
the third was Vṛṣagaṇa;
the fourth was Manyu.
Upamanyu for the fifth;
Vyāghrapāt for the sixth;
Śakti for the seventh.
Of the eighth [month] is Karṇaśrut;
of the ninth, Malīka;
of the tenth, Vasukra.
All these belong to the Vasiṣṭha lineage.
Thus thirty verses have been traversed.
Now, for the fourteen verses, Parāśara, the son of Śakti, is the seer (ṛṣi).
Among the remaining [seers], Kutsa is of the lineage of Aṅgiras.

Thus it is enumerated: "Vasiṣṭha saw the first fifty-eight of these; then in the subsequent [hymns]: Pṛṣadhra, Indrapramati, Vṛṣagaṇa, Manyu, Upamanyu, Vyāghrapāt, Śakti, Karṇaśrut, Malīka, Vasukra—these fourteen; Parāśara [saw] the others; Kutsa [is the seer of the final hymn].
The application [of the verses] has been explained.

Being purified by the impelling golden [hand], this god has mingled his juice with the gods. Pressed out, he goes around the filter, chanting like a Hotṛ-priest toward the measured, cattle-filled dwellings. *asya* (of him), *prepā* (impeller), *hemanā* (by the golden [hand]), *pūyamānaḥ* (being purified), *devaḥ* (the god), *devebhiḥ* (with the gods), *sam* (together), *apṛkta* (has mixed), *rasam* (his juice), *sutaḥ* (pressed out), *pavitram* (the filter), *pari* (around), *eti* (goes), *rebhan* (chanting), *mitāiva* (like measured [dwellings]), *sabaṃ* (dwellings), *paśumānti* (rich in cattle), *hotā* (the Hotṛ). *Asya*: of this Soma; *prepā*: impeller, from the root *pra-i* (to go); the form is derived with the suffix *kvip*; the acute accent on the case-ending is according to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. *Prepā*: by the impeller; *hemanā*: by the golden [hand]—there is a connection with gold in the text "he purifies with golden hands. Such a *devaḥ*: shining-rayed one, *rasam*: his own juice, *devebhiḥ*: with the gods, *samapṛkta*: he thoroughly mixes or joins together. [The root is] *pṛcī*.
Rigveda [Aṣṭaka 7, Adhyāya 4, Varga 11]:
Then the pressed Soma, having been filtered, goes around— that is, it passes through— the *pavitra* (strainer) made of woolen threads while making a sound, that is, while roaring.
In what way?

Just as the Hotṛ, the priest who invokes the gods, goes around the sacrificial sheds—those dwellings provided with animals, that is, those where animals have been tied up—as soon as they are constructed, so too [does he go].
Clothed in auspicious, well-fitting garments, the great seer pronouncing his utterances,
being purified, flow forth— far-reaching, watchful— at the banquet of the gods.

Auspicious, clothed in garments, accompanied by the Maruts, the great sage, reciting the words of the dwelling-place, flow hither; being purified, the far-seeing, watchful one, at the banquet of the gods. 2.
*Vibhadra*, *bhadrāṇi*, and *kalyāṇāni* mean "auspicious" or "welfare. *Samanyā*: *samanyā* is a name for battle;
[the suffix] *-ya* is applied in the sense of "skilled in that."

Wearing garments worthy of battle— clothing that is radiant— he, the great seer (*kavi*), who possesses far-reaching vision, praises the hymns that are most fit to be uttered; he, the discerning one (*vicakṣaṇa*) who perceives everything specifically,
the ever-watchful (*jāgṛvi*), [is present] at the feast of the gods (*devavīti*)— that sacrifice in which the gods partake— in the two pressing-boards (*cumbauḥ*).
"Enter, having caused the vessels to turn toward you.
The root *vṛc* has the sense of "entering";
thus, it means "cause them to enter."
"Being purified."
He is cleansed upon the woolly ridge, most glorious through his glory, patient toward us.
Flowing toward the sound, purify yourself; and do you gods protect us always with your blessings.

He is cleansed upon the woolly summit; men call him "Glory," he who is the patient endurer of glories. Flowing toward us with his sound across the desert, purify yourself. Do you protect us always with blessings. 3.

Among those who possess glory, you are the most glorious; among those dwelling on earth, you are the beloved one who delights all. O Soma, upon the high, imperishable, and unaging woolen filter, you are being cleansed and prepared by the officiating priests for our sake. Indeed, being purified, you resound loudly throughout the firmament.
"Vyūyam": the plural number is used for honor. O Soma, you—protect (pāta) us (naḥ) always (sadā), at all times, with most auspicious protections (svastibhiḥ). Protect! Guard! Preserve!
Sing forth! Worship the gods! Send forth Soma for great wealth.
Sweet, he flows through the sheep’s wool filter; may he sit within the jar with those who seek the gods.
Sing forth! Let us praise the gods; send forth the Soma for great wealth. Sweet, he flows through the sheep’s wool filter; may he sit within the jar by means of those who seek the gods. 4.
O singers, sing forth;
praise Soma with excellence.
Likewise, worship the gods; offer them adoration.
There is a transposition of persons;
or rather:
"We praise the gods; you, O Soma, be praised."
Furthermore, for the sake of great wealth—that is, to obtain abundant riches—distill the Soma; that is, impel it for the purpose of pressing.
(The dative case of the word *dhana* is used according to the rule: *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*).
Then the Soma, becoming sweet—that is, making itself sweet—passed through the filter, the woolen strainer, the *vāra*, or the *vāla*.
1. *ta-bhara.6*: Being purified (*pūyamānaḥ*), he does not exist.
2. *ta3-bha1.2*: One who makes [it] sweet (*svādukārī*); *bha4.7*: *svādukāri*.
He cooks exceedingly; he cooks.
Furthermore, our Soma, longing for the gods, sits down—that is, it enters—the vessel, the jar;
in both instances, the augment *āṭ* is added according to the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood.

The drop, the foremost of the gods, approaching, flows in a thousand streams for exhilaration; being praised by men according to the ancient law, [he honors] Agni and Indra for great fortune. 5. *induḥ*, *devānām*, *ūrpa*, *mukhyam*, *ā'yana*, *sahasra'dhāraḥ*, *pavate*, *madāya*, *nṛbhiḥ*, *starvāānaḥ*, *anu*, *dhāma*, *pūrvam*, *agni'indram*, *mahate*, *saubhagāya*. 5.

Approaching—that is, entering into—the primary state of friendship with the gods, Indra and the others, the Soma-drop (*indu*), flowing in a thousand streams—that is, by way of many kinds of streams—purifies itself for the exhilaration of the gods; it flows, streaming forth from the jars and other vessels. Praised by men, the leaders of ritual action, Soma goes toward his ancient abode, the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
He explains that very point:
He goes to Indra for great and abundant good fortune— that is, for auspiciousness.
Soma is "possessed of that" (tadvān) by virtue of being overcome by Indra.
The suffix *ac* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*.
Such Soma, "lowing" (making a sound), "approaches" (*abhyeti*) "step by step" (*padā padā*), that is, the various places or vessels.
Or alternatively:
Just as a certain boar makes a sound while treading upon the earth with its foot, so it is in this case.
The swans have come toward the stone; the bull-like hosts have approached Muniyu with haste.
O friends, they proclaim the irresistible, roaring Vāṇa, the one being purified, as he reaches the joint of the arm.
Like swans toward the water, the bull-like hosts have come from home to Tuṣala and Munyu; together with their friends, they proclaim the irresistible song of Pava-māna Āḍguṣya. 8.
The *haṃsāsaḥ* are those who act like swans when being struck by enemies, or perhaps the seers named *vṛṣagaṇāḥ*. Being terrified by the power (*amāt*) of their enemies, they [utter] *tuṣalam*.
The word *tuṣala* denotes speed; as Yāska has stated: "One who possesses *tuṣala*-strikes is one who strikes swiftly" (*Nirukta* 5.12).
They have gone forth, they have set out, they are proceeding toward the sacrificial hall—the *kṣipraprahārin* (swift striker), *manyu* (wrath), who regards himself as a foe—directed toward *soma*.
Then, the *sakhāyaḥ* (friends)—the singers who are friends by virtue of the relationship characterized as the praised and the praiser—[attain] *āḍguṣyam*, that which is to be approached by all.
Or else: [it refers to the soma].

The substitution of *g* for *ghoṣavat* [in *ghoṣavantam*] is due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group; the nasalization of the prefix *āṅ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). With reference to this Soma, who is worthy of praise, who is *durmarṣam*—unassailable by enemies, difficult to restrain, and hard to endure—they simultaneously utter, that is, they proclaim aloud, a specific kind of speech (*vāṇam*).
The meaning is that they perform singing characterized by that [sound].
He hastens with the speed of the wide-striding one; like cows lowing, they measure him as he sports at will.
The sharp-horned one makes himself vast; by day he is golden to behold, and by night he is dappled brown.

He rushes toward the speed of the wide-striding one; like cows lowing, they measure him as he sports at will. The sharp-horned one makes his fullness manifest: by day he is golden to behold, and by night he is bright-red.
That Soma speeds forth;
the meaning is that he goes with extreme rapidity,
following the impulse— the movement— of the wide-striding Self who is praised by many.

The cows— other travelers— do not measure, that is, they do not limit or cannot follow, Soma as he moves, plays, and wanders effortlessly and in vain (without exertion). Furthermore, he has sharp horns (*tigmaśṛṅga*).
*Śṛṅgāṇi* are splendors (*tejāṃsi*), so called because they "hear" (*śṛṇanti*) and "destroy" (*hiṃsanti*) darkness.
*Tīkṣṇatejaskaḥ* [refers to one] possessing sharp splendor. *Parīṇasam* is a synonym for "much."
He manifests—that is, produces—manifold splendor.
That Soma who exists in the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is seen as "hari," meaning golden-colored, during the day at the time of striking;
that is to say, he does not shine [at other times].
At night, however, it is seen as straight-moving (*ṛjra*), clear, and endowed with light;
this is the form of the root *dṛś* (to see) in the passive voice with the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*).

The Soma-drop, the steed of the waters, has flowed upon the mountain like a herd of cattle; the Soma, bestowing strength upon Indra for his exhilaration, strikes down the demon and drives away the attackers, acting as a hero and king of the community.

The drop, the prize-winner, upon the mountain; the floods of the cow-stall; in Indra, the Soma; together, impelling, for exhilaration; he slays the demon, drives away hostilities; making wide space, the king of the enclosure. 10.

1. *ga-ta-bha-rūpaṃ*: because of its metrical structure, there is no *nighāta* (suppression of accent). *Vinduḥ* means "having the nature of flowing"; *vājī* means "powerful"; *gavyoghāḥ* means "a mass of downward-pointing [streams] characterized by movement"; *vindre* means "possessing power" (*sahaḥ*), that is, producing strength; *vinvan* means "impelling"; *somaḥ* [flows]; *madāya* means "for the sake of intoxication"; *pavate* means "it flows. Soma, possessing the nature of flowing, powerful, a mass of downward-pointing streams characterized by movement, impelling the strength-giving power, flows for the sake of intoxication.
Furthermore, he destroys—that is, strikes down—the host of Rākṣasas;
furthermore, he completely oppresses—that is, utterly annihilates—the enemies, the ill-wishers.
Of what nature is he?
Bestowing desirable wealth, making it for his praisers, he is the leader, the lord of the host and of strength—thus says Soma.
Then, mingled with sweetness in a stream, milked by the stones, Indu flows through the fleece;
enjoying the friendship of Indra, the exhilarating god flows for the god’s intoxication.
Now, being mixed with sweetness, the drop, milked by the stones, flows through the wool; the god, enjoying the friendship of Indra, purifies himself for the exhilaration of the god. 11.
Immediately after the slaying, the Soma— milked from the mountain [the pressing-stone], pressed by the stones— is heard. Then,
making himself known, informing all, he causes this speech to flow, causing it to spread in every direction.
The meaning is that he utters a loud sound.
Worthy of being tasted, swelling with milk, he flows forth, impelling the honeyed stalk;
being purified as a continuous stream, making it ready for Indra, O Soma, you are poured out.

Worthy of being tasted, swelling with milk, you go forth; sending it forth, you go toward the honeyed stalk. Being purified, O Soma, you go toward the continuous flow, being poured out for Indra while making [it] ready. 14.
O Soma, you are *rasāyya*—the suffix *-āya* being added to the root *ras* according to the rules of the Uṇādi-sūtras;

thus, you are to be tasted. Swelling with milk, emitting a sound as you flow, and impelling [it], you go toward—that is, you reach—the honeyed stalk (*aṃśu*), which is full of sweetness and ready for the pressing.
"Aṃśu is of the measure of a drop," says Yāska (Nirukta 2.5).
By this, the Soma juice is designated.
Furthermore, O Soma, being sprinkled with water, you, as Pavamāna, while being purified in the filter, [produce] a continuous sound.
The root *tan* means "to expand."

O Indu, send down for us the divine rain—swift-moving, rich in nourishment, abounding in happiness, and quick to bestow gifts. Like a beautiful, loosened lock of hair, O Indu, seeking these lower winds that are our kin, search them out and flow forth to grant us wealth. **Sanskrit:** vṛṣṭiṃ no arṣa divyāṃ jigatvīm ilāvatīṃ śaṃgayīṃ jīradānum | stukāiva vītā dhanvā vicinvan bandhūn imān avarān indo vāyūn || 17 || **English Translation:** O Soma, pour down upon us the celestial rain—ever-moving, full of food, a dwelling place of bliss, and swift in its giving. Furthermore, O Indu, like a lovely, loosened lock of hair, you who discern these lower winds as our kinsmen—our friends through praise and song—flow forth, seeking and bestowing wealth. **Note on Vocabulary:** * **Vṛṣṭim**: Rain. * **Naḥ**: For us. * **Arbha**: Send, cause to come. * **Divyām**: Celestial, belonging to heaven. * **Jigatvīm**: Moving, flowing. * **Ilāvatīm**: Rich in nourishment (food). * **Śaṃgayīm**: Abounding in happiness or comfort. * **Jīradānum**: Quick to give or bestowing life. * **Stukāiva vītā**: Like a loosened lock of hair. * **Dhanvā**: Flowing, running. * **Vicinvan**: Discerning, searching out. * **Bandhūn**: Kinsmen, relatives. * **Imān**: These. * **Avarān**: Lower, terrestrial. * **Indo**: O Indu (Soma). * **Vāyūn**: Winds. **Explanation:** The poet addresses Soma, requesting him to bring down the heavenly rain characterized by abundance and ease. He likens this descent to a beautiful, loose lock of hair. Just as one might observe such a lock, the poet asks Soma to look toward the "winds" (vāyūn) situated below—the earthly powers—and to flow toward them as they approach him, seeking to find and reward his devotees. The term *bandhūn* (kinsmen) refers to those connected to the singer through hymns of praise. The final exhortation is for Soma to flow (*dhanva*) across the earth to fulfill this purpose.

Unknot me who am bound, O Soma, as you are being purified—granting me both the straight path and the crooked. Neigh like a bay steed, O God, as you are being grasped; run like a youth, O possessor of the dwelling. Unknot me who am bound, O Soma, as you are being purified—granting me both the straight path and the crooked. Neigh like a bay steed, O God, as you are being grasped; run like a youth, O possessor of the dwelling. Being purified, release me from my expanded bond of evil; separate me from sins. How so? Like one who unties a knot. (The form *viṣya* is the imperative of the root *vyadh*, used here in the sense of "separating" or "untying"). Furthermore, O Soma, grant me the straight path that is not crooked, and also the crooked [strength]. Being bay-colored (*hari*), and being grasped within the vessel, you neigh like a swift-running horse. Moreover, O God, a youth beneficial to men, or a slayer of enemies, a possessor of a dwelling—a *pastya* being a house—run toward me, or toward the jars.

O Indu, beloved for exhilaration at the divine service, flow forth with your stream upon the high, woolly summit! With a thousand streams, fragrant and inviolable, go around completely in the battle for booty, where heroes sit in the fray. O Indu, you who are beloved for exhilaration at the divine service—the sacrifice—flow forth with your stream upon the high, woolly summit! With a thousand streams, fragrant and inviolable, go around completely in the battle for booty, where heroes sit in the fray. O Indu, you who are beloved for exhilaration, sufficient for the divine service—that is, the sacrifice—flow forth with your stream, that is, with a mass of flowing currents, upon the high, woolly summit, which is the filter. Possessing a thousand streams, endowed with many forms, fragrant, and inviolable—meaning not harmed by anyone—go around completely in the battle for booty, which is the cause for obtaining food, in the conflict where men sit together.
Like spirited horses yoked to chariots, like coursers mingling in the race, these bright Soma drops flow;
O Gods, come hither to drink them.
1. ta3-bha4.5-vimuñca | 2.
ga-ta3-bha1.4.7—'avibhave' is not present | 3.
ta1.7-bhara-su—'pavitre' is not present |
4. *ta1-bha6-mu-śravaṇa* | 5. *ga-annālābhe dhananimitte*; *ta1.3.4.5.6.7-bhara-mu- annālābhāya nimitte*; *bha1.4-annālābhāya nirmito*.
Like stones, like chariotless horses unyoked, like coursers released in the race—these bright Soma juices flow; they are the gods whom the deities approach to drink. 20.
The stones are devoid of rays; that is to say, they are without ropes. They are without chariots, meaning they are devoid of chariots; they are unyoked, not employed for any purpose whatsoever.
The meaning is "unbound.
Such [beings], being created (*sasṛjānāsaḥ*) in the *āji*—that is, in battle—move with speed just like horses (*atyāsaḥ*) in a race; likewise here in the *āji*.
For the *ṛtvij*s drive (*ajanti*) here for the purpose of performing the ritual action; thus, *āji* refers to the sacrifice (*yajña*).

Being pressed in that [vessel], these bright and shining Soma juices flow swiftly toward the jars. Now, directly addressed: O gods, come near to those approaching Soma juices for the sake of drinking them.
Thus, O Indu, flow for us toward the feast of the gods; encompass us everywhere like a wave of homage among the plants.
May Soma grant us desirable, vast wealth, accompanied by heroic sons and formidable power.
O Indu, flow toward the feast for the gods; encompass us with a flood of homage. May Soma, dwelling in the vessels, grant us desirable and vast wealth—mighty and full of heroes. 21.
O Soma, flow for us toward our *devavīti*—the sacrifice (*yajña*) which is the gods' enjoyment (*vīti*), their partaking, or their arrival;
toward that, from the sky (*nabhas*), [flow] the water (*arṇas*).
By this, the Soma juice passing through the filter (*pavitra*) is designated.
Flow around, pour out from all sides, that wealth into the cups and the bowls.
From that, may Soma grant and bestow upon us desirable, longed-for, vast, increased, heroic—endowed with sons—fierce, and formidable wealth.
When the speech of the longing mind carved him out at the edge of the milk-stream according to the law of the eldest,
then the cows, lowing for the best, approached the Soma-drop in the jar as their beloved lord.

When the speech of the longing mind was hewing [the wood], or when, according to the law of the eldest, at the front of the dwelling, they came toward him with desire, lowing for their choice, the cows toward the beloved husband, Indu, in the jar. 22.
Yāska [states]: "The root *ven* means 'to desire' (*venate*), [being] a word for the act of longing" (Nirukta 10.38). [It refers to] the mind that is being desired.
He thinks: "If the speech of the praiser—
characterized as praise— fashions or refines him," the word *vā* is used in the sense of comparison.
As in the case of *dharman*.
The locative case is used according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.36 (*nimittakarmasaṃyoge*).

The speech (*vāk*) of the one who dwells there—of the one who is the eldest, of the one belonging to the countryside (*jānapadīya*), of the one standing at the front (*anīke*) or mouth (*mukhe*) of the roaring kṣatriya, whose organ of action (*karmendriya*) pertains to the sphere of security and well-being (*yogakṣema*) and which is the sustainer (*dhāraka*).
The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Just as one praises a most excellent king, so too does the speech of the praiser praise Soma; this is the meaning.

Immediately thereafter (āt), the cows—lowing (vāvaśānāḥ) and desiring him—came toward this very Soma (īm enam), who is the most excellent (varam), desirable (juṣṭam), sufficient for the exhilaration of the gods, the lord (patim) of the waters (mavasya), the protector, and who resides in the jar (kalaśe).
They come to mix it with their own milk.
1. Free from the rope of thirst (*tṛṣṇā*); [it is] the state of being free from the burden of the rope.
2. *Bha* and *Śukra* are [the letters] *śukra*. 3.

Because of the cause of *ta* and *bha*, there is the conjunction of action (*karmasaṃyoga*); because of the cause of *ma* 1 and 2, there is the conjunction of action; because of the cause of *ma* 4, there is the possession of the conjunction of action.
4. Ta-bha2.6-dharmodiśya.

The celestial bestower of gifts, the showerer of wealth upon the givers, the wise one flows forth for the sake of Truth, for the sake of the True One. He becomes the upholder of the law, the king of the righteous host; with his ten rays he bears up the earth. (The celestial one) is that which exists in heaven. (The bestower of gifts) is the giver of wealth and other things to those who give. He explains this very point: (the showerer of wealth). [From the root *pivi* meaning "to sprinkle," with the suffix *aṇ* according to Pāṇini 3.2.1]—he is the one who pours down desires for the givers. (The wise one) is Soma, possessed of excellent intelligence. For (the sake of Truth), for Indra who has become Truth, (for the sake of Truth), his own essence which has become Truth, he (flows forth), he flows forth abundantly. (The king), the shining Soma, (of the righteous host), of the virtuous strength, (the upholder of the law), he becomes the sustainer. Furthermore, with (ten), of that number, (rays)—meaning the fingers of the horses for the purpose of performing the ritual—he (bears up), he supports the abundant (earth). This is a form derived from the *ciṇ* suffix.

Flowing through the purifiers, the all-seeing King of both gods and mortals has become doubly the lord of riches. Indu bears the well-sustained and beautiful *ṛta*. Through the purifiers, being purified, the all-seeing one—the King of both gods, such as Indra and others, and also of mortals, of human beings—thus of both classes of people, becomes doubly the lord of wealth; not the lord of a little, but the master of many riches. By his nature as a substance, both his lordship and his abundance are intended to be expressed. Such is Soma; he exists in two ways, among both gods and humans. This Indu, Soma, bears the well-prepared, beautiful, and auspicious *ṛta*, which is water.
1. *ta* 1.2.7–*atha*; *ta* 3.4.5.6–*bha* 1.2.4.7–‘*tathā*’ is not present; *bha* 6–*yathā*; *mu*–*atha*. 2. *ta*–*asya*.

May the Soma juices, worthy of the gods, being poured out, flow toward our dwelling rich in heroic sons. May they, who are yoked for the journey, who possess all desirable things, who are like the most delightful Hotṛ-priests born of heaven, grant us their good favor. devāvyo naḥ pariṣicyamānāḥ kṣayaṃ suvīraṃ dhanvantu somāḥ | āyujyavaḥ sumatiṃ viśvavārā hotāro na divijo mandratamāḥ || 26 || Worthy of the gods, being poured out, may the Soma juices flow toward our dwelling rich in heroic sons. Yoked for the journey, possessing all desirable things, like the most delightful Hotṛ-priests born of heaven, [may they grant us] good favor. || 26 ||
*Devāvyaḥ*:
[This is derived] from the root *av*, in the sense of satisfying (*tarpaṇa*). The suffix *ī* is applied according to the rule "after *avitṛ*, *stṛ*, and *nṛ*, the suffix *ī* [is added].
The circumflex (*svarita*) accent of the case-ending *jas* is due to the rule "after a vowel that is either acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*), the *yaṇ*-substitute [is circumflex]."
May the Soma juices—those who satisfy the gods, being poured out and sprinkled all around into the vessels—flow toward us, bringing a dwelling with excellent sons;

likewise, may they, who are to be sacrificed to face-to-face or who bestow [gifts] face-to-face, and who are therefore desirable by all (*viśvavāra*), flow toward us with their benevolent mind (*sumati*).
Of what nature are they?

Just as the *holāra* priests praise the gods such as Indra and others, so too do the *divijaḥ*—those who sacrifice to the gods such as Indra situated in the sky (*divi*)—worship them. [In the compound *divija*,] the locative case ending is not elided according to the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix, the locative is frequently retained. They are *mandratamāḥ*: exceedingly intoxicating.

Thus, O God, flow for the sake of the divine service, O Soma, for the great outpouring, as the drink of the gods. For we indeed are established in greatness; in the assembly of heroes, while being purified, make the two worlds well-established. 27. Thus. God. For the divine service. Flow. For the great. O Soma. For the outpouring. Drink of the gods. For even from the great. Indeed. We are. Established. In the assembly of heroes. Make. Well-established. The two worlds. Being purified. 27.

O radiant one, worthy of praise, O Soma, who art to be drunk by the gods (*devapāna*), flow thus—purify yourself—for the sake of the great feast of the gods, for the drinking of the gods in this sacrifice spread out and extended by the gods. Then, being impelled by you, we shall indeed overcome even the great, those possessing superior strength, our enemies in battle where death is the common lot.
Furthermore, while being purified—that is, as you are being cleansed—make the two worlds, heaven and earth, our dwelling place, and establish us in friendship within that beautiful abode.

Like a neighing horse yoked by stallions, like a terrifying lion swifter than thought—by the paths that lead hitherward and which are rich in wealth, flow toward us, O Indu, bringing us favor and goodwill. 28. Like a horse, you neigh, yoked by stallions; like a terrifying lion, swifter than thought. By the paths leading hitherward, which are rich in wealth, flow toward us, O Indu, bringing us favor and goodwill. 28.

O Soma, you, the bull, being harnessed—joined together—with the priests who press the Soma, you neigh like a horse; you cry out with sound. Of what sort? Like a lion, you are terrible, a source of fear to your enemies.
Likewise, he is even swifter than thought, possessing greater velocity.
By means of the paths that are directed hitherward— those routes which are most straight and exceedingly swift—
the vowel *u* is replaced by *r* according to the rule "vibhāja-uc-chandasi."
O shining Soma, flow toward us with those paths; bring us *saumanasam*, that is, a state of well-being and joy.
1. The world of heaven (dyuloka) consists of the syllables *na*, *bha*, *ma*, and *u*.

A hundred streams, born of the gods, have been released; the seers cleanse these thousands of yours. O Indu, flow hither from heaven for our great gain; you are the leader to the prize of wealth. A hundred streams, born of the gods, have been released; the seers cleanse these thousands of yours. O Indu, flow hither from heaven for our great gain; you are the leader to the prize of wealth. O Soma, your hundred streams, born for the sake of the gods, have been let loose. Then the seers—the far-seeing officiants—purify these many kinds of yours, or rather, they cleanse them all at once. O Indu, flow toward us from the heavenly world for the sake of wealth that brings enjoyment, for the benefit of ourselves and our sons. If it is asked whence this wealth comes, he says: you are the one who goes before the vast abundance of riches; therefore, grant it to us.

Like the streams of light from heaven, the vigorous ones flow; like a wise king, he does not harm his friend. Like a son with his father’s deeds, strive with your powers; flow for this people, bringing them invincibility. Like the streams of light from heaven—that is, like the rays belonging to the days of the shining sun—are released vigorously; so too are the streams (sargāḥ) of Soma released. "Streams" (sargāḥ) means the flows; they are poured forth. [The form] is derived from the root *sṛj* in the sense of an action, with the suffix *lyuṭ*; in the Vedic language, the substitution of *ś* for *s* is common (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), and the change to *śer* is a Vedic peculiarity. This wise king, Soma, does not harm his friend, as if he were a friend. Striving with ritual acts (*kratubhiḥ*)—just as a son honors his father by his deeds—strive with your actions. Flow for this people, bringing them invincibility (*ajītim*); that is, act so that they do not suffer defeat. || 16 ||

Your honeyed streams have surged forth, when, purified, you pass through the sheep’s wool, beyond the waters. Flowing on, you purify the essence of the cows; being born, you have filled the sun with your rays. Your honeyed streams have surged forth when, purified by the *vasatīvarī* waters, you pass through the sheep’s wool, beyond the waters. Furthermore, O Pavamāna, you flow toward the essence of the cows, that is, their milk; and being born, you have filled the sun with your worshipful splendors.

1. O you who are abundant in splendor! 2. O you who shine like the sun! 3. Just as a son does not bring about the downfall of his father, so do you flow for this people (*viśe*) in such a way that there is no defeat; the meaning is: "protect."
O unaging and unconquered one, bellowing along the path of Truth, you, the bright one, shine forth according to the law of immortality.

As such, you flow for Indra, exhilarating and impelling the speech of the sages through their inspired thoughts. 32. Bellowing, along the path of Truth, you, the bright one, shine forth according to the law of immortality. As such, you flow for Indra, exhilarating and impelling the speech of the sages through their inspired thoughts. 32.
Being pressed, that Soma, repeatedly crying out—that is, sounding—along the path, the way, of *ṛta*, the truth-realized sacrifice;
and now directly perceived:
he is the abode, the place of *amṛta*, the immortal nature.
The meaning is "free from death.
Such a Śukra—you, who are white in color—shine forth, that is, you reign preeminently.
Full of *matsara* (intoxicating juice), you flow and purify yourself for Indra, for the sake of Indra.
Of what sort?
You flow on, impelling and setting in motion the voice—the sound—along with the thoughts of the poets, the singers.

O divine, well-winged one, flow toward Soma; swelling with streams through your ritual action at the banquet of the gods, O Indu, enter the jar that holds the Soma, crying out as you go toward the ray of the Sun. 33. Divine. Well-filled. Flow. Behold. Soma. Swelling. Streams. By your work. At the feast of the gods. Enter. O Indu. The jar. The receptacle of Soma. Crying out. Go. Toward the ray of the Sun. 33.

O Soma, you who are divine, dwelling in heaven, the well-winged one of excellent flight—you look down; behold from below. [The form *ava cakṣi* is derived from the root *cakṣ* with the suffix *sip* in the present tense (*laṭ*), using a substitution for the active voice (*parasmaipada*). What are you doing?

At the feast for the gods, in the sacrifice which is the place where the gods partake of the oblation, you flow, pouring forth streams by means of your ritual action. Furthermore, O Indu, enter the vessel that holds the Soma;
bellowing, make a sound, and go toward, approach the ray of the Sun, the impeller, the Āditya.

The bearer (of the sacrifice) sends forth three voices: the thought of Truth and the inspired wisdom of the sacred word (*brahman*). Like cows seeking their herd, they go toward the lord of cattle; like lowing thoughts, the hymns go toward Soma. tisraḥ | vācaḥ | īrayati | pra | vahniḥ | ṛtasya | dhītim | brahmaṇaḥ | manīṣām | gāvaḥ | yanti | go-patim | pṛcchamānāḥ | somam | yanti | matayaḥ | vāvaśānāḥ || 34 ||
Agni is the bearer and the sacrificer; he impels the three voices—the praises consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman.
Likewise, he impels the auspicious speech, which is the sustainer of the *ṛta* (the sacrifice), the support of the *brahman*, and the sovereign of the mind of Soma.
Furthermore, as cows go toward their bull, so do the cows, seeking him out, go toward Soma, the lord of speech, asking for the truth.
They approach to mix him with their own milk;
likewise, the prayers—the yearning, desiring singers—go toward Soma, approaching to praise him.

The milch-cows low loudly toward Soma; the inspired singers, inquiring with their prayers, [seek] Soma. Pressed and anointed, Soma is purified; the hymns and *triṣṭubh* verses lead him together toward Soma. 35. Soma. The milch-cows. Lowing loudly. Toward Soma. The inspired singers. With their prayers. Inquiring. Soma. Pressed. Is purified. Being anointed. Toward Soma. The hymns. The *triṣṭubh* verses. Together. Lead. 35.
1. With praises consisting of [words] possessing the sense of "bhā" (light).
2. And behold the sixfold [nature] of the sun. 3. Of the sun, which is everything.
The seven cows have pleased you; the seven milch-kine low, longing for the Soma.
The wise, the intelligent singers, inquiring with their hymns, ask questions.
Being anointed, being sprinkled with milk, the pressed Soma, having been extracted, is purified by the officiating priests.
Likewise, these seven *triṣṭubh* verses—these seven *arkas*, the mantras being performed by us—resound together and come into harmony with the *soma*.
Thus, O Soma, being poured out and purified, flow for our well-being;
enter Indra with a mighty roar, strengthen our speech, and generate inspired wisdom.
Thus, O Soma, being poured out, flow for us while being purified; enter Indra with well-being and with a mighty roar; increase our voice and bring forth the builder of the city. 36.
O Soma, being poured out— that is, being poured all around into the vessels— and being purified, do thou grant us (naḥ) this very well-being (svasti), which is non-destruction (avināśam);
[the augment] ā is added by the rule "it is also seen in the Vedic language" (chandasyapi dṛśyate).
In the word *pūrvapadāt*, the *ṣ* in *saḥ* is the *ṣaṃhitā*-form of *s*. [The forms] *priyā* and [the rest] have the vowel *ā* in place of the genitive case-ending.
Of that beloved Soma, or of those who bestow various dear things, of that Soma whose most beloved streams are for our protection—
may he swiftly grant us wealth.
(The form *prayacchatu* is derived from the root *yacchati* in the *leṭ* mood with the augment *si*).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as people do not give wages to a laborer who has not performed his work, so it is here.
May he, the increaser who grows strong while being purified, the bounteous Soma, protect us with his light—
by whom our ancient fathers, knowers of the path and seekers of heaven, snatched the cattle from the mountain.

He, the one who increases, the increaser, being purified—Soma, the bounteous one—has favored us with light, by which our ancient fathers, who knew the tracks and found the sun, heated the rock for the sake of the kine. 39.

He who has increased by bestowing his own portions upon the gods, the increaser, increasing himself; being purified by the purifier, the bountiful one, the sprinkler of desires—that Soma has protected us with light, with his own splendor.

By that Soma, our ancient ancestors, the Aṅgirases—the knowers of the tracks, who knew the footprints of the cows stolen by the Paṇis, the finders of heaven, or rather, the knowers of the sun—stole the cattle, they stole them from the mountain.
The meaning is that, having gone to a mountain mass enveloped in darkness by the brilliance of the moon, he took away their tracks. Here, the root *muṣ* (to steal) has "tracks" as its object.
Alternatively:
In the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *muṣ*, there is the elision of the phoneme [the nasal].
Having traversed the ocean in the first vessel, the king of the world, generating creatures,
the bull Soma— the Indu— being pressed, has grown great upon the woollen back of the filter.
The ocean has stepped forth in the first ordinance, the king of the world, generating offspring. As a bull upon the woolly summit of the filter, Soma, the pressed drop, has grown great. 40.
He is called *samudra* because from him the waters (*āpaḥ*) flow forth; he is the ocean.

Soma, the King who rains down waters, at the first expansion—that is, in the wide expanse of the world, the atmosphere—while generating and producing all creatures, has stepped across everything. [The form] *akrān* is derived from the root *kram* (to step) in the aorist tense, third person singular (*tip*), with the absence of the augment (*iṅ*), the doubling of the consonant, the elision of the suffix (*silopa*), and the change of the letter *m* to *n* according to the rule “*mo no dhātoḥ*” (the *m* of a verbal root becomes *n* before a following *n*).
The bull, the showerer of desires, being pressed and purified, the radiant drop—that Soma—has grown, increasing greatly upon the high, lofty, and wide-spreading filter.
The great Soma, the buffalo, performed that great deed when, as an embryo, he chose the gods;
while being purified, Indu generated power for Indra from his half and light for the sun.
Great is that which Soma, the buffalo, has performed: that as the embryo of the waters he chose the gods; flowing forth, he generated power in Indra and light in the sun, O Indu. 41.
1. The augment *aṭ* is applied according to the rule *ta-bha6-su*.
2. In the text of Ta (1.2.5.1.7), the phrase “or rather... of Soma” (*yadvā ...somasya*) is absent. 3. In Ta it reads *sarva jānaṃto vā*; in Bha6 it reads *sarva jānaṃto*.
4. "The waters flow from this [place], hence it is called *samudra*.
5. *ta1.2.5.6.7-avimaye*; *ta4-avisaye*.
The *mahiṣaḥ*—the great or the venerable Soma—performed (*cakāra*) that great (*mahi*) or abundant (*prabhūta*) deed.
What is that?

The "womb of the waters" (*apām garbhaḥ*)—being the embryo of the waters because he is both their progenitor and their offspring—that Soma chose the gods; that is to say, he caused them to share [the sacrifice]. Furthermore, as *pavamānaḥ* (the purifying one), the Soma being purified bestowed (*adadhāt*), that is, assigned, the power (*ojaḥ*) produced by drinking Soma upon Indra.
Likewise, Indu, that is Soma, generated light and splendor within the sun.
Rejoice in the wind for our desire and for our prosperity; rejoice in Mitra and Varuṇa while being purified;
rejoice in the host of Maruts, rejoice in the gods, and rejoice in Heaven and Earth, O divine Soma!

Exhilarate Vāyu for our sacrifice and for bounty; exhilarate Mitra and Varuṇa as you are being purified; exhilarate the host of Maruts; exhilarate the gods; exhilarate Heaven and Earth, O divine Soma! 42.
O Soma, do you exhilarate Vāyu; do you cause him to rejoice. For what purpose? For our seeking—that is, for our desire and for our command—and for the sake of wealth.
Likewise, being purified by the filter, you gladden—meaning you satisfy—Mitra and Varuṇa;
furthermore, you gladden the host, the strength belonging to the Maruts;
and similarly, you gladden—that is, you delight—the gods, Indra and the others.
O divine Soma, worthy of praise, gladden and exhilarate both Heaven and Earth;
having delighted them, grant us wealth—this is the meaning.
Straight in your joints, the slayer of the crooked, driving away disease and adversaries;
you who mingle the milk with milk and the cows with milk—of you, Indra, we are the friends.
Straightforward, among the joints, the slayer of the crooked; driving away disease and crushing the adversaries, blending the milk with milk from the cows—of you, O Indra, we are the friends. 43.
O Soma, being straight and moving straight, flow forth; that is, pour out.
Doing what?
Being the slayer of the crooked, that is, of affliction.
Driving away the Rākṣasa in the form of disease (amīvā),
and likewise driving away our assailants and enemies (mṛdhaḥ),
flow on; then, mixing the milk— the warm essence of the cows— with the milk of the cows, you go toward the vessels.

Moreover, O Soma, you are the friend of Indra; we are your friends, being united as companions through the relationship of the one who praises and the one who is praised, and the one who sacrifices and the one for whom the sacrifice is performed.
Flow as the brew of honey, flow as a fountain of wealth; flow to us with heroic sons and with fortune.
O Indu, being purified, flow sweet for Indra; flow to us with riches from the ocean.
Flow as the sweetener; flow from the spring of wealth. Flow toward us with a hero and with fortune. O Indu, being purified, make it savory for Indra; flow toward us with riches from the ocean. 44.
O Soma, flow clear—purify yourself as the distiller of the sweetness of honey, or as the condensed essence, the fountain and overflowing sap of wealth and riches.
Furthermore, flow toward us and bring forth a heroic son;
likewise, grant us Bhaga, the desirable wealth.
O Pavamāna, being purified within the waters, be sweet for Indra; become radiant. (1. *somapāna*; 2. *mādayasi*; 3. *meṣaṇīyāyājñāya*; 4. *dyotamāna*; 5. *śīghragamana*).
Bow down for us from the ocean, from the intermediate space—[grant] a chariot, wealth, or a son.
A chariot-horse or a cow gives milk;
as such, flow and give that [milk].

The pressed Soma flows in a stream like a swift horse that has been urged forward; like a river rushing toward the lowlands, the vigorous one has flowed toward [the vessel]. Purifying himself, he has settled in his wooden womb; the drop (Indu), being cleansed, has mingled with the products of the cow and with the waters. The pressed Soma, by means of his own stream, like a swift horse that has been urged on—*hitvā* is a form derived from the root *hinoti* with the suffix *knip*—and furthermore, like a river (*sindhu*) which, being powerful, flows toward a low-lying place, the vigorous Soma has flowed toward the low-lying vessel. Then, purifying himself, the Soma has settled in his wooden (*vanya*) womb, his place of origin, the jar. This very Soma of yours, O Indra, flows for you who desire it, into the vessels—wise, powerful, beholding the light of heaven, chariot-borne, and of true vigor; he who has been released like the longing of those who seek the gods. 46 This very Soma of yours, O Indra, flows for you who desire it, into the vessels—wise, powerful, beholding the light of heaven, chariot-borne, and of true vigor; he who has been released like the longing of those who seek the gods, meaning he was poured forth. 46 O Indra, for you who desire it—for your sake—that wise, powerful, and swift Soma flows into the vessels; he who beholds the light of heaven, who possesses a chariot, whose strength is true, and who, like the longing of those seeking the gods, has been released. 46. He was given forth; this is the meaning.

Purifying himself with ancient vigor, assuming the forms of his daughter, and clothing himself in a triple-layered protection within the waters, he goes forth like a Hotṛ-priest, chanting among the sacrificial rites. (47) With *pratena*—with ancient *vayasā*—vigor or food, *punānaḥ*—being purified; that is to say, flowing in a stream consisting of food. Such [Soma], *duhituḥ*—of the "daughter," the milker of all, namely the Earth—*varpāṃsi*—"forms" (*varpas* is a name for appearance; it covers the body); thus, *tiraḥ dadhānaḥ*—covering and concealing those forms with his own luster; and likewise *vasānaḥ*—clothing himself in *śarma*—a sacrificial hall provided with three enclosures (*trivarūtham*), or rather, that which wards off the three: cold, heat, and rain; *apsu*—standing in the *vasatīvarī* waters; *eṣaḥ*—this Soma; *hotā iva*—just as the Hotṛ-priest goes to sacrifices making sounds of praise, so too *rebhan*—uttering sounds, *śarmaneṣu*—in the *samanas*, where courageous and bold deeds are performed, i.e., in the sacrifices; *yāti*—he goes.
O divine Soma, being purified for the two bowls, flow around as a swift charioteer for us.
