The most sweet, honeyed, and true to the cosmic order (ṛta), like the god Savitṛ whose thoughts are truth.

Now, O divine Soma, you who are the charioteer, flow for us, being purified in the waters within the two bowls—sweetest, most honeyed, and true to the cosmic order (ṛta), like the god Savitṛ whose thoughts are ever true.

O divine Soma, being desired, you who possess a chariot—being purified upon the two pressing-boards of our own sacrifice—flow forth quickly and pour out into the *vasatīvarī* waters. Most sweet, the sweetest here, full of honeyed sweetness, possessing the *ṛta*, and possessing the sacrifice, you who are like a god, a deity whose praises are true—you, being such, flow forth.
Pour forth upon us divine treasures, pour forth all earthly riches as you are being purified—those by which we may obtain wealth in horses and the ancestral heritage of Jamadagni. 51.
O Soma, being purified by the filter, flow toward us—bring to us the celestial riches, those treasures existing in heaven.
Likewise, bring to us all the earthly riches, those treasures existing upon the earth.
And bring that power by which, through your own capability, we may attain wealth and cattle; bring that power to us.
Furthermore, "ārpaye" means: just as you bestowed upon Jamadagni wealth suitable for the sons of the Ṛṣis (ārṣāṇām), so too bestow (*abhyarpa*) it upon us.
Or alternatively:

just as you made the *ārṣeya*—the mantra appropriate for the Ṛṣis, which was the very property of Jamadagni—most delicious to the taste, so may you make such a mantra most delicious for us; thus the Ṛṣi named Kutsa makes this request.
Flow forth with this [stream], O Indu; bestow these riches upon us. Do not remain, O Indu, but flow forward.
Even through prayer, bring us treasures and wealth for the sake of sport and for the purpose of conquering our enemies; shake them down and protect us.
The meaning is that he gave it.
How so? Just as one desiring fruit causes a tree to shake when there is an unripe fruit upon it, even so [did he act].
The earth trembled at his roar, like that of a bull, whether he was growing strong in the marshy land or on the dry upland.
The one who is praised sent the enemies to sleep and, with his weapon, struck down the senseless foes.

Upon the earth—these [are his]. Of this one, whose name is Vṛṣan, for the sake of nourishment—whether in the state of hunger or in the state of satiety—for him who grows great—he caused to sleep; he struck them down and made them unctuous. Drive away the enemies; drive away the thoughtless ones from here! 54.
"Greatly" (*mahi*) means "very great" (*mahatīm*);
by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*).
"Vṛṣanāmanī" means "the two names of the showerer."
The raining down of arrows and the bowing down of enemies—
these two actions of this Soma become forms that bring happiness;
and these two actions are within my reach.
"One eats this while moving on a bed. Here, "battle" is understood because it is that which is accomplished by means of horses;
thus, battle is what is grasped in this context.
Or rather, they are "in the seizing," meaning in hand-to-hand combat accomplished by touch, and "in the slaying," meaning characterized by the destruction of enemies.
This very [hero], *nigutaḥ* (concealed), caused the enemies who were lying low to fall asleep; that is, he struck them down with his two [arms].
This is the meaning.
Furthermore, O Soma, making [the enemy] feel affection and causing him to flee from the battle, drive away those enemies,
our adversaries.
Likewise, drive away from here—from our presence—those who do not honor [the gods] and those who do not perform worship, as well as the nihilists (*nāstika*).
The root *añc* denotes the act of going.
Three purifiers are stretched out; you, being purified, run toward one of them.
You are Bhaga; you are the giver of the gift; you are Maghavan; O Indu, increase our wealth.

Mine! Three purifiers are stretched out; you go along one of them, flowing as you are purified. You are Bhaga; you are the giver of the gift; you are Maghavan for those who possess wealth, O Indu. 55.
O Soma, you reach—that is, you properly pervade—the three extended and wide-spread filters, which consist of Vāyu, Sūrya, and [the Earth].
Furthermore, being purified, you flow along—that is, you follow—that one filter made by the Unshakable One (Aja Ekapād).
Moreover, you are Bhaga, the one worthy of being honored.
Likewise, you are the giver of the gift and of the wealth. If it is asked how this [wealth] possesses the nature of wealth, it is said in reply:
O Indu, O Soma, you are the increaser of wealth for the liberal patron (maghavan); you are a liberal patron yourself, being exceedingly wealthy even beyond others.
This Soma, the all-knowing sage upon the mountain, the king of the entire world,
impelling the drops at the assemblies, O Indu, passes through the woolly filter toward the choice vessel.
This one, the all-knowing, the wise Soma, the king of the entire world, flows clear; impelling the drops at the assemblies, the Indu passes through the sheep’s-wool filter. 56.
The knower of all, the perceiver of everything, and therefore wise and intelligent; the king and master of the entire world and of every realm—this Soma flows and pours forth.
He explains this very point:
"In the sacrificial assemblies."

They know, they understand this here: 1. *ta* and *ma* are included in *ga*; 2. *bha* is pure (*pavitra*) among the pure syllables; *su-pavitrā*; 3. *ga* becomes [the result]; furthermore, according to *ta*, *bha*, *dha*, and *na*, it is "the state of possessing wealth" (*dhanatva*); according to *ta*, *ra*, *sa*, *ca*, *tha*, *pa*, *ya*, *la*, *va*, *bha*, *ra*, *sa*, *dha*, *na*, and *va*, it is "the state of possessing riches" (*dhanavattva*).
"Devān" means those who find or obtain; "vidathā" refers to sacrifices.

In these, the Soma—acting as a hero (*vīrayan*), impelling the drops of essence (*rasakaṇān*)—pervades (*vyati*) the filter (*pavitra*) on both sides (*samayā*), passing through it repeatedly (*vadhyaṃ avivabhaṃ vdhāraṃ dhāraṃ*).
The unassailable buffaloes lick the drops;
like greedy poets, they low toward him.
The wise ones urge him on with their ten fingers.
They anoint the form with the essence.
The unassailable buffaloes lick the drop; like eager poets they sing aloud. The wise ones urge it on with their ten fingers and anoint its form with the essence of the waters.
The great, worshipful, and therefore unassailable (avadhya) bulls—the gods—lick, that is, taste, the drops of Soma.
Furthermore, the gods, desiring the Soma, low at its place, that is, at the location of the streams of this Soma.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like poets (*kavayaḥ*) who are not greedy,

desiring wealth, the wise (*dhīrāḥ*) priests— skilled in their ritual duties— urge forth this Soma with ten fingers for the purpose of pressing it. Just as poets, the chanters, are made to resound while they praise, so too do they impel it.
Moreover, they thoroughly adorn—that is, they properly attend to—the form of Soma, the stalk, and the omentum, which are known as the *vasatīvarī* waters.
Hasten, O Soma; by means of your purifying flow, may we continually gather the wealth that has been made ready for us.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.
Hasten! O Soma, by means of your purifying flow, may we gather in the battle what has been won; may Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that forever. 58.
O Soma, with you as my companion— being purified by the purifying strainer—
I shall win the battle, which is the name for conflict.
In that battle, we shall distinguish— that is, perform with excellence— the many deeds that must be done.

Since we perform our rites with your assistance, therefore may Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi by name, Sindhu by designation, and also Pṛthivī and Dyau—may these, beginning with Mitra, honor us by bestowing wealth and other gifts.
The second hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "abhi naḥ," has both Ambarīṣa—
the son of King Vṛṣāgir— and Bharadvāja as its seers (ṛṣis) together. These and the three following [hymns] are in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
In this case, however, the *ekādaśī* is the *bṛhatī*;
Soma Pavamāna is the deity.
Thus it is enumerated: “*Abhi no* [is by] Ambārīṣa Ṛṣi; the [first] twelve are *anuṣṭubh*s, and the last two are *bṛhatī*s.”
The application is concluded.
Flow toward us for the winning of booty, O Indra, with your chariot that is much-desired,
bearing thousands, most brilliant, and all-conquering.
Bestow upon us, O Indu, wealth that is most excellent at winning booty, worthy of much desire, bringing thousands, highly resplendent, and all-conquering. 1.
Having come, bring to us—our own—splendor (*varcas*) that is most brilliant, bestowing strength or food, and consisting of wealth or a son;
what kind?
one that is desired by many and brings a thousandfold support.
1. *ta*-śabdayanti; *bha6*-śabdayanti. 2. *ta1.2.5.6.7*—‘the form of *moma*’ does not exist; *bha6*—*somasya*. 3. *ga*, *ta3*, *bha1.2.6.7*—‘*dīsa*’ does not exist.

"Bahuvidhabharaṇam" means endowed with the nourishment of many; thus says Yāska: "Tuvidyumnam" [means] either "one who has well-shined speech" or "one who has well-shined praise" (Nighaṇṭu 5.5). "Yahvam" means possessed of great fame or the like. "Vibhvasaham": "vibhva" is a name for the great; it means the overcomer of the great.

This Soma, being pressed and currently undergoing the pressing, flows through the filter made of sheep’s wool (*avyaya*).
Therein lies this illustration:
just as a man standing upon a chariot puts on his armor (*varma*) for protection.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *vyayi*, there is a Vedic elision of a phoneme (*varṇalopa*).

"Abhihitaḥ" means impelled from all sides, or alternatively, praised by the worshippers. That "indu," namely Soma, being "hiyānaḥ" (impelled) by the wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*) made of wood—the root *hi* meaning "to go" and "to increase."
Being filled by that, he flows with streams; "akṣāḥ" is the form of the root *kṣar* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense.

This *indu*, this Soma, being pressed and being purified— this one who, as the distiller of exhilaration, is impelled by the gods for the sake of intoxication— flows all around upon the invigorating, woolly filter. That Soma, who is exalted and preeminent at the sacrifice, desiring cattle— or rather, desiring milk and the like— proceeds with his stream,
moving like a bird through the atmosphere with its shining radiance.

For you indeed, O God, bestow eternal wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations; O Indu, you win for yourself riches that are thousandfold and possess a hundredfold essence. 4. For you indeed, O God, [bestow] eternal wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations; O Indu, you win for yourself riches that are thousandfold and possess a hundredfold essence. 4.

"O divine Soma, as such, you bestow wealth (*vasu*) and great power (*mahaḥ*) upon the mortal human being who offers oblations (*dāśuṣe*), that is, the sacrificer, for the sake of his numerous offspring and progeny; thus you cause them to prosper.

For according to the view that this constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), there would otherwise be a lack of *anighāta* (non-suppression of accent) due to the connection with the particle *hi*."
O Vṛtra-slayer, O Vasu, may we obtain a portion of this much-desired wealth;
may we be the ones closest to your nourishing food and your favor, O Adhigu.

ga—O Indu, O wise one, he bestows wealth; likewise, [bestow] wealth of many forms numbering in the thousands.
O Vṛtrahan, O Vasu, may we be the ones to whom you have bestowed much-desired wealth; may we be the closest recipients of nourishment and of the light of Agni. 5.
O Vṛtra-slayer, O Soma, destroyer of enemies, we are yours—belonging to you who are such as you are.
Therefore, O Vasu, O bestower of dwelling, O you who are desired by many, may we be most closely situated—extremely near—to the Vasu, the wealth and treasure bestowed by you.
Likewise, may we be closest to food (iṣas), and furthermore, O Agnigū, O Soma whose course is unseen, may we be closest to happiness (sunnasya). May we become so.

The five sisters bathe him who possesses celestial glory, who is pressed by the stones, the beloved and desirable one of Indra, the surging wave. (Twice). Him. Five. Of celestial glory. The sisters. Pressed by the stones. Beloved. Of Indra. Desirable. They bathe. The surging one. (6).

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: the "twice ten" (twenty) "sisters"—the fingers—moving here and there for the purpose of performing the ritual, "bathe" (*prasnāpayanti*) that Soma which possesses its own glory, which is pressed by the stones (*adrisaṃhata*), which is the "dear" and "desirable" one beloved by Indra and desired by all, and which has "waves" (*ūrmiṇam*) consisting of streams; they thoroughly sprinkle it with the *vasatīvarī* waters. "They purify it" is the syntactical link to what follows.

They purify with the fleece that beloved, golden-hued, swift steed, who indeed goes forth with exhilaration to reach all the gods. 7. They purify with the fleece that beloved, golden-hued, swift steed, who indeed goes forth with exhilaration to reach all the gods. 7.
They purify—that is, they cleanse—this Soma with the *vāra*, the woolen filter; he who is beloved by all, desirable, golden-hued (*hari*), and tawny-brown (*babhru*).
That Soma goes around together with exhilarating juice (*mada*) to all the gods, indeed to Indra and the other deities alone.

By means of this hymn of yours, O you who protect the one who accomplishes skill—[the hymn] of him who, like the sun, has established great glory among the patrons, he who is desirable. Of this [hymn], indeed, by your protection, [we celebrate] the one who accomplishes skill; he who among the patrons has established great renown, like the sun, he who is desirable.
The form *vaḥ* [is used here]; the substitution of *vas* is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
O you, by means of the protection (*avasa*) of this Soma, you become those who drink (*pāntaḥ*) the essence that accomplishes skill (*dakṣasādhanam*), the essence that accomplishes strength.

Like the sun (*svarṇa ādityaḥ*), this desirable (*haryataḥ*) Soma, who is longed for by all, bestows (*dadhe*) great (*bṛhat*) renown (*śravaḥ*)—that is, abundant food (*annam*)—upon the patrons (*sūriṣu*), the singers who impel the hymns of praise. That is to say, he establishes it [for them].
At your sacrifices, O Rodasī, the daughter of Manu, Indu, was born—the god who dwells on the mountains; may he prosper for you both, O you of mighty roar.
Maḥ! Vām! At the sacrifices, the two Rodasīs—Mānavī and Indu’s divine mother—were born from the mountain-dweller. The gods established him, the one of great power. 9.

O Mānavī, O daughter of Manu, O you who are born of Manu; O Goddess, O radiant one; O Rodasī, Heaven and Earth—you two, at your sacrifices, that Indu, Soma, was born. As a god, illuminating everything by his own splendor, he took his place upon the earth among the mountain-dwellers, the pressing-stones. The priests established that newly-born Soma upon the loud-sounding lower stone at the sacrifice; they struck him with the stones—that is to say, they chanted over him.
O Soma, you are poured out for Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, to drink; for the hero who bestows sacrificial fees, for the god who sits amidst the exhilarating draughts.
For Indra, for Vṛtra-slayer, to drink the Soma, you are poured out; for the man who gives sacrificial fees, and for the god who sits upon the exhilarating seat. 10.

O Soma, you are poured out all around into the vessels for Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, for the sake of the Lord— here the fourth case denotes purpose— for his drinking. You are poured out for the sake of Indra’s consumption.
Or [it is performed] with [grains] other than *amanī*.

Furthermore, for the sake of the sacrificial priests who possess the *dakṣiṇā*, and for the sake of Indra, the god who possesses that [sacrifice], you are poured out to bestow the fruit upon that man—the sacrificer—who sits (*sīdate*) in the sacrificial hall (*madana-āsada*) as a human being.
Those ancient Soma juices have flowed through the filters at the dawns;
snorting away those who are malicious from afar, they have driven off the thoughtless ones at morning.
Those ancient Soma juices have flowed through the filters at the dawns, snorting away those who plot evil from afar—those of perverted minds—at early morning. 11.
In the dawns, in the breakings of light, and in the manifestations, those ancient Soma juices have flowed and continue to flow through the filter.
Those Somas which were hidden away in secret, devoid of consciousness, and crooked-minded— [the Soma] has driven them away, bearing the name of a thief.
"They were cut down by Kauṭilya"—thus [it is said].
Those deceitful thieves were driven away at the very time of dawn;
and "driving away" (apaprothana) means propelling away (apapreraṇa).
Driving others away and repelling them by means of their power,
they become "those who flow forth"— this is the connection.
May we, along with our wise patrons, obtain him who goes before us for friendship— he who bears the scent of booty— and may we win him whose home is wealth.

Being pressed out with the stones, placed upon the ox-hide, they have sounded forth nourishment for us on every side—they who find wealth. (11) *suṣvāṇāsaḥ*, *vi*, *adribhiḥ*, *citānāḥ*, *goḥ*, *adhi*, *tvaci*, *iṣam*, *asmabhyam*, *abhitaḥ*, *sam*, *asvaran*, *vasuvidaḥ*. Placed upon the hide (*tvaci*) of the ox (*goḥ*), being known (*citānāḥ*) through the stones (*adribhiḥ*), being pressed out (*suṣvāṇāsaḥ*) by the pressing-stones (*grāvabhiḥ*), these Soma juices—finders of wealth (*vasuvidaḥ*)—have sounded forth (*asvaran*) nourishment (*iṣam*) for us on every side (*abhitaḥ*). That is to say, they bestow it.

These purified, wise Soma juices, mixed with curds, like suns visible to all, moving and firm in the clarified butter (ghṛta). 12. These—purified, cleansed by the filter; wise, possessing intelligence; mixed with curds, blended with curd; like suns, visible to all; moving, having the nature of motion; firm, remaining steady therein—in the clarified butter, known as the *vasatīvarī* water, these Soma juices, like suns, become visible in the vessels for all to behold.

Let not the mortal, who obstructs the pressed juice, enjoy that splendor of the flowing soma; slay the stingy dog, just as the Bhr̥gus struck down Makha. (13) Let not the mortal—the destroyer who creates obstacles to the rite—possess that well-known voice, the sound of the flowing *andhas* (the edible Soma). Let him not hear it. Likewise, O worshippers, strike down that stingy dog, one devoid of the means to accomplish the rite. Therein lies the illustration: just as in ancient times the Bhr̥gus struck down the one named Makha who had committed an offense, so too should you strike him down.

The kinsman has clothed himself in the filter; like a son for the enjoyment of his parents, he moves. Like a lover to a young woman, like a suitor to take his seat in the womb. The kinsman, Soma, who is related to the gods, has clothed himself in the *atka*, the filter which covers [the juice]; he envelops it, becoming bound within it. Therein is the illustration: just as a son covers himself for the sake of enjoyment (*bhuje*) between the two protectors (*oṇyoḥ*), namely his mother and father, so does he. Then this Soma moves (*sarati*) toward the *yonim*, the vessel that serves as his own chariot, in order to take his seat (*āsadam*).
1. [This concerns] those who are barren and those who have not yet given birth. Regarding this, there are two similes:
just as a paramour hastens to reach an unchaste woman, so does he [the breath].
Or it is just as when a suitor goes forth to obtain a maiden; it is like that.

That hero, the accomplisher of skill, who has propped apart the two worlds—he, the golden-hued one, has clothed himself in the filter, like a wise ordainer taking his seat upon his own womb. 15. He. Hero. Accomplisher of skill. Apart. Who. Has propped apart. The two worlds. The golden-hued one. In the filter. Has clothed himself. The ordainer. Like. His own womb. To sit upon. 15.
That Soma, the hero, is capable of accomplishing skill and accomplishing strength.
That Soma, by his own splendor, propped apart—meaning he supported—the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*).
He covered them; such is the meaning.

Furthermore, Hari—the golden-hued Soma—is the creator (vedhāḥ), not merely a disposer; just as a sacrificer enters his own home, so too does he envelop himself within the filter (pavitre) in order to settle (āsadam) in his own place, the vessel (yonim). He becomes firmly established there.

Soma flows through the sheep’s woolly strainers upon the ox-hide; bellowing, the tawny bull goes toward Indra’s appointed place. 16. Through the sheep’s woolly strainers, Soma flows upon the ox-hide; bellowing, the tawny bull goes toward Indra’s appointed place. 16.
This Soma flows through the sheep’s wool, through the fleece as purifiers; from them he flows toward the jar and pours forth.
Moreover, bellowing loudly upon the ox-hide, the bull, the showerer of desires, the golden-hued Soma approaches and reaches Indra’s own prepared and consecrated place.
‘Krāṇā śiśuḥ’: this sixth hymn belongs to Trita;
these four subsequent hymns are in the *uṣṇih* meter.
Pavamāna Soma is the deity.
And thus it is enumerated: "The eight krāṇa [verses] belong to Trita and are in the uṣṇih meter.
The application [of the verses] has been explained.

Taking his stride, the child of the great ones, impelling the vision of the Cosmic Order (ṛta), he has encompassed all that is dear; indeed, he exists doubly. krāṇā | śiśuḥ | mahīnām | hinvan | ṛtasya | dīdhitim | viśvā | pari | priyā | bhuvat | artha | dvitā || 1 ||

*Krāṇā*: from the root *kṛ*, with the suffix *śānac*; by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” there is elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). By the rule “*supāṃ suluk*,” there is the substitution of the vowel *ā* for the case-ending (*sup*).

Performing the sacrifice, Soma—the child, like a son, of the great and worshipful waters—urging forth his own juice, which is the illuminator or sustainer of the *ṛta* (the cosmic order) of the sacrifice, pervades and encompasses all beloved oblations. Moreover, he exists in a twofold manner;
that is to say, he abides both in heaven and upon the earth.

Anoint the two stones of Trita, for that secret place which is the beloved goal of the sacrifice, O presser, has been reached through the ordinances. 2. upa tritasya pāṣyo'raṃkta yadguhā padam | yajñasya suta dharmabhirartha priyam || 2 || Anoint the two stones of Trita, for that secret place which is the beloved goal of the sacrifice, O presser, has been reached through the ordinances. 2.

When Soma, my portion at the sacrifice, reached its place upon the two pressing-boards— which are secret within the secret [sanctuary], the *havirdhāna*, and as firm as stones— when he distributed himself there, immediately thereafter the officiating priests praise with the seven meters, such as the Gāyatrī and others, Soma, the supporter of the sacrifice and the one who delights;
or rather, they press Soma with the flowing waters, such as the *vasatīvarī* and others.
With the stream of Trita, he has sent forth three [streams] over the ridges;
the one of excellent wisdom measures out his paths.
Threefold, with the stream of Trita, he has sent forth wealth upon his back; the one of excellent wisdom measures out his journeys. 3.
O Soma, maintain for me, the performer of this sacrifice, the three pressings that belong to you, by means of your own sustaining power.

Furthermore, through the *pṛṣṭha* chants, bring hither Indra, the bestower of wealth, or inspire him with heroic vigor. The wise praiser, possessing excellent insight, measures out—that is, performs—the *yojanas*, the far-reaching hymns that effect the union [with the deity].
Since this is so, the meaning is: "Therefore, impel Indra toward the Sāmans."
When he was born, the seven mothers directed the wise one toward glory;
he has become aware that he is the firm foundation of riches.
As soon as he was born, the seven mothers instructed the wise one for the sake of glory; this steadfast one has taken heed of riches. 4.

The seven rivers, such as the Gaṅgā, or the seven meters, being born—that is, having manifested—as the wise ordainer (*vedhas*) and arranger of ritual action, instruct the *mānara*s for the sake of the glory and sovereignty of the sacrificer; they provide instruction by means of the scripture (the *śāstra*). Because Soma, who is firm, knows the riches of those who seek them, therefore, when his instruction is carried out, there arises for the sacrificers an abundance of wealth and other blessings.
In his service, all the guileless gods, being of one accord, become desirable delights; may they take pleasure in what [is offered].
In his service, may all the gods, being of one accord and free from malice, become desirable and sources of delight, when they take pleasure [in his offerings]. 5.
All the gods, free from malice, acting in accordance with the ritual act of this Soma, being of one accord and united, become objects of desire;
when these delighting gods enjoy this pressed Soma, then they become desirable.
Yami has brought forth for us to behold a beautiful child at the proper time—
the seer, most bountiful, who desires nothing at the sacrifice.
Him—the embryo—those who increase the cosmic order (ṛtāvṛdhas) have brought forth for all to behold: the lovely one, the seer (kavi), the most bountiful, desired by many at the sacrifice. 6.

The waters known as *vasatīvarī*, which increase the ritual action (*vṛtāvṛdhaḥ*) and cause the sacrifice to prosper (*yajñasya vardhayitryaḥ*), generated (*ajanayan*) this Soma for the sake of the sacrifice (*adhvare*) so that he might be seen (*dṛśe*). He is the embryo (*garbham*), situated like a fetus within the vessel.

What kind [of Soma]? Beautiful (*cārum*), auspicious in form to all; a seer (*kavim*), one of far-reaching wisdom; most magnificent (*maṃhiṣṭham*), most worthy of honor or most bountiful; and for that very reason, much-desired (*puruspṛham*), sought after by many. "The gods serve this Soma"—thus the connection with the preceding verse.
1. In Ga, Ta3, and Bha1.2.7, "ṛtvijaḥ" is absent.
2. In Ga, Ta3, and Bha4.5, there is "saṃyojana".
3. In Ga, Ta1.2.3.4.5, and Bha1.2.4.6, "sorya" is "somaḥ".

He goes by himself toward the two united ones, the great mothers of *ṛta* (the cosmic order), when they, extending the sacrifice, anoint it continuously. When the two united ones—the great mothers of *ṛta*, Heaven and Earth—are joined together, he approaches them by himself. When the officiants, extending the sacrifice, anoint it continuously with the *vasatīvarī* waters, then he approaches it of his own accord.

By your power, with the bright dice, you have opened the enclosure of heaven; impelling the thought of Truth at the sacrifice. (8) O Soma, by your *kratu*—whether through action or knowledge—with the *śukébhiḥ*, the bright, shining *ákṣabhiḥ*, like dice or the senses, you have driven away (*apa ṛṇóḥ*) the *vrájam*, the mass of darkness, from *divaḥ*, the intermediate space. [The root *ṛṇu* means "to go," belonging to the *tanādi* class. What were you doing? Impelling (*hinván*), sending forth your own essence which sustains the *ṛtásya*, the Truth of the sacrifice, at the *adhvaré*, the unimpeded ritual. By this, his presence in both worlds is expressed. The seventh hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "pra punānāya," belongs to the first Dvita. The meter and deity are as before. Thus it is enumerated: "Pra punānāya: six; the first is for Dvita. Its application is established.

To Soma, who is being purified, the ordainer, for whom the hymn is raised up—to him who delights in our prayers, bring forth a song of praise as one brings a wage; with our thoughts, satisfy him who finds pleasure in them. (1) The seer, having been twice addressed, speaks to himself: "To the *punānāya*—being purified by the filter; to the *vedhase*—the ordainer of rites; to the *matibhiḥ jujoṣate*—who is pleased by our prayers, or rather, who together with the prayers (*matibhiḥ*) of the worshippers finds delight in giving pleasure; to *Soma*, bring forth (*pra bhara*) the *vacas*—the speech that is *udyatam*—raised up; that is, accomplish it excellently. The meaning is: 'Praise him! In this matter there is a comparison: *bhṛtim na*—just as laborers accomplish their wages, so [bring forth the hymn]."

Anointed with the products of the cow, he flows around the sheep’s woolen filters; being purified, the golden-hued one makes for himself his three dwelling places. Anointed (*añjānaḥ*) by means of the products of the cow (*gobhiḥ*), such as milk and the like, Soma flows (*arṣati*) around (*pari*) the sheep’s woolen (*avyayā*) fleece-filters (*vārāṇi*). Furthermore, the golden-hued (*hariḥ*) Soma, while being purified (*punānaḥ*), makes for himself (*kṛṇute*) his three dwelling places (*trī ṣadhasthā*); a "dwelling place" (*ṣadhastha*) is so called because he stands (*tiṣṭhati*) within it—namely, the three locations consisting of the *droṇakalaśa*, the *āvanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt*.
1. [The syllables] *ta*, *ta*, *ma*, *anuṣaktaṃ* and *ca*; 2.

*ga*, *tta*, *bha*, *pra* and *erayan* (meaning "impelling" or "driving away"); *ta*, *bha*, *pra* and *erayan* (impelling or driving away). He flows around the honey-dripping vat through the sheep's wool filter.

O pressed one, now be praised with the songs of the seers! 3. Around the vat, honey-dripping, through the sheep's wool, he flows. Toward the songs of the seers, O pressed one, be praised now! 3. Around the vat, honey-dripping, through the sheep's wool, he flows. Toward the songs of the seers, O pressed one, be praised now!

That Soma, flowing with sweetness, moves around and reaches the wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*)—the vessel that receives the essence—having been brought there; he flows through the sheep’s wool, the unblemished fleece, the purifying filter.
The seven voices of the seers—the meters (*chandāṃsi*)—now praise this very Soma, for "nu" means "in praising."
Where is the beginning?

The leader of prayers, belonging to all the gods, the undeceivable Soma, being purified, the tawny one, enters the two vessels. 4. Leader of prayers, belonging to all the gods, the undeceivable Soma, being purified, the tawny one, enters the two vessels. 4.
Hari, who is green-colored, that Soma, being purified—that is, being cleansed—enters around the two *camū* vessels, the two pressing-boards.
Of what nature is he?
He is the leader of hymns (*matīnām*), or rather, the one who leads the hymners (*matīnām*) toward their own task; he is the one belonging to all the gods (*viśvadevaḥ*).
When it is being pressed, all the gods, beginning with Indra, indeed come toward the Soma;
therefore, he is accompanied by all the gods, and for that very reason, he is *adābhya*, meaning unassailable or uninjured by anyone.
Go forth along the divine powers according to your own nature, with Indra, upon a well-yoked chariot; being purified, O immortal one, together with the priests, O priest. 5.

O Soma, you, having mounted the same chariot together with Indra, go around—that is, proceed along—the divine powers belonging to the gods, following the armies of the gods. Of what nature? Being purified, that is, being cleansed.
"By the *vāghats*:
*vāghat* is a name for a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*). By the priests who impel the oblations, the immortal one—devoid of human attributes—is being carried forward."
Or alternatively:
being purified by the *vāghat*s—the officiating priests—O Man, you who bring wealth and other blessings to the singers and sacrificers, proceed around.

Like a prize-seeking steed, the god, pressed for the gods, flowing through the joints, pervading all, he runs forth. 6. pari | sarminam | na | vājayuḥ | devaḥ | devebhyaḥ | sutaḥ | vyānaśiḥ | parvamānaḥ | vi | dhāvati || 6 ||

Like a cloud, the seeker of booty, the shining god, being pressed for the sake of the gods, has been poured out; pervasive in the vessels and extending throughout them, Soma, the purifying one being cleansed by the filter, thus runs around and approaches the cups on every side.
*Vyānaśiḥ*: [derived from] the root *aśū* in the sense of pervasion (*vyāptau*).
Regarding the rule *āda-gama-hana*, the suffix *kip* is applied here because we observe its usage after roots such as *sad* in the Vedic language (*utsarga-chandasi sadādibhyo darśanāt*).
The augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule "aśnoteśca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19).
In this seventh anuvāka, there are eleven sūktas.
Among them, the first sūkta, consisting of six verses, begins with "sakhāyaḥ.
Parvata and Nārada, both belonging to the Kaṇva lineage, are the seers (ṛṣis).
Alternatively, the two Apsarases named Śikhaṇḍinī, who were the daughters of Kaśyapa, should be regarded as the seers of this hymn. The meter and deity are as before.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Sakhāyaḥ [is by] Parvata and Nārada, both sons of Kaśyapa; or [it is by] the two Apsarases, the Śikhaṇḍinīs."
The application of the hymns has been concluded.

O friends, sit down; sing forth to him who is being purified. Adorn him with sacrifices for his glory, as one would adorn a child. 1. O friends, sit down; sing forth to him who is being purified. Adorn him with sacrifices for his glory, as one would adorn a child. 1.
1. [The one] who causes [the soma] to flow;
2. [those] related to him. O friends—meaning you who have become friends, the praisers and officiating priests—sit down; that is, sit down to offer praise.
Now, sing forth—sing out pre-eminently—to Soma who is being purified and is being cleansed.

Adorn him thoroughly for the sake of splendor with sacrifices, with oblations worthy of worship, and with mixtures once he has been pressed. From that [pressing], adorn the pressed Soma on all sides with sacrifices, with the sacrificial offerings to be worshipped, and with the blending [of juices] for the sake of beauty.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a father adorns his young child, his infant son, with ornaments, so it is here.
At the Pravargya and Abhiṣava rites, there is one verse beginning with "samī vatsam.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'samī vatsaṃ na mātṛbhiḥ, saṃ vatsa iva mātṛbhiḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).
Let him join the gods like a calf with its mothers, he who wins wealth and possesses double power for our exhilaration.
Like a calf with its mothers, send forth this one who wins the household; toward the god-pleasing exhilaration that possesses double strength. 2.

O officiating priests, mix this Soma—the means of attaining the sacrifice, the means of attaining the home—with the mothers, that is, with the *vasatīvarī* waters which have become like mothers. How so? Just as they unite a calf with its mothers, the cows, so [should you do].
Of what sort?
One who is other than the gods, the protector of the gods; the cause of intoxication (*mada*); possessing double the speed (*dviśavasam*), or exceeding strength.
Alternatively, it means the gods and humans residing there between the two banks (*ṛkya*).
Unite with that Soma, who causes them to prosper through the gift of the *havirdhāna* shed.
May he who accomplishes skillful means purify [us], so that he may be most auspicious for the refreshment of the host, as he is for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Purify [us], you who are the means for skill; as [you do] for the host, for their enjoyment; as [you do] for Mitra and Varuṇa, most auspiciously. ||3||
Purify with the purifier that which is the means for skill, the means for strength, or the means for wealth and so forth—purify the Soma.
The root *pūj* belongs to the *ṛ* class (the sixth class).
From it, in the imperative (*loṭ*), by the rule "tasanasanayanaśca," there is the substitution of *ta* for *ti*. There is no absence of the *paśvādi* group [which would otherwise apply].

The meaning is: "May this Soma purify itself so that it becomes most beneficial (*śaṃtamah*), providing exceeding comfort (*atiśayena sukham*) for the host (*śardhāya*) of the gods for their enjoyment (*vītaye*) and for their drinking (*pānāya*), or likewise for Mitra and Varuṇa."
The voices have followed you, the finder of wealth, for our sake;
with cows we clothe your form.
Toward us, do thou, the finder of wealth, come hither; let our voices follow after thee. We clothe thy form with the products of the cow. 4.
O Soma, our voices (*vāṇīḥ*) praise you—*abhy-anūpata*—you who find wealth and are the giver of riches, for the sake of bestowing wealth and other gifts upon us.
"Nū" means in praising. We clothe you there with *varṇa*, the concealing essence, by means of *gobhiḥ*, that is, with products of the cow such as milk and the like; we clothe you thoroughly.
We cover [it] on all sides.
O Lord of our exhilarations, you are the celestial nymph among the gods in this soma-drop;
like a friend to a friend, be the best finder of the path for us.
O Lord of our exhilarations, O Indu, you are the celestial nymph of the gods; like a friend to a friend, be the one who best finds the way for us. 5.
1. [The syllables] *ga-ta-bha* are not present [in the text] as "by the mothers.
O Lord Indra, [belonging to] "us" (*naḥ*), that is, to our exhilarating drinks (*madānām*, *madakānām*), you, O Soma, are "one whose food is the gods" (*devapsaras*).
*Smara* is a name for form.
You are of radiant form.

As such, just as a "sakhā" (companion) or "suhṛd" (well-wisher) makes known the true path to a "sadhya" (dear) friend, so too, being the "gātuvittamaḥ"—the supreme finder of the way—become for us as well the one who reveals it. Be our guide.

O Soma, be with us; this is ancient. Make it ancient and perfect. Drive away every devouring Rakṣasa, even one who is Atri-like. Of what sort? One who is godless, lacking the nature of a god, and greedy for wealth. This Soma becomes the accomplisher for the sake of strength or for increasing power.
Likewise, this Soma exists for the sake of speed and for the purification and consumption by the gods.
Pressed out and poured forth,

this Soma becomes exceedingly sweet (*madhumattama*)— that is, possessed of an extreme sweetness— for the gods, Indra and the others, in their place; or rather, it becomes an absolute source of exhilaration.
O Indu, flow out when pressed, rich in cattle and rich in horses, O thou of excellent skill;
I have established thy pure color among the kine.
O Indu, flow for us with cattle and with horses; being well-pressed and most skillful, run! I have placed your bright color upon the cows. 4.

O Soma, you who are skilled in cattle, very strong, pressed out and poured forth for us—lead us toward wealth consisting of cattle (*paśumat*), which is the means for accomplishing our sacrifice, and wealth consisting of horses (*aśvavat*). [The root *dhav* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class and carries the sense of "to go.
Then, O Lord, I place—that is, I hold and mix—your pure, purified, or radiant portion (*pavamāna*) within the products of the cow (*paguṣu*), such as milk and other dairy substances.
O Indu, lord of the bay steeds, most excellent winner of the gods' favor,
be a guide for us among our friends, for our friendship and for our splendor.
O Lord of the tawny steeds, O Indu, you who are most effective in winning over the gods, lead us like a friend to a friend; be present for our splendor. 5.

O Soma, lord of our green-hued cattle, you who fall upon the enemies—O Pāṇḍu, most radiant in form, you who are beneficial to the officiating priests (panaryaḥ), may you become a light-bringer for us, a protector (paṇaḥ).
How so? Just as a friend becomes a light-bringer for a friend, even so [be you for us].
O Indu, you who possess all-encompassing power, drive away from us every godless and wondrous foe; as a conqueror, strike down the wood-worm-like oppressor.
O Indu, with your rim, drive away every godless devourer from us; as a conqueror, strike down the wood-eater.
O Soma, you who possess a thousand paths, make that ancient truth manifest among us.
Furthermore, drive away from us even the footless one who is godless by nature, as well as the winged one who is devouring by nature—the Rākṣasa.
Moreover, O Indu, overcoming the powerful enemies and subduing those who oppress, strike them down.
Likewise, drive away from here that Rakshasa-like person who is cruel, endowed with both truth and falsehood, and possessed of external and internal deceit.
The third hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "indramaccha," is in the auṣṇiha meter and has the flowing Soma as its deity.
The seer of the first triplet (tucas) is Abhimantra, the son of Cakṣurālaya;
the seer of the second is named Cabhū, the son of Manu.
The son of Aṣūpanāman is Manu, the third [Manu].
Thus, nine verses have been accounted for.
Of the remaining five [verses], Cākṣuṣa Agni is the deity.
And it is recited accordingly: "The three-verse hymns beginning with 'To Indra,' 'Pañcāgni,' 'Bhrākṣa,' 'Cāmana,' and 'Manu Āpsava' constitute the Pañcāgni.
Thus the application [of the verses] has been explained.
May these pressed drops, the tawny ones, go toward Indra, the bull;
the Soma-drops, born in streams, bestowing heaven.
May these pressed drops, the golden-hued Soma juices, go toward Indra, the bull; born in streams, they are finders of light. 1.

This pressed Soma, flowing for Indra, purifies itself for the sake of battle; it takes heed of the victor, as one who knows. This Soma, the winner of booty, being pressed, flows for Indra for the sake of battle. It takes heed of the victor—Indra—as one who knows; just as Indra is known by the worlds, so does it take heed of him. *Note:* The word *jaitrasya* (of the victor) is used in the genitive case with the sense of the dative (*caturthyarthe bahulam*), according to the rule "the use of the genitive is frequent in the sense of the dative. Furthermore, the rule "the mention of the action must be made" (*kriyāgrahaṇaṃ kartavyam*) applies here, whereby the object (*karma*) of the verb *cetati* (takes heed) is designated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Thus, the genitive is employed in the sense of the dative. The meaning is that the Soma knows the victorious Indra, just as Indra is known by all people.
In the exhilarations of this [Soma], may Indra take hold of the firm grasp; let him wield the bull-like thunderbolt, he who conquers the waters.
Flow forth for the feast of the gods, O Indu, with your streams and with vigor! O Soma, rich in sweetness, sit within our vessel.

O Indu, O Soma, flow with your own streams by your power and strength for the sake of the feast of the gods, that is, for the consumption of the gods. O Soma, being full of sweetness—that is, possessing an intoxicating flavor—sit in our wooden vat known as the *droṇa*.
"Sadaḥ" is the form of the root *sad* in the imperative mood.
He sat down.

Your drops, leaping up from the water, have strengthened Indra for exhilaration; the immortal gods have drunk you for the sake of immortality. 8. Your drops. Leaping up from the water. Indra. "Udaprutah" means those going toward the water known as *vasatīvarī*;
or alternatively,
those who cause the water to flow out.
"Your own 'drops'—the flowing juices—'for intoxication,' for the sake of exhilaration, 'have strengthened' Indra.
Then the 'gods,' Indra and the others, have 'drunk' you, the bringer of happiness, 'for immortality,' for the sake of deathlessness."

O pressed drops of Soma, being purified, flow toward us with wealth—ye who rain upon heaven, whose waters flow freely, and who find the light of the sun. 9. Toward us! O pressed Soma drops, being purified, shining as they flow into the vessels; O waters, by whom the earth was made resonant with fame—such as you are, O Somas, being purified, flow toward us and bring us wealth.
Of what kind?
Those who cause rain to fall from heaven.
By means of rains, the sky is made [to rain];
those who possess the world of heaven oriented toward rain are "finders of light" (svarvidas), the obtainers of everything.

Being purified and being cleansed, Soma, with his wave—that is, his own stream—flows through, or moves variously across, the woolen filter (*vāra*), the *vāla*, the purifier (*pavitra*).
Of what nature is this Soma? Being *pavamāna* (the one being purified), he flows while repeatedly making sound, "croaking" at the forefront of the speech of praise.

With their prayers they urge on the prize-winning steed who sports in the wood, passing beyond the sheepskin; toward the three-backed one, the hymns have resounded together. Our thoughts, that is, our praises, have intoned together toward that Soma; they celebrate him from all sides.

This is called the *saṃgrāma* [chant]; it is so named because it is produced in the *saṃgrāma*. Then, being purified (*punānaḥ*), Soma, generating sound (*vācam*) as he flows forth, pours himself out into the vessels (*amiṣyadat*).

The fourth hymn, consisting of twenty-six verses, begins with “parītaḥ. The seven seers, such as Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, and others, who were mentioned in the hymn “tvaṃ somāsi” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.67), are its seers. The first verse is a Bṛhatī, and the second is a Satobṛhatī.
This is a single *pragātha*:
the verse beginning with “*pari suvānaḥ*” is a third-verse *bhurig-virāṭ* consisting of twenty-one syllables and is in the *dvipadā* meter;
the sixteenth verse beginning with “*nṛbhir yamānaḥ*” consists of twenty syllables and is a *virāṭ* in the *dvipadā* meter.
The two *pragāthas* beginning with the fourth [verse],
the three beginning with the tenth, and the five *pragāthas* beginning with the seventeenth have Pavamāna Soma as their deity.

And thus it is enumerated: "The *parīta* [hymn] consists of twenty-six verses; the seven seers [are the authors]; the third and the two following are *prāgātha*; the eighth and the first are *dvipadā*; the [last] two are *bṛhatī*.
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been explained.
Let him fashion the pressed juice that has been filtered; Soma is the supreme oblation.

O officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), pour out (*pari pinvata*) the pressed Soma (*sutam abhiṣutam*) with the *vasatīvarī* waters after this ritual act, or after this entry. In the phrase "pour out from here" (*ito pinvata*), the substitution of *r* for *s* occurs according to the rule *chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.126), and the substitution of *s* for *t* occurs according to the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59). That Soma which is the most excellent and praiseworthy oblation (*uttamaṃ havir*) for the gods, and which is also beneficial to men (*nṛbhyo hitaḥ*), and that Soma which flows (*dadhanvān*) within the waters—the *vasatīvarīs*—or within the atmosphere; that Soma the Adhvaryu has pressed with stones. He pours it out around it; such is the connection. **Now, being purified by the sheep’s wool filters, flow forth, O fragrant one! When you are pressed, we shall rejoice in the waters with the juice, mixing you further with the products of the cow.** 2. Now (*nūnam*). Being purified (*punānaḥ*). By the sheep’s wool (*avibhiḥ*). Flow forth (*pari srava*). Uninjured (*ardhvaḥ*). Most fragrant (*surabhitaraḥ*). When pressed (*sute cit*). You (*tvā*). In the waters (*apsu*). We shall rejoice (*madāmaḥ*). With the juice (*andhasā*). Mixing (*śrīṇantaḥ*). With the products of the cow (*gobhiḥ*). Further (*uttaram*). O Soma, uninjured (*ardhvaḥ*) by anyone, most fragrant (*surabhitaraḥ*), you, now being purified (*punānaḥ*), flow forth (*pari srava*) from the sheep’s wool filters (*avibhiḥ*). When you are pressed, we, mixing you with the grain-meal (*andhasā*) and with the products of the cow (*gobhiḥ*)—such as milk—shall rejoice (*madāmaḥ*) in you who are established in the waters, the *vasatīvarīs*, which are more elevated (*uttaram*). **Being pressed, he flows forth for all to see, the exhilarator of the gods, the rite, the drop, the three-eyed beholder.** 3. Being pressed (*suvānaḥ*). For seeing (*cakṣe*). The exhilarator of the gods (*devamādanaḥ*). The rite (*kratuḥ*). The drop (*induḥ*). Three-eyed (*tricakṣaṇaḥ*). The Soma, being pressed, flows forth for all to see. Of what nature? The exhilarator of the gods, the performer of the rite, the drop (*induḥ*) because it flows into the vessels or because it shines, the three-eyed beholder of everything. **Being purified, O Soma, clothing yourself in the waters, flow forth in a stream! As the giver of jewels, you sit in the womb of Truth, O divine, golden fountain.** 4. Being purified (*punānaḥ*). O Soma (*soma*). In a stream (*dhārayā*). The waters (*apaḥ*). Clothing yourself (*vasānaḥ*). You flow forth (*arṣāsi*). As the giver of jewels (*ratnadhāḥ*). The womb (*yonim*). Of Truth (*ṛtasya*). You sit (*sīdasi*). The fountain (*utsaḥ*). O God (*deva*). Golden (*hiraṇyayaḥ*). O Soma, being purified, clothing yourself in the waters known as *vasatīvarīs*, you flow forth in a stream toward the filter. Then, as the giver of jewels, you sit in the womb of Truth, the place of the sacrifice. O shining God, you are a flowing fountain, truly golden—the source of gold—or rather, you are the delightful delighter of the gods. **Milking the heavenly, dear, ancient honey, he has sat upon the beautiful seat. The prize-winner flows toward the supporting vessel, shaken by men, the far-seeing one.** 5. Milking (*duhānaḥ*). Upward (*ūrdhvam*). Heavenly (*divyam*). Honey (*madhu*). Dear (*priyam*). Ancient (*pratnam*). The beautiful seat (*sudhastham*). He has sat down (*āsadat*). Toward the supporting vessel (*āpṛcchyam dharuṇam*). The prize-winner (*vājī*). He flows (*arṣāti*). Shaken by men (*nṛbhir dhutaḥ*). The far-seeing one (*vicakṣaṇaḥ*). 1. T3, 6–M1, 2, 4, 7 read *chandasaṃ*.

The Soma, being milked—[the Soma] which is *madhu* (sweet), intoxicating; *priya* (dear), causing delight; *divya* (divine), existing in heaven; and characterized by the *udhaḥ* (udder) of the Soma-creeper—has settled in the *pratna* (ancient) *sadhastha* (dwelling place). A *sadhastha* is a place where one stands together (*saha tiṣṭhati atra*); [it refers to] the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for it has sat there.
This is the form in the *saderluṅ* [aorist].

Then, having been questioned regarding the ritual action—that which is not to be asked—the Soma, who is the sustainer of the ritual action (*vāpṛcchyam karmaṇyāpraṣṭavyam*) and the possessor of food (*vājī*), rains down; that is, he approaches in order to bestow food upon the sacrificer, the one who maintains the ritual action.
Of what kind is he?
He is "shaken" (dhūta) by men—the officiating priests who lead the ritual—and purified within the inviolable house (*adābhyagṛha*).
Āpastamba has prescribed in his Sūtra: "With those [strainers], one shakes him four times, five times, or seven times."
Vvicakṣaṇa: the all-seeing observer.
Being purified, O Soma, watchful and dear one, you pass through the woolly filter;
you have become a sage, the best of the Aṅgirases; with your sweetness, you have mixed our sacrifice.

Being purified, O Soma, you are watchful; as another, you are dear while passing through the woolen filter. You have become a sage, the best of the Aṅgirases; with honeyed sweetness, mix our sacrifice. 6.
O Soma, you who are ever-watchful (*vijāgṛvi*), wakeful by nature, and beloved (*priya*), as you are being purified (*punānaḥ*), you flow forth through the sheep’s wool filter (*vadhryave vāre*).
Furthermore, as a wise sage (*vipraḥ*) and the most eminent of the Aṅgirases (*aṅgirastamaḥ*), you have become—the leader of the ancestors (*pitṝṇām netā*).
As such, sprinkle our sacrifice (*yajñam*) with your own honeyed juice (*madhvā madhunā*).
The form *miheḥ* is derived from the root *mih*, meaning "to sprinkle," with the suffix *san*.
Soma, the bountiful, dwells upon the mountain; he is the seer, the inspired sage, the far-seeing finder of the path.
You became a wise craftsman for the gods; you caused the sun to ascend in the sky.
Soma, the bountiful, flows on, the finder of the path, the seer, the inspired sage, the far-seeing. You have become the poet for the feast of the gods; you have made the sun ascend in heaven. 7.
Having poured forth, Soma—the sprinkler of desires—flows and streams.
Of what nature is he?
He is the best finder of the path (*gātuvittama*), the showerer (*vṛṣi*) who reveals everything, the inspired sage (*vipra*), and the far-seeing observer (*vicakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, O wise one, you are most skilled in action; you are most devoted to the gods, being exceedingly desirous of them.
Moreover, in the heavenly world, you cause the sun and the rice-grains to appear.
Soma, being pressed by the pressers upon the backs of the sheep, goes with a stream like two tawny mares; he goes with a gladdening stream.
Soma: *Ūm*! Being pressed by the pressers upon the backs of the sheep’s wool, he goes like a tawny horse with his stream; he goes with his gladdening stream. 8.
Being pressed by the pressing priests—the officiants who are performing the extraction—the Soma flows through the *snus* of the woolen filters;
the word *snus* is substituted for *sānu* according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.63.1 (*māṃspṛtsnūnām upasalyānām*), meaning "with the high-tufted strainers. It passes through, or exceeds, them.
The word *vu* is used in the sense of what is well-known.
Like a mare (*vaśvayeva*), that is, like a female horse, [the Soma] flows with a golden-colored (*haritā*) stream.
With a delightful (*mandrayā*), intoxicating stream, it approaches the wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*).
1. He attains the characteristic of the moon, which is like that of Ga-ta (the syllables *ga* and *ta*), *bha*, and *sa*.
2. Or [he attains] *ta*, *bha*, *va*, and *la*.
3. He attains *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *bha*, *ma*, *mu*, and *madhi*.

Following the tracks of the cows, Soma has flowed with the milk; he has flowed with the milks. Like the ocean, he has gone toward the enclosures; the exhilarating one flows for intoxication. 9. Following the tracks of the cows—with the cows—Soma has flowed; with the milks—he has flowed. Like the ocean—the enclosures—he has gone; the exhilarating one—he flows for intoxication. 9.
The Soma, possessing cattle (*gomān*) and joined with cattle (*goyuktaḥ*), flows down into the vessel in the low-lying place along with the products of cattle, such as milk and the like.
This is what is being said:
that Soma flows down together with the cows whose milk has been milked for the purpose of mixing with himself.
This is the form of the root *kṣar* in the *luṅ* tense.
Furthermore, just as waters go to the ocean, so do the "enclosures"—the juices in the form of soma-essences that are to be gathered—go to the *droṇakalaśa*.
This is the form of the root *gam* in the *luṅ* tense with the elision of the suffix *cli*.

Furthermore: *manda* means intoxicating; *soma* is for *mada*, that is, for the purpose of intoxication. It is *tośate*, meaning it is struck or pressed. The root *tośati* has the sense of killing (*vadha*).

O Soma, pressed by the stones, through the sheep’s woolly fleece, like a man entering a fortified city, the tawny one has entered; you have established your seat within the wooden vessels. 10. O Soma, pressed by the stones, through the sheep’s woolly fleece, like a man entering a fortified city, the tawny one has entered; you have established your seat within the wooden vessels. 10.

He, O Soma, being pressed by the stones—the pressing-granites—while being extracted, passing through the woolen filters (*vārāṇi*), which are made of sheep’s wool and serve as interposing purifiers; [the word] "you flow" (*ā pavase*) is the ellipsis.
That golden-hued Soma, being yellowish-green, enters into the jar situated above the two pressing-boards (*camvoḥ*).
Therein lies the illustration:
Unlike an ordinary person who enters one city after another,
you, O King, take up your seat and occupy your place in the sacrificial assembly within bowls fashioned from wood in the forests.

He has purified himself, passing through the fine [fibers], the holy one, like a war-horse seeking booty in the fray; Soma, being pressed, is to be celebrated by the wise, by the inspired singers with their hymns. 11. He has purified himself; through; the fine [fibers]; the holy one; in the contest; like a war-horse; seeking booty; to be celebrated; being pressed; by the wise; Soma; by the inspired singers; with hymns. 11.

Seeking strength—that is, desiring food—the subtle, that is, minute and fine, purifying—that is, the cleansing hairs of the filter—he makes pass through; that Soma is cleansed, or rather, is adorned. In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as a horse desiring victory is adorned for the fray in battle, so is he.
Of what nature is he?
He is "to be celebrated" (anumādya), worthy of praise by all; "purifying" (pavamāna), being cleansed by the wise officiating priests (ṛtvij) as well as by the sacred hymns (ṛc).
The suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffix] *vanip* [is added].
He is cleansed while being praised by wise sages who possess hymns of praise.
O Soma, for the banquet of the gods, you have swelled like a river with its flood;
with the juice of the stalk, exhilarating and wakeful, flow toward the vat that drips with honey.

And I, O Soma, by night and by day, for the sake of the Sun, O brown one, [dwell] upon your height; [we have flown] beyond the Sun who burns with heat, as birds fly beyond him. And I, O Soma, by night and by day—for the sake of the Sun, O brown one, upon your height—I [dwell]. We have flown beyond the Sun who burns with heat, who shines and blazes, situated in the highest place; we have flown beyond you who are of that nature. To reach you stationed there, we have flown past. How so? Like birds. Just as eagles and other winged creatures fly beyond the Sun, so too [have we]. [The root] *pastṛ* means "to go. From this, in the Vedic *liṭ* (perfect tense), there is the elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule *tanipaśyośchandasi*. In the *Grāvastotṛ* litany, regarding the preparation of the Soma being purified, there is one *ṛc*; therein, "being purified" (*mṛjyamānaḥ*) is the third verse. like Savitar, the god, he unrolls the covering.
Beholding him as their kin, certain celestial ones, radiant with wealth, have followed after him; like Savitar the god, he discloses the treasure. 6.

Immediately after that, the celestial ones—those dwelling in heaven known as the *vasurucaḥ* (shining with wealth)—beholding him, that is, seeing him, praised and extolled this Soma, their excellent kinsman.
Why immediately after that? It is said:
because the radiant god Savitṛ, the impeller of all, namely the Sun, does not yet open (*vyūrṇute*) nor dispel the veil (*vāra*), the obscuring darkness; therefore, they praised him.
For indeed, they praise Soma even before the rising of the sun.
O Soma, in thee the first [sages] who have spread the sacrificial grass have fixed their thought for great booty and for glory;
as such, O Hero, impel us toward heroic power.
To thee, O Soma, the first ones who have trimmed the sacrificial grass have offered their prayer for great strength and for glory. As such, O Hero, impel us toward heroic valor. 7.
O Soma, you are the first, the ancient ones;
or rather,
you are the foremost among all people by virtue of being the object of worship.
Those who have trimmed the sacrificial grass (*vṛktabarhiṣaḥ*):
those for whose sake the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) has been trimmed or cut are the sacrificers (*yajamānāḥ*).
For the sake of great strength (*vāja*), power (*bala*), fame (*śravas*), and food (*anna*), they have placed their thought (*dhiyam*, i.e., their intellect) in you (*tve*), having fixed it upon you.
Therefore, O heroic and capable Soma, you who are such, impel and urge us as well toward valor and capability in battle;
or rather,
impel us toward a heroic son and toward our own welfare.
From the great depth, as if from the ocean, they have milked out the divine nectar, the pure and most excellent essence;
they raised a chorus together toward Indra at his birth.
The nectar, the fresh, the praiseworthy—out of the great depth of heaven they have milked it forth; they raised a shout together toward Indra as he was being born. 8.

From the sky (*divaḥ*), from that lofty realm, the gods dwelling there have milked forth—that is, they have drawn toward themselves—the nectar (*pīyūṣam*) which is pure, excellent, and of the nature of Soma; that food which is worthy of praise (*ukthya*) and most eminent. From the great depth (*maho gāhāt*) of the vast sky, they have milked it out. Then, the singers chant together; they offer praise to that Soma as it is being produced, directed toward Indra.

And now, O Pavamāna, when you with your might stand over these two worlds, heaven and earth, and over all these beings, you spread yourself abroad like a bull stationed among the herds. (9) O Pavamāna Soma, immediately thereafter (*adha*), just as you stand over these two worlds (*rodasī*)—heaven and earth—and over all (*viśvā*) these created beings (*bhuvanā*) with your power (*mujmanā*), so doing, you spread yourself abroad (*vi tiṣṭhase*) throughout the worlds. Therein lies the illustration: just as (*na*) some bull (*vṛṣabhaḥ*) stands firmly established (*niḥṣṭhāḥ*) within a herd (*yūthe*) or a multitude of cows, even so do you stand firmly established among the created beings who occupy that place.

Soma, being purified in the woolly fleece like a playful child, flows as he is pressed; the drop (indu) with a thousand streams and hundredfold vigor. Soma, being purified, in the woolly fleece, like a playful child, flowing as he is pressed, he flows forth. Of what sort? Possessing a thousand streams, endowed with many currents, having hundredfold vigor, the radiant drop (indu).

This one, being purified, rich in sweetness, possessing the *ṛta*, flows for Indra as the exhilarating drop (*indu*), a sweet wave, a winner of booty, a finder of wide space, and a bestower of vital strength. (11) Being purified—that is, being cleansed—rich in sweetness, endowed with *mādhurya*, possessing the *ṛta*—that is, possessing the cosmic order or sacrifice—the *indu* (the drop), which is by nature flowing, sweet-making, a mass of streams of essence, flows—that is, it pours—for Indra, for the sake of Indra. Of what sort? A winner of booty (*vājasaniḥ*)—a giver of food; a finder of wide space (*varivovit*)—an obtainer of wealth; a bestower of vital strength (*vayodhāḥ*)—a giver of life-force.

Flow forth, O Soma, overcoming those who seek battle, driving away the Rākṣasas, and clearing the difficult paths; well-armed and victorious, subdue the enemies. 12. Flow forth! Overpowering those who seek battle, driving away the Rākṣasas, clearing the difficult paths, well-armed and victorious, O Soma, subdue the enemies. O Soma, you who are such, flow forth. Doing what? Overpowering—that is, surpassing—the *pṛtnyūn*. [In the word *pṛtnya*,] the vowel *a* is elided before the suffix *kyac* according to the rule "the vowel is dropped in *kavyadhvara-pṛtnya* when followed by *kyac*. Thus, it refers to enemies desiring combat. Overpowering them means overcoming them. Likewise, [flow forth] clearing the difficult paths (*durgahāṇi*).
1. In the herd of cows that have gone [to the pasture]; with the great herd of cows. 2.
The upholder of the cosmic order (ṛtāvā).
3. The sacrificer (yajamāna).
Driving away—that is, removing and destroying—the *rakṣases* that are difficult for even some to overcome;
moreover, being well-armed with excellent weapons, flow on, overwhelming and subduing the enemies.
The eighth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “*ayā rucā*,” belongs to Anānata Ātreya, the son of Parucchepa; it is composed in the *āṣṭi* meter and has Pavamāna Soma as its deity.
Thus it is enumerated: “*ayā rucā*: a triplet by Anānata, the son of Parucchepa, in the *āṣṭi* [meter].
The application [of this hymn] has been explained.
With this golden luster, purifying himself, he overcomes all hostilities with his own yoked companions,
like the sun with his own yoked companions.
The stream of the pressed juice shines as he purifies himself, ruddy and tawny.
When he encompasses all forms with his hymns, with these pressed-out hymns.

Being purified with this golden, shining stream, he overcomes all hostilities with his self-yoked [rays], like the sun with his self-yoked [rays]. The stream of the pressed juice shines as it is being purified, the ruddy, tawny one; when he encompasses all forms with his hymns, with these hymns of the pressed juice. Being purified—that is, being cleansed—the Soma, with this golden, green-colored, shining stream, overcomes—that is, destroys—all hostilities, that is, all demons. Therein lies the illustration: just as the sun (*sūra*) destroys darkness with his self-yoked rays, so does he. The repetition of "with his self-yoked" (*svayugvabhiḥ*) is for the sake of emphasis. Alternatively, the Soma, joined with the stream, overcomes the demons by means of his own joined splendors. The stream of that *suta*, the pressed Soma, shines—that is, it blazes. Being purified, the tawny (*hari*) Soma becomes ruddy (*aruṣa*), that is, radiant. That Soma, with these hymns—meaning with those possessing the quality of carrying essence—and with these hymns—that is, with splendors—goes around, that is, pervades, all forms, that is, all the stars.
You found that treasure of the leaves; you cleanse yourself with your mothers in your own abode through the prayers of Truth.
Like a chant from afar, it is there where the cooked offerings rejoice.
Shining with threefold red rays, he has distributed [the light]; he has established vital strength.

You found that wealth of the Paṇis; you shall cleanse yourself with the mothers in your own home, by the meditations of *ṛta* in the home. Like a *sāman* from afar, that *sāman* is heard where the meditations rejoice. Shining, he has established food through the threefold, ruddy mothers; shining, he has established food. O Soma, you found—that wealth of the Paṇis—the cattle consisting of riches stolen by the Paṇis; you obtained it. Furthermore, by the "meditations" (*dhītayaḥ*), the sustainers, the "mothers"—the *vasatīvarī* waters—of *ṛta*, the sacrifice, you "completely cleanse" yourself, becoming perfectly pure, in your own "home," which is the sacrificial dwelling. Just as the sound of a *sāman* is heard from a distant place, so too is your *sāman*-sound heard by all. This is said with reference to the pressing of the Soma. Wherein—in that sound—the "meditations," the sustainers of the ritual, the sacrificers, "rejoice. Shining, Soma, through the "threefold" mothers—the *vasatīvarī* waters who support the three worlds—and through the "ruddy" ones, the radiant splendors, "establishes food" for his praisers; he bestows it. He establishes food once more, and so forth.
1. ta4.5-tatsutasya; bha6-tatsutasya | 2. ta5-bha2.6-dhārā parvati | 3. ta1.2.10.7-yatayaḥ; bha6-yataḥ yaḥ |
He moves toward the eastern quarter, perceiving with his rays; the divine chariot exerts itself, the beautiful chariot.
Hymns have come forth to glorify Indra, inciting him to victory.
For with the unshakable thunderbolt and with the unshakable [chariot], he prevails in the battles.

Toward the eastern quarter he goes, observing keenly; he strives with his rays, the visible one. Divine is the chariot, the visible chariot. The manly hymns have come, gladdening Indra for victory, when the thunderbolt and the chariot are both unshakable in battles—both are unshakable.

Observant and knowing, Soma follows and pursues the ancient, eastern direction, the far-reaching quarter. Moreover, your divine chariot—visible to all, worthy of being beheld by everyone—unites and comes together with the rays of the sun.
[The repetition of "the visible chariot" is for the sake of emphasis.]
Then the manly hymns (*puṃsy-ukthāni*), which are songs of praise, go toward Indra; they reach him.
Likewise, for the sake of victory—that is, for the purpose of winning—those hymns gladden Indra as they cause him joy.
And likewise, the thunderbolt (*vajra*) goes toward that Indra.
Whenever, in battles— that is, in conflicts— you two, O Soma and Indra, were unshaken and unsubdued by enemies, and you both existed together,
then there occurred the arrival of hymns of praise and other such rites.
The repetition of the word "unshaken" (anapacyutā) is for the sake of emphasis.
The ninth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with “nānām,” has Śiśu, a descendant of Aṅgiras, as its seer;
the metre is Paṅkti with five feet;
and the deity is Soma Pavamāna.
And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "The four [verses] beginning with nānā, and the pāṅka [hymn] beginning with śiśu.
The application (viniyoga) has been explained.
Our various thoughts and the religious observances of men differ;
the carpenter seeks the broken wood, the physician the sick man, and the priest seeks one who presses the Soma—O Indra, flow for us, O Indu!

O Indu, flow for Indra! Our various thoughts, the sacred laws of men, the carpenter, the healer of the broken, the physician, and the priest—all these desire one who presses the Soma. Flow around for Indra, O Indu! 1.
With these hymns beginning with "pari," [the seer], providing mental diversion while the Soma flows without ceasing, speaks for the sake of its non-repetitiveness (ajāmitva).
O Soma, our *dhiyaḥ*—our ritual acts—become many, of various kinds (*nānā*), belonging to diverse types;
the word *vai* serves to indicate what is well-known.
The syllable *u* is a filler.
These various duties (*vratāni*)—that is, the actions—of these people are manifold. A carpenter desires his own unerring craft of wood-cutting.
Likewise, the physician—the healer—desires the *ruta*, which means disease.
Brahmā desires the *brāhmaṇa*, the sacrificer who is pressing the *soma*. But I desire *tāhaṃ tvat-parisravaṇa*, the flowing forth from you.
Therefore, O Indu, O Soma, flow forth completely for Indra, for the sake of Indra.
With aging plants, with full cups of birds,
with stones that fulfill desires, O Indu, flow around for Indra who seeks the golden one.
With the aging plants, with the full ones, with the desires of the birds, with the stones, with the heavens—[the Soma] desires that which possesses gold; O Indu, flow around for Indra! 2.

1. O you two who have gone through fear in battles, in conflicts; 2. O you two from whom [the poison] flows away, O you two who bear that which flows away. The arrows are made with aging, worn-out plants.
Likewise, they are fashioned from the feathers of birds, which serve as the wings of arrows;
and likewise, they are fashioned by us from whetstones that are bright and intended for sharpening arrows.
With these tools, the smith desires the primordial Person who possesses gold.
Thus do I desire your praise;
therefore, O Indu, flow forth for Indra.
Then the physician Kāruha pressed out the stone-rolling [Soma];
like those seeking wealth who follow various thoughts, we stand waiting for Indra—O Indu, flow forth for Indra!

The artisan, I myself, then the physician, the one who cleanses with a stone, the impeller—possessing various thoughts, we who are the gatherers of wealth—stand following thee like cattle; O Indu, flow forth for Indra. 3.

The seer (ṛṣi), having commenced the Soma sacrifice, while the Soma was flowing from the *daśāpavitra* filter, performed a search for the seers—preceded by the recitation of preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*)—for the removal of obstructing sins. At that time, he said: "I am the *kāru*, the maker of hymns (*stoma*).
From that [comes] *tataḥ*, which is a name for lineage (*saṃtāna*).
He from whom this [world] is stretched out is therefore the father;
or, he who is stretched out [from it] is therefore the son.
A physician is one who prepares medicine.
The meaning is that it is abundant for the sacrifice, according to the Vedic scripture: "Everything he causes to prosper through the threefold knowledge.
Likewise, she is one who grinds stones.
"He destroys the barley by parching it on the grinding stones and sand.
Or alternatively:
"He destroys—that is, he grinds into powder—the barley that has been parched upon the grinding stones and so forth."
Alternatively, it refers to the preparation of parched grain, flour-mixtures, parched groats, and so forth;
or it is that mother or daughter,
because of her connection with the act of bowing.
Indeed, a mother is naturally inclined toward her offspring through acts such as suckling at the breast;
or a daughter [is so inclined] for the sake of service.
Thus, by attending to all [these], we—who possess diverse thoughts, diverse actions, and who desire wealth—have stood here, having settled ourselves within this world.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
*gāvaḥ*. Here, the substitution of *śas* for *jas* follows Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Just as cows attend to the cow-pen and serve it by providing their own milk, so do we also serve it.
Knowing this, O *Indu*, O Soma, flow forth for Indra; stream from the ten-strand filter.
Thus, these activities are preceded by honor and solicitation.
Regarding this, the Nirukta states: “*Upalaprakṣaṇī* means one who cleanses upon stones, or one who throws stones.

*Kāruhaṃ asmi kartā stomānām*—I am the maker, the performer of hymns; *tataḥ*, from that [source], means a name for lineage, or for a father, or for a son. *Bhiṣak* means a physician. *Tataḥ* is a term for progeny, whether referring to a father or a son.

"Like those who wash stones with a sieve, like sons or daughters of various names and forms, possessing diverse thoughts and diverse actions, seeking wealth and desiring riches, we have taken our stand upon the world like cattle. (Nirukta 6.5–6)
The draft-horse draws the chariot easily; the penis is the summoner of laughter for the two hairy testicles. The frog desires water; O Indu, flow around us with your power.

The horse; the draught-animal; the chariot for comfort; the one who calls out to those laughing; the penis; the two hairy ones; or perhaps the frog is the divider; he desires [it]; O Indu, flow forth for Indra! 4.
The horse, reaching its goal, desires a comfortable and auspicious chariot;
those who possess counsel—namely, the ministers and attendants—desire speech that is either humorous or satirical;
and so too does the penis.
"‘Śepo vaitasaḥ’ refers to the male generative organ," says Yāska (Nirukta 3.21).
Just as the *śepa* desires the two hairy [testicles],
so does the frog.
1. By those [rays] which are worn out;
2. by the rays intended for sharpening;
3. and that.
